story:
Amelia wanted a book about trucks. Big trucks. She looked at the shelves. So many books. She could not find trucks anywhere.

She picked a book. She opened it in the middle. There were dogs, not trucks. She flipped back some pages. Still dogs. Then she turned to the front of the book. She pointed at the letters. "Dog," she said slowly. The letters were the same on the cover. So this was a dog book. No trucks here.

She put it back. She found another book. She opened the front page first this time. She pointed again. "C-A-T," she said. "Cat!" That was not trucks either. Her mother laughed. "You are a good letter spotter," she said.

Then Amelia saw a card on the wall. It said AMELIA. She touched it. Her name! The librarian had made it for her. She held up the card. The letters went A, then M, then E. She waved the card at her mother. "Look! A, M, E," she said. Her mother wrote AMELIA on a piece of paper. Amelia looked at the card. She looked at the paper. Same letters. Same order. She grinned. Then she ran to the shelves and opened the next book at the front, where the words begin.

Scarlett woke up tired from her long sleep. She rolled out of bed and went to find Grandma. "Let's hang the wash outside," said Grandma. Scarlett held Grandma's hand all the way to the yard.

While Grandma pinned up the towels, Scarlett looked at the grass. Something small and shiny lay by the fence. It was a little lighter. Scarlett bent down and looked at it. She did not pick it up. She ran back to Grandma. "I see something by the fence," she said. "It looks like the thing Daddy uses."

Grandma walked over with Scarlett. "That is a lighter," said Grandma. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." Grandma picked it up and put it high in her pocket.

Scarlett helped pin one small sock. The wind made it flap and flap. "It's dancing," said Scarlett.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Mama set down a bowl of red strawberries. Aubrey smelled them with her nose. "Yummy smell," she said. She heard them plop in the bowl with her ears. She touched one with her fingers. It felt bumpy and cool.

But Aubrey had a problem. She did not want the green tops cut off. "Try one first," said Mama. "Pass me the big one," Aubrey said. Mama passed it over. Aubrey held her nose closed with her fingers. She took a bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. "Oh!" she said. She let go of her nose. She took another bite. Now it tasted sweet and strong. "It's back!" she said. She took a big bite and smiled. "Lucky me, strawberries taste so good."

Livia went to the art gallery with Mama. Big paintings hung on the walls. "Red," said Livia, pointing. "Yellow. Blue." Mama smiled and nodded.

In the corner there was a paint table just for kids. Livia wanted to paint a sky. She dipped her brush in blue. She made her sky. It was so dark. Too dark! Her sky looked almost black. "Yucky sky," Livia said, and she almost cried.

A boy next to her pushed a pot of white paint close. "Here," he said. Livia stirred some white into her blue. She mixed it round and round. The brush made a little noise on the pot.

The blue grew light. Her sky turned soft and pale. Livia chased her brush across the paper. Up, up, up went the light blue sky.

"That is a good sky," said Mama.

Thomas stands in the bathroom. Daddy runs the water for his bath. Thomas touches the sink with one finger. The sink feels warm. Daddy says, "The hot tap is for me. Only me." Thomas keeps his hands in his lap.

Thomas washes his hands in the cool water. He dries them on the big rough towel. The towel tickles his fingers. Daddy lifts him down. "Don't forget your cookie," Daddy says. There is one cookie on the little table. Thomas takes it. He holds Daddy's hand all the way to the door.

Outside, Thomas sees his red bike. He starts to run to it. Then he stops. He turns around. "Helmet," he says. He runs back and gets his helmet from the step. He puts it on his head. Daddy claps. Thomas climbs on his bike. "Ready!" he calls.

Nora ran to the door. "Bus! Bus!" she called. Big brother Sam had his boots on. Nora wanted to go too.

She opened the door a little bit. The cold air came in. It touched her arms. "Brr!" said Nora. The wind was loud by the door. She shut it fast.

"Nora needs her coat," said Mom. "A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside." Mom held the pink coat down low. Nora pushed her arm in. One arm. She pushed the other arm in. Two arms. "My turn," said Nora. She pulled the zipper. Up, up, up. It went zzzzzip all the way!

"Now I am warm," said Nora. She patted her coat like a soft sheep. At the bus stop, the wind blew again. Nora did not feel it. Her coat kept her body warm and cozy. "My coat did it," said Nora. Sam zipped his coat too. "Zzzzzip!" they said together. Then the big bus came, and it was loud. Nora held Sam's hand and smiled.

Miles went to the library with his dad. He saw a tablet on a small table. The screen was dark. "How do I make it light up?" he asked. Dad showed him the little button. Miles pressed it. The screen lit up!

Miles tapped the drawing app. It opened. He drew a big bus. The bus was yellow. He drew a heavy elephant next to the bus. Tap, tap, tap. His finger made the picture. One little tap made a big thing happen.

Then the screen went dim. "It needs power," said Dad. "A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall." Miles found the charger. He carried it to Dad. Dad plugged it in. Soon the screen was bright again. Miles drew one more picture. Then he pressed the button, and the screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the table, just where he found it.

"Can I use it again next time?" Miles asked.

"You sure can," said Dad. "You put it away all by yourself."

Cooper was playing with his blocks. He stacked them tall, one by one. His sister Mia came in. "Can I play too?" she asked. "Yes," said Cooper. "You put one on. Then I put one on." They took turns. The tower grew and grew.

Then Cooper tipped the blocks over. Crash! They fell all over the rug. Cooper laughed. He slid one block across the floor. It went far under the chair. The blocks were everywhere. Mia said, "Look at this mess."

Cooper ran to the window. He wanted to see the wet street after the rain. A big truck went by outside. Then he looked back at the rug. The blocks were still there. Nobody had picked them up. Cooper walked back. "We played with them," he said. "So we clean them up." Mia smiled. He picked up the red blocks. She picked up the blue ones. They put every block back in the basket. "Good job," said Mama from the door. Cooper clapped his hands. "All done!"

Sara went to the library with Dad. She saw a big book with a wild tiger on the cover. She wanted it very much. But a boy took the tiger book first. Sara felt sad. She sat on the floor and hid her face.

Dad sat down next to her. "Can you tell me how you feel?" he asked. Sara looked up. "I feel sad," she said. "I wanted the tiger book." Dad nodded. "Let's ask the librarian for another tiger book."

They walked to the big desk together. The librarian smiled. "We have one more tiger book," she said. She put it in Sara's hands. Sara felt excited. She hugged the book. The boy brought back the first tiger book. He looked sad. Sara showed him her book. "You can have this one," she said. He smiled big. Sara sat with Dad and opened her book. "Roar!" she said.

Declan ran to the block corner. Max was already there. "Can I play too?" Declan asked. "You can play later," said Miss Jo. "Max is using them now." Declan sat down. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Miss Jo. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Declan watched Max stack. A tall tower grew. One block would not stick. "It keeps falling!" said Max. "Try a different block," said Declan. He handed Max a flat one. Max put it on the top. The tower stood tall. Then Max yawned. "I'm done now," said Max.

"Is it later now?" Declan asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Yes. Now it is later." Declan clapped his hands. He picked up a red block. "Yesterday I made a small tower," he said. "Today I will make a big one. And tomorrow, even bigger!" He set the red block down. The tower began.

Charlie sat at the kitchen table. Mama put warm toast on her plate. "Can I do the butter?" asked Charlie. "Yes," said Mama. She handed Charlie a dull knife. "I will watch you."

Charlie poked the toast with the point of the knife. The toast tore. Butter fell off in little bits. "Oh no," said Charlie. "What happened?"

Mama turned the knife over. "Try the flat side," she said. Charlie looked at the flat side. It was wide and smooth. She pushed it across the bread. The butter went thin. It covered the toast. One, two, three strokes, and the whole slice was shiny. "It works!" said Charlie.

"Now the milk," said Mama. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. One, two, three. Not one drop spilled. "Look at that," said Charlie. Mama pointed out the window. A yellow flower nodded in the sun. Charlie took a big bite of toast. "Best toast ever," she said.

Madeline sat in a big chair at Grandma's house. Today was her birthday. There was a cake on the table. It was pink with white frosting.

"Look at the candles," said Mom. Madeline counted them. "One, two, three, four." She stopped. "Four candles? I am five today!"

Mom looked at the cake. "You are right," she said. Mom took out one more candle. She put it in the frosting. Now there were five candles, one for each year.

Grandpa lit the candles. The little flames danced. Everyone sang the birthday song. Madeline blew as hard as she could. All five flames went out. The smoke curled up like a ribbon.

Then Madeline waited for her cake. The frosting was cool on her tongue. Her friend Sam sat next to her. He had crumbs on his chin. Madeline gave him her napkin. "Thank you," said Sam.

Grandma cut more cake for everyone. Madeline licked her fork. "Best cake ever," she said. Grandma smiled and gave her a hug.

Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. Grandma was at the little table. A kettle sat on the grill. "I want to see the bubbles," said Maria.

"Come and stand by me," said Grandma. Maria stood close to Grandma. The kettle went puff, puff. White steam rose up. Maria reached out one finger. "Stop," said Grandma. She held Maria's hand. "Steam is hot. It can burn. Stay back."

Maria took one step back. Then one more step. She watched the steam curl up high. The steam went up, up, up. Then it was gone. Maria clapped her hands. "I see it, Grandma! I see it from here!"

Grandma poured tea into her cup. Maria helped wipe the table with a cloth. She wiped it slow, then fast. The kettle went quiet now.

Maria sat by Grandma's feet. "More steam soon?" she asked. "Soon," said Grandma. Maria waited in her new hat. The steam would come again. And she would stay back.

Alice went to the store with her brother. Alice was hungry for a snack. Mom said, "Let's find aisle five."

Alice looked up at the big signs. She saw a sign with a 5 on it. "Is that five?" she asked. Mom smiled and nodded.

Alice held up her fingers. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." She looked at her hand. She looked at the sign. It was the same five!

She tried to walk to the sign. "This way!" she said. Her brother followed her. They turned down aisle five.

There were the crackers on the shelf. Alice reached for the box. "We found it!" she said. Mom put the crackers in the cart.

On the way home, Alice counted the crackers in her bowl. "One, two, three, four, five," she said, and ate them all up.

Lydia went to a big game with Mama and Papa. The stadium was huge. So many people sat in the seats. Lydia sat with her cousins too. The players ran and ran on the field.

"The blue team runs so fast!" said Lydia. She skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt jumpy and happy. The blue team ran more than the red team. So Lydia clapped for the blue team. "The blue team wins!" she said.

Papa shook his head. "Look at the big board," he said. Lydia looked up. She counted, "Red has three. Blue has two." Her cousin pointed. "More points at the end wins," he said. Lydia watched and waited. The red team scored one more. Four! The game ended. Everyone cheered for red. Lydia clapped too. "More points win," she said. "I want to count next time!"

Emilia went to the store with Dad. She wanted a big red apple. She ran down the aisle. She bumped into a boy. His block tower fell down. The blocks went deep into a big basket and all over the floor.

The boy looked sad. "My tower," he said. Emilia said, "Sorry." Then she picked up the blocks. She put them in a tall pile. The boy put one on top. Emilia put one on top too. They took turns.

Then the boy gave Emilia a block. "You can put the last one," he said. Emilia smiled. She set it on the very top.

Dad came back with two apples. He gave one to the boy too. The boy's mama said, "What a nice present." Emilia took a big bite of her apple. "We made a tower," she said.

Chloe wanted to play the guessing game. Mom put five things on the kitchen table. "Close your eyes," said Mom. "No peeking!"

Chloe closed her eyes tight. First came a crunchy cracker. Chloe nibbled it. "My mouth tastes it!" she said. "My tongue!"

Next came a bell. Mom rang it softly. "My ears hear it!" said Chloe.

Then Mom held up a red apple. Chloe peeked one eye. "Stop peeking!" laughed Mom. Chloe closed it again.

"Now touch this," said Mom. Chloe put her hand in the box. Something was bumpy and cool. She rubbed her fingertips over it. "My skin feels it!" she said. "My skin says bumpy!" It was a pineapple, bumpy all over.

Last, Mom opened the cinnamon jar. Chloe sniffed. "My nose smells it!" she said. "Pee-yew!"

Mom laughed and gave her a hug. "Five senses, five guesses. You did it!" Chloe clapped and took a big bite of apple. "Crunchy," she said.

Andrew went to the little pool by the lake. His dad came too. Andrew wanted to get in the water all by himself.

First Andrew sat on the edge. He pushed and pushed. His arms were too small. He could not climb out over the side. A duck went pop into the lake, but Andrew stayed stuck.

Then Andrew saw the ladder. It went right into the water. He put his foot on the first step. Then the next step. Step by step, he climbed down into the pool. "I did it!" said Andrew. He held the rail and kicked his feet. He was not shy anymore.

When it was time to go, Andrew used the steps. Up, up, up he went. It was easy. "The steps help you get in and out of the water," said Dad. Andrew yawned a big yawn. He was ready for his nap. He waved to the duck and said, "Bye bye, lake."

Chloe wanted to make her own breakfast. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. Chloe held the little knife with butter on it. She spread slow, slow, slow. The butter made the toast shiny. "Look, a butter lake!" she said.

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup with both hands. She poured. A drop ran down the side. She licked it off her finger. "Mmm, one little slip," said Daddy with a smile.

Then Chloe ran to play. The milk sat on the counter. "Uh oh," said Daddy. "The milk has to go back in the fridge, to keep it cold." Chloe picked up the big jug with both hands. She set it on the fridge shelf, way down low.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy and gray. "The rain can come," said Chloe. "My milk is safe and cold." She took a big bite of buttery toast.

Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt funny and her hands felt weak.

"Will it hurt?" she asked Grandpa.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Grandpa. "Now smell the flower with me. Breathe in slow and deep."

Emilia took a big slow breath in. Then she let it out. She did it again. Her tummy felt better. Her hands felt strong.

"Look, there is a long line of kids waiting," said Grandpa. "Let's count them while we breathe."

They counted one, two, three kids. The nurse came in with a small tray.

"I can do it," said Emilia. "I will breathe like a flower."

She breathed in slow and deep. The nurse gave the shot. It was just a tiny pinch!

"Can I pick a sticker now?" asked Emilia.

"Yes, pick any one you like," said the nurse.

Emilia chose a shiny yellow star.

Henry ran to the park with his teddy. He smelled the smelly pond water. "Yuck," he said, with his nose.

Then Henry heard a sound with his ears. It was a big truck! The truck went by the gate. It made the gate swing shut.

Henry's teddy fell out of his arms. The teddy landed under the dark tunnel slide. Henry looked with his eyes. He could not see the teddy. The tunnel was dark.

"I can't see in the dark," Henry said.

His dad came over. Dad switched on his big phone light. Now Henry could see! There was teddy, down on the ground.

Henry reached in with his hands. He touched the soft teddy and hugged him tight.

"Lets talk about the ocean next," said Dad. "Can you hear waves with your ears?"

"Yes," said Henry. "And I can taste my snack now!"

Henry went to the library today. Yesterday he could not go, because it rained. Today the sun was out, and Mom held his hand.

"Good morning," said the man at the desk. Henry looked around. It was morning, and he had eaten breakfast at home. He had eaten eggs, and he had licked his spoon clean.

Henry wanted the bear book. Last week the bear book was gone. Now the shelf was empty again.

"Where is the bear book?" Henry asked.

"It comes back tomorrow," said the man. "Someone is reading it now."

"Tomorrow is a whole sleep away," said Mom with a smile.

Henry found a duck book instead. He sat on the soft rug. He turned the pages slowly. The duck said quack, and Henry laughed.

"Now we read," said Mom. "Later we can take the duck book home."

"Tomorrow we come back for bears?" Henry asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow."

Henry patted the cover. "See you tomorrow, bear book," he whispered.

Hayden ran to the library playroom. He wanted the red ball. But the ball rolled under a shelf.

Hayden got down on his knees. He saw the ball, far away. He reached. Too far! His tooth felt loose. He wiggled it with his tongue.

A girl named Mia came over. She held a big toy box. "I can help," she said. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys. This box can hold them all."

Mia put in one block. Then a doll. Then a teddy bear. Then she reached far under the shelf with her long arm. Out came the red ball!

Hayden clapped. "Toys help toys!" he said.

He dropped the ball in the box. The ball bounced up. It bounced so high it hit a picture of an elephant on the wall. The elephant looked like it winked.

Hayden gasped. "The elephant wants a turn!"

So Hayden rolled the ball to the picture. The ball bounced back. Hayden caught it.

The librarian smiled. "Time to close the playroom," she said softly.

Hayden held the ball to his ear. "Shh," he whispered. "The ball is sleeping."

Mia closed the lid of the toy box, very gently.

Lincoln put on his blue coat. He went to the corner store with Dad. The store smelled like bread and apples. A shiny case held ten cookies.

"Can we buy five?" Lincoln asked. Dad said yes. The shop lady put them on a plate.

Lincoln counted them. "One, two, three, four, five."

Then Dad bought two more. "Now we have seven," Lincoln said. "Seven is more than five!" He saw the plate had more cookies now. Adding cookies made more.

At home, they ate the cookies. Lincoln bit one. It was sweet and a little crunchy. He counted again. "Six." He ate another. "Five." The plate got emptier and emptier.

Soon there was just one left. Lincoln ate it. He looked at the plate. He counted, but there was nothing to point to. "How many now?" he asked Dad.

Dad smiled. "Zero. Zero means none."

"Zero cookies," Lincoln said. The plate was all empty. "Zero is less than one!"

Then Lincoln turned the empty plate over like a hat. "Look, Dad! Now the plate has zero cookies on the bottom too!"

Joshua went to the big hall with Mom. The sky was cloudy. Everyone brought food for the shared meal. There were breads and soups and a big bowl of grapes.

"First we say our blessing," said Grandma. "A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food."

Joshua wanted to say it too. He stood on his tiptoes at the desk where the cups sat. He looked at the grapes. "Who grew these?" he asked.

"The grape farmer," said Mom.

Joshua smiled. He took a big breath. "Thank you for the food," he said. "And thank you, grape man!"

Everyone clapped. Then everyone ate. A dog outside went, "Bark, bark!" Joshua waved his grape at the window and said, "Hello, dog! Want a blessing too?"

Anna went to the playground with her lion. The lion was a soft toy with a dark mane. Anna held him tight.

A boy was at the swings. Anna wanted a turn. She hid behind her mom. The boy waved at her. Anna peeked out. Then she said, "Hello." The boy smiled big. "Hello," he said back. "Do you want a turn?" Anna nodded. "Yes, please."

Anna sat on the swing. The lion did not fit on her lap. He fell in the sand. "Sorry, lion," Anna said. The boy picked him up. "Thank you," said Anna.

Then Anna wanted to go higher. She could not reach. "Mom, can you help me push?" she asked. Mom pushed. Up went Anna, up to the sky. The swing felt like flying.

"Do lions fly?" the boy asked. Anna thought hard. "This lion can," she said. She held him up high. The wind moved his dark mane. The lion flew through the air, all the way to the top of the swing.

William went to a big festival with his dad. There was food everywhere. There was a pretend playground made of hay bales. William ran there first. Then he fell off a low bale, right on the soft grass. He got up and tried again. This time he did not fall.

Then William's dad said, "Our friend Maria invited us to eat." At Maria's table, everyone held hands. Maria's mom said, "We say grace before we eat. It is a short prayer of thanks." Maria smiled at William. "Would you like to say it?" she asked.

William felt shy. He held his dad's hand. He said, "Thank you for the food. Thank you for friends." Everyone at the table said, "Amen." Maria gave him a big spoonful of rice. The food was warm and good. "You said it," said Maria. "Now we eat!"

Blake walked on the nature trail with Dad. She wanted to learn her five senses. "You can do it," said Dad. "Let's find them one by one."

Blake found a pine cone. She touched it. "I used my hands!" she said. She smelled a flower. "That was my nose." She saw a red bird. "My eyes saw it!" Then a big truck rumbled by. It was so loud. Blake covered her ears with her hands. The sound got quiet. She lifted her hands. The truck was loud again. She put her hands back. Quiet again. "My ears hear!" she said. "And my hands make it quieter."

Then Dad poured water from his bottle into a cup. Blake took a little sip. "My mouth tastes it!" she said. "That makes five. Hands, nose, eyes, ears, mouth." A drop of rain fell on her nose. "That's neat," said Blake. "My nose felt that, too."

Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was piled thick on the window ledge. Miss Maya had a big jar of blocks. "Let's count them!" she said.

Everyone sang the counting song. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Axel sang loud. He loved that song.

Then Miss Maya said, "Axel, count the red blocks."

Axel pointed. "One, two, three, four, six."

His friend Pia stopped him. "Wait! You skipped a number. What comes after four?"

Axel scratched his head. He sang the song in his head. One, two, three, four, five. "Five!" he said. "Five comes after four, then six."

"Try again," said Pia.

"One, two, three, four, five, six." Six red blocks! Axel jumped up. "The song helped me!"

Miss Maya smiled. "Count the blue ones now."

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten blue blocks!

"Ten!" shouted Axel. "Ten is the last one!"

Michael jumped out of the car. He ran to Grandma's door. Today was a big holiday, and the whole family would come. Michael wanted to see his cousins most of all.

He looked in the kitchen. Only Grandma was there, stirring a pot. He looked in the living room. Only Grandpa sat in his chair. "Where is everybody?" Michael asked. "They will come soon," Grandma said. "On holidays, families gather together." Michael sat by the window to watch.

One car came. Then another. Then three more! The door opened and his cousins rushed in. "Michael!" they shouted. They hugged him and spun him around. Later, everyone ate together at the long table. Michael got sleepy before the cake came. Grandma carried him to the couch, and he fell asleep still smiling.

Bennett sat in his big car seat. His baby sister sat in her small one. "Fast car!" said Daddy. The car went fast down the big road. Then the cars made a line. The car went slow.

Bennett had a little drum on his lap. He banged it. BANG, BANG, BANG! It was so loud. The baby woke up. She cried and cried.

"We call that loud," said Daddy. "Loud and quiet are opposites. Can you try quiet?"

Bennett held his sticks. He tapped the drum, tap, tap, tap. It was so quiet. The baby blinked. She yawned. She closed her eyes and went back to sleep. "She likes quiet," Bennett whispered. He tapped again, tap, tap, tap.

Soon they stopped at Grandma's house. Daddy put a cold drink in Bennett's hands. Grandma held a hot plate of yummy pancakes. "Fast car, slow car," said Bennett. "Loud drum, quiet drum. I did it!" Then he ate every yummy bite.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Violet wanted to make her feel at home. But Grandma looked sad at breakfast. "I miss my little girl," Grandma said. Violet was puzzled. Grandma was old. How could she have a little girl?

Mom opened a big box of photos. There was a photo of a small girl. The girl had paint on her nose. She was hugging a fluffy sheep toy. "That is me," said Mom. "I was little once." Violet looked and looked. "Grandma is your mom?" she asked. Grandma laughed a funny laugh. "Yes," said Grandma. "I am your mom's mom."

Violet got her crayons. She drew Mom as a little girl, with the sheep and the paint. Grandma hung it on the fridge. "Now I am not sad," said Grandma. She gave Violet a big hug, right there in the sunny kitchen.

Snow was falling on the park. Andrew wore his red hat and puffy coat. "Let's slide first," said Mom. The slide was fast and snowy at the top. Andrew zoomed down, whee, whee, whee.

Then they walked to the little farm. A fat pig snuffled in the straw. His nose was warm on Andrew's hand. There was a grill near the snack hut. A man was cooking. It smelled good, but Andrew did not go near. Mom said, "Stay back. It is hot."

Andrew saw a duck and ran to the fence. When he turned around, Mom was gone. He looked left. He looked right. No red coat. His tummy felt jumpy.

Then Andrew remembered. He walked to the snack hut. The man at the counter had a uniform. "I can't find my grown-up," said Andrew. The man looked out the window. "There she is," he said.

Mom ran over fast and hugged Andrew tight. "You did just the right thing," she said. Andrew held her hand all the way back to the slide. "One more slide," said Mom. "Then hot cocoa."

Blake went to the library with her dad. She wanted a new book about a duck on a lake. She found one with a big green cover. It was her favorite kind of new.

Now it was time to check out the book. There was a line. Blake stood behind a boy with red boots. A girl ran up and pushed past everyone. She got to the front. The librarian shook her head. "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn," she said. The girl walked back to her spot at the end. She stood very still. Then it was the boy's turn. Then it was Blake's turn.

"Can I take this book home?" Blake asked. "Yes, you can," said the librarian. She stamped the green cover. Blake held the book all the way to the car.

Iris did not want to sleep. She pulled on her shoe under the blanket. "Is today library day?" she asked.

Mom sat on the bed. "Yes, it is today," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now."

Iris looked out the window. The sky was dark. "But now is night," she said.

"The library was this morning," said Mom. "We read the bear book. That was today, too."

Iris thought hard. This morning was today. Now was today too. One day could hold both! She wiggled her toes. "Yesterday we went to the park," she said. "My hands got sticky from the pear."

"That's right," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done."

"Tomorrow I want new books," said Iris.

"Tomorrow comes later," said Mom. "Sleep now, and tomorrow will come."

Iris pulled off her shoe and set it by the bed. She closed her eyes. Mom tickled her nose with a soft kiss.

"Later, I will dream about books," said Iris.

"Yes," said Mom. "Later is a good time for dreams."

Iris hugged her bear and waited. She heard the house go quiet. One tick at a time, the clock walked toward tomorrow.

"Goodnight, today," Iris whispered.

Oliver sat at the paint table at summer camp. He was painting a big lion. The lion had a yellow mane and a long tail.

"Can I paint the tail too?" Oliver asked his friend Mia.

"Yes," said Mia. "You can use my red brush."

Oliver painted the tail. Then the bell rang for snack time. He put his brush down in the paint cup. He shut his paint box and ran to the snacks.

The next morning, Oliver came back to paint. He picked up his brush. The bristles were hard. They did not bend at all.

"What happened to my brush?" Oliver asked.

The teacher held it up. "The paint dried on it," she said. "The brushes get rinsed clean so the paint does not dry on them."

Mia handed Oliver her brush. "I rinsed mine in the water cup," she said. "Feel it. It is soft."

It was soft like a kitten's tail. Oliver dipped it in blue. He painted a big sky above his lion.

At the end, Oliver carried his brush to the water cup. He swished it round and round. The water turned blue like the sea.

Brielle stood in the reading corner. She wiggled one toe inside her shoe. She was waiting for her very first library card.

The librarian smiled. "Here it is," she said. "Now you can borrow a book."

Brielle looked at the shelf. She wanted the book about the long, long train. But a boy sat near it. He hugged his knees and looked at the floor.

"Storytime is starting," the librarian said. She sat down on a small chair. She held up a funny book about a duck. She opened it wide.

The boy peeked at the duck. Then he got up. He put himself down on the carpet, right by her feet.

Brielle watched. The librarian read aloud to the children. Her voice made the duck quack. The boy laughed.

Brielle took her train book off the shelf. She put her new card in her pocket. She sat down next to the boy to listen too.

"Quack, quack," said the librarian.

Brielle laughed and clapped her hands.

Aiden went to the park with his red ball. The sun did shine on the green grass. Aiden felt happy. He ran far across the field. Then he saw a girl by the swings. She sat on the ground. Tears ran down her face. She was crying.

Aiden felt sad for her. He walked over slowly. "Why are you crying?" he asked. "I am sad," she said. "My dog ran far away. I miss him." Aiden wanted to help. He had an idea. He held out his red ball. "Do you want to play?" he asked. The girl wiped her tears. She took the ball. She stood up.

Aiden felt excited. He chased the ball. The girl chased it too. She laughed out loud. Then Aiden pulled a rubber chicken from his bag. He squeezed it. It made a silly squeak. The girl laughed even more. Aiden threw the ball high. "Catch it!" he called. The girl jumped up and caught it with both hands. "Again!" she said.

Matteo loved hide-and-seek at daycare. Today he found the best spot. He stood behind a short bookshelf. Then he covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the toys. He could not see the table. He could not see his friends. "Nobody can see me," he thought.

But Priya walked right up to him. "I see you, Matteo!" she said. Matteo moved his hands. The room came back. He could see the blocks with his eyes. He could hear Priya giggle with his ears. How did she find him? He asked her. "I could see your shoes," she said.

Next, Matteo hid again. This time he kept his eyes open. He watched Priya look behind the big doll house. He heard her feet go tap, tap, past his shelf. She did not see him. He won!

After the game, Miss Dana called everyone for snack. Matteo smelled the apples with his nose. He touched his cup. It felt warm, not too hot, because Miss Dana poured it. "The sun can burn your skin outside," she said, "so we put on hats." Matteo tasted the sweet apple. Then he ran outside to play on the little grassy hill. "Can I roll down?" he asked. "Yes," laughed Priya, "but keep your eyes open."

Beatrice woke up on a sleepy morning at Grandma's house. In the corner sat a shiny violin in its black case. "What is that, Grandma?" Beatrice asked. "That is my violin," said Grandma. She opened the case. "This is the bow." Beatrice wanted to hear it play.

Grandma handed her the bow. Beatrice held it in her fist. She poked the violin with the stick. Squeak! The sound was funny. Beatrice laughed. Then she poked it again. Squeak, squeak! One, two, three squeaks. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "Watch me first." Grandma put the bow on the strings. Then she pulled it across, slow and smooth. A sweet sound flew around the room like a bird.

"Can I try?" asked Beatrice. "Yes," said Grandma. She helped Beatrice lay the bow on the strings. "Now pull it across," said Grandma softly. Beatrice pulled. Music! Real music came out. "I did it!" said Beatrice. She played one note. Then two notes. Then three. Grandma clapped her hands. "Play it again," said Grandma. So Beatrice pulled the bow across the strings one more time, and the little song went on and on.

Lily sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. "Can I write my name?" Lily asked. "Yes, let's try," said Grandma.

Lily held the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard on the paper. The letters came out big and wobbly. One letter looked like a stick. Her L came out wrong. Lily made a sad face. "It won't do what I want," she said.

Grandma sat close by. "Watch my hand," she said. Grandma pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Lily looked and looked. Then she tried it. Pinch, pinch, rest. She wrote an L. Then an I. Then more letters. L, I, L, Y. "Look, Grandma, look!" said Lily. Grandma smiled big. On the paper, the name stood clear and neat, letter after letter, all the way across the empty page.

Henri was awake early. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shoes. He packed a triangle sandwich in his bag. "A triangle has three sides," he said.

At the classroom door, Henri stopped. His tummy felt funny. It fluttered like a small bird. He held Mama's hand tight.

"My tummy feels fluttery," Henri said.

"I felt that way on my first day too," Mama said. "Feeling nervous is okay."

Henri looked at the door. He took one step. Then another step. Inside, a boy was chasing a ball across the rug. The boy smiled at Henri. Henri smiled back.

"My tummy is quiet now," Henri said. He let go of Mama's hand and ran to chase the ball too.

Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find something pretty to look at. First she saw the big grill by the benches. It had a small fire inside. It was hot. Grandma held her hand. "We stay far from the fire," said Grandma. The fire made the grill go hiss and pop. So standing far away was the good thing to do.

Next Josephine saw a picnic table. On the table was a little bag. The bag was open. Inside were round red things and round yellow things. They looked like candy. Were they candy? Josephine wanted to touch them. She did not touch them. She kept her hands right at her sides.

"Grandma, come and see," she called. Grandma came and looked. "Those are not candy," said Grandma. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Grandma picked up the bag and put it in her pocket. She said Josephine was very kind to come get her.

A boy ran up. He beg, beg, begged to see the pretty round things. "No," said Grandma. "Not for touching." The boy and Josephine ran to the swings instead. Josephine pumped her legs. Up, up, up she went. "Look at me!" she called. Grandma waved and waved.

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She wanted to find a book all by herself. The bookshop was warm and friendly. Books sat on the shelves like little rows of colors.

Brooklyn found a big book of letters. She pointed at the first one. "That is A," she said. "A goes a, a, apple." Dad smiled. She turned the pages. B went buh. C went kuh. She sang the letter song all the way to P. Then she stopped. "The end," she said. She shut the book.

Dad shook his head. "Not yet," he said. "Keep going." Brooklyn opened the book again. She sang past P. Q went kwuh. R went ruh. Her voice got louder. She kept turning pages. S, T, U, all the way on.

Then she saw the last page. "Z!" she shouted. "The song ends at Z!" A lady at the desk looked up and clapped. Brooklyn laughed. The alphabet started with A and ended with Z. Who knew there were so many letters hiding after P?

At dinner, Brooklyn spelled her name with peas on her plate. "B, R, O," she said. Dad added the rest. Brooklyn ate the letter O first.

Sara had a garden at the farm. She dug little holes in the brown soil. She put tomato seeds in one hole. She put carrot seeds in another hole. Then she watered them with a small can.

The next day, Sara forgot her spots. "Where did my tomatoes go?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. He helped her make picture labels. Each label had a tomato or a carrot on it. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," said Grandpa. Sara pushed a tomato label into the dirt. Then she pushed a carrot label in too. "Now I know, now I know!" she sang.

Little green sprouts came up. Sara looked at the labels. The tomato sprout grew by the tomato label. The carrot sprout grew by the carrot label. "Hello, little tomato," she said. A pretty butterfly landed on the tomato leaf. It stayed there for a long time. Sara watered her sprouts and whispered, "Grow big, grow big."

Victor was at school. It was snack time. Ms. Beth had a big jug of apple juice. She poured juice into little cups.

Ben pushed to the front. "Give me juice!" he said. Ms. Beth shook her head. "Try again," she said. Ben frowned. Then he said, "Juice, please." Ms. Beth smiled. "Of course!" She poured him a big cup.

Victor watched all this. He was very thirsty. He wanted juice too. He waited in line. His tummy felt jumpy. Then it was his turn. "Juice, please," said Victor. Ms. Beth poured his cup all the way up. "Thank you," said Victor. "You are welcome," said Ms. Beth.

Later, Victor bumped into Ben's elbow. Juice spilled on the table. "Sorry," said Victor. Ms. Beth helped wipe it up. "It was an accident," she said. Afterward Victor felt warm inside, not sleepy, just happy. On the way to the rug he heard Ben say, "Blocks, please." The teacher said yes. Victor smiled and sat down with his empty cup.

Harrison had a big pot on the balcony. "We can grow lettuce," said Dad. Harrison put three seeds in the soil. He patted the soil until it was smooth. Dad wrote the letter L on a stick. "L for lettuce," said Harrison, and he pointed at the stick.

Every day Harrison looked. One sprout. Then two. Then three little green leaves. He counted them. "One, two, three," said Harrison.

One day the sun was hot. The lettuce hung down low. "It looks sad," said Harrison. He felt worried. Dad gave him the watering can. "Give them a drink," said Dad. Harrison tipped the can. Drip, drip, drip, all over the leaves.

The next morning, Harrison ran to the balcony. The lettuce stood up tall. "One, two, three," he counted. All three plants were up. "They wanted water," said Harrison. Dad smiled. "More water tomorrow," said Harrison, and he filled the little can.

Joshua was playing with his blocks. Then he heard a noise. Thump, thump, thump. It came from the hall. Joshua felt scared. His tummy felt tight. His dog, Biscuit, ran to the door. Biscuit began to bark.

Joshua wanted to know what made the noise. But he felt too scared to look. He remembered what Grandpa said. "When you are scared, tell a grown-up you trust." So Joshua called out, "Daddy!"

Daddy came fast. He held Joshua's hand. They walked to the hall together. Daddy turned on the light. "Let's listen," he said. Thump, thump, thump. It came from the big tree by the window. A branch was tapping the glass.

Daddy opened the window a little bit. He moved the branch away. The tapping stopped. Joshua felt happy now. His tummy felt calm. "The tree made that noise," Joshua said. "The wind pushed the branch," said Daddy. Joshua smiled big. He felt so excited. "Biscuit, we found it!" he said. Biscuit wagged his tail. Joshua gave Daddy a cool high five. Then he ran back to his blocks. He was not scared anymore.

Claire ran into Grandma's kitchen. She wanted to make soup for her teddy bear. Grandma gave her a big pot and a wooden spoon.

Claire found some pretend food. There were red apples and yellow pears. They looked so real. Claire put one in her mouth.

"Spit it out, sweet pea," said Grandma. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat."

Claire spat it out. Then she stirred her pot. She put in pretend apples and pretend pears. She held the spoon up to teddy's mouth. "Slurp, slurp," said Claire. Teddy was full!

Outside, a bird began to sing its last song of the morning. Claire carried her pot to the window. A little red leaf flew past the glass and landed in her pot.

"A leaf in my soup!" said Claire. "That is the best surprise ever." Grandma laughed and clapped her hands.

Isaac climbed into the car. He held his snack. But Bunny was gone! "Where did Bunny go?" he cried. Mom looked under the seat. It was too dark to see. "We can't see in there," said Mom. Isaac felt like crying.

"Wait!" said Mom. She opened the glove box. She took out a flashlight. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots," said Mom. She clicked it on. Mom shined the light under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore! Isaac leaned over and looked.

"I see a tail!" he shouted. "Bunny is there!" Isaac reached down. His arm was too short. Mom unbuckled him. Then he reached again. His fingers touched soft fur. He pulled and pulled. Out came Bunny! "Bunny!" Isaac hugged her tight.

"Now we can go," said Mom. She drove past the kitchen shop on the corner. Isaac waved at it. The car went round and round the bend. "That bend makes me dizzy!" Isaac laughed. Bunny sat on his lap all the way home. "No more dark spots for you," said Isaac. Mom smiled and kept driving.

Natalie sat on the playroom floor. Her tummy felt hungry for a game. Mama held up a big blue bag.

"This is the feely bag," said Mama. "Put your hand in. Don't peek!"

Natalie put her hand inside the bag. She felt something round. It was smooth. It had a little bounce.

"A ball!" she said. "A red ball!"

Natalie pulled it out. She looked at it. It was not red. It was yellow!

"Oh," said Natalie. "I could feel it was a ball. But my fingers did not tell me the color."

Mama smiled. "Want to try again?"

Natalie reached into the bag. She felt something soft and squishy. A sock! But what color? She had to look. She pulled it out fast. Green!

Then Mama hid a red car in the bag. Natalie felt the little wheels. She felt the smooth top. But she shut her eyes and squeezed it. Still no color came to her fingers.

"Is it red?" she asked.

"Look and see," said Mama.

Natalie opened her eyes. Yes! The little car was red.

"One more," said Natalie. She filled the bag with her blue blocks herself. Then she closed her eyes tight and reached in.

Mama laughed. "You can feel the blocks, Natalie. But only your eyes can find the blue."

Natalie peeked with one eye. There it was. Blue!

"My eyes are so good," said Natalie. She gave the bag a big hug.

Margot sat at the little table. The tablet lay in front of her. The screen was dark and still. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen with her finger. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. Still nothing. "Why won't it wake up?" she asked.

Teacher Ben came over. He was a grown-up, so he knew about tablets. "Press the button," he said. He pointed to the small button on the side. Margot pressed it. The screen lit up. It was bright and full of colors. Her tap had not worked, but her press did.

She pressed the drawing app and drew a big cat. It had long whiskers and a winter scarf, because outside the window snow was falling. When she was done, she pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, just where it belonged.

"I did it," Margot said, and she clapped her hands.

Wesley was a small boy who loved the forest. He found a flat stump under a big tree. He put three pinecones and two leaves on top. "This is my shop," he said.

A squirrel came near and sat still. Wesley waited. The squirrel did not pick anything. Then his friend Mia came down the path. "I am the shopkeeper," said Wesley. "You can be the shopper." Mia picked one leaf. She paid him with a small stone. Wesley put the stone in his pocket.

"Now I can be the shopper," said Wesley. "You be the shopkeeper." Mia stood by the stump. Wesley walked around the tree first. Then he came back. He picked one pinecone and paid with the stone. He put the pinecone in his bag to carry home. "Good shop," said Mia. The squirrel watched from the branch above.

Gabriella went to Miss Penny's music room. Miss Penny had a small drum. She wanted Gabriella to clap the steady beat. Gabriella wanted to sing "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" all by herself. But first she had to clap.

Gabriella clapped. Her claps went fast, faster, fastest. "Too fast," said Miss Penny. "Let's try marching." Miss Penny marched around the room. Gabriella marched too. Her footsteps went one, two, one, two. They stayed even and they kept going. "Like this!" said Gabriella. She clapped along with her marching feet. Clap, clap, clap. The claps were even now. The claps kept going too.

"Now sing," said Miss Penny. Gabriella sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, yes sir, yes sir." Miss Penny played the drum. Gabriella clapped the steady beat and sang every word. Miss Penny clapped too. "I did it!" said Gabriella. Miss Penny smiled and gave her a hug.

Hazel went to the library with Dad. She wanted the big red book about a chicken. The shelves were tall. She could not reach it.

A boy named Sam stood by the shelf. He had a book in his hands. Hazel reached up high. Her hand bumped Sam's book. The book fell down with a thump.

"Sorry," said Hazel. She picked up the book. She gave it back to Sam. Sam smiled. "Thank you," he said.

Hazel wanted the red chicken book still. She asked the librarian. "Please, can you help me?" The librarian reached up high. She took down the red book. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you," said Hazel. She sat on the soft rug. Dad sat next to her. Hazel opened the book. The chicken had fresh yellow feathers. Sam came and sat too. They read together, page by page, until the story swung its happy ending.

Logan stood in the library with his mom. He wanted a book about trucks. He could not take it home. The lady at the desk said, "You need a library card."

Logan reached up on his toes. "Can I have one?" he asked. The lady shook her head. "A grown-up helps a child sign up," she said. So Mom sat down at the desk. She wrote on the paper. Logan watched and held his book against his knee.

Then the lady made a little card. It was blue and shiny. It had Logan's own name on it! She put it in his hand. Logan gave the book to her. She beeped it. Now the book was his to take home. "Thank you," Logan whispered. He squeezed Mom's hand and skipped to the door.

Emily was at Grandma's house. She wanted a cookie. She saw a big jar on the shelf. There were little marks on the jar. "What are those marks, Grandma?" Emily asked. Grandma said, "Those are words. Words tell us things."

Grandma lifted Emily up so she could see. Emily pointed at the jar. "What do the words say?" she asked. "They say Cookie Jar," said Grandma. Emily looked and looked. Words on a jar! Words were telling her what was inside!

Then Emily saw a box on the table. It had words too. "What does the box say?" she asked. "It says Crackers," said Grandma. Emily clapped her hands. Words on boxes! Words everywhere!

There was a little card on the door. It had words on it. "What does the card say?" asked Emily. "It says Welcome," said Grandma. Emily smiled. Words on signs! Words told her things all day.

Grandma brought a book to the soft chair. She sat Emily on her lap. "Books have words too," said Grandma. She opened the front of the book. She turned one page, then the next. She read from the front to the back.

Emily leaned on Grandma's warm neck. Her neck did not hurt at all. It was comfy and soft. Grandma read about a little green frog. The frog sat on a slimy rock by the pond.

"More words," said Emily. "Read the front to the back again!" Grandma turned to the first page. She began to read. Emily listened, happy and warm.

Dylan wanted to go to the park. He could see the swings from the window. The park was across the street. He called, "Grandma, park!"

Grandma came with her shoes on. She took the bread out of the oven first. The pan was hot. She used a big glove so her hand would not get hurt. Dylan stayed back from the oven. He saw steam go up, up, up.

Outside, the sun was warm. The street was in front of them. Dylan saw a red truck go by. He held Grandma's hand. They looked left. They looked right. They walked across the street together, hand in hand.

At the park, Dylan found crunchy leaves. He stepped on them. Crack, crack! Grandma sat on the bench. A little girl dropped her ball. Dylan picked it up and gave it back. She smiled big.

When they got home, Dylan was sleepy. He got into his bed with his bear. "We held hands," he said to the bear. Then he closed his eyes.

Stella stood by the play table. Three kids were there. They rocked a baby doll and stirred a pot.

Stella wanted to play too. She walked closer. She stood very still. Nobody looked up.

She touched the doll's blanket. The kids kept stirring. Stella felt like crying a tiny bit.

Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend I am the doctor," she said.

Ben looked up fast. "Okay! The baby has a scratch on her knee."

Stella got a bandage from the toy box. She patted the doll. "All better now."

"You are a lucky baby," said Mia. "The doctor came today."

Then Mia held up a spoon. "Let's pretend this soup is magic soup!"

The pot bubbled with giggles. Stella stirred and stirred. The kitchen got very busy.

"More soup, Doctor?" Ben asked.

"Yes please," said Stella. "Magic soup for everyone."

Zoey was in the garage with Grandpa. He had a little guitar made of wood. "You can play it," Grandpa said.

Zoey picked a string. The sound was funny. It went boing, not a nice note. She picked another string. Boing again. "It sounds wrong," she said.

Grandpa sat down next to her. "The strings need tuning," he said. "Then the notes sound right." He turned the little pegs at the top. Zoey watched. He turned one peg a tiny bit.

Zoey picked the string again. Now it made a sweet note. Not boing. A real note! "I want to try," she said. Grandpa helped her turn a peg. Very slow. Very small.

Zoey picked the string. The note sounded mean and wobbly. Too far! Grandpa smiled. "Turn it back a little," he said. Zoey turned it back. She picked the string. Sweet note.

"Again!" said Zoey. She picked every string, one by one. Grandpa tapped his foot to her song.

Sienna put on her new backpack. It sat on her back. It was very heavy. She walked to the school playground. Her legs felt slow.

"Oof," said Sienna. She could not run. The bag pulled her back.

A boy named Tom ran up. "That's a backpack," he said. "It rides on your back."

Sienna sat on the bench. She opened the bag. She looked in. Three teddy bears! Two books! One drum!

"Too many toys," said Sienna. She took out the teddy bears. She took out the drum. The bag got thin and light now.

Sienna stood up. The air felt good on her face. She ran to the slide. Tom ran with her. They laughed all the way.

Adam sat at the little table at school. Miss Kim put out ten fresh leaves for counting. Adam touched each leaf one by one. "One, two, three," he said. His friend Mia counted too. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Miss Kim sang the counting song, and everyone sang the last word together. "Ten!"

Adam wanted to write ten on his paper. He wrote a big 1. Then he stopped. The other numbers had one shape each. Ten looked different. "Why does ten need two numbers?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled and knelt down beside him. "Ten is a 1 and then a 0," she said.

Adam wrote the 1. Then he wrote the 0 right after it. Mia looked over at his paper. "That is ten!" she said. Adam picked up a leaf and gave it to Mia. She took a tiny bite of her apple and grinned. Then Adam counted all ten leaves again, tapping each one. Ten leaves, ten numbers, one happy boy.

Georgia sat on Grandma's big striped chair. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Uncle Sam clapped. Grandma clapped. Georgia clapped too.

Georgia wanted to know who would win. She asked, "Who won the game?" Uncle Sam said, "Not yet. We have to wait." So Georgia waited. She hugged her soft bear. She watched the TV.

The game went on and on. It was night outside now. Daddy pointed at the screen. "Look. Both teams have the same score," he said. Georgia looked. The numbers were the same. Same and same.

"Who won now?" Georgia asked. Grandma smiled and said, "Nobody won. When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie." Georgia said the word slowly. "A tie." She liked that word.

Then one team kicked the ball, and it went in! The big number changed. Everyone jumped up. Uncle Sam lifted his arms. Grandma laughed out loud. Georgia stood on the chair cushion, and Grandma said, "Feet on the floor, sweetheart." So Georgia slid down and stood by Grandma's knee.

"It is not a tie now!" Georgia said. "That team has more!" Everyone clapped for her. Georgia clapped too, and hugged her bear tight.

Rehmat was playing in the backyard. She wanted to make a cold drink for her doll, Dolly. It was a hot day, and Dolly sat in the sun.

Papa brought out a bowl of ice cubes. Rehmat picked one up with her fingers. She touched it and pulled her hand back fast. "Cold, cold!" she said. She dropped the ice cube right into Dolly's cup. She touched it again with one finger. It was still cold.

Rehmat looked at the shiny ice with her eyes. She heard it go plink in the cup with her ears. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled like water. She licked it with her tongue. It tasted like water too. "Your drink is ready," she said. She put Dolly under a tree, out of the sun. Then she touched her own cold, wet cup and smiled. "Papa, Dolly calls this her mountain of ice," she said. Papa laughed and helped her add one more piece.

Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his little blue car. It was his favorite toy.

The car slipped out of his hand. It went down, down, down. "Where did it go?" said Colton. "Where did it go?"

Colton looked by the apples. No car. He looked by the bread. The bread was in a thick plastic bag. No car there either.

A teacher named Miss Kim worked at the store. She saw Colton looking sad. "Small toys can roll," she said. "They roll far."

Near the carts, there was a big couch for sale. Colton got down on his knees. He peeked under the couch. Something blue was there! He reached his arm in. His fingers touched the little car. He pulled it out.

"My car!" said Colton. "It rolled under the couch!"

Mama helped him stand up. Miss Kim smiled and gave him a sticker with a star on it. Colton held the car with both hands now. He would draw a picture of the blue car when he got home.

"Mama, hold my hand too," said Colton. So she did.

Leo went to the park with Dad. Leo held Dad's hand. The sun felt hot on his head. His water bottle felt cold in his hand.

Leo saw the big slide. He wanted to go on it. He climbed the ladder with Dad right behind him. At the top, Leo lay down on his tummy. He put his head down first.

Dad said, "Not head first, Leo. At the playground, go down the slide feet first."

Leo sat up. He turned himself around. His feet went first. Whoosh! Down he went. His socks felt rough on the slide. He landed in the sand on his feet.

"Again!" said Leo. He climbed up again. Feet first. Whoosh! He kicked the sand at the bottom and laughed.

Then Leo saw a shiny can in the sand. He reached for it. Dad came fast and picked it up. "Not that one," said Dad. "It has sharp edges." Dad put it in the trash.

Leo stayed close to Dad. They sat on the bench. Dad opened the cold water bottle. Leo drank a little sip.

"More slide?" asked Dad.

"Feet first!" said Leo. He ran to the ladder.

Peyton sat on the rug at math club. Ten toy ducks sat in a row. Her teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Count them for me."

Peyton counted fast. "One, two, three... um..." She forgot where she stopped. "Ducks are tricky!"

Her friend Leo laughed. "They do not even wiggle!"

Peyton looked at her hands. She tried again. She held up one finger for each duck. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Miss Kim put out two plates of pretend cookies. "Which group has more?"

Peyton counted the cookies. She put up a finger for each one. "This plate has seven. That plate has four. Seven is more!"

"You may pick one cookie," said Miss Kim with a smile.

Peyton picked the sweet pink one. "Mmm, counting makes cookies fair!"

Amira wanted to make cookies for her family. She stood at the little table in the cooking classroom. The teacher put out a big bag of sugar. Amira picked up the bag. She tipped it over the bowl. The sugar poured out fast. Too much sugar fell in. Sugar went all over the table.

The teacher brought a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Amira looked at it. It had a little line inside. Amira filled the cup with sugar. She stopped at the line. Then she poured it into the bowl. Not too much, not too little. Just the right amount.

Amira measured the flour too. She measured a little spoon of vanilla. The teacher put the tray in the hot oven. Amira waited and watched from far away. Soon the cookies were done. She put them in her sheep lunchbox to carry home. "My family will know I made these," said Amira. Her dad took a big bite. "These are so nice," he said.

Baby Ben was sleeping in his crib. Brielle stood on her tiptoes. She wanted Ben to like her.

"Can I hold his hand?" she asked.

"Shh, soft hands," said Mom. "You can put one finger in his hand."

Brielle counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." She picked her pointer finger. She put it in Ben's little hand.

Ben held tight! His small fingers gripped her finger.

"He got me!" said Brielle. She giggled.

She pulled a tiny bit. Ben still held on. He was so strong for a baby.

"You are so cute," she whispered.

Ben opened his eyes. Sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the crib.

Brielle waited. She waited some more. Then Ben blinked at her.

"Hi, Ben," she said.

Mom clapped her hands, very softly. "He likes you," she said.

Brielle counted again. "One finger, one baby, one big sister."

Ben squeezed her finger one more time.

"Again tomorrow?" Brielle asked.

Bennett ran into the backyard. "Can I get in the tub now?" he asked. A big tub of water sat by the fence. It was tall, and it sparkled in the light.

"I want to jump in!" said Bennett. He lifted one foot.

"Not yet," said Grandma. She put her hand in the water. "The sun made it too hot. We will add cold water and mix it." Bennett watched. Grandma turned the hose on. The water went round and round.

"Now let me check," said Grandma. She put her hand in again. "It is warm now. Not hot. You can get in."

Bennett put in his toes. "It feels nice!" He splashed with both hands. "You do the checking every time?" he asked.

"Every time," said Grandma. She smiled and held his hand so he would not slip.

Sebastian went to the library with his mom. The craft table had smooth white paper and cups of paint. The librarian smiled. "You can paint one half of the paper," she said. "Then fold it while the paint is wet."

Sebastian dug his brush into the red paint. He painted one wing on one half of the paper. One wing, one dot, one line. Then he folded the paper in half. He pressed it with his hands.

"Open it," said the librarian. Sebastian opened the paper slowly. Two wings! Both sides matched. "A butterfly," Sebastian said. The wet paint had made a print on the other half.

"Mine has one wing only," said a girl next to him. She had let her paint dry. "Try again," said Sebastian. "Fold it while it is wet." She painted blue on one half. She folded it fast. She opened it. Two blue wings, the same on each side.

Sebastian carried his butterfly to the kitchen window at home. He hung it up with tape. "One butterfly," he said. "Two wings. Both the same." His mom clapped her hands.

Jules sat at the dinner table. His tooth felt wiggly. He wiggled it with his tongue.

Dad put down his fork. Dad did not eat. Dad made a big sigh.

"What is wrong?" asked Jules.

"I feel nervous," said Dad. "Tomorrow I go to my new job. My tummy feels funny."

Jules felt surprised. He thought only kids got scared. Grown-ups were so big!

"You get scared too?" asked Jules.

"Yes," said Dad. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Jules felt happy inside. He ran to get his teddy. He put teddy near Dad's plate.

"Teddy helps me when I'm scared," said Jules.

Dad hugged teddy. Then Dad smiled a big smile. Dad took a big bite of dinner.

"Teddy works," said Dad. "Teddy works!"

Noah stood at the train station. He held a red paper sign. It said "Grandma" in wobbly letters. He had drawn it all by himself. One letter looked a bit wrong. But Mom said it was still good.

The train came in. It was very long and loud. People stepped down, one by one. Then Noah saw her. "Grandma!" he shouted. She waved and hugged him tight. "I get to stay for a whole week," she said.

At home, Noah showed Grandma his toy train. "Dad has a train too," said Noah. Grandma laughed. "When your dad was little, he had a blue bike. He fell off it lots of times. Then one day he rode it all the way to the shop." Noah stared. "Dad was little? Like me?" "Yes," said Grandma. "Just like you."

The next day, Noah rode his trike in the yard. He fell off. His mouth turned down. "That's okay," said Grandma. "Your dad fell too." Noah got back on. He pushed and pushed. Then the trike rolled fast down the little hill. "I did it!" said Noah. "Tell me another dad story tonight!" Grandma smiled. "I will," she said.

Sadie stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her new lunchbox with a little boat on it. She liked the blue sails best.

At lunch time, Sadie could not find her lunchbox. Another girl had one just like it. The same boat. The same blue sails. The other girl looked sad too. "That one is mine," Sadie said softly. "But this one is mine," said the girl.

Then Sadie's teacher came. She opened the lid. Inside, there was a name. It said Sadie. "This one is Sadie's," said the teacher. The other girl opened the other box. That lid had her own name. It said Mia. Now they each had the right lunch.

After lunch, Sadie asked the teacher for a marker. She wrote Sadie on her coat tag too. She wrote it on her backpack. At home that night, Sadie helped Mom stir the soup for dinner. Then she found her old teddy. "We will write your name too," she said. She printed the letters, one by one. "There. Now you can always come back to me."

Levi ran to the big paint table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. A big, round, orange pumpkin. But he looked and looked. There was no orange paint.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Levi, counting the pots. "Red, yellow, blue." No orange anywhere. He frowned at the empty paint cups. His pumpkin could not be a green pumpkin. Or a blue one. Pumpkins were orange.

Levi dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a thin red circle. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow pot. He swirled the yellow right on top. The red circle turned orange! "Orange!" shouted Levi. He painted the whole pumpkin orange. It looked like a giant sunset egg, glowing on the paper.

He held it up high. "I made orange!"

Everett ran to the big tree at the playground. The sky was cloudy and soft. Under the tree was a pretend kitchen. There were cups and pots and one long stick for a spoon. "I will cook soup," said Everett. He took all the pots. He took all the cups too.

Then Mia came to the tree. She stood very still. She had no pot. She had no cup. Her hands were empty. "I want to cook too," said Mia. Everett looked at his pots. He looked at Mia's empty hands.

"You can use this pot," said Everett. He put a pot in her hands. He put a cup in her hands too. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too," said Mia. She smiled big. Now they both had pots. Now they both could cook.

"Stir, stir, stir," said Everett. "Stir, stir, stir," said Mia. They stirred the leaf soup under the cloudy sky. Ben ran over. He had no pot. Everett looked at his last pot. "You can use it too," said Everett. Ben stirred and stirred. Three friends cooked soup by the big tree. "More leaves for the soup!" said Ben.

Wyatt wanted warm milk. He followed Dad into the kitchen. Dad turned a knob on the stove. The pot went on the little burner. Wyatt could not see anything. The burner did not look hot at all. Wyatt reached out his hand. Dad caught it gently. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," Dad said. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot." Wyatt stepped back. He sat on his stool and watched. The milk got warm. Bubbles came up, small and slow. Dad poured the milk into Wyatt's cup. It was warm, not cold like before.

Wyatt carried his cup outside. He stayed close to Dad in the backyard. The grass was wet under his shoes. A bee buzzed by the big flowers. Wyatt did not touch the bee. He watched it fly away. Dad picked up a sharp tool from the ground. Dad put it far back on the shelf. Wyatt sipped his milk. "I like the warm taste," he said. The sun came out. The wet grass began to shine. Dad held out his hand. Wyatt took it and held on tight. "One more sip," said Wyatt, "and then can we look for birds?"

Margot sat at the dinner table. She had five toy monkeys with her. They sat next to her cup. "Time to sing," said Margot.

She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one monkey fell off. Margot put it in her lap. "How many now?" she asked. She counted, "One, two, three, four." Four monkeys sat by the cup. She sang again. One more monkey fell off. Now three. Then two. Then one. The last monkey fell off, and her lap was full.

Daddy slid her plate closer. "Little monkeys need dinner too," he said. Margot lined up the monkeys. She pointed at each one. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. All five monkeys sat back up again. "Maybe they should not jump on the bed," said Margot. Then she took a big bite of her peas.

Matthew went to the farmers' market with Dad. There were big baskets of carrots and potatoes. "Let's buy some," said Dad. "You can help cook supper." Matthew picked three carrots. They felt bumpy in his hand. A fish seller next door waved. "Look at the shiny fish!" said Matthew. "Yes, very shiny," said Dad.

At home, Dad put the carrots on the counter. Matthew looked closely. The carrots had dirt on them. Brown dirt, right on the top. "Dirt," said Matthew. "I don't want dirt in my soup." He felt worried. "We can fix that," said Dad. He lifted Matthew up to the sink.

Matthew turned the water on. The water ran cool over the carrots. He rubbed them with his hands. The dirt came off. It went down the drain. "Look, Dad! The dirt goes away!" Dad smiled. "Good scrubbing," he said. Then they rinsed the potatoes too. Scrub, rinse, clean. Scrub, rinse, clean. Soon every carrot was orange and shiny.

Dad chopped the carrots with a big knife. Matthew stood back, far from the knife. He watched Dad put the pot on the stove. "You can stir when it cools," said Dad. The soup bubbled and smelled good. Mom came home and sniffed the air. "Mmm! Who made this?" she asked.

"I did!" said Matthew. "I scrubbed the dirt off!" They all sat down together. Matthew ate his soup. The carrots were soft and sweet. "Clean carrots, yummy soup," said Matthew. Dad gave him a high five. "Scrub, rinse, clean," said Matthew, and he took one more bite.

James was at Grandma's house. He put on his red coat all by himself. One arm went in. Then the other arm went in. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He tugged it gently. Zip! It closed.

"Good job," said Grandma. "Now we can play outside." James ran in the snow. His hands got cold. He had lost one mitten by the big tree. He looked and looked. There it was, under the bench.

Grandma held his mittens. "Try your coat pocket," she said. James pushed both mittens in. The pocket held them snug. They stayed put.

Later they went inside. James was thirsty, so Grandma gave him milk. They ate a cheese sandwich together.

"Thank you, Grandma," said James. He patted his pocket. The mittens were still right there.

Chloe woke up early. Snow was on the ground! "A snow day!" she cheered. She pulled on her boots. She put on her mittens. Out she ran into the backyard.

The snow was cold and soft. Chloe made a big snowball. She patted it with her red mittens. Snow fell from the sky and tickled her nose. She laughed and laughed.

Then Mom called, "Time for a snack!" Chloe ran inside. She wanted hot cocoa. Mom made it, and Chloe watched from her chair.

Soon Chloe wanted to go back out. She grabbed her mittens. But they were wet! Water dripped from them. Her boots were wet too. "Oh no," said Chloe.

"Hang them up to dry," said Mom. Chloe clipped her mittens to the rack. She set her boots by the door. They dripped, drip, drip.

Chloe waited by the window. She watched the snow. At last her mittens felt dry. Her boots felt dry too. On they went! Chloe ran outside fast. She picked up her snowball. "Still here!" she said, and gave it a big pat.

Avery sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. "Mama, we went to the park tomorrow!" she said. Mama smiled and shook her head. "The park was yesterday," Mama said. "Yesterday is the day before today." Avery tapped her ear. Did she hear that right? "Yesterday?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "It already happened."

The car went past the bakery. Avery saw a thin bird on a fence. "Look, a bird!" she said. "It is there now," said Mama. "Now means right this minute." The bird flew away. "Where did it go?" Avery asked. "It will come back later," said Mama. "Later means not now, after now."

"Can we go to the park again?" Avery asked. "We can go tomorrow," said Mama. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Avery clapped her hands. The car turned onto their street. Tomorrow felt far away. But now the car was stopping. Now they were home. Avery jumped down from her seat. "Tomorrow, park!" she called. "Park tomorrow!"

Nova went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she stayed home. Today the sun was out. Nova wanted the ice cream truck.

"Is the truck here now?" she asked Mom.

"Not now," said Mom. "The truck comes later."

Nova waited. She went down the slide. She played in the sand. A funny pigeon walked by her bag and pecked at the strap.

"When is later?" Nova asked.

Mom held up her watch. "This clock shows what time it is," said Mom. "See the hands move. When they get to the three, it is later."

Nova watched the clock. The hands moved slow, slow, slow. She kissed the watch face. Then she heard a bell.

The ice cream truck came around the corner.

"Later is now!" said Nova.

"Today it is," said Mom, laughing. "And tomorrow we can come back."

Elias sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse came in with a small tray. "What is that?" Elias asked. "It is your shot," said Dad. The nurse cleaned his arm with a cold wipe. Then came a quick pinch. Elias blinked. It was done!

Then Elias saw a red box on the wall. It was small and hard. "What is that red box for?" he asked. The nurse held up the used needle. "This goes in here," she said. She dropped the needle through the little slot. Clunk. It stayed inside. "So nobody gets poked," she said.

"The needle goes in and the box keeps it?" asked Elias. "Yes," said Dad. "The needle goes in and the box keeps it." Elias watched the slot close. The needle could not come back out. It was safe in there.

Afterward, Dad took Elias to the ice cream shop. Elias got a small pink cone. He took a big lick. "My shot is all done," he said, "and the needle is in the box." Dad smiled and gave him a thumbs up.

Raphael was at Grandma's house. Today was painting day! Grandma set out big paper and bright paints.

"I will paint a sun," said Raphael. He made a big yellow circle. He added orange rays all around. "It looks so sunny!" He wanted to touch it. He poked the sun with one finger.

"Oh no!" The yellow smeared. The sun had a smudge on it now. "My sun!" said Raphael. "It got all blurry."

"Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries," said Grandma. "Let's wait and watch."

Raphael sat very still. He watched his painting. He touched the squishy paintbrush instead. He did not touch the paper. Dad came in with a snack. They ate apple slices together.

Then Grandma said, "Touch it now. Very gently."

Raphael tapped the sun. It felt dry and smooth. Nothing smeared! The sun stayed bright and round.

"It worked!" said Raphael. "I waited and it dried!"

"Thank you for waiting," said Grandma. She hung the painting on the fridge.

Raphael grinned at his sunny picture, then ran to get more paper.

Anthony ran into the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. A big game was starting soon!

Anthony sat with Mama, Papa, and Aunt Jo. Everyone wore green shirts. Anthony looked down. His shirt was plain and gray.

"I want a green shirt too!" said Anthony.

Aunt Jo opened her big bag. She pulled out a small green shirt. Anthony pulled it on over his gray one. Now he matched everyone!

The game began. The crowd on the screen made a big noise. Lots of fans wore green, just like Anthony's family.

A man at the next table wore green too. He waved at Anthony. Anthony waved back.

"Smart shirt," said Papa with a big smile.

The team ran fast. Anthony jumped up. He clapped and clapped. The green fans on the screen clapped too.

Aunt Jo held up her cup. "Go, green team!" she called.

Anthony held up his little cup of water. "Go, green team!" he shouted.

The room went quiet. Then the screen showed a green player run, run, run. He sent the ball far across the field.

Everyone jumped up. The whole restaurant made one big noise.

Anthony hugged Papa's leg. His green shirt was bright in the light of the big screen.

Willow loved playtime at school. Today the teacher put out three big mats. "Let us sort," said Miss Kim. "Animals go here. Toys go there. Foods go on the blue mat."

Willow picked up a little cow. She put it on the animal mat. She picked up a soft ball. She put it with the toys. Then she saw something funny. A banana was hiding among the toy cars!

"Look," said Willow. "The banana does not fit here." Her friend Sam ran over. "It is the odd one out," said Sam. "It is the one that does not belong in the group." Willow held the banana up. The cars were all the same hard toys. The banana was soft food.

Willow put the banana on the blue food mat. Miss Kim smiled. "You learn fast," she said. Willow clapped her hands. "A mat is a good tool for sorting!" she said. Then she ran back to find more odd ones out.

Sofia wanted to make her own breakfast. Mom said, "You can help." The toast was warm from the toaster. Mom had put it on the plate.

Sofia picked up the butter knife. She took a little butter. She spread it slow and soft. The butter melted and made the toast shiny. "It looks real yellow now," she said. Mom smiled. "You pay attention so well," said Mom.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the big cup with two hands. She poured and poured. The milk went up to the very top. She walked to the table. Step, step, wobble. Milk spilled over the edge. It ran down the cup and onto her hand.

"Hmm," said Sofia. "The cup was too full." She tried again. This time she stopped pouring before the cup was full to the top. She left a little room. She walked to the table. Step, step, wobble. This time nothing spilled at all. Sofia took a big sip. "I did it, Mom!" she said. Mom clapped her hands.

Anthony looked out the window. Snow was everywhere. No school today! "Snow day!" he shouted. He jumped on the rug. "One sock, two socks, boots, coat, hat!" said Mom. Anthony counted each thing as he put it on. Then he ran outside.

Outside, the sky was dark and gray. Anthony made one big snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it forever. He carried it inside. He set it in his red bowl. "Stay right there," he told the snowball. Then he went to build a rainbow tower of blocks.

The tower got very tall. One block, two blocks, three blocks, four. Boom! It fell over. Anthony laughed. Then he remembered his snowball. He ran to the bowl. The bowl was full of water. No snowball at all. Just a wet puddle. "My snowball ran away!" he cried.

Mom came over. "Look," she said. "The snow came inside where it is warm." Anthony dipped his finger in the water. It was cold water, and that was all. He grinned. He got a spoon and scooped a fresh scoop of snow. "I will watch you this time," he told it. He sat down. One minute, two minutes, three. The snow got small, then smaller. Drip, drip, drip. "Got you!" said Anthony, and he patted the puddle with his spoon.

Myles went to Dad's office. He saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I use it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "First you press this little button."

Myles pressed the button. The screen lit up. It went from dark to bright! Dad tapped a green square. "This is the drawing app," he said.

Myles took the tablet. His finger slid across the screen. A red line followed his finger! He moved his finger again. The line went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. "I made a line," said Myles. The line looked like a squiggle. Myles gave it two eyes. "Now it's a snake," he said. Dad looked up from his work. "A red snake on a green grass day," he said.

Outside, a truck rumbled down the street. Myles drew a long line under the snake. "The snake has a road now," he said.

Soon Myles was tired of drawing. "All done," he said. Dad helped him press the button again. The screen went dark. Myles put the tablet in the drawer, all by himself. "Good job," said Dad. Myles smiled and folded his hands on the desk. "Snakes need naps too," he said.

Liam was three today. His party was at the park. There was cake and balloons. Grandma brought a big box. The box was all wrapped up in paper.

"Is it a truck?" Liam asked. He shook the box. He could not see inside. The paper hid the present. He squeezed it. He held it up to his ear. "Maybe it is a drum," said his cousin Mia. "Maybe it is a duck," said Grandpa. Everyone laughed.

Liam wanted to know now. He picked at the paper with his little fingers. "Not yet," said Mom. "We sing first." So Liam waited. It was hard to wait. He tapped his toes.

Then they sang happy birthday. Liam blew out his candles with Mom right beside him. Then Mom said, "Now you can open it." Liam tore the paper off. Inside was a big red truck! He could not see it before, but now he could. "My truck!" Liam shouted. He pushed it down the hill. "Beep beep," said Grandpa. "Coming through!" said Liam.
