Matteo wanted to read his puppy book all by himself. He sat on the rug and held the book. He looked at the pages. "That looks funny," he said. The puppy's legs were up in the air. The little words were upside down too.

Matteo frowned. "Big problem," he said. He turned his head to one side. The puppy still looked upside down. He turned his head the other way. Still upside down. Matteo laughed a big laugh.

Mama came over and sat close. "You made the pictures pop upside down," she said with a smile. Matteo turned the book around in his hands. Now the puppy stood on his four paws. The little words stood up straight too. "There he is!" said Matteo. He opened the front cover. He turned page after page, one at a time, all the way to the back.

"Read it to me," said Mama. Matteo pointed at the words. "Puppy runs fast," he said. Mama nodded and clapped. Matteo hugged the fresh, smooth pages. Then he flipped the book upside down one more time. The puppy hung by his ears. "Silly puppy," said Matteo. He turned the book right side up again. "Good night, puppy."

Rose sat high in the big stadium. Her dad sat next to her. Her friend Mia sat on the other side. Down below, the players ran fast. Rose watched the ball go up and down the court.

A player threw the ball. It went right through the hoop. The crowd made a big noise like a storm. "Look, the ball went in the hoop!" said Mia. Rose clapped and clapped. Then the players threw the ball through the hoop again and again. Every time it went through, the crowd cheered.

After the game, Dad took Rose to a small hoop. He handed her a ball. Rose planted her feet on the ground. She aimed at the hoop. She threw the ball. It went up, then down, then right through the net. "I did it!" Rose said. Mia laughed and jumped. Rose picked up her spotted ball and lined up for one more throw.

Max climbed the steps of the school bus. It was his first day of school. He sat by the window. He held his little bag. He wanted a friend, but he did not have one yet.

A boy sat down next to him. The boy looked at the floor. He did not say anything. Max took a big breath. Then he said, "My name is Max. What is your name?" The boy looked up. He smiled. "I am Sam," he said.

Now Max had a friend. Sam showed Max his sweet red apple from his lunch box. They looked out the window together. A big dog ran by, and both boys laughed. At school, the teacher said, "Sam, you can sit next to Max." Sam sat down and whispered, "This bus is fun." Max nodded and waved out the window at the dog.

Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted red apples. Dad said, "We need one, two, three, four, five apples." Sienna put apples in the bag. One, two, three, four, five. The bag felt heavy.

A man at the store smiled at her. "How old are you?" he asked. Sienna held up three fingers. Then she said, "I am three!" The man clapped. "Three is a good age," he said.

At the bread shelf, Sienna counted buns. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Then more. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten buns in a row. Sienna tapped each bun softly as she said the numbers. Dad waited. He let her take her time.

A song played over the speakers. Sienna began to dance. She twirled near the cart. Her shoe landed in a messy puddle by the fruit. Dad laughed. "One wet shoe," he said. He wiped it with a paper towel. "Now let's count our apples again," said Dad. Sienna opened the bag. "One, two, three, four, five!" she said.

Snow was falling outside. Logan pressed his nose to the window. "Snowy!" he shouted. Mom helped him put on his big puffy coat. She zipped his red boots. On went his warm hat.

Outside, the wind whooshed. "Windy!" said Logan. The snowflakes tickled his cheeks. His dog, Bingo, ran in circles. Bingo dug in the snow and found his old bone. "Good boy!" said Logan.

Logan scooped up a snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it forever. He carried it inside. He set it in a cup on the table. "I will keep you," he told the snowball. Then he ran back out to play more.

Later, Mom called, "Snack time!" Logan ran to see his snowball. He looked in the cup. The cup was empty! There was only a little puddle of water. "Where did it go?" he asked. He touched the water. It was wet and cool. His snowy ball had melted in the warm house. Logan clapped his hands. "It turned into water!" he said. Bingo came and licked the puddle. Logan yawned a big, sleepy yawn. "Night night, snowball," he whispered. Mom carried him off to his cozy bed.

Gabriel ran to the playground. He wanted the big slide, not the small one. The gate to the water park was shut. Gabriel pulled and pulled. It would not open. "Mama, help!" he called.

Mama came fast. Gabriel had tried slow. Mama pushed the gate. Click! It swung wide open. "Look," said Mama. "Open and closed are opposites." Gabriel laughed. He pushed the gate shut. Then he pulled it open. Shut, open, shut, open. What fun!

The water sprinklers were on. Splash, splash! The water felt cold. The sun felt hot. Mama held out a towel. Gabriel dried off, all warm. Then it was quiet. Only the little birds sang. Gabriel waved at the gate. "Bye, gate!" he said. He closed it all by himself.

Juliette was on the swim team. Every day she went to the tall pool with her mommy. She practiced kicking in the water. Her teacher was called Coach Ben.

One day the sun was very hot. Juliette felt slow and hot. The team took a break. All the other kids drank from their bottles. Juliette looked in her bag. Her water bottle was not there. She had left it at home.

"I forgot my bottle," she said. Coach Ben brought over a big water bottle. "Players drink water during breaks," he said. "Especially on hot days." Juliette drank and drank. Soon she felt better. She got back in the pool and kicked fast.

After practice, Mommy helped Juliette pack her bag. The water bottle went in first, every single day. At dinner that night, Juliette told Daddy all about the hot pool. "I will always stay with my water bottle," she said, and took a big sip from her cup.

Brooklyn waited at the bus stop with her grandma. It was cold. "Time for your coat," said Grandma. Brooklyn picked it up. One arm in. One arm in. Now the zipper. She pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. She tried again. Slowly it went zip, zip, zip, all the way to the top. "I did it," said Brooklyn.

Then she got warm and took the coat off. She dropped it on the ground. A furry dog walked by. A boy dropped his carrot. People's feet went tap, tap, tap. Brooklyn's coat went under the bench. Soon she could not see it. "Where is my coat?" she asked. She looked down. She looked under. There it was, dusty on the ground.

The bus came near. Brooklyn put her coat on again. One arm in. One arm in. Zip, zip, zip. Then she saw a little hook on the bus stop pole. She hung her coat on the hook. It stayed up high. It did not touch the ground. "My coat is safe," she said. Grandma smiled. "Bus is here," she said. "I dream of warm cocoa at home," said Brooklyn. She took her coat off the hook and climbed the bus steps.

Audrey had a cough. It came out in big bounces. "Time to call the pharmacy," said Dad. He picked up the phone. He called Mr. Blue at the corner store. "Your medicine is ready," said Mr. Blue.

At the pharmacy, Audrey saw a yellow sign. The floor was slippery from a wet mop. She held Dad's hand and walked slow. Mr. Blue had a small bag. He had a triangle of white paper taped on it. It said Audrey. Dad paid for the medicine.

At home, Dad gave Audrey a spoon of medicine. She swallowed it down. Later, Mom made warm soup. Audrey took two bites. Then she pushed the bowl away. "I can't eat more," she said. "That is okay," said Mom. "When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much." Audrey yawned. Her blanket was soft. Her cough was small now. "Good night, soup," she said.

Mia turned four today. The party was at the big park. Grandma brought a cake with four candles. Mia wanted to light them all by herself.

She grabbed the little matchbox. Dad took it gently. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," he said. "You get to make the wish." Mia pouted a bit. Then Dad lit the candles one by one. The sky was cloudy, so the flames looked extra bright.

Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out. Everyone clapped. "Happy birthday, Mia!" said her friend Sam. Grandma cut the cake with a safe knife and gave Sam the first big slice, because Sam had skipped his nap and looked sleepy.

Mia handed out plates to everyone. She even saved a seat for Grandpa. Then she licked frosting off her thumb and said, "Next year, can I watch Dad light them again?" Dad laughed. "Yes," he said. "Every year."

Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse smiled at him. "Do you know how to wash your hands?" she asked. "With soap?" said Dylan. "Yes! With soap, for twenty seconds. That is a slow count to twenty."

The nurse took Dylan to the little sink. She put soap on his hands. "Can you count to twenty?" she asked. "I can try," said Dylan. They rubbed and counted together. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. The bubbles went down the drain. Dylan's hands were clean and shiny. "Now the germs are off," said the nurse. "We wash our hands after the toilet too."

Then the nurse gave Dylan a snack. A cracker, and a little cup of apple juice. Dylan looked at his hands. He looked at the cracker. He jumped up. "Wait!" he said. He ran to the sink. He put on soap. He counted to twenty all by himself. "Twenty!" he shouted. His hands were clean.

Dylan ran back and took the cracker. "I washed first!" he said. The nurse clapped. Dylan munched his cracker and smiled. He looked out the window at the whole wide world. Then he took a big sip of juice.

It was a rainy day, so Asher went to the store with his mom. The store had a big wall of crayons. Asher wanted a blue crayon for his rain picture.

A girl named Mia stood there too. She held a dark blue crayon. "That is not blue," said a boy next to her. "It is too dark." Asher felt worried. Maybe there was only one true blue.

Mia put the crayons on the floor. "Let's line them up," she said. Asher helped. First came a light blue, like the sky. Then a middle blue. Then a dark blue, like the night. "They are all still called blue," said Mia. Asher smiled.

He picked two blues, a light one and a dark one. Mom paid for them at the desk. At home, Asher drew rainy clouds. "Light blue for morning," he said. "Dark blue for bedtime."

"Two blues," said Mom. "One box, both true."

Romy wanted her teddy bear. He sat high on the toy shelf. Romy was small. The shelf was big.

She pushed her toy truck to the shelf. The truck went fast. Then it went slow, slow, slow. It stopped. Romy was mad at the truck. "You did not help," she said.

Then she saw the stepping stool. Papa had put it by the shelf. It had a yellow sign on it that said Romy. She climbed up, up, up. She reached the teddy bear! Then she climbed down, down, down.

Papa came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," he said. He held the cup while Romy hugged the cold teddy bear tight.

"Papa, up and down are opposites," said Romy. "I went up to get him. I came down to hug him."

Papa smiled. "You teach me something new every day."

Then teddy's hat fell off. A tiny mouse toy was hiding under it! "A surprise!" said Romy. She put the mouse in teddy's lap and gave them both a kiss.

Naomi stood in the reading corner. She held her new library card with both hands. It had her name on it in red letters. Today she could pick one book to take home.

She found a big book about stars. Inside was a blank white page at the back. Naomi took out her crayon. She wanted to draw a big yellow circle on that page.

The librarian knelt down beside her. She said, "That book is shared with many other people. We take care not to tear it or write in it."

Naomi looked at the page. Then she looked at the little boy reading on the mat. He would read this book next week. And a girl would read it after him. The book belonged to them too.

Naomi put her crayon away. She asked the librarian for a piece of paper. She drew her big yellow circle on the paper instead. Then she put the paper inside her coat, safe and flat.

The librarian smiled. "Would you like to borrow the star book?" Naomi nodded. She held the book with clean hands and carried it to the desk. "My first book," she said. The librarian stamped it gently. "Two weeks," she said. Naomi hugged the book all the way home.

Layla stood in the kitchen. She wanted to know what Mom was making. She used her eyes to look. She saw a big pot on the stove. Mom stirred it. It was too heavy for Layla to lift.

Layla used her ears to listen. She heard the pot go pop, pop, pop. She used her nose to smell. Mmm, it smelled like soup.

"Smell with your nostrils," said Mom. "Your nose has two openings called nostrils."

Layla touched her nose. She felt two little holes. She wanted to count them. Mom held up a small mirror. Layla looked in. She saw one opening. She saw two. Two nostrils!

Then Mom gave her a taste. Layla used her tongue. It was warm soup.

"Yum!" said Layla. She jumped up and down. "Is this a gift?"

"Yes," said Mom. "A gift from our kitchen."

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house. "Grandma now?" she asked. Daddy shook his head. "Not now, Paisley. Grandma is later. First we drive, then we get there."

Paisley looked out the window. A cow stood in a wild, grassy field. "Cow now!" she said. The cow went behind a hill. "Cow gone now," she said. Daddy laughed. "That's right. Now means right this minute."

Paisley thought about that. Yesterday she had painted an egg at Grandma's house. It was yellow. Today she wanted to paint a blue egg. Tomorrow she would show it to her friend Sam.

"Snack now?" Paisley asked. Her tummy made a little growl. Daddy reached back and gave her a banana. "Now you can eat," he said. Paisley ate it all up.

Soon a red roof came into view. "Grandma's house now!" she said. Grandma waved from the door. Paisley ran to her. "We can paint now?" she asked. Grandma held up her hand. In it was a small white egg, all ready. "Yes, Paisley. Right now."

Audrey was in the playroom with her toy ducks. One duck, two ducks, three yellow ducks. Her friends Ben and Mia came in. "Let's play Duck Race," said Mia. Audrey knew this game. Everyone lines up the ducks. Then everyone counts to three. Then everyone pushes a duck to the wall. Mom sat by the door, folding slow, warm towels.

The first race started. "One, two three, go!" The ducks slid on the soft rug. Mia's duck won. "Hooray, Mia!" said Audrey. They played again. This time Ben's duck won. Then came the third race. Audrey's duck was winning. But Mia picked up her duck and moved it. "Now my duck is at the wall," said Mia. "I win."

Ben put his duck down. "That's not the game," he said. Audrey put her duck down too. She did not want to play like that. Nobody pushed any more ducks. The rug was quiet. Mia's face went hot and red. A box of crayons tipped over and the crayons began to spill out, but Mom came over slow and caught them.

"Feeling sad, Mia?" Mom asked. Mia nodded. Audrey held out her hand. "Want to try again? We all follow the same game," said Audrey. Mia wiped her eyes. "Okay. Same game." They lined up the ducks. One duck, two ducks, three yellow ducks. "One, two, three, go!" This time nobody moved a duck. Ben's duck won fair and square. Everybody clapped, even Audrey, even Mia.

Mom gave out apple slices. They were sweet and crunchy. Audrey took her slice and sat close to Mia. "Good game," said Mia. Audrey smiled and patted her yellow duck. "Same game tomorrow?" said Audrey. "Same game tomorrow," said Mia, and they bumped their apple slices together.

Charlie ran to soccer practice. Coach Nina had a big red ball. "One ball, one game," she said. "Everyone gets a turn to kick it."

Charlie wanted to kick first. He ran up fast. He grabbed at the ball with both hands. "Not yet," said Coach Nina. "Maya is first today."

Charlie sat down on the grass. Waiting felt so long. He puffed out his cheeks like a frog.

Then he saw some cones nearby. He lined them up. He put a pinecone on top of each one. "Look, a tower with a star shape on this one," he said. Maya laughed and kicked the ball far. Then Ben kicked it. Then it was almost his turn, and his tower was done.

"Charlie, your turn," said Coach Nina. Charlie jumped up. He ran to the ball. He sent it rolling all the way to Maya. She sent it back.

"Nice kick," said Maya. "Nice tower," said Charlie. "You are a friendly kick sender."

After practice, Charlie waved goodbye. "Same time next week," said Coach Nina. "And I get to build the tower," said Maya.

Iris sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a small scratchy sound, like a tiny animal at the door. She was hungry now. "Is dinner soon?" she asked. Mom said, "Yes. Soon means in a little while." Iris waited. She counted the spoons on the table. One spoon, two spoons, three spoons. Yesterday she had pasta. Today she would have soup. Tomorrow she would have pasta again.

"One, two, three," said Iris. Mom set down the bowls. "Now we eat," said Mom. The soup was warm and yummy. Iris ate it all up. She was not mad anymore. Her tummy was happy.

"After dinner we will have a treat," said Mom. "Later," said Iris. "Yes, later," said Mom. Iris licked her spoon and smiled. "One, two, three spoons of soup for me."

Milo had big news. His tooth was wiggly. He ran to the kitchen. Mom was on the phone. "Mom! Mom! My tooth!" he said. Mom held up one finger. She was still talking. Milo waited. He wiggled his toe instead.

The phone went quiet. Mom smiled at him. "Yes, Milo? What is it?" she asked. "My tooth wiggles!" said Milo. "May I show Dad?" "Of course," said Mom. "Thank you for waiting, Milo."

At dinner, Dad was telling about his shiny new mug. Milo opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He took a bite and waited. Dad stopped talking. There was a quiet moment. "Now, Milo," said Dad. "My tooth wiggles!" said Milo. Dad looked at it. "Wow," he said. Milo grinned. Later, Mom tucked him into bed. The dog came to lick his hand. "Sorry, dog," said Milo. "You cannot sleep here." He closed his eyes. "Good night, tooth."

James sat at the little table. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. He would paint her favorite flower. But the flower in the book was pink. James had red, blue, yellow and green paint. He had white paint too. But there was no pink.

James looked and looked. He painted a green stem. He painted a green leaf. He stirred his brush in the water and waited. The teacher, Miss Ada, smiled at him. "Take your time," she said. James tapped the table. He tapped his chin. Then he dipped his brush in the red paint. He put a big red dot on his tray.

Next he dipped his brush in the white paint. He stirred it into the red dot. Round and round went the brush. Slowly, the red dot turned pink! James gasped. "It turned pink!" he said. He painted the pink flower on the card. It looked just like the one in the book.

Then James had a small surprise. A drop of pink paint fell off his brush. It landed on the blue paint. Miss Ada laughed. "Now you have a purple spot," she said. James laughed too. He painted the purple spot next to his flower. Grandma would love it.

Lily stood on a little stool in the restaurant kitchen. The cook, Ben, gave her warm toast. "Can I be your helper?" Lily asked. "Yes," said Ben. "Let's make breakfast for Dad."

Lily took the butter knife. She spread the butter, slow and smooth. The butter got soft and shiny on the toast. "Good job," said Ben. "Now the milk."

Lily picked up the big jug. She poured fast. Milk splashed out onto the table! "Oh no," said Lily. Ben wiped the table with a cloth. "Try again," he said. "Pour slowly this time."

Lily tipped the cup high, but she poured slowly, slowly. The milk went up, up, up. It stayed in the cup. No splash. No spill.

"Look, Dad!" said Lily. She set the cup on the tray next to the toast. Dad smiled big. "Milk and toast, my favorite." Lily looked at the clean table. "More milk, Ben? I can pour."

Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish. She saw birds. Then she saw a small gray kitten. "I want that one," said Ella. Dad said, "Okay. We will need food and a warm blanket too." Dad carried the big bag of food. It was heavy and strong. Ella carried the little blanket.

At home, Ella opened the cage. The kitten ran fast. It went under Ella's bed. It did not come out. Ella looked and looked. "Where did it go?" she said. The phone did ring, but Ella stayed very still. She sat on the floor by the bed. She waited. She waited more.

Then one little paw came out. Then the whole kitten came out. Ella sat very still. The kitten walked to her. It sniffed her hand. It rubbed her arm. "Hello," said Ella softly. The kitten sat in her lap.

Ayla stood in the band room. Her drum sat on the floor. Ben had a drum too.

"Can we play together?" Ayla asked.

"Yes," said Ben. "Let's try."

They played. Ayla went fast. Ben went fast too. Then faster. Then fastest. The sound got all mixed up. They stopped.

"Why did it sound funny?" Ayla asked.

"Maybe we went too fast," said Ben.

Miss Kay came over. She tapped her drum one, two, three, four. Slow and steady. "Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together," she said.

Ayla listened. Then she tapped one, two, three, four. Ben tapped too. Same speed.

"Now let's play," said Ayla.

They played. Slow and steady. Together.

"Shop for drums with me next time," said Ben. Ayla smiled and zipped her jacket straight up. Then she tapped the beat one more time, just for fun.

Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was empty. She wanted more rice.

"Please may I have more rice?" she asked. Daddy smiled. He gave her a big spoonful. "Thank you," said Sienna.

Then she reached for the milk. Oops. The cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. "Sorry," said Sienna. Daddy wiped it up. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Sienna ran to get a towel. She wiped and wiped. One, two, three swipes. The table was dry again.

Then a knock came at the door. It was Mateo, her new friend from the playground. He sat down at the table too. Mama gave him some rice. "Gracias," said Mateo.

Sienna blinked. What did that mean? "Gracias means thank you," said Mateo. "We say it in Spanish."

Sienna tried the new word. "Grah-see-as," she said slowly. Mateo laughed and clapped. She tried again. "Gracias!" This time it slid out just right.

Mama put a cookie on Sienna's plate. Sienna looked at Mateo. "Gracias, Mama," she said.

Mateo held out his hand for a high five. "Gracias to you too," he said.

Camille sat down at the dinner table. Grandma put a big bowl of peas in front of her. "These are for you," Grandma said. Camille grabbed the spoon and started eating right away.

"Can I have some peas too?" asked her brother Leo. Camille looked at the bowl. She pushed it across the table to him. Leo put some peas on his plate. Then he pushed the bowl back. "Your turn," he said. Camille took some more. Back and forth the bowl went. Camille giggled. Sharing made the bowl go around like a ride.

Dad used a knife to cut the bread. "One piece for you, one for Leo," he said. Two pieces, both the same size. Camille looked at them. The same! That felt good.

After dinner, Grandma held out a small box. Inside was a shiny red hair clip. Camille put it in her hair. She ran to the mirror. Then she thought of Grandma standing there. She ran back and gave Grandma a hug. "Thank you," she said. Grandma smiled big. "Thank you back," said Grandma. "And now I thank you for this hug."

Jaxson followed Mom into the kitchen. They had shopped for apples, and his tummy was hungry. Mom put a pot on the stove. "The stove is hot," Mom said. She turned the knob. Jaxson stayed back and watched. The pot went sizzle, sizzle. Mom stirred the apples with a big spoon.

Then Jaxson saw something on the wall. It was a little box with holes. He wanted to poke it with his spoon. "Mom, what is this?" he asked. Mom came right over. "That is an outlet," she said. "We never put fingers or spoons in outlets." Mom gave him a job instead. "Put the napkins on the table," she said.

Jaxson carried the napkins one by one. He set them down just right. Then he sat on his chair and waited. Soon Mom brought warm apple sauce. Jaxson took a big bite. "Yum," he said, and licked his spoon.

Bennett stood by his window. "Can we go to Mia's house now?" he asked. Mama shook her head. "Not now, sweet boy. We go tomorrow." Bennett frowned. He wanted the round swing in Mia's yard. He would miss it if he stayed home.

"Is tomorrow now?" Bennett asked. "No," said Mama. "Tomorrow is the day after today. First we sleep. Then it is tomorrow." Bennett looked at the sky. "Sleep first?" he asked. "Sleep first," said Mama.

Bennett put on his pajamas. He hugged his bear. He got into his little bed. "Now I sleep," he said. "Then tomorrow comes." Mama kissed his head. "Yes. Sleep now. Fun later." Bennett closed his eyes.

The sun came up. Bennett opened his eyes. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked. Mama smiled. "It is tomorrow! It is the day after today." Bennett jumped up. "Now we go to Mia's house now!" He found his shoes. He held the door handle. "Mia! I am coming!" he called. Mama laughed. "Let's go, Bennett. Let's go."

Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was so thirsty. "Milk, please!" she said. Dad gave her a cup, and she drank it all up.

Then Mom brought in the laundry basket. "Can you help sort?" Mom asked. Rosalie jumped up. She held up a sock. "A sock!" she laughed. She put it with the teddy bear and the toy truck.

Mom shook her head, smiling. "No, no. Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes." Rosalie gasped. She looked at the shirt in her hand. She looked at the hat. She put them all in one pile, quick quick quick. Then she put the teddy bear with the toys.

"Look, Mom! Clothes here! Toys there!" The pile was big. Dad clapped loud. "What a good helper. That calls for a gift." He slid a warm cookie onto her plate. It smelled sweet. Rosalie took a big bite. "Yum!" she said.

Jaxon went to Milo's house. Milo had a big drum on the floor. It was red like a rainbow stripe. "Want to sing?" Milo asked. "Yes!" said Jaxon.

They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Milo clapped his hands to the beat. Jaxon clapped too. One, two, one, two. But his hands got tired. They hurt a little. Jaxon stopped and looked at his hands. Now what?

Then he had an idea. He stamped his feet instead. One, two, one, two. His feet made the beat! "Look, Milo!" he said. "My feet can do it!" Milo tapped the drum, and it made the beat too. Boom, boom, boom. Jaxon tapped his knees. Tap, tap, tap. That made the beat as well.

They sang the whole song from the start to the end. Jaxon did not forget one word. He stamped, tapped his knees, and Milo hit the drum. Boom, tap, stomp. "Again!" said Jaxon.

Benjamin ran out to the backyard. Today was his first soccer game. He was on the blue team. He wanted to kick the ball right away.

The coach called everyone to the grass. "Time to warm up," she said. Benjamin did not want to wait. He reached for the ball. His legs felt stiff like a sleepy caterpillar.

So Benjamin joined the line. The team ran in a big circle. They touched their toes and stretched up high. A butterfly flew by, and Benjamin laughed.

Then the game began. Benjamin ran fast. He kicked the ball far. His legs felt loose and strong. After the game, the coach gave him a juicy orange slice. "Good running today," she said. Benjamin smiled and took a big bite.

Wyatt sat at the art table. He wanted to make a paper sailboat. His boat needed a triangle sail. But Wyatt only had a square.

"Oh no," said Wyatt. He felt upset. "I need two triangles."

Miss Ana came over. "I can help," she said. She took the square. She took the scissors. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open. Two triangles! Wyatt clapped his hands.

"My turn to try," said Wyatt. Miss Ana gave him a new square. She held the scissors with him. Snip, snip. Two more triangles!

Wyatt picked a big triangle for the sail. He glued it on the boat. Then he glued a circle for the sun. He glued a square window and a rectangle door.

A cat walked past the window. Wyatt planted his boat on the shelf.

"Look, Miss Ana!" said Wyatt. "My boat has a triangle sail!"

Hazel wants to play firefighter with Ben. But she does not feel like a firefighter yet. Ben has the big red hat. He gets to squirt the hose. Hazel just holds the bucket.

"Can I have a hat too?" she asks. Miss Jo looks in the dress-up box. She finds a little red hat. She sets it on Hazel's head.

Hazel looks in the mirror. "Now I am a firefighter!" she yells, loud at first, then soft. Ben walks slow like a firefighter. Hazel walks slow too. They march around the middle of the rug.

Then Baby Bear needs help. Baby Bear is stuck on the toy chair. "A firefighter can save him!" says Hazel. She climbs the two small steps. She holds Baby Bear close. She pats his head. "You are safe now," she says.

At home time, Hazel gives back the little red hat. "More firefighters tomorrow," says Ben. Hazel smiles and waves. "Me and my hat," she says. "See you tomorrow, Baby Bear."

Grandpa came on the big bus. He was staying for a whole week. Ali jumped up and down. "You can sleep in my room!" said Ali. "I will show you everything."

Grandpa had a bath. Then he called out, "Oh no! I cannot find a towel!" Ali ran to the door. "I know where the towels are!" he said. Ali opened the cupboard. "Here, Grandpa! The towels live in here." Grandpa took a big blue one. "You are a good host," said Grandpa. "A host shows a guest where things are." Ali stood very tall.

So Ali showed Grandpa more things. "Here is the bathroom. Here is your cup. Here is my tidy toy box." Grandpa smiled and smiled. The next morning, Grandpa could not find his socks. Ali looked in the cupboard. He found a sock. Then he found something else. "Grandpa! Your hat is in with the towels!" Grandpa laughed. "The bus was bumpy. My hat jumped out!" Grandpa put the hat on Ali's head. It fell down over his eyes. "I can't see!" said Ali. Grandpa laughed. "Then let me hold your hand."

Clara rides in the car to the ball field. The grass smells green and fresh. Her team wears red shirts. Clara loves her red shirt.

The coach blows a whistle. It sounds loud and high. "Time to play ball," the coach says. Clara runs to the dirt. She does not know where to stand. She stops and looks around.

The coach pats a spot near first base. "Stand right here, Clara," the coach says. "Watch the bat. When the ball comes, you will get it." Clara stands on the spot. Her shoes feel dusty and warm. She waits. It is quiet for a moment. Then a bat goes crack. The ball rolls toward her. Clara bends down and picks it up. She holds it high.

"Good job, Clara!" the coach calls. Clara smiles big. The coach shows Sam where to stand next. Clara claps for Sam. The team plays until the sun goes soft and orange.

"Same time next week," the coach says. Clara waves her glove in the air.

Luka went to the library with his dad. He was excited to find a book about trucks. He ran to the shelf. But the truck book was gone. A girl had it in her hands. Luka felt angry. He stomped his foot and made a loud sound. The girl looked scared and held the book tight.

Dad knelt down next to Luka. "Try slow, deep breaths with me," he said. Luka took one big breath in. Then he let it out slowly. He did it again and again. His body began to calm down. His fists were not tight anymore. The girl watched him breathe.

She brought the book over. "We can share it," she said. Luka smiled. He was happy now. They sat together at a low table. Luka read about a big red fire truck. The girl pointed at a dog in the picture. They laughed at the sweet little dog drinking water. "Friends can wake up a sleepy story time," the librarian said with a smile. Luka turned the page.

It was a summer morning at the community centre. Sienna ran to the craft table. "Crackers!" she said. There were two bowls of crackers.

Teacher Maya knelt down. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Sienna looked and looked. She could not tell. "I don't know," she said. Her lip began to cry-ready wobble.

"Count them," said Maya.

Sienna pointed at the small bowl. "One, two, three, four." She looked up. "Four!"

Then she counted the big bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She bounced. "Six!"

"Six crackers," she said. "Six is more than four!" She held up the big bowl like a trophy.

Outside the window the sky turned stormy, but Sienna did not care. She held out the big bowl to her friend Leo.

"Six crackers," she said. "You take one, and we can count again."

Parker stood by the green pool wall. The water went splash, splash. His feet did not want to go in. "Too big," said Parker. Up on the tall chair sat a lady in a red suit. "Who is that?" Parker asked. "That is the lifeguard," said Dad. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it." Parker looked up. She could see every kid from up there. She waved at him. Parker sat down at the edge. He put one toe in. The water was warm. He kicked his legs. The water made little waves. His toy boat began to float away. Parker chased it with his toes. The lifeguard saw him lean too far. She climbed down fast. "Hold my hand," she said. Parker held it and stepped in. "Yay!" said Parker. "I am swimming with help." Dad clapped. The boat bumped against Parker's tummy. The lifeguard smiled and went back up high to watch.

Emily wanted to wear her scarf today. It was cold outside. Her scarf was red and soft. Daddy got his scarf too. His scarf was blue and long.

"Look," said Emily. She held up her scarf. It was small. It went up to her knees. Daddy put his scarf on. It went down past his coat.

"Mine is short," said Emily. "Yours is long."

"Yes," said Daddy. "Long and short are opposites."

Emily spun around fast, then stopped slow. The long scarf flapped like a tail. Could a scarf swim in the wind? She waved it and it swished. The pot on the stove made steam. Mommy stirred it. "Hot," said Mommy. "Stay back."

Emily touched the cold window. "Brrr!" Then she found Daddy's old mitten on the shelf. It was tiny. It had been his when he was small!

"Is that true?" Emily asked. Daddy laughed. "Really true," he said.

Milo went to the farmers' market with Dad. He saw big red tomatoes and long orange carrots. "I want to grow my own," said Milo. Dad bought three little seeds and a small pot.

At home, Dad helped Milo put soil in the pot. Milo pushed the seeds down into the dark dirt. He gave them a drink of water. Then he had to wait. Every day Milo stood by the pot. Every day the pot looked the same. "Where are my plants?" he asked. "Soon," said Dad. "Keep the pot near the window, and keep waiting."

Many days went by. Then one morning, Milo looked at the pot. Something small and green was poking up out of the soil. Milo ran to Dad. "A little green thing came up!" he said. Dad smiled. "That is called a sprout," said Dad. "A sprout!" said Milo. He touched the pot softly, very gently, like petting a bird in its nest. Then he got more water for his sprout.

Hunter ran to the school playground. He put his hand in his pocket. His little blue dinosaur was not there.

"Oh no," said Hunter. "Where is my dinosaur?" He wanted to run far away and look all alone. Then he saw his teacher, Miss Amy. She was standing by the gate.

"Miss Amy, my dinosaur is lost," said Hunter. "Can you help me look?" Miss Amy smiled a kind smile. "Yes, Hunter. We will search together. That is the safe thing to do." So they did not look apart. They looked side by side.

They peeked under the slide. No dinosaur. They peeked in the sandbox. No dinosaur. Then Miss Amy looked by the swings. "Hunter, come here!" There was the blue dinosaur, sitting on the big red ball. Hunter hugged him close. "You found him because we looked together," said Hunter. "May I pretend he is flying now?" Miss Amy laughed. "Yes, you may." Hunter held his dinosaur up to the sky.

Daniel sat in his car seat. He held his doll tight. "Are we there now?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later." Mama pulled the car past one tree. Then two trees. Then three trees.

"Is it later yet?" asked Daniel. "Is it later now?"

"Later means some time after now," said Mama. "Not right away."

Daniel looked out the window. Now he saw a red truck. Now he saw a cow. Now the cow was gone, like it was lost behind the hill.

"Is it later yet?" he asked again. They passed four trees. Then five.

"Yes," said Mama. "Now it is later. We are here today, just like we said."

Daniel hugged his doll. He clapped his hands. "Later came after now!"

Felix was in the kitchen. His tummy was rumbling. Lunch was coming soon.

First, Felix ran outside to the yard. He patted the big brown dog. The dog licked his hand. "Stinky dog," Felix said with a giggle.

Then Felix came back in. He sat down at the table. Mama put bread and cheese on a plate. Felix reached for the bread.

"Wait," said Mama. "Where did your hands just be?"

Felix looked at his hands. He thought for a moment. "On the dog," he said. "I patted the dog!"

"What do we do after we pet an animal?" asked Mama.

Felix wondered. Then he jumped down. "Wash hands!" he said. "Wash, wash, wash!"

He ran to the sink. Mama turned on the water. Felix pushed the soap pump. Bubbles grew on his hands. "Bubbles!" he said.

Mama helped him rub. They rubbed and rubbed. "Sing the song," said Mama. Felix sang his counting song. When the song was done, the hands were done.

Mama held a towel. Felix dried his hands, one at a time. His hands smelled like soap now. Not like dog at all.

Felix climbed back to his seat. He picked up the bread. "Yum," he said, and took a big bite.

After lunch, Mama said, "Potty time." Felix ran to the bathroom. He stopped and looked back.

"Wash, wash, wash," he said to himself. And he did.

Chloe was in the kitchen. Her coat was on the chair. She wanted to put it on all by herself. Her mom was making soup, so Chloe had time to try.

She pushed her arms in. The coat felt big and warm. Then she pulled the zipper up. It went up, up, then it stopped. The zipper was stuck! It had caught her sweater. "Oh no," said Chloe.

Her mom came close and watched. Chloe did not pull hard. She pulled the zipper back down, just a little. The sweater came free. The zipper slid up again, all the way to her chin. Chloe smiled. "I did it!" she said. She hid her hands in her sleeves, then popped them out. "I'm a wild kitty," she said, and she patted the wooden table with her mittens.

Alexis lived in the city, but today he was at Grandpa's house. It was a rainy day. His socks were warm and dry inside.

"Can I have some grapes?" Alexis asked.

"You can have three," said Grandpa.

Alexis looked at the bowl. He picked one big grape. He picked two small ones. He looked at his hand.

"Grandpa, do big grapes count as more?"

"No," said Grandpa. "One grape is one. Three grapes are three."

Alexis put one big grape on the plate. Then he put one more. Then one more. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three."

"Three!" said Grandpa.

Then Grandpa said, "Let's clap for the cookies. They need ten minutes in the oven." Grandpa set the timer. Alexis clapped while they waited.

The timer rang. Grandpa took out the cookies. Alexis counted them on the plate.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

He gave one warm cookie to Grandpa first.

Abigail lost her bunny. The bunny was her favorite toy. She looked under her bed. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

Abigail looked behind the big chair. She found a dust ball and one sock. Still no bunny. Her tummy felt sad. She sat down on the rug.

Then she thought hard. "When did I hold bunny last?" she said. "I had bunny at snack time. I ate my apple." She ran to the snack table. There was her chair. There was her cup. And there, under the chair, was bunny! Bunny had slid down when she ate.

Abigail hugged bunny tight. "I found you," she said. "You were near the last snack spot."

Mama came in. "There you are," said Mama. "You look happy." Abigail held up bunny. "Bunny was hiding by my chair," she said. Mama smiled. "Good thinking. Now let's clean up the crumbs."

Abigail helped wipe the table. Then she put bunny on her lap. She gave bunny a kiss on the soft ear. "Next time I will look here first," she whispered. Bunny's ear flopped over, real and warm, as they both slid off the chair to play.

Ellie went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish, birds, and one small gray kitten. "Can we take her home?" Ellie asked. "Yes," said Dad. "She will be ours to care for."

At home, the kitten drank from her little bowl. Then she went to sleep. Ellie played with her toys on the playground mat. Later, the kitten came back to the bowl. She sniffed it. She turned away.

"Why won't she drink?" Ellie asked. Dad looked in the bowl. "The water is all gone," he said. "Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day." Dad held the bowl. Ellie helped him fill it with clean water from the tap. The kitten ran over. She drank and drank.

The next morning, Ellie looked at the bowl first thing. It was empty again. She carried it to Dad. "She needs new water," said Ellie. Dad filled it up. The kitten purred and rubbed Ellie's leg. "I'm sorry it was empty," Ellie whispered. The kitten drank, then chased her tail.

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. There were only three pots. "One, two, three," he counted. A red pot. A yellow pot. A blue pot.

Dad sat on the grass with him. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," said Dad. Leon tapped each pot. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. "Red, yellow, blue." But where were the other rainbow colours? Leon felt sorry for his rainbow. A rainbow needs more colours.

He dipped his brush in the red pot. He dipped it in the yellow pot too. He swirled the brush on the paper. The paint turned orange! Leon gasped. Red and yellow made orange. Next he mixed blue and yellow. The paint turned green, green like the grass. He mixed red and blue. The paint turned purple, purple like a plum.

Leon painted a big rainbow. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. He held it up to the sky. "Look, Dad! My rainbow!" The paper did not sink. It waved in the soft wind, bright as the ocean in a story. Dad clapped his hands. "Paint it again," he said. So Leon dipped his brush in the red pot once more.

Connor was three years old. He was going on a big trip. His family drove a long, long way. Then they walked into a hotel room. "We are here!" Connor yelled.

Connor opened his little brown bag. He pulled out his swimsuit. "Beach time!" he said. But when he looked out the window, he saw white snow. Lots and lots of snow. Big flakes fell on the glass.

Daddy laughed softly. "We packed warm coats, not swimsuits," he said. "Snowy places need mittens and boots." He helped Connor find his red mittens. Mommy helped too. She zipped up his puffy coat.

Then Connor saw something. He put on his mittens, and his hands got warm. His coat went on, and his whole body got warm. Warm clothes for snow. Swimsuits were for sunny beach days.

Connor ran to the window. He pressed one mitten hand on the cold glass. "Bye bye, snowflake," he whispered. The little white dot melted away under his warm, red mitten.

Aiden sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The room smelled like popcorn. Uncle Ben handed Aiden a warm bowl, but Grandpa held it first, so it would not be too hot.

On the TV, men ran fast on green grass. Aiden saw a big white net. "The ball must go over the net," Aiden said. He pointed with one small finger at the screen.

A player kicked the ball. It went low. It went under the bar and into the net. The crowd on TV jumped up. Everyone in the room jumped too. "Goal!" they shouted. Aunt Maya clapped so loud. "Goal! The ball went in the net!"

Aiden clapped too. "In the net! Goal!" He counted on his fingers. "One goal. Two goals. Three goals." Each time a ball went in, everyone cheered.

Later Grandpa set out paper and red paint. "Can you paint a goal?" he asked. Aiden painted a green field. He painted a net with a ball inside it. He dipped his finger in the paint and made a dot right in the net. Uncle Ben looked at the painting and laughed. "That one is a goal too," he said.

Hayden went to the pharmacy with his mom. His tummy felt funny, so they picked up some medicine. The pharmacist said, "Wash your hands well, okay?" Hayden nodded. He wanted to be a good hand washer.

At the bathroom sink, Hayden reached for the tap. Mom stopped him fast. "Wait. Let me check the water first." She put her hand under it. "It is too hot. We need warm, not hot." She turned the tap a little. "Now it is warm." Hayden put his hands in. It felt nice, like soft rain on his fingers.

Mom said, "Now soap. We count to twenty." Hayden rubbed the soap. One, two, three. Bubbles grew on his hands. Four, five, six. He made a bubble shadow on the wall. Seven, eight, nine. Mom held the next towel ready for him. They counted all the way. Ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty. "Rinse!" said Mom. Hayden rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean and shiny. "All done," he said, and held them out for the towel.

Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Beth played a song on her small drum. Boom, boom, boom. All the children clapped along. Eva clapped too. Boom, boom, boom.

Then Miss Beth sang a rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva opened her mouth. But the second line was gone. It would not come out. "Where did the words go?" Eva asked. Miss Beth smiled. "Let's sing it again and see."

So they sang it again. And again. And again. Each time, Eva sang more words. Soon she knew the whole rhyme. She had sung it so many times that the words stayed in her head, all by themselves.

Miss Beth counted the claps. "Let's clap a big number," she said. "Ten!" They clapped ten times. Eva sang and clapped at the very same time. It was a huge smile on her face.

"Now I know it by heart," Eva said. She sang the rhyme one more time, all alone, and everyone clapped.

Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. But he looked in the paint box. No orange! "Oh no," said Weston. "My pumpkin needs orange. Orange is my favorite color."

Grandma set out little cups. Red paint sat in one cup. Yellow paint sat in another cup. Blue paint and green paint sat there too. "Try stirring," said Grandma. Weston dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in yellow too. He stirred and stirred. The paints mixed in the cup. "Grandma! Look! It turned orange!" His brush was orange. His pumpkin was orange. It looked so real and round.

Then Weston tried green and blue. That made a dark color, like the night sky. He giggled. "Paint is like a puzzle," said Grandma. Weston touched the wet pumpkin. It felt cool and slippery. Just then, the paint cup tipped over. Red paint ran across the table like a little river. Grandma laughed and grabbed a towel. "Now the table is red!" she said. Weston held up his orange brush. "I can fix it!"

Jackson went to the park with Gran. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his hat. A leaf fell from the big tree. The wind blew it round and round. "It is windy," said Gran. Jackson chased the leaf. He laughed when it jumped away.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Jackson felt drops on his nose. "Oh no, my hat is wet," he said. Gran opened her big umbrella. She held it over Jackson's head. The rain could not get him anymore. His hair stayed dry. "Come close," said Gran. They shared the umbrella. It kept the rain off both of them.

They walked home under it together. Jackson pointed at a picture on a wall. It showed kids in snow boots and mittens. "When it is snowy, you wear warm clothes," said Gran. Jackson hoped it would snow soon. He would wear his red mittens. For now, he stayed cozy under the umbrella. "Hold my hand," said Gran. Jackson squeezed it tight.

Wren sat at the big table. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her name all alone.

Mama sat next to her. "Hold the pencil like this," said Mama. She showed Wren how to pinch it near the tip. Wren tried. Her fingers felt funny at first.

Wren pressed down hard. She made a big W. Then she made an R. But the R was dark and thick. SNAP! The pencil tip broke off. The point was gone.

"Uh oh," said Wren. "Why did it break?"

"You pressed too hard," said Mama. "Try pressing soft and gentle."

Mama turned the pencil in the sharpener. The tip came back, new and pointy. Wren held it again. This time she pressed light, like a feather on the paper. She wrote W, then R, then E, then N. No snap. The letters sat on the line in a row.

Wren smiled at Mama's face. "Look! I did it all alone!"

"Yes you did," said Mama. She gave Wren a hug. Wren wrote her name one more time, soft and slow, all by herself.

Jasmine stood in the big school cafeteria. She held her tray with both hands. On the tray was a tasty apple and a cup of milk.

Jasmine saw a boy with a red shirt. He looked shy, just like her. He whispered, "Who is that lady?"

"That is my teacher," Jasmine said. "Teachers help the children in a class."

The boy smiled a little smile. Then he walked to the teacher and said, "Hello." The teacher said, "Hello! I am Miss Kim." She took his tray and set it on the table so his hands were free.

Jasmine wanted to say hello too. But her milk tipped over. Plop! The milk made a big white puddle on the table.

"Uh oh," said Jasmine. "What will we do?"

Miss Kim came with a cloth from the kitchen. She wiped the table. Wipe, wipe, wipe. The puddle went away and the table was dry. "Now you can skip to your seat," said Miss Kim.

Jasmine skipped all the way to the table. She sat next to the boy with the red shirt. "Hello, I am Jasmine," she said.

"Hello, I am Sam," he said. "Your apple looks tasty."

Arthur ran up to Ben's door. He could not wait to play.

"I have a big dragon," said Ben. "He is green and scary!"

"No," said Arthur. "My dragon is friendly. He helps people."

Ben frowned. Arthur frowned too. Now what?

"Wait," said Ben. "Can our dragon be both? Scary to bad guys, and friendly to us?"

"Yes!" said Arthur. "Let's say he is friendly, but very big."

They shook hands. The dragon was friendly and very big. Arthur clapped.

Then Arthur saw a blue blanket on a chair. He put it in a basket. He made a soft round nest. The dragon could sleep there!

"Now the dragon is a baby," said Arthur.

"Then we must feed him," said Ben.

Ben got a cup of water from the sink. His mom watched and helped him pour. Arthur held a spoon very carefully.

The baby dragon yawned. He went to sleep in the nest.

Arthur whispered, "Shh. The baby is sleeping."

Ben whispered too, "Can a baby dragon fly?"

"Not yet," Arthur whispered back. "First he has to grow big."

They sat by the nest. They waited for their friendly dragon to grow.

"Here, dragon," said Arthur softly. "Wake up soon."

Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His plate was full of rice. He took a big bite and chewed slowly.

"Dada," he said, "can I sleep in my party shirt tonight? It has gold stars on it."

Mama smiled. "Party shirts are for parties," she said. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in."

"But I love the gold stars," said Muhammad.

After dinner, Mama filled the tub with warm water. Muhammad had a bath. He splashed a little and washed his toes. Then Dada helped him dry off with the big soft towel.

Muhammad ran to his room. His party shirt hung on the chair by his desk. He touched the gold stars one more time. Then he looked at his drawer. It was open. Inside were his soft blue pajamas with little moons.

He put on the pajamas. They felt warm and cozy. He climbed into bed and pulled the blanket up.

"Mama," he said, "the stars can wait for a party. My moons are here now."

"Good night, Muhammad," Mama said. She turned off the light.

Maya turned four today. Her party was at the park. There was a big table with cake. Her grandma stood near the cake. There were balloons and a song.

Maya sat by the presents. Her friend Ben gave her a red truck. Maya opened it fast. Then she saw a shiny box. She jumped up and ran to it. Grandma put a hand on her arm. "Did you say something to Ben?" she asked. Maya looked back at Ben. He was looking at the ground. Maya ran back to him. "Thank you for the truck," she said. Ben smiled big. "You can push it with me," he said. They pushed the truck down the hill together. It did not spill anyone's juice. Maya asked, "Is the juice okay?" Ben said, "Yes, it is fine."

Later Maya felt too excited to sit. She spun around and got dizzy. "I feel sick," she said. Grandma held her hand. "Sit with me and breathe," Grandma said. Maya sat. Soon she felt better.

The cake had four candles. Dad lit them with a match. Maya watched from her chair. She made a wish. Then she blew out the candles. Everyone clapped. Ben handed her a piece of cake. Maya looked up at him. "Thank you," she said. Ben giggled and gave her a high five.

Hazel went to the grocery store with Dad. She carried her little bunny in the cart. The cart went slow down each aisle. Hazel looked at the apples. Then she looked down at the cart. Bunny was gone.

"Bunny is lost," said Hazel. She looked under the bread. No bunny. She looked behind the milk. No bunny. Dad looked too. The store had so many shelves and so many boxes.

Then Hazel saw a big pile of paper bags. Things can end up inside other things, she thought. She peeked into a bag by the carrots. Something soft was in there. It was bunny! Bunny had been tucked in the bag all along. "I found you," said Hazel. She gave bunny a big hug.

Dad put the apples in a bag too. The bag made a crunchy sound. Hazel laughed and held bunny tight. "One more aisle," said Dad. "Let's go slow," said Hazel. Bunny rode home on her lap.

Athena ran out to the backyard. Dad sat on the step with his tea. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Athena chased a yellow leaf past the swing. Then she saw something neat at the far fence. A train went by there! She wanted to count the cars.

She ran toward the fence. The grass was cold and wet on her toes. She looked back. She could not see Dad. The big hedge was in the way. Athena stopped. Her tummy felt small and tight.

Then she heard Dad's voice. "Athena? I cannot see you!" She ran back fast. The grass whooshed under her feet. There was Dad, waving from the step. She could see him again. He could see her too.

"You went too far," said Dad. "Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out." Athena held his hand. It felt warm. Her toes felt cold. "Warm hand, cold toes," she said. Dad laughed.

They sat together on the step. The train went by again. Choo, choo! Athena counted the cars. "One, two, three, four!" Dad kissed the top of her head. The tea was hot, so Dad held it. Athena snuggled close. "Stay where you can see me," she said. "Yes," said Dad. "Right here."

Ellie sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said Mommy. "Then we get ice cream."

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick pinch! It was done. Then the nurse did a new thing. She put a small bandage over the spot on Ellie's arm. "You can pick one," said the nurse. Ellie saw a red bandage, a blue bandage, and a bandage with stars. "Stars!" said Ellie. The stars were yellow and shiny. "Mommy, look, one, two, three stars!"

At the ice cream shop, Ellie held up her arm. "My bandage has stars," she said. The girl at the next table looked. "Wow, you are so smart," said Mommy. Ellie licked her pink ice cream. Outside, the rain began to tap on the window. Ellie ate slow, one lick at a time, and the stars stayed dry on her arm.

Ayla sat in Grandma's cozy reading nook. The window was cloudy outside. Grandma held up a card with a big S on it.

"This is S," said Grandma. "It says sss, like a snake."

Ayla pressed the card to her ear. "It is quiet," she said. Grandma laughed.

"Can you find things that say sss?" asked Grandma. "Let's play a hunt around the room."

Ayla looked. She looked high. She looked low. The sun peeked out from the clouds and made a warm spot on the rug.

"Sun!" said Ayla. "Sss-un. Sun starts with sss!"

Grandma clapped. Ayla pulled off one shoe. "Sock!" she said. She held it up. "Sss-ock. Sock starts with sss too!"

The sand bucket sat by the door. Ayla touched the sand with one finger. It was soft and bumpy. "Sand," she whispered. "Sss-and."

Grandma nodded. "Sun, sock and sand," she said.

Ayla counted on her fingers. "Three things. All S!"

Then she picked up the card again. She looked all around the room. What else could say sss?

"Grandma, what about the snake in your book?"

Nathan woke up early. Today was the festival day. He stood by his drawer and looked and looked. "I cannot pick," he told Mama. Mama smiled and waited. Nathan pulled out his red shirt. Then he pulled out his blue shirt. He held them both. He waited some more. Then he found it. His yellow shirt with the sun on it. "This one," said Nathan. "It is my special shirt."

At the festival, the street was full. Drums went boom, boom, boom. Nathan smelled sweet popcorn and warm bread. He held Papa's hand. They walked up a little hill to see the whole street. It had rained in the morning. The road was still wet, and the lights danced on it.

Nathan looked around. Grandma wore her long green dress. Papa wore his big white cap. His cousin Maya wore shiny gold bangles. "Everyone has special clothes on," said Nathan. "Just like me." Maya laughed and spun around. Her skirt went round and round. "You look like the sun," she told Nathan. Nathan puffed out his chest. "I am festival sun," he said. And he danced all the way down the hill.

Lea stood at the gate of the school playground. She held her teacher's hand. "I am hungry," said Lea. Her tummy made a little growl.

The teacher smiled. "We will have snack time soon," she said. "First we play." Lea let go of the gate. She ran to the slide. The slide was high, but Lea slid down fast. She laughed. She played with a soft toy animal in the sandbox. She made a big hill of sand.

Then a bell rang. "Snack time," said the teacher. Lea ran to the table and sat down. She grabbed her little cup and took a big drink. She munched on her crackers. "Snack time comes after play," said Lea. The teacher nodded. Lea ate all her snack and smiled.

Luna ran up to the bookmobile. The shelves were full of books. She picked one about a little red fox. "This one," she said. The librarian smiled. "Would you like your very own library card?" Luna nodded and nodded. She got a small card with her name on it. It felt like a gift.

The librarian stamped the book. "This is the due date," she said. "The book has to come back by that day." Luna held the fox book tight. She did not want to give it back, not ever. At home, she read it many times. But when the day came, Mom said, "Time to move the fox book into our bag." Luna frowned. "Will the shelf be empty without it?" she asked. "No," said Mom. "Another kid will read it next."

Luna carried the book to the bookmobile. She put it right on the shelf. Then she found a new book about a big yellow moon. The librarian stamped it. Luna hugged it and waved goodbye to the little red fox.

Jasmine stood far from the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It missed. She threw again. It missed again.

Her furry dog, Biscuit, ran to get the beanbag. He gave it a little lick, then dropped it in her hands.

"One, two, three steps," Jasmine counted. She took three steps closer to the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! She threw it again from the same spot. It went in again.

Then Dad rolled her the big ball. She held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy, but she caught it.

"Good job," Dad said. "Even a doctor has to practice new things."

Jasmine laughed. She stepped back far from the hoop. "Watch me, Biscuit," she said. She ran closer, and threw.

Emile sat in a little chair at the vet. A puppy slept in a basket next to him. The puppy was brown with one white ear. Emile gave the white ear a soft pat.

"Time for a collar," said the vet. She held up a small tag. It was shiny and round. Emile picked it out all by himself. Then the vet asked for his phone number. Emile said it slowly, and his mom helped. The vet put the number on the tag. "Why does the puppy need our number?" Emile asked. Mom smiled. "If the puppy gets lost, the tag tells people how to reach us," she said. The tag went on the collar with a little click.

At home, the puppy ran in the grass. Emile gave him water in a blue bowl. He gave him a kiss on his soft head. "I love you, puppy," Emile said. The tag went glint, glint in the sun. Emile held the tag in his hand and read the number. Then he let the puppy sniff it. The puppy wagged his tail, and they went inside together.

Clara sat at the big art table. She was drawing a blue fish. The marker slipped. Now her hand had a blue mark too.

Clara looked at her hand. "Oh no," she said. Would the blue mark stay there forever?

Miss Jo held up Clara's hand. "These are washable markers," she said. She took Clara to the little sink.

Clara put her hand under the water. Miss Jo added soap. Clara rubbed and rubbed. The blue mark began to fade. Then it was gone!

Clara looked at her clean hand. She had made the mark go away. She drew a small green butterfly on her paper. Then she drew a tiny green dot on her other hand. "Watch this," she said to her friend Sam.

Clara washed her hand again. Soap, water, rub. The green dot vanished. Sam clapped his hands.

"You can draw a cute fish on me next," said Sam. Clara picked up the orange marker.

Maeva and Dad went to the airport. Grandma was coming on a plane. "We wait here," said Dad. "This is the arrivals area. Families wait here to meet people coming off a plane." The doors opened. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" Maeva would yell. But it was not Grandma. A lady with a red hat came out. Not Grandma either. Then the doors opened one more time. Grandma! She hugged Maeva so tight.

The next day they all went to the park. Grandma brought a kite in her bag. That was a surprise. Maeva held the string and ran. The wind caught the kite. The kite went up and up. It flew far over the trees. "I did it!" Maeva would yell. Grandma laughed and clapped.

At the picnic table, Dad cut the bread. He made warm sandwiches for everyone. Maeva took a big bite. "Best picnic ever," said Grandma. The kite danced in the sky above them.

Paisley sat on the blue rug at daycare. Miss Jo held up ten paper shoes. "Let's count them," she said. Tom started. "One, two..." Then he stopped. His face went red. "I forgot what comes next."

Miss Jo smiled. "Try the shoe song," she said. She sang it. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Tom sang with her. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door!" He clapped his hands. "It rhymes! The words rhyme together!"

Paisley wanted to try too. "Three, four, shut the door," she sang. The words felt bouncy in her mouth, like a joke that tickled. "Five, six, pick up sticks."

Tom picked up a crayon from the floor. "Look! I picked up a stick!" Everyone laughed. Then they all sang more. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." They laid ten crayons in a neat row on the rug.

Paisley could see the row of shoes and the row of crayons. She counted them all by herself. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Tom patted her arm. "You did it," he said. Paisley sang the last part softly. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen."

Julia put on her soft pajama shirt. It was bedtime, but her teddy bear looked sad. His mouth was turned down in a frown. "Are you sad, Bear?" she asked. She gave him a hug. Bear's face felt better after that.

Then Bunny came along. Bunny's eyes were wide and her mouth was open. "You look scared," said Julia. So Julia tucked Bunny under her sweet blue blanket. Bunny stopped shaking. Julia smiled a big smile. She was happy now too.

Dino stomped in with a big frown and grumpy eyebrows. "You look angry, Dino," said Julia. She stuck one sticker on his nose. It was a star sticker. Dino's frown turned into a grin. Julia yawned. She tucked everyone into bed. "Goodnight, friends," she said. Then she closed her eyes and dreamed of stars.

Jack walked home with Dad. He held the leash in both hands. His new dog, Bella, trotted beside him. She had a shiny black nose and a wagging tail.

Jack had a chocolate treat in his pocket. He took it out. "Treat for you, Bella!" he said. Dad stopped him gently. "No, Jack. Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate." Jack looked at his treat. Then he looked at Bella. He felt worried.

Dad reached into his bag. "You can give her this instead." It was a dog treat, shaped like a little bone. Jack held it out on his flat hand. Bella took it softly. She wagged her tail fast. A bird began to sing above them. "Good dog," Jack said. Bella licked his cheek. Jack laughed and held her leash tight all the way home.

Jacob ran to the big backyard. Grandpa was there by the grill. The grill was hot, so Jacob stayed back. He could hear the food sizzle.

Jacob saw something small on the grass. It was brown and shiny. It had a little flame button on it. It was a lighter. Jacob wanted to pick it up. But he did not. He stopped his hand.

"Grandpa, I found something!" Jacob called. Grandpa came right away. He picked up the lighter. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," said Grandpa. He put it in his pocket, far up high.

Then Grandpa said, "The food is ready. We can share it together." They sat at the brown picnic table. Jacob ate a warm bun. Grandpa gave him a cool cup of water. "Hot and cold," said Jacob, touching the cup with both hands. Grandpa smiled and held Jacob's hand.

Charles sat at the dinner table. His sister Mia had a shiny red apple. Charles wanted it very much.

He reached across the table. He grabbed the apple quick. Mia's face went sad. "That is mine," she said. She did not laugh. She looked like she might cry.

Charles put the apple back on her plate. He thought hard. "Can I have the apple, please?" he asked. Mia smiled a big smile. "Yes! We can share it." Their mom cut the apple in two. Half for Charles. Half for Mia. Mom poured milk for each of them too. The milk was cold and sweet.

"Can I have your paint tomorrow?" Charles asked Mia. "Yes, if you ask," said Mia. "Ask, ask, ask," said Charles. Dad laughed. "That is the way."

The apple was crunchy. Charles ate his half slow. Mia ate her half too. After dinner, Charles felt warm and happy. His tummy was full. Then he yawned. Soon his eyes closed and he fell asleep in his chair.

Mom picked him up. "My big boy," she said softly. "He asked."

Brooks was at the big pool. His swim team was playing a game. They had to push a ball across the water. Brooks wore his red cap. His friend Mia held a rubber sheep. The sheep could float. They let it hide under a snowy white towel before the game.

The coach blew the whistle. Brooks kicked hard. The ball came to him. He pushed. The ball went past his hands. It missed the goal. Brooks felt his face go hot.

But then his team began to cheer. "Try again, Brooks! You can do it!" they called. Mia waved the sheep. The ball came back. Brooks pushed it again. This time it went in. The team splashed and cheered louder. "Good try, good try, good try," they sang. Brooks laughed and splashed back at them.

Aiden was at the big hall with Grandma. Everyone was making food. Soon they would all eat together.

Grandma held Aiden's hands. "In Japan, we say itadakimasu before we eat," she said. "It gives thanks for the food."

Aiden wanted to say it just right. He tried. "Ita... ducky... moose!"

Grandma laughed. "Almost! Try again."

"Ita-daki-masu," said Grandma, slow and slow.

Aiden puffed out his chest. "Ita-daki-masu!"

"That's it!" said Grandma. "Say it loud so the whole table hears."

The food came out. The bowls were big and warm. Aiden waited. He did not grab the bread. He had big eyes and a big want.

"Now, Aiden," said Grandma.

"Itadakimasu!" said Aiden.

"Itadakimasu!" said everyone back.

Then they all ate. Aiden took a big bite of rice. "Mmm," he said. "Is it true? The word tastes good too?"

Grandma smiled. "Words don't taste, silly."

Aiden giggled. "My tummy says thank you."

"My tummy too," said Grandma.

After the meal, Aiden put on his red boot. Then he lost the other one. "I need my boot!" he said.

"It's under the table," said Grandma.

Aiden reached down. He pulled it out. "Found you, boot!"

He pushed his feet in and stomped. "Ita-daki-stomp!"

Grandda laughed big. "You are a silly one."

At the door, Aiden waved. "Bye, hall! Bye, food!"

Grandma took his hand. "Say it one more time for the walk home."

"Itadakimasu!" Aiden shouted.

A bird flew up off the fence.

"Look," said Aiden. "The bird heard me!"

Kayden wanted Grandpa to read his book. But Grandpa could not find the words on the page.

Kayden used his eyes to look. He used his ears to listen. Where were the glasses? He touched the soft couch. He touched the cold table. "Two, three, four places," he counted.

Then Kayden smelled toast with his nose. He followed the smelly, warm smell to the kitchen. Grandma was there. "Do you remember winter?" she asked. "You wore mittens so your hands stayed warm." She handed Grandpa his glasses from the counter.

Grandpa put on his glasses. He opened the book. Now he could see the words. He read the story to Kayden.

"The glasses help me see more clearly," Grandpa said.

Kayden tasted the sweet toast. He clapped his hands. "Again," he said. "Read it again, Grandpa."

Blake was at daycare. She wanted to build a big tower. She put a block in the box, then took it out again.

Baby Sam crawled over. Sam put toys in the box. Blake took them out. Sam put them in. Blake laughed.

"You two," said Miss Kim. "In and out are opposites."

Blake tried it herself. Block in. Block out. In, out, in, out. Sam clapped his small hands.

Then Blake made her tower. It was big. It grew fast. Sam knocked it down, slow and soft, with one little push. Blake did not cry. She built it again.

At snack time, Miss Kim gave out warm muffins. "Careful, they're hot," she said. Blake blew on hers. Then she drank her cold milk.

Sam pointed at the box. "Da," he said.

Blake put a ball in the box. Sam pulled it out. They played the game until it was time to go home.

"Bye, Sam," said Blake. "You are not alone. I will sit by you tomorrow."

Theodore went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about spiders. He found a green book with a big spider on the cover. He opened it at the back. The pages felt funny that way. The words ran the wrong way. He turned the book around. He began at the front. Now the spider story started right. One spider, two spiders, three spiders on a web.

"Mom, who made up this spider story?" Theodore asked.

Mom took him to the librarian. The librarian pointed to the cover. She put her finger on a name. "This is the author," she said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Theodore looked at the name. It said Anna Lee. So Anna Lee wrote the words. Every page, all the spider words.

Theodore held the book tight. He found another book by Anna Lee. It had a bear asleep in a cave. He carried both books to the desk. "These are Anna Lee's words," he told the librarian. She smiled and stamped the books. Theodore counted them out loud. "One book, two books." Then he sat by the window and turned to page one.

Clara ran to the music corner at school. She was so excited. A big purple drum sat on the rug. Clara hit it with her hands. Boom! Boom! The sound was loud and fun. Clara laughed and laughed.

Then she saw her friend Ben. He was sad. He had his hands over his ears. "Too loud," Ben said. His face looked scared. Clara stopped drumming. She felt confused. She loved the drum. But Ben did not love it. She thought and thought. The same drum, but two different feelings!

Clara looked around the room. She found a box of magnets on the shelf. She held one up. "Want to play magnets, Ben?" she asked. Ben took his hands off his ears. He smiled a big smile. He was happy now. The magnets clicked together. They filled the whole rug with click, click, click sounds.

Miss Maya came over. "What a quiet game," she said. Then came a small surprise. The magnet stuck to the drum. Clara gasped. "Look, Ben! The magnet likes your drum too." Ben tapped the drum very, very soft. Tap. Tap. "I like it now," Ben said.

Sofia stood in the school hallway. It was her very first day. She held her red backpack with both hands.

The hallway had a big window. Sofia looked out. She could see the school bus parked by the door.

A boy got on the bus. He waved and waved at Sofia. Then he stood up in his seat to wave more. The driver turned around. "Sit down, please," the driver said. "On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats."

The boy sat down. Then he waved from his seat instead. Sofia waved back. His hand went left and right through the window glass. She saw that sitting down still let him wave. "Look at that," Sofia whispered.

A girl named Mia walked up next to her. "Do you see the bus too?" Mia asked.

"Yes," said Sofia. "The boy sits and waves. He does not stand. What else can you see from here?"

Mia pointed at the field. "Sheep!" she said. Two white sheep stood by the fence. One sheep walked to the other sheep.

Sofia clapped her hands. Then the teacher called, "Line up, everyone!"

Sofia and Mia got in line. Sofia turned for one more look. The bus doors closed with a big whoosh, and off it went down the road.

John sat in his big car seat. The car went fast. "Slow down, Daddy," said Mommy. Daddy drove slow by the cows. The cows were big. The birds were small.

John was hungry. Mommy had a cup of cold juice. John took a sip. The cup was not full now. Soon the cup was empty. "All gone," said John.

Then Daddy stopped the car. Daddy got a thermos of hot soup, but Daddy held it himself. "It's hot, so I pour," said Daddy. Daddy poured some soup into a clean cup. He poured too fast and the cup got too full. Some soup spilled. Daddy wiped it up with a napkin. Then Daddy poured slow. He stopped before the top. "This cup is full," said Daddy. "It is not empty."

John held his cup with two hands. He looked inside. The soup went all the way up. John smiled at Daddy and took a tiny sip.

"Wag your tail," John said to the dog in the next car, whose bone sat on the seat.

Maya ran into the garage. Dad had a surprise in his bag. It was a little flute called a recorder! "I want to play it now," said Maya. Dad showed her the holes on top. "Put your fingers on the holes," he said.

Maya blew into the recorder. It went squeak! That was not a nice sound. She looked down. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. She pressed her finger flat and hard on the hole. She blew again. Out came a real note! "Dad, listen!" she said.

Then Maya lifted one finger. The note changed! She put the finger back. The note went back. She lifted another finger. A new note came out. Maya played up and down, up and down. Dad tapped his foot. "Play it again!" he said. Maya smiled and blew a long, happy note.

Zayn ran to the bat. One, two, three, swing time! "Hold on, Zayn," said Coach Ben. "You need your helmet first."

Zayn stopped. He touched his head. "Why?" he asked.

"The batter wears a helmet to protect the head," said Coach Ben. He set the blue helmet on Zayn. It felt big and a little cold at first.

Zayn looked around. Every batter had a helmet. Mia had one. Sam had one. One, two, three helmets on the bench!

Zayn stood at the plate. He gave a little wave to his mom. Then the ball came. Zayn swung. Ping! The ball flew far. It went over the grass and began to fall down, down, down near second base.

"Run, Zayn, run!" his team called. Zayn ran, and his helmet stayed on tight the whole way.

William was on the swim team this summer. Every morning he went to the big pool. Coach Sam had a fun game for the team today.

At the small end of the pool, Coach Sam put a floating net in the water. Then he dropped a beach ball next to William. "In soccer, we try to get the ball into the net," said Coach Sam. "We play soccer in the water today!"

William pushed the ball with his hands. The ball bobbed away. It went past the net. It did not go in. Mia, on his team, splashed and pushed it back to him.

William tried a new way. He kicked the ball with his foot under the water. Kick, kick, kick. The big splash made the ball roll. It rolled and rolled. It rolled right into the net!

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Mia clapped her hands. Coach Sam blew his whistle. William laughed and jumped up and down. The water went splash on his nose.

"Now you kick it to me!" said Mia. William lined up the ball with his foot. He gave it a big kick. "Here it comes!"

Lily sat in the little reading corner. A soft rug was under her feet. Books sat on low shelves all around. She found a big red book. It had a dragon on the cover. The dragon had fire coming out of its mouth.

"I love this one," said Lily. She hugged the book. It felt rough on the cover. But books had to stay at the library. Lily's face went sad.

The librarian came over. She smiled. "Would you like a library card?" she asked.

"A card for me?" said Lily. "Yes!" So Lily wrote her name. The librarian made a shiny new card.

The librarian laughed. "Your card lets you borrow books. You can take them home to read."

"Home? This book can come home with ME?" Lily hugged the dragon book again. She put it in her bag. The bag had a strap that would hang on her hook at home.

At bedtime, Lily read about the dragon. It blew fire at a big hill of socks. "Silly dragon," said Lily. She patted the book. "You live at the library. But tonight you sleep here."

She put the book by her pillow. "Night night, dragon," she whispered.

Ethan stood at the door of his class. A big dragon was blocking the way. It was really Ben in a green dragon costume, and Ben was very still.

Ethan wanted to get past. He tried to squeeze by. The dragon wiggled and did not move. Ethan almost fell.

Then Miss Ana came close. "Say excuse me," she said in a gentle voice.

"Excuse me, dragon," said Ethan.

The dragon turned his head. He stepped to the side with a swish of his tail. The way was open now.

"Thank you, dragon," said Ethan.

The dragon bowed. "Excuse me is how a knight gets past a dragon," said the dragon.

Ethan walked through the door. He felt like a real knight with a shiny sword. At the craft table he picked up the glue.

"Please can I have the blue paper?" he asked. The teacher smiled and gave him two pieces. He made a tall, tall castle with a flag on top.

At home time, Ben fell down and did not cry. Ethan helped him up.

"Sorry I bumped you," said Ben.

"That's okay," said Ethan.

They marched out together, two knights side by side.

Colton ran to the play table at daycare. Miss Ana had a big box. "It is a guessing game," she said. "Close your eyes."

Colton shut his eyes tight. He could not see anything. But he could hear Miss Ana shake the box. Rattle, rattle!

"Now touch," said Miss Ana. Colton put his fingertips on something. It felt bumpy all over. His fingertips knew it! "A pinecone!" he said. He opened his eyes. Yes! It was a pinecone.

Next he felt something soft. Soft like a baby duck. "A feather!" he said. He was right again. Then he touched something smooth. Smooth and cool. "A rock!" It was a smooth stone.
