The kids smelled snack next. Colton's nose sniffed warm apples. He could taste the sweet apple too. Yum!

Later, Miss Ana gave him paint. Colton made a messy picture with his hands. "Feel this!" he said to his friend. "Bumpy paint!"

His friend touched it and laughed. "Bumpy!" said his friend.

Today was Ellie's birthday party in her classroom. There was a cake on the table. There were cups and plates. On the wall, a big paper owl would hang over the party. Ellie held it up high. "I will hang you, owl," she said. The owl hung there and looked down at everyone.

A new boy named Sam came in. He had never met Ellie before. "How old are you?" Sam asked. Ellie held up her fingers. She counted them. "One, two, three," she said. Sam laughed. "Three? But your mom said four!" Ellie looked at her hand. One finger was hiding down low. She lifted it up. "One, two, three, four!" she said. "I am four!" She wiggled the four fingers. Sam held up four fingers too. "I am four also!" he said.

Then Ellie went around the room. She asked her grandma. Grandma held up six fingers, and everyone laughed. She asked her friend Mia. Mia held up three fingers. Ellie looked everywhere for one more cup. The pink cup was lost! It was under the chair. Ellie found it and put it on the table. Then everyone sang. Ellie blew out the candles with a big puff. "Happy birthday, Ellie!" they all said. Sam waved four fingers at her and grinned.

Lucy was at the park with her mama. Grandma was coming to visit. Lucy wanted to see Grandma so much. She felt excited. When she felt excited, her legs wanted to bounce. They boing, boing, boinged. Her mouth wanted to shout. "Grandma! Grandma!"

But Grandma was not there yet. Lucy looked down the path. She saw a boy near the swings. He was crying. He felt sad. His kite was stuck in a tree. "I can help," Lucy said. She waited while Mama got the kite down. The boy stopped crying. He smiled a big smile.

Lucy heard a loud dog bark. She felt scared. She held Mama's hand. The dog ran past. It did not stop. Lucy let out her breath. She was not scared anymore.

Then Lucy saw a red balloon floating away. She felt angry. "Come back, balloon!" she said. But the balloon went up, up, up. Then, surprise! The wind blew it back down. It landed right in Lucy's hands. She laughed.

Lucy's legs began to bounce again. Boing, boing, boing. She took a big breath. She sat on the bench. She counted the clouds. One, two, three. Then she heard a voice. "Hello, my Lucy!" It was Grandma! Lucy ran with the red balloon. Grandma opened her arms wide.

Everly sat in the big red seat. Her mama sat next to her. The stage had many chairs and shiny horns. A woman began to play a quiet song on a violin.

Everly wanted to clap. She lifted her hands. Then she looked around. Nobody else was clapping. Everyone sat still and quiet. So Everly kept her hands in her lap. She waited.

The music went on and on. Everly tapped her toes. The toe taps matched the beat, tap, tap, tap. She played the toe game in her shoes. She hummed her nursery rhyme inside her head. Twinkle, twinkle, little star. She sang it to herself, all the way to the end.

At last the music stopped. The violin came down. Then everyone clapped at once. Clap, clap, clap! Everly clapped too, loud and fast. A lady in front turned and smiled at her.

Later they sat in the lobby. Everly ate a salty pretzel from the snack table. "Next song, I will wait," Everly said. "Then I will clap and show I liked it." She took another big bite of her pretzel.

Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He had a red hat on his head. He wanted to write his name. Miss Ana gave him a pencil. Nathan held it in his fist. The letters came out big and wobbly. Then his pencil made a fat, fuzzy line. The line was wide and soft, not sharp at all.

"Why is my line so fuzzy?" Nathan asked. Miss Ana looked at the pencil. "The tip is dull," she said. "Can you fix it?" asked Nathan. Miss Ana took the pencil to the sharpener. She turned it round and round. Grown-ups did the sharp part. Nathan waited with his hands in his lap.

Miss Ana gave the pencil back. The tip was pointy now. Nathan held it with his fingers, nice and easy. He drew the N. The line was thin and dark. Then A, then T, then H. "Nathan!" he read out loud. His friend Sam leaned over. "Your N looks like a little hat!" Nathan laughed and made one more N, just to see it again.

Margot sat on the couch with Dad. The big game was on TV. Uncle Ben was there too. Everyone was shouting and clapping.

Margot watched the players run. She could not tell them apart. "Dad, which team is which?" she asked. "Look at the shirts," said Dad. "Each team wears its own colors. The red team is ours. The blue team is the other team." Margot looked hard. Red shirts ran one way. Blue shirts ran the other way. Now she could see them! "Red team, go!" she shouted. A red player kicked the ball. Goal!

"Can I wear red too?" Margot asked. "Yes," said Uncle Ben. He hurried to get his red scarf. He wrapped it around her neck. It was soft and warm. Margot snuggled under the blanket with Dad. Her legs were cozy. The dog was lazy on the rug. The red team ran down the field again. "Go, go, go!" said Margot. Dad gave her a high five. "That one was ours," said Margot. "I can tell now."

Jordan made a circle in the dirt with his finger. It was his own little spot in the school garden. Miss Ana gave him three seeds to plant. Jordan pushed the seeds down, not too deep. Then he covered them up with soft brown dirt. He gave the seeds a drink of water from his small green can.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He looked and looked. There was only dirt in his circle. No sprout was up yet. "Maybe they need more water," said Miss Ana. So Jordan watered the seeds again. Every day he came back. Every day he shared his water with the dirt.

Then one morning, something small and green stood up in the dirt. It was a sprout! Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little sprout," he said. "I will bring you more water tomorrow."

Ethan wanted a story before bed. He ran to get his book. But he could not find his mom. He waited on the bed and hugged the book.

He opened the book by himself. He started at the back. He turned a page. The picture showed a dog at the end of a long day. On the next page, the dog was already home. "That is all mixed up," Ethan said. The dog barked in one picture. Then it slept. Then it played. It made no sense at all.

Mom came in. "Ready for your story?" she asked. Ethan held up the book. "It is all mixed up," he said. Mom smiled. "Try the other way," she said. Ethan flipped the book over. Now he held the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. First the dog woke up. Then it barked at a cat. Then it went home. Then it slept. The story went the right way, all the way to the back cover.

Ethan snuggled down under his blanket. "The front is the start," he said. Mom kissed his head. "Good night, Ethan," she said. Ethan closed the book and patted the front cover.

William jumped into the car seat. "Library time!" he shouted.

Daddy started the car. William looked out the window. He saw a dog. He saw a cow. "Animals everywhere!" he said.

At the library, William ran to a big shelf. He wanted a book about animals. He looked and looked. He saw books about trucks. He saw books about food, with apples on them. No animal books. Where were they? His animal book felt missing.

A librarian came to help. "Follow me," she said. She pointed to a shelf. All the animal books sat there together. Birds, bears, and one big elephant on the cover.

"The animal books live in a group," she said.

William reached for the elephant book. He hugged it tight.

Back in the car, he held it on his lap. At home, he drew an elephant with his gray crayon. "Big ears!" he said.

Daddy laughed. "Let's read it again."

Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. He looked in the paint box. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was no orange paint.

"I need orange," said Michael. "The pumpkin is orange." Grandma smiled. "Let's see what we can do," she said. Michael dipped his brush in the red paint. He put red on the pumpkin. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He put yellow on top of the red.

The brush went round and round. The red paint mixed with the yellow paint. The pumpkin turned orange! Michael touched the paint with his finger. It felt slimy. "Look, Grandma!" he said. "Red and yellow made orange!" Grandma laughed softly. Michael picked up his pumpkin. He held it up to the window. "It looks just like a real one," he said.

Madelyn woke up in her little bed. The sun was bright in her window. She heard spoons and cups in the kitchen. She ran down the hall. Mama, Papa, and Baby Sam were at the table. There were eggs and toast and milk. "Good morning," said Mama. "Good morning," said Madelyn. She sat down and ate her toast.

Yesterday Madelyn had wanted to plant seeds. Papa had said, "Not now. Later." Today she asked again. "Can we plant the seeds today?" "We can," said Papa. "First we eat breakfast. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast. Then we go outside." Madelyn ate two eggs. She drank all her milk.

Then Papa got the seed packet. Madelyn dropped three seeds into her hand. They went out to the big pot by the door. The dirt was soft and cool. Madelyn pushed each seed down with one finger. One seed got stuck to her thumb. She shook her hand and it fell in. Papa gave her water in a small cup. She poured it on the dirt.

"Now the seeds stay in the dirt," said Papa. "Tomorrow we will look at the pot. Tomorrow is the day after today." Madelyn patted the dirt. "Good night, seeds," she said. "See you tomorrow." The pot sat still and quiet in the sun.

Hailey was at Grandpa's house. She wanted to show Grandpa her new red ball. She ran down the hall. "Grandpa!" she shouted.

Mama put her hand up soft. "The baby is sleeping," she whispered. "We use a quiet voice."

Hailey looked at the baby. The baby's eyes were closed. Hailey made her voice very small. "Grandpa," she whispered.

Grandpa smiled and whispered back, "Hello, Hailey." They rolled the red ball to each other on the rug. The ball went tap, tap, so soft. Grandpa rolled it to Hailey. Then Hailey rolled it to Grandpa. They took turns, back and forth.

Outside, a truck rumbled by on the street. Hailey covered her mouth. But the baby still slept.

Then the baby woke up. She was not sad. She made a happy sound. Hailey held up her ball and whispered, "My turn, baby. You can share."

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box. He pulls and pulls. The box does not move. It is too heavy.

His friend Mia has a pillow. It is light. Carter lifts it up high. It is easy! "Look," says Mia. "Heavy and light are opposites." Carter puts the pillow on top of the box. The tower grows, one soft pillow at a time.

Now Carter wants a faster tower. He runs to get more pillows. Then he stops. He goes slow and careful. The pillows stay on top. The tower stands tall. Teacher Sam brings warm cocoa in little cups. "Hot," says Teacher Sam. "Blow first." Carter blows. He sips. "Cold now!" The tower is big. Carter is small. But his tower is the tallest in the room. "Again tomorrow," says Carter.

Blake went to the garden center with Dad. She wanted to plant a little garden. Blake picked carrot seeds and pea seeds. She held the seed packets tight.

At home, Dad helped her dig in the dirt. Blake dropped the seeds in. She patted the soil down. Then she watered it with her small blue can.

One day a green weed grew near her peas. Blake pulled it, gently, gently. Out it came. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom! "Wow," said Blake. "The roots grow down into the soil!" Dad laughed. "Yes, they do." Blake patted the soil back down. Her pea plant stayed snug, roots down below, growing and growing.

Soon the peas were tall. Blake picked one and had a taste. "Sweet!" she said. Dad had a taste too. "Mmm," he said. "My peas win the number one prize." Blake giggled and picked one more.

Matteo pulled his blanket up to his chin. "Mom," he said, "is today the library day?"

Mom sat on the bed. Her face was soft in the lamp light. "Yes," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now. And we went today."

Matteo thought hard. He remembered the morning. He had picked three books. He had hugged them all the way home. That was today.

"But I want to go again," he said. "Can we go now?"

Mom shook her head gently. "Now it is bedtime. The library is closed. You can go later."

"How long is later?" asked Matteo.

"Later comes after you sleep," said Mom. "When you wake up, it will be tomorrow. Tomorrow we can read your new books."

Matteo looked at the books by his pillow. Yesterday he had no books. Today he had three. Tomorrow he would open the first one.

"The sun went away today," said Mom. "Now it is dark. The snow will fall while you sleep."

Matteo snuggled down. His blanket felt warm. "Today was a good day," he said.

"Yes," said Mom. "And tomorrow is coming soon."

She kissed his cheek. Matteo closed his eyes.

"Read to me tomorrow," he whispered. "The bear book first."

Harper went to the pharmacy with her dad. She had to use the toilet. After that, they went to the little sink. Dad put soap on her hands. "We count to twenty," said Dad. Harper rubbed and rubbed. "Ten, eleven, twelve," she said. Her hands felt slippery.

Then Dad turned on the water. The water ran over Harper's hands. The slippery feeling went away. "Where did the soap go?" she asked. "The water washed it off," said Dad. Harper held up her hands. "My hands are not slippery now!" she said. "Slippery gone, slippery gone," she sang.

A small boy pointed at the sink. "My turn," he said. His mom helped him wash. Harper gave him a quick wave. "Count to twenty," she told him. On the way out, Dad bought a bandage for his knee. Harper carried the little bag all the way home.

Gabriel rode his bike to Grandma's house. Snow fell from the sky. It fell on the grass. It fell on Grandma's red door. Gabriel looked down. "The snow is white," he said. All the snow was white.

Gabriel wanted to draw the snow. He got white paper. He got a white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up! White on white was invisible. Grandma gave him a hug. "Try again," she said. Gabriel looked at the paper stack. He picked the blue paper. He drew white snow on it. Now the snow showed up! White on blue was easy to see.

Gabriel added a yellow sun. He added a green tree. Grandma made hot cocoa, and she chewed a peppermint while he drew. Then Gabriel saw a surprise. Outside, a red bird sat on the white snow. It looked just like his yellow sun on blue sky. He drew it fast. "Snowy red bird," he said.

Eliana went to the art gallery with her papa. There was a painting of a big red monkey. Eliana touched the monkey's tail. Her finger left a smudge on the wet paint. "Oh no," said Eliana. A kind woman said, "The paint is still wet. It can smudge if you touch it." Eliana looked at her fingerprint in the tail.

Then the woman took Eliana to a little table. There were three pots of paint. "This one is red," said the woman. "This one is blue. This one is yellow." Eliana said the names out loud. "Red. Blue. Yellow." She said them again, like a song.

"Now you can cook up a new colour," the woman said with a smile. Eliana put her brush in the red pot. Then she put it in the blue pot. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned purple! Eliana gasped. It was like magic, but her hands had done it.

She painted a purple monkey drinking a big glass of juice. The monkey looked thirsty, so she painted him a river too. "Don't touch it yet," Eliana told papa. "We have to let it dry." They sat and watched the purple monkey. They waited and waited, until the paint was dry.

Ethan sat at the little red table. His teacher, Miss Ana, put out two bowls. One bowl had apples. One bowl had grapes.

"Count them," said Miss Ana. "Then tell me which has more."

Ethan pointed at the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." He touched one apple two times. "Seven!"

Miss Ana smiled. "Count them again. Watch your finger. Touch each apple just once."

Ethan made a line with his finger. He pointed at each apple, one at a time. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples. He had counted one apple twice before. Now he got it right.

Then he counted the grapes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven grapes.

"The grapes have more!" said Ethan. He clapped his hands.

Miss Ana laughed. "You counted so carefully, Ethan."

"Can we count the naughty crayons next?" asked Ethan. "They keep rolling off the table!"

Miss Ana put the crayons in a long line. Ethan pointed at each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten crayons," said Ethan. "Ten is a lot!"

Hannah sat by the train window. Rain tapped on the glass. She watched the drops slide down, down, down. "Faster, rain," she said. The rain did not listen.

Then Hannah wiggled in her seat. Her tummy felt funny. "Daddy, I need to go potty," she said. "Can the train stop at our house?" Daddy laughed a little. "The train can't stop at our house. But we can walk to the bathroom on the train." Hannah's eyes got big. "A bathroom on a train? Where?"

Daddy held her hand. They walked down the bumpy aisle. Hannah held her arms out like a bird. "Wobble, wobble," she sang. A man in a yellow hat smiled at her. At last they found the little train bathroom. It was so small! "It's a tiny potty room," said Hannah. She used it all by herself, with Daddy waiting outside.

When she came out, she felt much better. "Daddy! Now I know a secret," she said. "Trains have bathrooms hiding inside them." Daddy nodded. "And guess what else? Cars can stop at a rest stop on a long drive, so people can use the bathroom and stretch." Hannah stretched her arms up high. "Like a tall giraffe," she said. Then she pointed at the window. "Look, Daddy! The rain stopped!" The sun made a little rainbow on her seat.

Eleanor was so excited. Tonight was Diwali night! Mama gave her a basket of little clay lamps. "These are called diyas," said Mama.

Eleanor set them out in a row. One, two, three, four, five. They were cool and smooth to touch. "Why are they dark?" Eleanor asked. "Watch Papa," said Mama.

Papa came with a long match. He did not let Eleanor touch the flame. He tipped the flame into each little diya. One, two, three, four, five. Each one glowed! The dark lamps turned into golden lights, one by one.

"Wow!" said Eleanor. "The flame makes them bright!" Papa smiled. The diyas sat in a shiny row on the messy table. Together they lit up the whole night. Eleanor clapped her hands. "More diyas next year!"

Sophie planted little seeds in the dirt. Her grandma helped her pat the soil. "Now we wait," said Grandma. Sophie wanted the peas right away. But nothing happened that day.

Each morning Sophie came back. The sun came out. Rain came down. A small green sprout turned into a tall vine. It grew up a stick.

Then Sophie found something odd. A fat green thing hung on the vine. "What is it?" she asked. "That is a pod," said Grandma. Sophie pulled the pod off. She popped it open with her fingers. Inside were little green peas, all in a row! Sophie laughed and picked more pods. It was getting late, and a big pink pig statue stood by the garden gate. "Time to go home and eat our peas," said Grandma. Sophie held her pods tight all the way home.

Elias stood at the big kitchen table. Dad put onions in a bowl. "We will make soup," Dad said. Elias loved soup. He wanted to help make it.

Dad picked up a knife. The knife was sharp, so Dad did the cutting. Elias watched from his chair. He passed Dad the salt. He stirred the big spoon in the pot. Dad held the pot. It was hot, so Elias only watched that part.

Then Dad cut an onion. Tears ran down his face. Elias felt worried. "Dad, are you sad?" he asked. He whispered, "Like a little mouse, I will hug you."

Dad smiled through his tears. "It is just the onion," he said. "Cutting it makes my eyes sting and water." Elias looked at the onion. It looked small and quiet. It was not a mean onion. It just made eyes water.

The soup bubbled. Dad wiped his eyes with a towel. "All ready," he said. Elias carried the spoons to the table. Mom came in and sniffed the air. "Mmm," she said. Elias sat down and took a big bite. "I helped," he said. "And the onion made you cry."

Sara sat at the kitchen table. Mama put a little cake in front of her. It was still warm from the oven. "Can you name your five senses?" Mama asked. Sara wanted to say them all. She held up one finger. "Eyes see," she said. She looked at the pink cake. Then she held up another finger. "Ears hear." She listened. The clock went tick, tick.

Two fingers more. "Tongue tastes," said Sara. "Hands touch." She patted the soft table. But now she stopped. One sense was missing. She thought and thought. Then she leaned close to the cake. She sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled sweet like strawberries.

"Nose smells!" Sara laughed. She sniffed again. "The nose knows," said Mama. Outside, a bird sat high in the tree. Sara watched it shake its wings. Then she took a big bite of cake.

Isla ran to the big slide at the playground. Her friend Max ran to the small slide. "Big!" shouted Isla. "Small!" shouted Max. They laughed and ran again.

Max said, "Those words are opposites." Isla said, "Let's play the opposite game!" Max ran fast. Isla walked slow. Max was quiet. Isla was loud. Max sat in the sun. It was hot there. Isla sat in the shade. It was cold there. "Brrr," said Isla, and she put her towel on the cold bench so she could sit too.

Then Max said, "Sleepy!" Isla thought hard. She closed her eyes. Then she popped them open wide. "Awake!" she shouted. Max fell down laughing in the grass. "Your turn," said Isla. Max grinned and shouted, "Up!" Isla jumped up as high as she could go.

Samuel put on his coat for shape hunt time. "Find a square!" said Miss Maya. Samuel found a square block. He counted its corners. One, two, three, four.

Next Miss Maya said, "Find a triangle!" Samuel found a triangle cracker at snack time. He almost ate it. "Silly me," he said, and giggled.

Then Miss Maya said, "Find a rectangle. A rectangle has four sides and four square corners." Samuel looked and looked. He saw a circle clock. Not that. He saw a square rug. Not that. Then he heard the door open. It was Ben, coming in from outside. Samuel looked at the door. He counted the corners. One, two, three, four. Four sides too!

"The door is a rectangle!" Samuel shouted.

Miss Maya laughed. "You found a big one," she said. Samuel touched the door. It felt cool and smooth. The room went quiet as everyone looked. Then Ben knocked on the rectangle. Boom, boom. Samuel knocked too.

Olivia wanted the big red swing in the yard. Her cousin Sam wanted it too. They both ran to it. They both grabbed the chain at the same time.

"Me first," said Sam. "No, me first," said Olivia. Then Grandma came out. She looked at the cloudy sky and said, "We can fix this. Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another."

Olivia asked, "So who goes first?" Grandma said, "You can count to ten. Then it is Sam's go." Sam counted to ten. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Then it was Sam's go. Sam counted to ten. Then it was Olivia's go.

Olivia pumped her legs. The swing went up high. Sam held the gate wall and waited. Then they traded again. One go, then another go. The sun came out. Olivia laughed and said, "Your turn, Sam. I will hold the wall next."

Logan ran into the baby store. "A baby is coming!" he said. "We need tiny socks, Mommy!" Mommy smiled. Logan followed her down the big aisle.

Then Logan saw a baby doll in a crib. He patted it hard. Bump! The doll's head fell over. Logan frowned. A lady who worked there came close. "A new baby must be touched very gently," she said. Logan looked at his hand.

He tried again. He stroked the doll's soft hand, slow and light. The doll stayed still. "I did it!" said Logan. Then the doll made a tiny sound, "Wah!" Logan jumped. "Mommy, the baby talks!" He picked cozy blue socks for the real baby. "Come on, baby brother," he whispered. "Hurry to my house!"

Mila sat at the art table. She had a big piece of paper. She drew a yellow sun. Then she drew a red apple. "What should I draw next?" she asked herself. "A dog," she said, and drew a small brown dog.

Next to her, Ben drew too. He drew a yellow sun and a red apple. The teacher called, "Time to clean up!" Both pictures went into one big pile. When Mila came back, she saw two papers side by side. Both had a sun and an apple. "Which one is mine?" she asked.

The teacher came over. "Look for your name," she said. Mila had not written her name. She looked down at her hands. There was red paint on one finger. Her apple had a smudge on it, from her own hand. She picked up that paper. Under the smudge, she saw her dog. "This one is mine!" she said.

Ben found his paper too. It had no smudge. Then Mila got a crayon. She wrote M-I-L-A at the top. "Now everyone will know I made this," she said. She smiled and sent her picture off to the drying rack.

Ellie ran to the white ball on the grass. It was soccer day at the park. Her coach was there. Her mom was there too.

Ellie kicked the ball. Then a boy on her team kicked it into the net. Everyone cheered. But a man in a striped shirt blew his whistle. He shook his head. The boy yelled, "No! We want the point!"

Ellie felt worried. She asked her coach, "Who is that man?"

The coach said, "He is the referee." Ellie waited. The coach said more. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Ellie looked at the referee. He pointed to a line on the grass. The ball had gone past the line. That was why he blew the whistle.

The game went on. Ellie kicked the ball to her friend. Her friend kicked it into the net. This time the referee clapped his hands. "Good goal!" he said.

The team did not win the game. But they got juice boxes after. Ellie sat with her mom by the gate. She waved to the referee. He waved back.

Brooks runs to the playground. The sun is warm. The swings squeak, squeak, squeak. His friend Mia is by the little playhouse. She hugs a toy bear.

"Let's play house," says Mia. "I am the mom." Brooks wants to be the mom too. He holds the bear's small hand. "No, I want to be the mom," he says. Mia makes a sad face. Brooks makes a sad face too.

Then Mia says, "When we play house, we each pick a role. You can be the dad, or the baby." Brooks thinks. He does not want to be the baby. "I will be the dad," he says. "The baby bear can be the baby." Mia smiles.

Broks rocks the bear near the toy bed. He pats its back, one pat, two pats, three pats. He sings a soft song. The baby bear goes to sleep. Mia claps. "You are a good dad," she says.

Brooks hugs the bear. "Next time," he says, "I can be the baby." Mia laughs and claps her hands. "Yes! And I will rock you to sleep."

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The bell at the door gave a little ring. Inside, a tall lady named May was waiting at a big table.

"Snack time," said May. She put down two plates. One plate had crackers. The other plate had apple slices.

"Which group has more?" May asked.

Clara pointed at the crackers. May smiled. "Let's count and see."

Clara touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the apple slices. "One, two, three, four."

The crackers had more. Clara clapped her hands.

Then a boy named Sam came to the table. He was hungry. May said, "Clara, can Sam have one cracker?"

Clara picked up one cracker. She gave it to Sam. Sam sat down next to a little toy car he had brought.

"Count again," said May softly.

Clara touched the crackers. "One, two, three, four."

Now the crackers and the apple slices were the same. Clara looked and looked. Taking one cracker away had made the number one smaller.

"Sam can have an apple slice too," Clara said. She pushed the plate toward him.

Sam took a big bite and smiled.

Lena sat in a big chair. The waiting room had fish in a tank. A little fish pushed a pebble with its nose. The peblem rolled and made a small puff of sand. Lena smiled at that.

Then a lady called her name. The dentist gave Lena a soft toothbrush. It had minty paste on it. Lena brushed her teeth, up and down. Her mouth got full of foamy bubbles. She was about to swallow them. Then she stopped. She turned to the sink. She spit the foam out. "Good job," said the dentist. "After brushing, you spit the toothpaste out instead of swallowing it."

Lena looked in the little mirror. Her teeth were shiny. "Can I push the button for water?" she asked. The dentist nodded. Lena pushed it. Water ran and washed the foam away. "All done," said Lena. "My teeth feel awake!"

Raphael stood at the lake pool. The water looked so cool and blue. But he did not want to put his face in.

His teacher Miss Jo smiled. "Try blowing bubbles in the water," she said.

"Bubbles? Like soap bubbles?" Raphael asked.

"Yes, but you make them with your mouth," said Miss Jo.

Raphael leaned down. He took a little breath. He blew out through his mouth. Plop, plop, plop! Big bubbles popped up by his nose.

He laughed a big laugh. "I made bubbles! The water made them pop!"

"Now let's do it again," said Miss Jo. "Big ones this time."

Raphael put his face close. He blew and blew. Bubbles went everywhere.

Miss Jo clapped. Raphael splashed his feet. "Bubbles, bubbles, more bubbles!" he said.

Then he dipped his whole chin in. The cool water tickled him like a feather. He giggled under the bubbles.

Dad waved from the side. "Look at my bubble boy!" he called.

Raphael blew one more big bubble and shouted, "Watch me, Dad! Plop, plop, plop!"

The lights went out. The TV went dark too. Matthew sat on the back step and frowned.

"No TV?" he asked.

"No power tonight," said Dad. He held a flashlight. "Want to see something?" He shined it on the floor. The light made a big white circle. Matthew put his hand in it. His hand glowed!

"What can we do now?" Mom asked. She found a board game. She found Matthew's book about the bus. She found his new puzzle with the ducks.

Matthew clapped. They sat on the grass in the backyard. Dad put the flashlight on a chair so it would stay bright. Mom rolled the dice. Matthew moved his little red piece. Beep, beep, he said, like a bus.

Later the lights came back on. Matthew looked at the TV. Then he looked at the game.

"More game?" he said. "And more ducks?"

Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. "I can do it," she said. Dad made the toast, because the toaster was hot. Then he put the toast on Aubrey's plate.

Aubrey picked up the butter knife. She dug the hard butter with it. The butter was cold from the fridge. It made a big hole in her toast. "Oh no," said Aubrey. "My toast broke."

Dad got the butter dish from the counter. That butter had sat out all morning. It was soft. Aubrey touched it with the knife. The soft butter spread easy and smooth. No holes! "Look, Dad," she said. "Soft butter works."

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one hand. She poured slow with the other hand. A little milk ran down her foot. She giggled. "Sticky foot," she said. Dad wiped it up with a towel. Then she tried again, even slower. Not one drop spilled.

The dog barked at the door. "He wants breakfast too," said Aubrey. She filled his bowl, slow and careful, all by herself. "Good boy," she said.

Zoey ran to the book corner at daycare. She wanted the bear book. The one with the sweet little bear on the cover. But the shelf was big and full.

"Where is my bear book?" she said.

Her friend Mia held up a book. "This one?"

"No," said Zoey. "That one has a dog."

Teacher Ben came over. He patted the shelf. "Look at the front of the book," he said. "The title is the book's name. This one is called Blue Dog."

Zoey looked. The big letters said Blue Dog. "That is the dog's name place," she said.

"You find it," said Teacher Ben. "Turn the book front side up."

Zoey held a book. She looked at the front. "Happy Bear!" she read.

"That's it!" said Mia. "The title is its name."

"One book, two books, three books," said Zoey. "Happy Bear is mine."

She sat down. She opened the cover. First page, then next page, all the way to the back.

"Read it to me?" she asked.

Teacher Ben sat on the little red rug. "One bear," he began, "two bees, three trees."

Zoey leaned on his arm and turned the page.

Eliana sat in her car seat. "Are we going to the park?" she asked. "Not today," said Mama. "We are going to the dentist. He will look at your teeth." Eliana made a funny face. "How can he see inside my mouth?" she asked. "It is dark in there, like a little cave." Mama smiled and kept driving.

At the dentist's office, Eliana climbed up into a big chair. It went up and up, like a ride. The dentist leaned over. "Open wide," he said. Eliana opened her mouth. Then a bright light came on above the chair. Eliana squeezed her eyes shut. "Too sunny!" she said. The light made her squint, like when she looked at the sky.

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Try these," he said. Eliana put them on. Now she could keep her eyes open. The bright light shone down above the chair, right into her open mouth. "I can see every tooth," said the dentist. "So that is what the light is for," thought Eliana. The dentist counted her teeth, one, two, three.

After that, they got a snack. Eliana was hungry. She ate a crunchy apple. It tasted sweet. "No dirt on this apple," said Mama with a laugh. "The dentist likes clean teeth." Eliana smiled her biggest smile. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked.

Edouard held his very first library card. It was blue and had his name on it. He was so happy.

At the library, Edouard saw a big dinosaur book. "A DINOSAUR BOOK!" he shouted. A girl at the next table looked up. She was reading. An old man was reading too. Edouard's mom bent down. "We use quiet voices here," she whispered. "So others can read."

Edouard looked around. Everyone was reading. He made his voice very small. "Can I have this one?" he whispered. The librarian smiled and stamped the book.

At home, Edouard sat on his bed in his bedroom. Mom read the dinosaur book to him. Then Edouard took his crayons and began to draw a big green dinosaur with sharp teeth.

"I will read it again tomorrow," he whispered, hugging the book.

Eliana stood at the gate. The playground looked very big. She wanted a turn on the swing, but the line was long.

A boy named Tom ran past her. "We go inside soon!" he said. "Miss Bloom will read the class rules."

"What are rules?" asked Eliana.

"You will see," said Tom.

Inside, Miss Bloom held up a big paper. "These are our class rules," she said. "We all follow them. Rule one is, we take turns."

Later, on the playground, the sky turned stormy and gray. Eliana ran to the slide. A big kid pushed in front of her.

Tom tapped his arm. "Rule one," he said. "We take turns."

The big kid looked at Eliana. "You first," he said.

Eliana slid down fast. "I like rules!" she called.

Then Miss Bloom blew a whistle. "Time to look for our class dog poster!" she said. "Line up, friends."

Eliana hopped to her spot in the line.

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. He held his little toy plane. Today he would see the dentist for the first time. "I want to be brave," he said. "But what do I do there?"

Mom smiled. "The dentist will count your teeth," she said. Brooks looked out the window. He made his plane jump from knee to knee. Soon the car stopped. They were at the dentist.

A kind lady in a blue coat said hello. "Open wide," she said, "so I can see every tooth." Brooks opened his mouth. Then he closed it. "Like this?" he asked. She shook her head and smiled. "Open it big, like a lion's roar." Brooks opened his mouth very wide. The little mirror went in. "I see all your teeth!" she said. Brooks felt proud. He gave his toy plane a big jump of joy. "Roar!" he said.

Lillian wanted to see her happy face. She ran to the big mirror in the hall. First she smiled a big smile. The mirror girl smiled too. "I am happy!" said Lillian.

Then she tried a sad face. Her mouth went down. Her eyes looked watery. The mirror girl looked sad too. Lillian laughed. Faces can change like that!

Lillian made a scared face. Her eyes got wide. Then she made an angry face. Her eyebrows came down low. "Grr," she said. Mommy came to look. "Show me happy," said Mommy. Lillian smiled so big. Mommy smiled back.

Lillian had an idea. She turned off the light. The hall went dark. Her tummy felt funny. She turned the light back on. The mirror girl was there again, smiling. "There you are!" said Lillian. She waved her hand. The mirror girl waved too. "Come shop with me," Lillian told her. They walked to the kitchen, hand in hand with Mommy.

Parker put on his bear ears. He was a bear today. His friend Milo was a robot.

Parker wanted to tell everyone about the park. He started to talk. But Milo was already talking about his robot ship. Parker talked louder. Then Milo talked louder too. Now nobody could hear anything.

Their friend Nia held up a little bell. "One voice at a time," she said. She rang the bell once. Milo finished his story about the dark spaceship and the moon park. Parker watched him and waited. He held his words in his mouth like a balloon.

Then Nia pointed at Parker. "Now you." Parker let his balloon go. He told about the big slide at the park. He told about the duck that went splish. Everyone listened. Everyone clapped.

Then Milo gave Parker the red robot hand. "Your turn to be the robot." Parker took it. The robot hand went beep, beep, beep, all the way to the moon.

Sophia ran to the bowling lane. It was her birthday party! Mommy, Daddy, and all her friends were there. The shoes were red and shiny. The ball was very heavy. Sophia pushed it with both hands. Roll, roll, roll. The ball bumped the pins. Crash! They all fell down. "Again, again!" said Sophia.

Sophia held up three fingers. "I am three!" she said. Daddy smiled. "You were three yesterday," he said. "Today is your birthday. Today you turn four." Sophia looked at her fingers. She put one more up. One, two, three, four. "I am four now!" she shouted. Her friends clapped. "Today I am four, today I am four!"

Then Daddy carried in a real birthday cake. He lit the candles, and Sophia watched from her seat. She did not forget to make a wish. She blew and blew. Out went the candles! Everybody sang. Sophia ate her cake with a big spoon. "Best birthday ever," she said. "Happy birthday to me!"

Parker was at school. It was paint time. He wanted to paint grass. But the green pot was empty. "Oh no," said Parker.

His teacher Miss Jo came over. "What do you need, Parker?" "I need green paint," he said. She smiled. "Try the blue paint and the yellow paint."

Parker dipped his brush in blue. He put blue on the paper. Then he dipped in yellow. He put yellow on top. He stirred it with his brush. The paint turned green! Parker jumped up. "It's green! I made green!"

He painted long green grass. His friend Mila looked over. "I need green too," she said. "Blue and yellow," said Parker. "Mix them like this." Mila mixed her paint. Her paint turned green too. She painted a green slide in her picture. "We did it," said Mila.

Later they ran outside to the old slide. The grass by the slide was green, just like the paint. Parker laughed. "Blue and yellow make green," he said, and down he went.

Hailey wanted a sandwich like a tent. Her dad made lunch and cut it with a safe knife. "A triangle," he said. He put the plate in front of her.

The triangle looked scary at first. It was too pointy, Hailey thought. Then she touched one corner with her finger. "One," she said. She found another corner. "Two." She reached the last one. "Three." The triangle had three corners. She slid her finger down one side, then the next side, then the last side. Three sides, too. "It has three sides and three corners!" she said.

Hailey took a big bite. One corner was gone. "Now it is a little tent," she said. Her dad laughed and gave her a napkin. Her pet cat jumped up to see. Hailey held up her sandwich so the cat could look at the shape too.

Natalie had a little orange ball. She played on a team. Today the game was outside in the backyard.

Dad put up a hoop. "If the ball goes through the hoop, we score," Dad said. Natalie threw the ball. It hit the rim and fell down. She did not score yet. A feather floated by. It landed on the grass.

"What if I throw it higher?" Natalie asked. "Try it and see," said Dad. She picked up the ball. She stepped on a crunchy leaf. Then she threw the ball up, up, up.

The ball went through the hoop. It fell down and bounced on the grass. "We scored!" Natalie shouted. She knocked the ball with her hand, and it bounced again. Dad clapped. "One more?" he asked. Natalie giggled and picked up the ball.

Isla loved the rocket ship game at school. Today it was her turn to be the pilot. Ben held the big cardboard door. Isla jumped into her seat and got ready to pretend they would fly far, far away.

"One, two, three," she counted. Ben shook his head. "It goes the other way," he said. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown." Isla felt her cheeks go warm. She tried again.

"Ten, nine, eight." Her voice got louder. "Seven, six, five." Ben held the door tight. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Isla jumped up so high her shoes clapped the floor. Outside the window, a cow in the field looked up. Ben laughed and laughed. "Again!" said Isla, sitting right back down. "Ten, nine, eight."

Mila found her toy cat on the rug. The cat had a long tail and a short tail, because there were two cats. "Which one is big?" she asked. Mom smiled. "The gray one is big. The white one is small."

Mila wanted to give the cats water. She carried a little cup. She walked fast, then slow. Oh no. The water jumped out. It made a puddle on the floor. Mila stepped in it. Her socks got wet. "My socks are wet," she said. "I need dry socks." Mom brought new ones. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mom. Mila touched the wet sock, then the dry sock. They did not feel the same.

Mom made warm milk after. It was hot, so Mom held the cup. Mila waited until it was cold. She took a little sip. "Cold now," she said. The big cat got a dry spot in the sun. The small cat sat by the door. "Sleep well, cats," said Mila. She patted the long tail, soft and slow.

It was dress-up day at school. Levi put on a big red hat and a fuzzy vest. He wore it at lunch time. A piece of banana fell on the vest. Then he painted with a brush. A blue dot went on his sleeve. Then it was nap time. Levi took off the hat and the vest. He dropped them on the floor.

After nap, Levi wanted the red hat again. He looked and looked. It was under the coats! It was squashed and messy. His friend Mila laughed. "The floor ate your hat," she said.

Teacher Rosa gave a gentle smile. She held up a big basket. "Dirty clothes go in this basket," she said. "Then we can wash them." Levi lifted the vest up high. He threw it in. Swish! Mila clapped. "Two points!" she said. Levi threw the hat in too. It landed right on top of the vest.

The next day, the vest was clean. No banana. No blue dot. Levi gave the vest a big hug. "You smell like flowers," he said. He put it on and marched around the room. Then he found two paint dots on his sock. He pulled it off and threw it at the basket. It hit the rim and fell in. "Three points!" said Mila. Levi bowed.

Jack ran to the sand pit at the park. A big pile of blocks sat in the middle. His friend Mia was already there.

Jack grabbed all the blocks. He put every block in his own pile. "My blocks," he said. He started to build a tall tower alone.

Mia sat down with an empty spot in front of her. She had nothing at all. Her mouth turned down at the corners. She looked at the ground.

Jack looked at his pile. Then he looked at Mia. He picked up a round block. "Here," he said. "You can have this one." He chose more blocks, one by one, and put them in front of her.

Mia smiled. "Now we both have some." She stacked a red block, then a blue one. Jack put a green block on his tower. Their towers grew tall side by side.

When they were done, they knocked them down and took turns stacking them up again. Jack clapped his hands. "Your turn, then my turn," he said.

The sun shone on the sand. "Same blocks, same fun," said Mia, and she handed Jack the last round block of all.

Beau sat on the little red chair. He had a big drum in front of him. He hit it hard with the stick. BOOM! The sound was very loud. A baby in the back row woke up and began to cry.

The music teacher, Miss Ana, came over. "Let's try something new," she said. Beau looked at the drum like it was a puzzle.

He hit it again, softer. Boom. The baby stopped crying. "That is a nice sound," said Miss Ana. "It is true," said Beau. "Little hit, little sound."

He hit the drum hard one more time. BOOM! The loud sound filled the whole room. Then he tapped it soft, boom, boom, boom. Miss Ana clapped. Beau smiled and tapped his drum all the way to the end of the song.

Declan sat in his car seat. The sun made the window hot. He touched it quick. "Ouch," he said. "That part is hot," said Grandma. Declan kept his hands on his lap. He looked out at the cars. Beep, beep, went a horn. The car stopped at the park.

Declan jumped out. He saw his friend Mia ride a bike. He wanted to ride too. He ran to her bike. He put his foot on the pedal. Then he stopped. He ran back to the car. "My helmet," he said. Grandma buckled it under his chin. The strap did not slip.

Declan pedaled the bike. He went fast, then slow. He fell once on the soft grass. His knee bumped, but the helmet kept his head safe. Grandma kissed his knee. "Try again," said Mia. Declan got on the bike. The fresh air rushed past his face. He pedaled all the way to the big tree.

Arlo had a red jersey. His team was called the Little Foxes. Every Saturday they played a game. Every Tuesday they had practice.

On Tuesday, Arlo sat on the grass. "I don't want to practice," he said. "I want to eat my juicy orange." Coach Mia smiled. "You can eat after practice," she said. "First we learn to catch."

Arlo stood in line. Coach Mia threw the ball. It bounced off his hands. Thump. It fell in the grass. "Hmm," said Arlo. "Why did it fall?"

Then practice began. Arlo tried again. He held out his hands. He squeezed them shut. He caught the ball! He jumped up and down. "I caught it! I caught it!"

Saturday came. The game began. The ball flew high in the sky. Arlo held out his hands. He squeezed them shut. He caught the ball!

"Wow," said Arlo. "Who taught me that?" He looked at Coach Mia. He thought about Tuesday. He thought about the grass. He thought about the ball bouncing off his hands.

"Practice," said Arlo. "Practice helped me catch!" Coach Mia gave him a big thumbs up. Then Arlo ate his juicy orange. "Sweet," said Arlo, "just like the game."

Levi found a big cardboard box in the living room. He climbed in. "This is my car!" he said. "Beep, beep!"

His sister Mia ran over. "No, it is a boat," she said. "Row, row."

Levi frowned. "Car!"

"Boat!" said Mia.

Levi wanted the box to be a car. Mia wanted it to be a boat. They both pulled on one side. The box tipped over. Uh oh.

Mama came in. "How about turns?" she said.

Levi went first. He sat in the box. "Beep, beep!" said Levi. He drove to get a teddy bear. The bear sat in the back seat.

Then it was Mia's turn. "Row, row," she said. She paddled with a block. The bear rode in her boat too.

Next Levi had an idea. "Now it is a house," he said. They both fit inside. They fed the bear a crunchy pretend cracker. He was a sleepy bear. They sang him a song.

"I remember," said Levi. "The box can be anything!"

"Anything," said Mia. "Even a rocket?"

Levi grinned. "Count with me. One, two, three. Blast off!"

Jack ran to the car. He held a small box. Inside was his new puppy! The puppy was white with brown ears. Jack named him Max. Max begged for a treat right away. "Okay, one treat," Jack said.

The next morning, Mom said, "Max needs a checkup." Jack frowned. "The doctor? Max can't sit in a big chair!" Mom smiled. "Not that kind of doctor."

They walked into a small office. Jack looked around. He saw a cat in a basket. He saw a rabbit with one white feather stuck to its cage. "Why are there pets here?" Jack asked. "Is this a pet store?"

"No," said a kind woman in a blue coat. She listened to Max's heart. "I am a vet. A vet is a doctor for animals." Jack's eyes went wide. A doctor just for pets!

Max barked once. The vet gave him a clean bill of health and a biscuit. Jack held Max's leash all the way home. "Max, you were so brave," Jack whispered. Max wagged his little tail.

Elijah put on his skates at the ice rink. The ice looked fresh and shiny. But first, Dad said, they would watch the big game. It was on the big screen above the snack bar. Mom, Grandpa, and his friend Mia sat on the long bench with him.

The players ran fast up and down the court. Elijah watched the ball go in the hoop. The people around him clapped and cheered. "Go, go!" Elijah shouted. His eye followed the ball the whole way.

Then a loud sound came from the game. Tweet! All the players stopped running. They stood still on the court. Elijah tugged Dad's sleeve. "Why did they stop?" he asked. Dad pointed at the man in the striped shirt. "That is the referee," Dad said. "The referee blows a whistle to stop play." The referee held the little whistle up to his mouth.

Elijah waited. The game started again. The players ran once more. Then, tweet! The whistle blew again. The players stopped again. Elijah laughed. He clapped his mittens together. "They stopped again!" he said. Mom gave his cold cheek a kiss. Then Elijah took Dad's hand and stepped out onto the fresh ice.

Isaac sat at the dinner table. His feet felt cold. He had kicked off his socks under the table. Mom set down his plate. It had ten little peas on it. "Count them," said Mom. "One, two, three," said Isaac. He pointed at each pea. "Four, five, six." He touched the last ones. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." "Good counting," said Mom. Isaac ate the peas, one by one.

Then he looked under the table. He saw one sock. He reached down and grabbed it. But his other foot was still cold. Where was the other sock? Isaac looked and looked. "I only have one," he said. Dad got down on the floor. He made a funny noise and peeked under his chair. "Here it is," said Dad. He held up the second sock. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks," said Dad. Isaac put on one sock. Then he put on the other sock. Now his feet were warm.

After dinner, Isaac helped Mom wash his hands at the sink. The water was warm and soapy. Dad washed the plates and cups. "Ten plates," Dad said with a laugh. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Isaac counted too. "Four, five, six." Dad helped with the rest. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Then Dad turned off the light. It was still early, so Isaac picked a book. He sat on Mom's lap with his warm sock feet. "One story," said Isaac. "Two stories," said Mom with a smile.

Margot sat on her bed. She had a big crayon and one piece of paper. She wanted to write a note to Grandpa.

She wrote: ILOVEYOUGRANDPA. All the letters ran together in one long line. "Look, Bunny!" she said. "One, two, three, four letters. More letters. More letters. All in a big hug!"

Grandpa came in. He held the paper. He turned it around. He looked and looked. "Hmm," he said. "Is it a secret code?"

Margot frowned. "It says I love you, Grandpa!"

Grandpa smiled. "I need a space between the words. One word, then a little space, then the next word."

Margot made tiny dots with her crayon. Pop, pop, pop. One space. Two spaces. Three spaces. Now the note said: I LOVE YOU GRANDPA.

Grandpa read it out loud. He gave Margot a big hug. "Best note ever," he said.

Then Margot found her stinky sock under the bed. She dropped it in the basket. "Even socks go in their own space," she said. Grandpa laughed and laughed.

Noah ran into the backyard. His team was waiting on the grass. All the kids had green shirts on. Noah had a green shirt too.

The coach blew the whistle. "Pass the ball," she said. Noah kicked the ball to a boy. But the boy had a blue shirt. The blue boy ran away with the ball. Noah stood still. He had given the ball away.

"Look for green shirts," said his friend Mia. Noah looked around. He saw green shirts here and there. Mia waved her arms. Her green shirt was bright in the sun. Noah kicked the ball to Mia. Mia kicked it back. The green team cheered.

After the game, Noah sat on the grass. He patted the ball like a horse going slow. "Good ball," he said. "Next time I will guess right. I will look for green." A bee buzzed by the fence. It was getting late. Dad called from the porch, "Time for dinner, Noah." Noah picked up the ball and ran home across the soft green grass.

Gabriel woke up and saw the sun. He was so excited. "Park day!" he shouted.

Then the sky turned dark. Rain hit the window. Tap, tap, tap. Gabriel could not go to the park now. His face felt sad. He sat on the floor.

"I wanted to swing," he said. A big tear ran down his cheek.

Mom knelt down beside him. "We need a new plan," she said. "Can you help me?"

Gabriel wiped his eye. "Okay," he said.

They got two chairs. Mom put a red blanket over the top. It made a tent. Gabriel crawled inside. "Wow!" he said. He brought his bear and his book. He shone his little flashlight. The tent glowed.

A loud boom of thunder came. Gabriel felt scared. He held his bear tight. Mom came in and held his hand too. The scared feeling got small.

Then Gabriel laughed. His fort was fun. He was happy inside it. "Mom, look! I am not sad now!" he said.

Mom smiled at him. "Come in, it's cozy," said Gabriel.

Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted red apples. He held Mama's hand in the middle of the big aisle. A girl stood by the apples with her dad. "I went to the park tomorrow," she said. Then she shook her head. "No, not tomorrow. Yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." Theodore looked up. He saw the apples. He kicked his shoe softly on the floor. "Mama, we got apples yesterday," he said. "That was yesterday," said Mama. "Today we get more." "And tomorrow we eat them," said Theodore. "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow." She put three red apples in the bag. One apple sat in the dark bottom of the cart. "Can we eat one now?" asked Theodore. "Not now," said Mama. "Later, at home." At home, later came. Mama cut the apples. Theodore sat close and waited. "Tomorrow we get more," he said. Mama smiled and handed him a slice. "Tomorrow," she said.

Leon sat on the big couch at Mr. Ted's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Leon could not remember who was winning.

"Papa, who has more points?" Leon asked.

"Look up high," said Papa. He pointed at the wall on the TV screen. "That is the scoreboard. It shows how many points each team has."

Leon looked. One team had a big number. One team had a small number. The team with the big number was winning.

"The red team is winning!" Leon shouted.

"Good eyes," said Mr. Ted. He bit into a cold, frozen popsicle. "Ooh, my teeth!"

Everyone laughed. Leon's shoe string had come untied, so he tied it himself.

Then the red team scored again. The scoreboard changed. The number got bigger.

"Look, look!" Leon said. "More points!"

Daniel was at school in the cooking classroom. He was making bread for his family. He mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Then he touched the dough. "Yuck!" said Daniel. "It's all sticky!"

The dough stuck to his fingers. It stuck to the table. "My bread is ruined," said Daniel. "It will never be bread now." His teacher smiled. "Cooks knead dough," she said. "Watch me." She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

"Now you try," she said. Daniel pushed the dough. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his fingers! Push and fold, push and fold. Soon the dough felt soft and smooth. "You did it!" said his teacher. Daniel laughed. "I made dough with my hands!" Later, his teacher put the bread in the oven where it was safe. Daniel waited and sniffed the air. "Mmm," he said. "Mama will smell this from home!"

Luca ran to his toy box in the dark shed. He wanted his blue ball for the yard. The shed had no window. It was very dark in there. Luca grabbed a ball. "I found it!" he shouted.

He ran out to the green grass. He looked at his ball. It was not blue. It was red! Luca laughed. "The dark tricked me," he said. He ran back inside the shed. It was still dark. He felt two more balls with his hands. He could not tell which one was blue.

Then he had a big idea. He pulled the balls out into the sun. One ball was yellow. One ball was green. And there, under the bench, was his blue ball! Luca kicked it high. It bounced on the grass by the yellow flowers. "Best ball ever," said Luca. "Best day ever, too."

Wesley ran into the band room. He wanted to play the big violin today. He picked it up and held it upside down. He plucked the strings. He swung his arm. The violin made a sad, wobbly sound. "That is not right," said Wesley.

The music teacher came over. She smiled. "A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument," she said. She turned the violin around. She put it under Wesley's chin. She placed the bow in his little hand. Wesley pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang out loud and sweet.

Wesley laughed. "It likes being right side up!" he said. He played again and again. His mom peeked in the door. "Is that my big boy?" she asked. Wesley played one more note. Then he took a crunchy cracker from his pocket and grinned. "I can play now, Mom!"

John sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. He tried to draw a circle. His circle came out wobbly. It went up, then down, then up again.

"You can use my cup," said Mia. She pushed her cup to him. John put the cup down on his paper. He held it with one finger on top. He traced his crayon all around the bottom of the cup. He lifted the cup up. There it was. A round circle, nice and neat.

"It's a circle!" said John. He traced it again and again. Around the circle he drew triangle rays for the sun. Then he drew a square house and a rectangle door.

"Look what the cup did," said John. Mia smiled and traced her own circle. "The cup helps," she said. The sun had a curly smile at last.

Myles ran to the backyard with his hat. "Today I will wear my sun hat!" he said. The sun felt warm on his nose. Then a big cloud came. Where did the sun go? The cloud hid it! Now the yard felt cold. Myles shivered. "Mom, the sun is gone!"

Mom brought his sweater. "Clouds can hide the sun," she said. "But wait. It may peek back out." So Myles waited by the fence. The wind blew. His naughty hat tried to fly away! He held it tight.

"What is that?" asked Myles. A turtle sat by the rocks. It was cold too. It did not move at all. "Is the turtle going to freeze?" Mom said no. "It just likes warm sun, like you."

Then the cloud moved. The sun came back! The turtle stretched its legs. Myles took off his sweater. His hat stayed on. "Hello again, sun," said Myles.

Camille wants to see the bubbles in the pot. Grandma fills the pot with water. Then she sets it on the stove.

"Stay back," says Grandma. "Steam is hot. It can burn."

Camille wants to be brave. She takes one step. Then she stops. The steam is like a little white cloud. It goes up, up, up. It reaches her cheeks from far away. It feels warm, not cold like ice. Camille jumps back.

"Too hot," she says.

"Come hold my hand," says Grandma. "We can watch from here."

Camille holds on tight. She counts the bubbles. One, two, three, four. The water goes pop, pop, pop.

"Steam, bubbles, pot," says Camille.

She watches it all from her safe spot. Maybe tonight she will dream about little white clouds.

Madison wanted to build a rainbow in her backyard. She dumped out her big toy box. Red blocks rolled on the grass. Blue blocks too. Yellow blocks went everywhere.

"I will sort them," said Madison. She made a red pile. She made a blue pile. She made a yellow pile. All the red things sat together in one group. All the blue things sat together. All the yellow things sat together.

Then she saw a green block. It was hiding in the blue pile! "You do not go there," she said. She put it in its own green group.

A toy snake was green too. Madison held him tight. "You live with the green things," she said. She shut her toy box with a bang.

Then she lined up all the piles. Red, blue, yellow, green. "It's a rainbow snake," she whispered, and she wiggled him all the way home.

Sophie sits in the car. The baby sits in his little seat. He is coming home today.

Sophie counts the things in the car. One blue bag. Two blankets. Three baby socks. All the things are for the baby.

Sophie has no things. "Mom," she says. "I miss you. It was just you and me before." Mom turns around in her seat. "I miss that too," Mom says. "It is okay to feel left out, Sophie. Big sisters can feel that way."

Mom holds out her hand. Sophie holds it. Mom's hand is warm. Then the baby makes a small sound. His face goes deep red. He is hungry.

Dad stops the car. Mom feeds the baby. Sophie waits. Then Mom says, "One cookie for my big girl." Sophie takes a bite. The baby watches her with big eyes.

"Hello, baby," says Sophie. "This is my cookie. I will share."

Benjamin was at daycare. He saw Mila crying by the toy shelf. Her doll had fallen on the floor. "She got hurt," Mila said. "She is sad."

Benjamin picked up the doll. He looked at its face. The doll did not cry. The doll was still and quiet. "Toys cannot really feel," said Teacher Rosa. "But you can pretend they do."

Benjamin had an idea. He held the doll close. He gave the doll a big hug. "There, there," he said softly. He patted the doll's back, just like his mom did for him. Mila stopped crying. She watched.

"Is the doll better now?" she asked. "Yes," said Benjamin. "The hug was magic." He laid the doll on a little blanket. He fed the doll a pretend apple. "Eat it all up," he said.

Mila smiled. She brought a stuffed bear. "The bear is scared," she said. "There is a big pretend mountain, and he has to climb it." Benjamin made his voice deep and brave. "I will help you, bear."

The two friends climbed the pretend mountain together, step by step, across the soft blue rug. "We made it to the top!" Benjamin shouted. The bear and the doll sat side by side, looking down at the whole daycare room.

Aurora hurried into Grandma's kitchen. The whole family was there. Cousins, aunts, uncles, everyone! Big pots sat on the stove. Uncle Ben stirred them with a long spoon.

"Time for the blessing," said Grandma. "We sing it before we eat."

Aurora blinked. Sing it? She thought blessings were spoken. "Can I lead it?" she asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You are lucky. It is your turn."

Aurora stood up tall. She took a big breath. Then she sang. But the tune came out wiggly and wrong. It sounded like a sleepy old cat. The little cousins giggled.

Aurora's face went hot. She wanted to hide under the table. But Grandma smiled and held her hand.

"Try again," said Grandma. "Slowly this time."

Aurora picked up a pencil from the counter. Grandma had drawn little notes on paper. Aurora looked at the notes. Then she sang again. She sang slowly. She sang each note in order.

This time the tune came out right. One note, then the next. The whole family joined in. Their voices filled the kitchen. Even baby cousin Sam hummed along.

When the song ended, Grandpa clapped. "That was the best one yet," he said.

"Tomorrow you can lead it again," said Grandma.

"I want to sing it twice!" said Aurora.

Grandma laughed and handed her the pencil. "We will sing it twice, and you can hold the notes."

Violet walked into the big house with her mama. There were little lamps everywhere. They looked like tiny stars.

"I want to light one," said Violet. Mama held her hand. "Flames are for grown-ups," said Mama. "But you can pick which lamp I light."

Violet looked and looked. She picked a small blue lamp on a low shelf. Mama took a match and lit it. The little flame came up. It was warm and bright. Violet watched from her step back.

There was a plant in the corner with big green leaves. Shadows from the lamps danced on the plant. One shadow looked like a bear. "Is it scary?" asked Violet. "No, it is just a leaf shadow," said Mama.

Violet picked more lamps for Mama to light. "This one, and this one," she said. Mama lit each one. Soon the whole room glowed. More lamps made more light.

Grandma came over and smiled. "You chose well," she said. Violet stood very still and watched the flames. "Our house shines," she whispered. Mama gave her a soft hug. Then Violet pointed at one more lamp, a red one, way up high. "That one too," she said.

Violet ran to school after breakfast. She was not late today. It was playtime in the yard.

"Let's play hide-and-seek," said her friend Mia. "You seek first, Violet."

Violet put her hands on the tree. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around.

Mia was still standing in the open. Ben was half behind a bush. Nobody was hidden yet.

"You counted too fast," said Mia. "Count slowly, Violet. We need time to hide."

Violet put her hands back on the tree. "One, two, three." She went slowly now. "Four, five, six." She heard little feet running. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

She turned around. The yard was quiet. Mia was not in the open. Ben was not half behind the bush. Violet looked behind the slide. No one. She looked by the sand. Then she saw two shoes under the coats on the fence.

"Found you, Mia!" said Violet. Mia laughed and jumped out.

"You counted slow," said Mia. "Now I got to hide."

Violet smiled. "Your turn to seek," she said. "I will count to ten for you."

William loved his little red truck. It was his very special toy. At summer camp, Miss Amy said, "Truck time, friends!"

Ben reached for the truck. William grabbed it fast. Ben's face went sad. William held the truck tight.

Then William had an idea. He walked to the shelf. He put the red truck up high, where only Miss Amy could reach. "I put it away," he said. "It can wait for me."

William found a big blue truck. He held it out to Ben. "Your turn first," said William. Ben smiled a big, friendly smile. He pushed the truck across the grass. It made a loud brmm sound. Then he gave it back. "Your turn, William!"

They took turns all morning. At water play, they filled a bowl and floated leaves in it. "You pour, then I pour," said Ben.

William's hands did not grab. They waited. And waiting made the game last a long, long time.

When camp was over, Miss Amy took the red truck down from the shelf. William hugged it all the way home.

Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. Rehmat wore her red coat. The coat hung open. The big door made wind. The wind blew the coat open wider. "Oh no!" said Rehmat. Her tummy felt cold.

Mama said, "Look at the zipper. It has two sides. Pull the tab up." Rehmat looked down. She saw two sides. She saw the little tab. She pulled the tab up. The two sides joined together. Zip! The coat closed. "I did it!" said Rehmat. She jumped up and down.

A man at the bank dropped his pen. Rehmat picked it up. She gave it back. "Thank you," said the man. "Sorry it fell," he said with a smile. Rehmat smiled too.

Then Rehmat wanted to try again. She pulled the tab down. The coat opened. She pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed. "Zip, zip, zip," sang Rehmat. Mama laughed. "You are so fast," said Mama. The wind blew again. This time the coat stayed warm and shut. "My turn to hold your hand," said Mama.

Luka sat at the paint table at summer camp. He had a pot of yellow. He had a pot of blue. He wanted to make green, like the grass.

"Try a little blue first," said his teacher, Mia. Luka dipped his brush. He stirred the blue into all the yellow. Swirl, swirl, swirl. Now the whole pot was green. Luka poked at it with his brush. He tried to find some yellow. It was gone. The blue and the yellow would not come apart again.

Mia smiled. "Next time, keep a little of each aside." She gave him a fresh pot of yellow. Luka kept a small bit safe in a cup. Then he mixed the rest, slow and careful. Green! He laughed. "Mother, look!" he called across the field. "Green like the grass!" His shy friend Pip peeped over and clapped.

Joshua ran into the school cooking room. Today he would make bread for his family. Miss Ana put a bowl on the big table. "First we stir," she said. Joshua stirred the soft, squishy dough. It felt like warm mud between his fingers. "Naughty dough, you keep sticking to me!" he giggled.

Then Joshua wanted butter on his bread. He opened the little fridge. The butter was hard and cold. He pushed it with his spoon. It would not spread. It just broke the bread into pieces. One piece, two pieces, three pieces. "Oh no," said Joshua.

Miss Ana smiled. She put the hard butter on the counter. "We will let it sit," she said. Joshua waited. He counted to ten. He smelled the sweet bread baking. Miss Ana touched the butter. "Try now," she said. Joshua pushed his spoon. The butter was soft! It spread over the warm bread, one swipe, two swipes, three swipes.

Joshua held up his bread. "Mama will love this!" he said. He gave the spoon one more happy stir.

Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. A big red truck sat on the rug. Charlie wanted it right now.

Ben had the truck first. Charlie reached out to grab it. Her hand touched the truck. The wheel scratched her finger. "Ouch," she said. The truck felt bumpy and hard.

Miss Amy knelt down beside them. She held up a little timer. "Ben, when the timer rings, your turn is done," she said. Charlie sat on her leg and waited. The timer rang. Ding! Ben lifted the truck high. He almost tossed it. Then he stopped. He put it in Charlie's hands, gently, like a baby bird.

The truck was warm from Ben's hands. Charlie pushed it across the rug. Vroom! Then the timer rang again. Now it was her turn to be done. She walked to Ben. She held the truck out softly.

"Your turn," said Charlie. Ben smiled big. Then he let her push the truck one more time, together.

Miles sat in the car with his blanket. He was going to get his first haircut. "I like my hair," said Miles. Mom parked the car. They walked in together.

The barber put a cape on Miles. It was blue and big. Snip, snip went the scissors. A little curl fell down. It landed on the cape. The barber brushed it into his hand.

Miles watched Mom take out a small envelope. She put the curl inside. "Why?" asked Miles. Mom said, "To remember your first haircut." Miles smiled. He held the envelope all the way to the car. The curl was soft, like his blanket. Mom buckled him in. Miles looked at the envelope. "We keep it," he said.

Parker wanted to paint at school. But the paint cups were missing. "They are drying," said Miss Ana. "We washed them yesterday. They will be dry today."

Parker looked at the big clock on the wall. "When will it be time to paint?" he asked. Miss Ana pointed at the clock. "The clock shows what time it is," she said. "The little hand moves. When it points up, it will be paint time."

Parker watched the clock. He stacked blocks. He looked again. The hand moved a tiny bit. He read a book about a bear. He looked up. The hand moved some more.

"Now!" called Miss Ana. The paint cups were dry. Parker dipped his brush in red. He made a big sun. "Tomorrow," he said, "I will paint a moon."

Anna was at the school playground. Her bunny was gone. "Where is bunny?" she said. She looked under the slide. No bunny. She looked by the swing. No bunny. Anna sat down on the short wall. She wanted to cry.

Then her big sister came. "I can help you look," said Mia. "Two people can look." Dad came too. "Now we all can look," he said. Anna looked by the sand. Mia looked by the park gate. Dad looked in the toy box. Dad lifted a small coat. The coat was folded on top of something soft. There was bunny!

"My bunny!" said Anna. She hugged bunny tight. More people looked, and they found her. "Let's go home," said Dad, and Anna held Mia's hand all the way.

Milo went to the park with Dad. He saw a big red hoop on the grass. "I want to throw my ball in," said Milo. He threw his ball at the hoop. The ball hit the rim and bounced away. It rolled down the hill. Milo ran after it, but he felt dizzy from spinning around. Dad caught the ball for him.

Then Milo found a small beanbag in the toy bag. He threw the beanbag at the hoop. It did not bounce away. It hit the rim and went flop. It fell soft and slow, right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Milo. He threw the beanbag again and again. Each time it went flop, flop, right in.

Dad held out a big ball. "Now catch it with both hands," said Dad. Milo held out both arms. The ball came down and Milo caught it in a big hug. Milo laughed and laughed. The world felt sunny and good. He filled his arms with the ball and ran to Dad for one more throw.

Eli wanted a story about a big red truck. He could not find one at daycare. He looked in the little basket. He looked under the rug. Then he found a book with a truck on the top.

Eeli sat down with the book. He opened it from the back. Miss Ana came over. "Books start at the front," she said. She turned the book around. "We read from here." She pointed to the first page. Then she put her finger under the little black marks. "These are words," she said. "I read the words out loud." She read them, and the story came out!

Eli turned a page. There were no words there, just a picture of the truck going fast. "Read this one!" he said. Miss Ana smiled. "There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read." So they just looked at the picture together.

Eli got another book. He opened it at the front. He put his finger under the words. "Read these!" he said. Miss Ana read them all. Eli clapped. At pickup time, he ran to his dad. "Dad, read the words!" he said, holding up the book.

Today was Daddy's birthday. Lena wanted to make him a cake. She helped Mama crack the eggs. The batter dripped off the spoon. Lena frowned. "It is so runny!" she said. "It will spill all over. It can't be a cake." Mama smiled. "Watch the oven," she said. Mama poured the batter into a pan. Then Mama put the pan in the oven. Lena stood back, far from the hot door. She waited. She wiggled her toes. "Is it still runny in there?" she asked. Mama said, "You will see."

The kitchen got warm. A sweet smell filled the room. Lena sniffed and sniffed. The timer rang and she gave a little yell. Mama put on big mitts. She pulled out a real cake. It was tall and golden. Lena poked it with one finger. It was soft, but not runny at all. "Mama, look!" she said. "It got thick!" Mama cut one slice for Daddy. Lena drew a fox on his card. Daddy took a big bite. "Best cake ever," he said. "Lena made it!" Lena grinned and clapped her hands.

Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Baba. Red paper lanterns hung from the ceiling. Lillian wanted to see the lion dance.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were so noisy. Lillian hid behind Mama's back. The big lion came out. It was red and gold. But the lion did not move.

Mama held her hand. "Look at the lion," she said. "Listen to the drums." The drummer hit the drum. Boom! Then the lion jumped. The drummer hit it again. Boom! Then the lion shook its head. Lillian saw it. The drums made the lion dance!

She came out from behind Mama. She clapped her hands to the beat. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! The lion hopped to her. It blinked its big eyes. Lillian laughed and clapped some more.

Henry put on his red shoe. Then he put on the other one. "We are going on a trip!" he said. The car was packed full of bags. Dad started the engine. Henry sat in his seat and looked out the window.

The sky looked stormy and gray. "Will the rain stop our trip?" Henry asked. "No," said Mom. "We will drive right past it." The rain tapped on the roof. Tap, tap, tap. Then the sun came out. Henry clapped his hands.

Soon they got to the airport. Airports are busy places. Henry saw big planes out the window. He wanted to run to them fast. "Wait," said Mom. She held out her hand. Henry remembered. In busy places, he stays close to his grown-up. He grabbed Mom's hand and held it tight. Together they walked through the crowd.

"Can I see the planes?" asked Henry. "Yes," said Dad. "Hand in hand, all the way." Henry held on. They walked and walked. Then they stopped at a big window. A huge plane zoomed up into the sky. Henry pressed his nose to the glass. "Up, up, up it goes!"

Ibrahim looked out the window. White flakes fell from the sky. "It is snowy today," said Mama. "Snowy!" said Ibrahim. He put on his boots. He put on his puffy coat. He ran outside and made a snowball. His hands felt cold. Very cold. "Ow," said Ibrahim. He ran back to Mama. "Hands are cold!" Mama held his little red hands. "Your mittens," she said. "Mittens keep your hands warm." Ibrahim remembered his mittens. They were on the shelf by the door. He pulled them on. His hands felt warm. Good and warm. He made a new snowball. He threw it at the fence. Then he heard a beep. His toy robot sat in the snow by the door. "Robot is outside!" said Ibrahim. He picked the robot up with his warm mittens and hugged it all the way inside.

Evelyn lived in a little house with her mama. One morning, Mama put on a song. The song had a steady beat. Evelyn patted her knees, but too fast. Mama clapped slow. Clap, clap, clap. Evelyn tried again, slow like Mama. Clap, clap, clap. Now her claps fit the song.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat sat on the red hat." Evelyn wanted to sing it too. She sang, "The cat sat on the..." Then she stopped. The next word was gone. She could not find it.

She looked at the floor. There was her red block. She held the block and thought. Hat. Block did not sound right at the end. She tried more words in her head. Cat, hat, bat, mat. "Mat!" said Evelyn. "The cat sat on the mat!" Mama laughed and clapped. "Yes! Mat rhymes with cat. Both end the same."

Evelyn stood up tall. She sang the whole rhyme. She clapped on the beat while she sang. Clap, clap, clap. Mama clapped too. Evelyn sang it one more time, all by herself.

"Again, Mama!" said Evelyn. "Sing it again!"

Kinsley went to the park with Dad. She saw a big red ball near the slide. She wanted to play with it. A boy named Tom had the ball. Tom threw the ball to his friend. His friend ran off with it. Then the friend stopped. He turned around and said, "Thank you, Tom!" Then he ran back to play. Kinsley watched with wide eyes.

Kinsley wanted a turn too. She walked to Tom. "Can I have the ball, please?" she asked. Tom smiled and rolled the ball to her. Kinsley caught it. She held it tight. The slide was wet and slippery, so she played on the flat square of pavement instead. She kicked the ball high. It flew over the bench and landed in a bush. Kinsley felt worried. "My ball is stuck," she said. Dad came over. "I can help," he said. Dad reached in and got the ball out.

Kinsley hugged the ball. "Thank you, Dad," she said. Dad smiled. Tom waved from the swings. "Come play!" he called. Kinsley ran to him over the square tiles. She passed the ball to Tom.
