Tom caught it. "Thank you, Kinsley!" he said. They laughed and kicked the ball back and forth. Dad sat on the bench and watched. The sun went down slow. "Time to cook dinner," said Dad. Kinsley took his hand. "Bye, Tom! Thank you for playing!" she called. Tom waved his big wave.

Paisley held Mama's hand at the shelter. Cats and dogs sat in little rooms with doors. "They wait here," said Mama. "They wait for a family to take them home."

Paisley walked past the dogs. She walked past the cats. Then she saw a small gray cat. The cat looked back at her. "This one," said Paisley. "This one waits for me."

A helper opened the door. The cat rode home in a box with holes. At home, Paisley set out water. She set out food. "Kittens get scared," said Mama. "Let's be quiet." Paisley sat very still on the floor.

The moon came up. The cat peeked out of the box. It sniffed the water. It drank a little sip. Paisley saw the water go down in the bowl. She put a bit more in. The cat drank again. "You were thirsty," whispered Paisley. The cat curled up next to her. Paisley petted its soft fur, very, very gently.

Georgia put on her big farm hat. The hat was too loose. It fell over her eyes. "I want to help," she said.

Farmer Ben smiled. "You can sort this basket," he said. "Find the soft things. Find the rough things." Georgia touched a feather. It tickled her hand. "Soft," she said. She touched a pinecone. It was bumpy and hard on her fingers. "Rough," she said. Then she touched a soft blanket. Her hand felt the softness right away.

"My hand knows!" said Georgia. "My skin tells me soft or rough." Farmer Ben nodded. "Yes, your skin feels it," he said. Georgia touched the baby chick's fluffy feathers. Soft. She touched the old wooden fence. Rough. She laughed and clapped.

Then Georgia found a smooth stone. It was not soft like the feather. It was not rough like the pinecone. "This one is in the middle," she said. She put the stone in her pocket. She ran to show her mama. "Feel this!" said Georgia. "My skin can tell!"

Olivia stood by the little clock at school. It was time to go outside. Miss Ana held up Olivia's coat. "Can you try?" she asked.

Olivia pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat sat on her shoulders. Now the zipper. She pinched the tab and pushed it up. It would not go. It slid down instead. The coat opened wide. "Look," said Olivia. "Down makes it open." She tried again. She pushed the tab up, slowly, slowly. Zip! The coat was closed.

At recess, Olivia ran and jumped. She got very warm. So she pulled the tab down. The coat opened all by itself. Cool air came in. "I did it," she said. Her friend Ben wore a different coat. His zipper went down too. After play, Miss Ana said it was almost time to wash hands, like a little bath for fingers. Olivia zipped her coat up again. "All done," she said.

Axel sat down at the dinner table. He was very hungry. "Peas tonight!" he said. Mama put the plate in front of him.

"Let's count them," said Mama. "One, two, three, four, five." Axel counted five green peas. Then he counted his fingers too. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Five fingers, five peas!"

Then Axel saw his birthday card on the table. It had a big red mark on it. The mark looked like this: 5. "What is that?" he asked. "That is five," said Mama. Axel's eyes got wide. "That is my five? The same five?" He held up five fingers next to the card. "Five and five! They match!"

"Now eat your peas," said Mama. "Don't forget your carrots too." Axel ate fast. Then he smiled big. One tooth was missing in front. "I want to count to ten now," he said. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

After dinner, Axel ran to the door. There was a number on it too. He pointed at it and shouted, "That says five too! I found another one!"

Milan loved story time at school. He wanted a story now. He ran to Teacher Rosa.

"Can we have the story now?" he asked.

Teacher Rosa smiled. "Not now. Now means at this very moment. First we have snack. The story comes later."

Milan sat down. He looked at the clock. He ate his crackers. He drank his water. He waited and waited.

"Now?" he asked again.

"Not yet," said Teacher Rosa. "Now you are eating. Later we will cook pretend soup in the story."

Milan kept waiting. He stacked a coin on the table. He watched the bright fish swim in the tank. He waited some more.

Yesterday the story was about a red bus. Today the story would be about soup. Tomorrow there would be a new story too.

At last Teacher Rosa clapped her hands. "Snack is done. The story is now!"

Milan jumped up. "Now, now, now!" he said.

He sat on the rug and hugged his knees. "Once there was a big pot," Teacher Rosa began.

Milan leaned in close to hear.

Jaxson was playing in the yard. He dug in the dirt with his little shovel. His hands got dirty. His sister, a big girl named Mia, called him in for lunch.

Jaxson ran to the table. He saw bread, cheese, and apple slices. He counted them out loud. One apple, two apples, three apples. He reached for his plate.

Mia held up her hand. "Stop. Look at your hands." Jaxson looked. There was dirt on his fingers. Mia pointed to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Jaxson walked to the sink. Mia turned on the water. It felt warm and bubbly. The soap smelled like lemons. Jaxson rubbed his hands together. The bubbles took the dirt away. He rinsed and dried them on the soft towel.

Then he sat down and picked up his apple slice. It was clean and sweet. Jaxson smiled. "Wash first, then eat," he said. Mia laughed and gave him a kiss on his head. After lunch, Jaxson yawned and whispered, "Bath next."

Zoe went to the park with Mama and Dad. The park had big trees and a lake. "Look, a deer!" said Dad. Zoe waved at the deer. It ran away.

Zoe found a pretty rock by the water. It was gray with white lines. She put it in her pocket. Then Zoe saw a big wheel on a car. It was parked in the mud. The wheel spun and spun. Mud went splat on the grass. "The wheel made the mud fly!" said Zoe.

Dad opened his backpack. He took out a camera. "Smile, Zoe," he said. Click! He took a photo of Zoe and the rock. Click! He took a photo of the deer track in the mud. Zoe helped Dad find more things to snap. A tall tree. A red bird. The lake.

At home, Zoe felt sad. "I miss the park," she said. Mama opened the photo book. There was Zoe with her rock. There was the tall tree and the red bird. "We can look any time we want," said Mama. Zoe held her gray rock tight. "Again," she said. "Show the deer track again."

Billie stood in the kitchen. The pot on the stove went puff, puff, puff. "Hot," said Mom. "Stay back." Billie stayed back. She touched the cold milk carton instead. It felt smooth and cool.

Then Mom said, "We need apples. Let's go to the store." The store was big and bright. The doors went swing, and in they walked. Billie held Mom's hand. But then she saw a red swing toy on a shelf, and she stopped to look. When she looked up, Mom was gone. Billie asked herself, "What do I do now?" She knew the answer. Find a store worker. She saw a woman at the checkout with a green vest. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. The woman smiled and took her hand. Mom came running, and Billie hugged her tight. "Let's get those apples," said Mom.

Hayden wants to wash his hands. He stands by the sink. Mom turns the tap. First the water runs cold. Then it runs warm. Mom checks it with her hand. "Just right," she says.

On the shelf, Hayden sees something. Little red dots in a bottle. They look like candy. He wants one. He reaches up high. "Wait," says Mom. She puts her hand out. Hayden stops.

"Those are not candy," says Mom. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." She takes the bottle down. She clicks the cap shut. She puts the bottle up high, far away.

"Can I wash my lion now?" asks Hayden. He holds up his special toy lion. Mom laughs. "Yes. Hold him up to the water." Hayden holds the lion under the tap. Cold water runs over the lion's paws. Hayden laughs too.

Mom dries the lion with a soft towel. Hayden hugs him tight. "All clean," he says.

Aaron ran to the playground. He wanted his little blue car. He looked in his pocket. The car was not there.

"Where did you go?" Aaron asked. His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Retracing your steps," she said. "Go back to each place you went, in order."

Aaron thought hard. First he had gone to the swings. He walked back to the swings. He looked under the seat. No car. Next he had gone down the slide. He walked to the slide. He looked at the bottom. No car. Last he had played in the sandbox. He ran to the sandbox. There, in the sand, was the blue car!

"I found it!" Aaron said. He held it up high. Miss Kim clapped. "Let the car ride down the slide," she said. Aaron set the car at the top. It zoomed down. Aaron laughed and chased it across the cloudy sky's little shadow on the ground.

Asher skipped to the sink. It was snack time at summer camp. His team sat at a cozy table with apple slices.

Asher turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. But there were no bubbles. He looked and looked. Not one bubble.

He called to his friend Maya. "Look at my hands. No bubbles!"

Maya held up her hands. They were full of white bubbles. "I used soap," she said.

Asher found the soap bottle. He put one pump on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed the soap and water together. Bubbles! Lots of bubbles! They popped on his fingers.

"Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles," he sang.

He counted to twenty with Maya. Then he rinsed and dried his hands. His hands were clean and warm.

Asher picked up an apple slice. "I love bubbles," he said. He took a big, happy bite.

Mya stood in the storytime room. The rug had striped pillows on it. Today Mya would get her first library card.

The librarian smiled at her. "Sign your name here," she said. Mya wrote the letters, one by one. M, Y, A. The card was blue and shiny.

"Now you can borrow a book," said the librarian. Mya wanted a book about trucks. She looked on the shelf. She saw a book about bears. She saw a book about paint. No trucks. She looked again. Still no trucks.

Mya tapped her chin. Then she walked back to the librarian. "Can you help me find trucks?" she asked.

"I help people find books," said the librarian. "That is my job. Let's look together." They walked to the other side of the room. The librarian pulled out a big red book. It was all about trucks!

Mya hugged the book. "I did it," she said. "My first book."

The other kids began to clap. Mya held up her card and her truck book. "One card, one book, one happy day," said Mya. The librarian laughed and stamped the book. "Bring it back next week," she said, "and we'll find two."

Luka sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to be brave today. The nurse came in with a tray. "Let's check you all over," she said.

First, Luka used his eyes to see the tray. He saw a small light, a sticker, and a lemon slice. Next, he used his ears to hear the doctor knock. Knock, knock. Then Luka used his nose to smell the lemon. "Does it smell like orange juice?" he asked. "Smell it and see," said the nurse. Luka sniffed. It smelled sharp and lemony.

"Now touch the cotton ball," said the nurse. Luka used his fingers to touch it. It was soft like a cloud. "Last thing," said the nurse. "Taste the lemon." Luka used his tongue. He thought it would taste sweet like orange juice. He took a little lick. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!"

"Does my tongue always know?" Luka asked. "It knew today," said the nurse. She gave him water. Luka drank it all. Then he put the sticker on his shirt. It was a gold fish that looked like it could swim in the sea. On the way home, Luka waved the lemon slice at his mom. "Taste it," he said. "It is sour." His mom took a tiny bite and made a funny face too.

Jordan sat at the big table. His whole family was there. Grandma was there too. The restaurant had a huge screen on the wall. A big game was on. Jordan wanted to cheer like the big kids.

The blue team ran fast. Jordan jumped up. "Go blue team!" he shouted. He clapped and clapped. But then everyone at the table went quiet. Uncle Max laughed. "Jordan, we like the red team!" Jordan's face turned warm. He had clapped for the wrong team.

Then the red team scored a goal. Everyone stood up and cheered. They clapped so loud. Jordan saw what made them cheer. So he stood up too. He clapped his hands and yelled, "Go red team!" Grandma gave him a high five. Jordan cheered loudest of all.

Liam stood in the school computer lab. A tablet sat on the big table. He wanted to draw a big sun on it. He did not know how to begin.

Miss Ada showed him the round button. Liam pressed it with one finger. He waited. The screen lit up. Liam clapped his hands. "I made it wake up!" he said.

Miss Ada tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. Liam picked yellow. He drew a big round sun on the screen. Then he drew wiggly rays. The tablet felt smooth and warm in his hands.

Time to put it away. Liam picked up the tablet with one hand. It tipped and slid. His tummy jumped. He caught it just in time. "Hold it with two hands," said Miss Ada. Liam held it with two hands, one on each side. He held it tight. The tablet did not tip. It did not fall. It sat safe and still.

Liam walked slowly to the shelf. He set the tablet down soft as a kitten. Miss Ada smiled and pushed the button. The screen went dark. Liam waved at the sleeping tablet. "Bye bye, sun," he said.

Madison stood at the running track. Her dad held out a red beanbag. "Throw it in the hoop," he said. Madison looked at her friend Nina. She threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. It did not go in the hoop.

"Try again," said Nina. Madison looked at the hoop. She kept looking at it. She threw the beanbag. Plip! It went right in. "My eyes helped me!" said Madison. Her dad clapped his hands.

Then Dad rolled a big ball to her. "What if it's too big?" asked Madison. "Hold it with both hands," said Dad. The ball came near. Madison held out both hands. She caught it! She stood up straight like a tall pig statue by the fence. Then she threw the beanbag again, still looking at the hoop. In it went. "Again!" said Madison.

Arlo woke up and put on his shoes. He was ready for school. He ran to the window. Everything outside was white.

"No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day. A snow day is a day when school is closed because of snow."

Arlo looked outside. "Can I touch it?" he asked.

"Put on your boots," said Mom. She helped him tie the laces tight. His pet dog, Biscuit, barked at the door.

Arlo stepped into the backyard. The snow was cold on his hands. His boots sank in. He made a footprint. Biscuit stepped next to it and made a paw print. Two prints side by side!

Arlo found his red sled. He pulled it up the small hill. He sat down and pushed. The sled did not move. He pushed again. Still nothing.

Then he wiggled to the top of the snowy slope. He sat and slid. Whoosh! He went fast down the hill. The snow made him slide!

"Again!" said Arlo. He climbed up and slid down. Up and down, over and over. Biscuit ran beside him every time.

Mom called from the door. "Hot cocoa is ready."

Arlo held the warm cup with both hands. He looked at his hill. "Snow day is the best day," he said. Biscuit licked the air and wagged his tail.

Leon went to the hair salon with Mama. It was his first haircut. The hairdresser was named Nan. She had a big chair and shiny scissors.

Leon climbed up into the big chair. Nan put a soft cape on him. Then Leon saw the fish tank. Three orange fish were swimming in it. One fish went round and round. Leon turned his head to see the fish. Snip! went the scissors, too long on one side.

"Hold still like a statue," said Nan, smiling. "Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly." Leon looked at the fish one more time. Then he sat very still, like a statue. He counted the fish in his head. One fish, two fish, three fish. Snip, snip, snip. Nan cut all around his head.

Mama held his hand the whole time. At last Nan took off the cape. Leon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I see a little rainbow!" said Nan, pointing at the shiny scissors catching the light. Leon laughed. He was a tired, happy boy. Mama picked him up and hugged him tight. "Home now," she said, "to cook your supper."

Owen did not want to go to the doctor. "Shots make me grumpy," he said. Mom laughed. "No shots today. Just a checkup." Owen held his toy bear. The bear needed a checkup too.

First the doctor looked in Owen's ears. "Ears are for hearing," she said. Owen heard the paper crinkle under him. Then she looked in his eyes. "Eyes are for seeing." Owen saw a sticker chart on the wall. He sniffed the air. "This room smells like my bread at home," he said. The doctor laughed. "Your nose knows!"

The doctor held a tiny cup. "Taste this," she said. It was sweet. "Yum," said Owen. "Your tongue did that," she said. Then she put a cotton ball in his hand. "Squeeze it." It was soft and squishy.

"Now take off your shoes and socks," said the doctor. Owen pulled them off. He put his bare toes on the cold floor. "Brrr!" he said. Then the doctor put a soft towel under his feet. His toes felt warm and fuzzy.

"Your feet can feel things too," said the doctor, "like soft grass under bare toes." Owen looked down. He wiggled his toes on the towel. The towel tickled, just like grass!

At home, Mom let Owen play in the yard. He took off his shoes again. He stepped on the green grass. "Tickle, tickle, toes!" he shouted. Then Owen put his bear in the grass. "You can feel it too," he told the bear. He ran in a circle, laughing. "My feet are so smart!"

Anna sat at Grandma's table. The bowls were hot. Grandma had stirred the soup, and Mom had carried it over. Anna picked up her spoon. She took a big bite.

Then she looked up. Everyone else was sitting still. Their hands were folded. Nobody was eating. "We say thank-you first," said Grandma. "Many families say a thank-you before they start eating." Anna put her spoon down. She folded her hands too.

Grandma lit a little candle. She was the grown-up, so she held the match. "Thank you for the soup," Grandma said. "Thank you for the bread," said Mom. Anna wanted a turn. "Thank you for the cow," she said. "The cow helped make the milk!" Everyone smiled.

Grandma pointed at Anna. "Your turn was the best one," she said. Then Grandma blew out the candle. The smoke went up in a thin line. Anna watched it curl and vanish. "Now we eat," said Grandma. Anna took her spoon again. The soup was still warm.

Edouard wanted to read the pet book. It had a soft red cover and it smelled like paper. He opened the book. But he started at the back page. He ran his finger from the right side of the page. The picture looked all jumbled.

His teacher Ms. Lily sat down next to him. "Let me help you," she said. She put his finger at the left side of the page. "Start here." Edouard slid his finger from left to right. One word, two words, three words. "The... dog... runs," he said. He held the book tight in his lap. The words made the picture make sense.

"Did I read it?" Edouard asked. "Yes, you did," said Ms. Lily. Edouard turned to the next page. He began at the left side all by himself.

Claire wants to paint at daycare. Today the paint is all used up. "We will get more paint tomorrow," says Miss Ana. Claire sighs. Tomorrow feels far away.

Yesterday Claire played a game outside. But today is a cloudy day. Miss Ana says, "We can play inside now. And soon we will have a snack." Soon. What does soon mean? Claire waits. She builds a tower. She reads a book. Then the snack table comes out.

"See?" says Miss Ana. "Soon means in a little while." Claire eats her crackers. The wait was not long at all. After snack, Miss Ana brings out new crayons. "Soon we can draw too," she says. Claire smiles and waits. Soon is easy now. "Crackers first," says Claire. "Drawing later."

Zoey sat on the rug at daycare. She had cardboard, tape, and a big want. She wanted to build a toy car for the class fish rug. "My car can give the fish a ride," she said. First she cut four squares. Four square wheels, one for each side. She taped them on and gave the car a pull. The car bumped. It stopped. It would not roll. Why not?

Ben rolled by on a truck. His truck had round wheels. Round like a circle. Zoey looked at her square wheels. Then she looked at his circle wheels. Hmm. Could that be it? She asked Miss Pam for help with the scissors. Miss Pam held the scissors and cut four circles. Zoey taped them on herself. Round wheels, one for each side.

Zoey pulled the car again. It rolled! It rolled all the way across the rug. "Look, look!" she said. Ben put his fish on top. The fish rode and rode. "You were brave to try again," said Miss Pam. Zoey smiled and gave the car one more pull. Around and around the rug it went, riding the happy fish home.

Elizabeth was at daycare. It was snack time. Miss Jo put green peas on every plate.

Tommy looked at his peas. "Yuck!" he shouted. Miss Jo gave him a sad little frown. Nobody clapped for Tommy.

Then Mia looked at her peas. She folded her hands. "No, thank you," she said. Miss Jo smiled big. "Of course, Mia. Here are carrots instead."

Elizabeth wanted carrots too. She held her breath. "No, thank you," she said, straight and tall, like a small queen.

"Carrots for Elizabeth!" said Miss Jo.

After snack, Elizabeth pretended her carrot was a butterfly. One orange wing, two orange wings. "Please fly to me," she said. The carrot flew up, up, up.

"Thank you, butterfly," said Elizabeth. "Thank you."

Alexander stood at the bus stop with Mama. He had on his blue coat. The zipper was open. "I can do it," he said. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. Then it slid back down. He tried again. This time the zipper stayed. "I win!" said Alexander.

Little drops began to fall. Drip, drip, on his nose. "Oh no," said Alexander. "Rain." Then he felt something on his coat. It was a soft part at the top. What could it be? "That is your hood," said Mama. "The hood is the part of a coat you can pull up over your head." Alexander pulled it up. It covered his head like a turtle shell.

The rain went drip, drip, drip. Alexander stayed dry. He looked up at the hood. "Did you keep me dry?" he asked. The bus came. Alexander climbed in, not wet at all. His hands were tired from the zipper, but he smiled. "My hood works," he said.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Olivier was so happy. On day one, they went to the big park. Grandpa sat on the green bench. He opened his bag. He took out bread. "This is my bread," said Grandpa. "Our family has made it for a long, long time. My own grandma taught me."

Olivier took a little bite. It was warm inside. How did it get so soft? "Can I help make it?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "We will cook it together tomorrow."

The next morning, they stood in the kitchen. Grandpa gave Olivier a bowl. Olivier put in flour. Grandpa poured the water. Olivier mixed it with a spoon. The dough was sticky and stiff.

Then Grandpa said, "Now we push it and fold it." Olivier pushed the dough. He folded it. He pushed it again. The dough began to feel different. It became soft and stretchy! "Look, Grandpa! My hands did that!" said Olivier.

Grandpa put the dough near the warm oven, where grown-ups watch. They waited. The dough got big and puffy. Grandpa slid it in with his big gloves. Soon the kitchen smelled wonderful.

At the park, they sat by the pond. A sign said, "Feed the ducks, not the geese." Olivier laughed. He held his warm slice of family bread. He took a big bite and said, "Grandpa, can we make it again tomorrow?"

Eleanor was a little child with curly hair. She played at the park with Grandma. "I want a snack," Eleanor said. Grandma said, "Soon. We go home for dinner next."

Eleanor slid down the slide. Her hands felt the smooth metal. She heard a dog bark with her ears. She saw a red kite up high. She smelled flowers with her nose.

Then Eleanor sniffed the air. "I smell dinner, Grandma! It is soup!" Grandma laughed. "We can smell dinner before we see it. Good nose." They walked home fast. In the kitchen, Daddy stirred the big pot. Grandma gave Eleanor a small taste from a cool spoon. "Soup!" Eleanor said. It was warm and good. Daddy filled her bowl.

Henri sat at the big table in the community hall. His grandma sat next to him. Bowls of soup were coming down the long table. Henri picked up his spoon.

Then everyone at the table reached out their hands. Hands went from person to person, all around. Henri held his spoon tight. His hand could not hold a spoon and a hand too.

Grandma smiled at him. "We hold hands while we say the blessing," she said. Henri put his spoon down on the table. It made a little click. Now his hand was free. He took grandma's hand on one side. He took a kind man's hand on the other side.

Everyone closed their eyes. Grandma said the blessing out loud. Her voice was soft and thick like warm honey. The soup smelled good. Outside the window, a green hill sat under the sky.

Then hands let go. Henri picked his spoon back up. He ate his soup, bite by bite. Grandma gave him bread. "Good job, Henri," she said. Henri smiled and took another big sip.

Sofia lived by the sea. The beach was big and sandy. But today she was going somewhere new. Today she was going to the pool!

Sofa grabbed her furry towel. Mama helped her carry her swim bag. They walked past the sand and the waves. Soon they saw the pool. It was bright blue and shiny. Sofia jumped up and down. "I want to swim right now!" she said.

A boy was standing by the pool. He was dripping wet. Sofia ran to jump in too. A lifeguard called out, "Stop! Take a shower first." Sofia stopped fast. "A shower?" she asked. "Yes," said the boy. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." So Sofia ran to the little shower. The water went splish splash. Then she skipped back to the pool.

"Can I jump in now?" Sofia asked. "Yes, you can!" said Mama. Sofia held Mama's hand. She kicked her legs in the water. "Look at me!" she cried. "I am swimming!" The water went splash, splash, splash.

Bennett held his swim bag. He was at the pool with Dad. Today he would learn to swim.

The changing room floor was wet. Bennett saw it shine. Why did it shine like that? He wanted to find out.

Bennett started to run to the pool door. "Walk, please," said Dad. "Wet floors around a pool are slippery, so people walk instead of run."

Bennett stopped his feet. He took little steps. Walk, walk, walk. His feet did not slide at all. Then he looked at Dad's feet. Dad walked too. Dad's feet did not slide either.

A big kid ran past them. His feet went slip, slip, slip. He wobbled like a jelly. A grown-up held his arm and said, "Walk, please."

Bennett kept walking. All the people in the hall walked. Nobody slid. Nobody fell.

He got to the pool door. The water was blue and bright. Bennett looked up at Dad.

"Everyone is walking," said Bennett. "I am walking too."

Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week! Anna waited in the kitchen by the window. She counted the things on the table. One cup for Grandma. One cup for Anna. Two cups!

A car pulled up. Grandma was here! Anna ran to the door. She wanted to hug Grandma. But Grandma had so many bags. Her arms were full. No room for a hug.

"Hello, Grandma!" said Anna. She waved her hand up high. Grandma put down one bag. She waved back. "Hello, Anna!" said Grandma.

Then the bags were inside. Grandma's arms were free at last. "Now I can hug you," said Grandma. The hug was big and warm.

They made toast together. Mom held the knife and cut it. Anna ripped a paper napkin into pieces for their messy crumbs. Anna counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four!"

"That was my best hello ever," said Anna, waving again.

Brielle wanted to play outside. She looked out the big window. Today was a windy day. The trees waved their leaves. "Windy," said Brielle. Mom put a hat on her head. "Hold on to your hat," said Mom.

Brielle ran out to the grass. The wind puffed her cheeks. Then the wind pulled her hat. Off it went, fast across the yard! Brielle chased it. The hat rolled like a wheel. Her dog Max ran too, his nose sniffing the air.

The hat stopped by the bush. Brielle picked it up. She hugged it tight. Then she put it back on her head. The wind came again. Off went the hat again! Brielle laughed. "Silly wind," she said.

Brielle held the hat with both hands. She carried it like a little bowl. The wind could not take it now. Mom came out with her own hat on. "That wind is strong," said Mom.

Brielle and Max walked to meet Mom at the gate. The wind tickled Brielle's hair. "It can blow my hat," said Brielle. "But not today." She sat down in the soft grass and held her hat on her lap.

Eliana ran into the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a cake on the table. Everyone clapped for her. "Why is everyone so happy today?" she asked. Grandma sat down next to her. She held out a thick photo album. She opened it to a small photo. It showed a tiny baby. "That is you," said Grandma. "That is the day you were born. Today we celebrate that day. It is your birthday." Eliana looked at the baby. Then she looked at the cake. The cake had three candles. Daddy lit the candles with a match. Then he blew out the match. Eliana blew at the candles. They went out. Everyone cheered again. Eliana pointed at the snow outside the window. "The baby is in here," she said, "and the snow is out there." Grandma laughed and hugged her tight.

Riley went to the park with her dad. The wind was blowing. It puffed her hair all around. Sand flew up from the sandbox. A little bit went toward her face. Riley blinked fast. The sand did not get in her eyes.

"Why did I blink?" she wondered. She looked in her dad's little mirror. She saw tiny hairs on her eyelids. "Dad, what are these little hairs?" she asked. "Those are your eyelashes," said Dad. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes."

Riley wanted to see more things. She used her eyes to watch a red kite go up. She used her ears to hear it snap in the wind. She used her nose to smell popcorn popping. Dad bought some, and she used her tongue to taste the salty bits.

Then Riley touched the grass with her fingers. It was soft and a little wet. A ladybug landed right on her hand! "Hello, little friend," she said. The wind blew again. Sand flew by her face once more. Riley blinked, and her eyelashes caught the sand. Her eyes stayed clean and dry. She laughed and blinked again, just to feel them work.

Elliot wanted to have a tea party. He wanted one so, so much. He set his teddy bear on a little chair. He set his rubber duck on another chair. "Tea time!" he called.

Then Elliot had a problem. The teapot was empty. Mom was busy, and the tea things lived up high. His shoulders drooped. How could he have tea with no tea?

Then he looked at the empty cups. He picked one up and tipped the empty teapot over it. He made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug, glug." Nothing came out, but he said, "There! Full!"

He handed a cup to the duck. "Here is your tea, duck." He handed a cup to teddy. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" He blew on his own cup. Then he took a big pretend sip. "Mmm. Juicy tea," he said, and he giggled.

Mom peeked around the door. "May I have tea too?" she asked. Elliot poured her an empty cup, glug glug glug. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" he said. Mom blew on it and sipped. "Best tea ever," she said. Elliot clapped. "More tea, everyone!" he shouted. "Glug, glug, glug."

Isaiah went to the store with Mom. He saw a big basket of apples. He wanted a red one. He grabbed for an apple with both hands.

A girl named Mia was there too. She was waiting for her turn. Mom knelt down softly. "We say please when we ask for something," she said. Isaiah let go of the apple. "May I have one, please?" he asked.

The store man smiled. He picked a shiny red apple. He put it in the bag. "Thank you," said Isaiah. Mia took her turn next. She got a green apple. "You can hold the bag," said Mom. Isaiah held it all the way to the street. The bag was full and heavy. He kept walking, one step at a time.

At the car, Mom opened the bag. There was a small surprise inside. A tiny sticker of a happy apple sat on top. "For you," said Mom. Isaiah put it on his shirt. "I said please," he said. Then he took a big, crunchy bite.

Grayson was going on a big trip. The car was packed full. "Camping today!" Daddy yelled.

The car went up a hill. Then it went down the hill. Grayson counted the trees. "One tree, two trees, three trees!"

Then the car stopped. Daddy made a sad face. "I think we took a wrong turn," he said. The road was small and bumpy. No campsite was here.

Mommy held up a big paper with roads on it. "Look, this is a map," she said. "It shows roads and places. It can help us find the way."

Grayson leaned over the seat. He saw little lines and dots. "Is our campsite on there?" he asked. Mommy pointed to a spotted dot. "Yes! Right there."

Grayson put his finger on the dot. "Go this way!" he said. Daddy turned the car around. They found the big road again. One road, two roads, three roads.

Soon they saw tents and a lake. "We made it!" Grayson yelled. He jumped out and hugged his spotted teddy bear. "The map found us!"

Charlotte got a new bike for her birthday. She loved to ride it fast. But one day her long hair got in her eyes. She fell off her bike. Her legs felt weak and she sat on the grass.

"Mama, my hair is in my way," said Charlotte.

"Then it is time for your first haircut," said Mama.

They went to the barbershop. Charlotte saw the big chair. She saw the scissors. The scissors looked sharp.

"Will the scissors hurt me?" she asked.

"Cutting hair does not hurt," said the barber. "You will see."

Charlotte climbed into the big chair. The chair went up and up. The barber snipped one little snip.

"That is all?" said Charlotte. "I did not feel it!"

She watched in the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They rolled off the cape like tiny curls of paper. It did not hurt at all.

"More," said Charlotte. "You can do more."

The barber smiled. He cut and cut. Soon Charlotte had short, bouncy hair. It was out of her eyes.

At home, Charlotte rode her bike again. Her hair stayed back. No more falls.

"I love my haircut," she said.

Today was a big day at Luke's house. Grandma was making challah bread. It was bread just for the holiday. "Can I taste it now?" Luke asked. "Not yet, little one," said Grandma. "First we make it."

Luke stood on his step stool. Grandma gave him dough. "Push it down," she said. Luke pushed. The dough went flat! Then Grandma showed him how to fold it over. Luke folded and folded. The dough looked like a little nest now.

The bread went into the oven. Grandma put it in, not Luke. The oven was hot. They waited and waited. Luke's tummy made a growl. At last the bread came out, big and gold. Luke's hands were empty no more. He held a warm piece. He took a bite. "Mmm!" said Luke. "It tastes like a happy day!"

Hailey and Grandma went to the grocery store. It was cold outside. Grandma handed Hailey her red coat.

"Can I do it myself?" asked Hailey. "Yes, you can," said Grandma.

Hailey pushed both arms into one sleeve. The coat wiggled like a worm. She laughed and fell over on the soft bench. "That is not right!" she said. Her arms were stuck together in one long sleeve. She could not even pick up her juice to drink it.

Grandma smiled. "Try again, Hailey."

Hailey pulled her arms out. Then she put one arm in one sleeve. She put her other arm in the other sleeve. The coat felt just right now. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. Click! It was zipped all by herself.

"Is it true I did it all alone?" asked Hailey. "All alone," said Grandma.

Outside, they walked past the garden by the store. A little brown dog wore a tiny coat too. "Look, Grandma!" said Hailey. "He knows the sleeve trick too!"

Jayden sat at the little table on the grassy hill. Paint day at summer camp! Miss Rosa put a flat tray in front of him. "This is called a palette," she said. "It holds your paint." Jayden dipped his brush. He named his colors. "Red. Yellow. Blue." He counted them too. "One, two, three." On his paper, red ran into blue. It made a big purple puddle. But Jayden wanted green, and his paper was stuck all purple now. His lip wobbled. "It's okay," said Miss Rosa. "Try the palette." Jayden put one drop of blue on the tray. He added one drop of yellow. He mixed them with his brush. The paint smelled like spring, and it turned green! He painted a big green grassy hill. "Green!" he laughed. Miss Rosa clapped, and Jayden painted one more.

Henri sat on the train with Mama. The seat was bumpy under him. He held his cup of milk with two hands. "Where are we going?" he asked. "To the beach," said Mama. Henri looked out the window. Trees went by fast. Then the trees stopped, and there was sand. There was the big blue sea.

At the beach, Henri saw the water. The waves went up and down. "Waves!" he shouted. He wanted to splash right now. He ran to the wet sand. But Mama called, "Wait for me, Henri." Henri stopped. He stood and watched. A wave came in and touched his toes. Then he stepped back to Mama.

"Why do I wait?" Henri asked. "Little ones go near the water with a grown-up watching," said Mama. She took his hand. Her hand was warm and strong. His own legs felt weak after the long train ride. Now Mama was right beside him.

Together they walked to the water. A big wave came. Splash! It went over their feet. Henri laughed. "Again!" he said. Another wave came, and Mama held his hand tight.

Hudson sat at the little table. He wanted to paint green grass. He looked in the paint cups. Red, yellow, blue. No green paint at all.

Hudson frowned at his paper. "I need green for the grass," he said. Miss Amy came over. She waited with him. She did not hurry him.

Hudson put his brush in the yellow cup. He painted a big yellow blob. Then he put his brush in the blue cup. He painted blue right on top of the yellow. He swirled the brush around and around.

The blob turned green. Hudson stopped. He looked and looked. "It's green!" he said. He painted tall green grass all the way up the paper. Then he painted a purple flower next to the grass.

At tidy-up time, Hudson sang a little song while he put the brushes away. He scratched an itch on his nose. There was a small green spot on his nose too. Miss Amy smiled at him. "Green grass boy," she said.

Alice sat in her car seat. The sun was warm on her hands. "Are we at Mia's house now?" she asked. "Not now," said Mama. "Today we go to the store. Tomorrow we go to Mia's house." Alice made a sad mouth. "I want to go now," she said. Mama kept driving.

The store had big doors. The doors went whoosh. Alice held Mama's hand. They picked a heavy bag of apples. Alice helped put it in the cart. The apples rolled and bumped. "Mia likes apples," said Alice. "Yes," said Mama. "You can bring some tomorrow."

In the car, the sun began to drop. It made long shadows on the road. Alice yawned. "Is it tomorrow yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "First comes night. You will sleep. When you wake up, that is tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today." Alice looked out the window. The streetlights came on, one by one.

Alice ate an apple in her seat. Her eyes felt heavy. At home, she slept in her little bed. When she woke up, the sun was back. "Is it today again?" she asked. Mama smiled. "It is a new today," she said. "Now it is tomorrow." Alice clapped her hands. "Mia's house!" she said. She put the apples in her small bag, one, two, three.

Everly wanted her red blocks. But the block box was in the car. It was dark outside. "Can I get my blocks now?" she asked. "Later," said Mama. "First we have dinner, then later we get blocks."

Everly ate her dinner. She tasted the lemon in her water. "Sour!" she said, and made a funny face. Mama laughed. Everly drank more water.

"Is it later yet?" Everly asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Now we wash hands." Everly washed her hands. "Is it later now?" "Not yet. Now we put on pajamas." Everly put on her pajamas.

Papa went out to the car with a flashlight. Everly waited at the door. Now she heard the car door open. Now she heard Papa's feet on the steps. Now Papa set the block box down. "It is later," said Papa.

Everly sat on her bed. She stacked one block, then two, then three. The tower went up and up. "I got them later," she said. She yawned big. Mama tucked the blocks under the bed. "Blocks again tomorrow," said Mama. Everly closed her eyes and held her bear tight.

Ellie sat at the dinner table. She looked at her plate. There was rice and a piece of broccoli. The broccoli looked like a little green boat.

"I want pancakes," said Ellie. "We had pancakes yesterday."

"Yes," said Mom. "Yesterday is gone. Today is rice day."

Ellie felt upset. Her bottom lip went down. "I want pancakes now."

Dad sat down next to her. "Pancakes are for morning," he said. "Tomorrow, when you wake up, we will eat breakfast. Good morning, Ellie. Pancakes for you."

Ellie thought about that. Morning was when she woke up. Morning was breakfast time. She could almost see it. She would open her eyes. The sun would be in her window. She would smell pancakes.

"Okay," said Ellie. "Tomorrow morning, pancakes. Today, rice."

She picked up her fork. She pushed the rice around. The broccoli boat sailed on top. "Look, Dad. The boat is sailing."

"Now we eat dinner," said Mom. "Later, we will wash hands and brush teeth."

"Now dinner," said Ellie. "Later, teeth. Tomorrow, pancakes and morning."

"That's right," said Dad.

Ellie took a big bite of rice. Then she made the little green boat sail right into her mouth. "Next stop, tomorrow!" she said.

Dylan ran to the park with his red truck. The sun was warm. The weather was just right for playing outside. He felt so excited. His tummy was full of breakfast, and his truck bed was full of little stones.

Dylan pushed the truck across the grass. Vroom, vroom. Then he heard a loud thump. A boy named Sam had tripped by the slide. Sam sat on the ground. His face looked sad, and then he looked angry at his shoes. He rubbed his knee.

Dylan felt a little scared for Sam. He walked over slowly. "Are you okay?" he asked. Sam looked up. His sad face began to change. He nodded his head. "Yes," Sam said. "That helps. Thank you." Dylan held out his hand. Sam took it and stood up.

Then Sam pushed the truck too. Vroom, vroom, they went, side by side across the warm green grass.

Anthony woke up early. "Is today the library day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is today," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now." Anthony clapped his hands. "Right now! Right now!" he said.

At the library, Anthony picked books. One, two, three books. He heard kids reading. He saw a story time sign. "Can we go now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later, after we find our books." Later came, and they sat in the story circle.

On the way home, Anthony held Mom's hand. "We went to the library yesterday," he said. Mom shook her head. "No, that was today," she said. "Yesterday is all done. Tomorrow is a new day." Anthony thought. "Tomorrow can we go back?" he asked. Mom laughed. "Tomorrow we will bake a cake. You can help. But not now, now we walk home." Anthony smiled. "One, two, three books for today."

Sofia sat in the car with her mama. They were going to the dentist. It was her very first time. "My tummy feels funny," said Sofia. "That is called worried," said Mama. "You can hold my hand." Sofia squeezed Mama's fingers. One, two, three squeezes. The car seat was warm. The window smelled like sunshine.

At the dentist, a kind lady looked in Sofia's mouth. "How can you see behind my teeth?" asked Sofia. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. "Watch," she said. She put it near Sofia's back teeth. Sofia saw her own teeth in the little mirror. One tooth, two teeth, three white teeth!

After that, Sofia got to hold the tiny mirror herself. She reached up and saw her ear in it. She giggled. "Mama, look! The little mirror shows everything!" In the car going home, she held a sticker on her knee. "The dentist was nice," said Sofia. "Can we count my teeth again tomorrow?"

Michael was shy at school. He liked to watch first. Today his class had a dress-up corner.

"Let's play getting ready," said Teacher Amy. "First we eat breakfast." Michael sniffed the play toast. He could smell the wooden toast, but it was just pretend. He laughed.

Next the dolls needed a nap. Michael patted a doll. He covered it with a small blanket. "Shh," he whispered. The doll slept and slept.

Then it was time to dress up. Michael wanted to wear the big red shoes. He pushed them onto his bare feet. His toes hurt. The shoes would not fit right. He sat down and tried again. Still wrong.

His friend Ben came over. "Watch me," said Ben. Ben put on his socks first. Then he pushed on his shoes. The shoes slid right on. "Socks first," said Ben.

Michael took the red shoes off. He wiggled his feet into the socks. Then he pushed on the shoes. They fit! He stood up and stomped around the rug.

"I did it!" said Michael. Ben clapped. Teacher Amy clapped too. Michael was not shy anymore. He stomped his feet all the way to the play kitchen.

Lincoln stood by the little bed. His new baby sister was in it. She was small and warm. She made a tiny sound.

Lincoln had a cracker in his hand. He wanted to share it. "Baby, want a bite?" he asked. He held it out to her. The baby turned her head away.

Mom came in. "Not a cracker, Lincoln," she said. "A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food." Lincoln looked at the bottle on the table. "Can I fetch it?" he asked. Mom smiled and gave him the bottle. It was warm in his hands.

Linlin watched Mom feed the baby. The baby drank and drank. Her tummy went round. She did not cry now. "She likes milk," Lincoln said. He patted her soft blanket. Then Mom went to wash dishes. Lincoln was not alone. He sat by the bed. He sang a little song, and the baby closed her eyes.

Charlie stood at the basketball court. The hoop was tall and far away. Charlie had a big red ball under her arm. Sam had five beanbags in a long row. "My turn, my turn," said Charlie. She picked up all the beanbags at once.

Sam's face went sad. Sam had no beanbags left. Coach Rosa knelt down beside them. "Taking turns," she said softly. One beanbag, then two beanbags. "You throw one. Then Sam has a turn." Charlie looked at the beanbags. One, two, three, four, five. She gave four to Sam. She kept just one.

Charlie threw her beanbag at the hoop. It went up, up, up. Then it came down and sat on the rim. It did not fall in. Sam threw one. Sam's beanbag went in. "Yay!" said Charlie. She clapped her hands. Then it was Charlie's turn again. This time her beanbag went in. The hoop made a little swish.

Then Coach Rosa rolled the big red ball to Charlie. Charlie held out both hands. Pat, pat, went the ball on her fingers. She caught it with two hands. "I caught it!" she said. Sam clapped too. Then it was Sam's turn to catch. Charlie rolled the ball, slow and gentle, all the way to Sam's two hands. "One throw for you," said Charlie. "One throw for me."

Lincoln ran to the school garden with his teacher, Ms. May. He had tiny carrot seeds in his hand. He made little holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in and patted them down. "Grow, grow, grow!" he said.

Every day Lincoln ran to the garden. One morning, little green leaves popped up. Lincoln clapped his hands. Then he saw green leaves in the wrong spot too. They grew between his carrots, close and messy. What a puzzle! "Are these baby carrots?" he asked himself. "No, they are too thick and all over the place."

Lincoln grabbed one thin stem and pulled hard. "Stop!" said Ms. May. "That one is a weed. Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them." Lincoln let go fast. "So the messy leaves are bad?" he asked. "Yes," said Ms. May. "Pull those out, and leave the carrot leaves alone."

Lincoln pulled the weeds one by one. The dirt looked neat again. His carrots had room to grow tall. Then, one sunny day, Lincoln saw something orange in the dirt. He pulled it up. It was a carrot! "Look at this!" he shouted. He held it up high, and his hands smelled like fresh dirt and salty sea air from the playground breeze. "Ms. May!" he called. "My seed made a carrot!"

Nora was at Grandma's house. Cookies were waiting on a plate. Nora wanted one, and they looked crunchy.

"Nora, first we wash," said Grandma. "You scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds." Nora put soap on her hands. She rinsed fast, right away. "That was too quick," said Grandma. "The soap did not have time to work."

Nora tried again. She made lots of bubbles. Grandma said, "We count slowly to twenty." They counted together. One, two, three. Nora kept scrubbing. The bubbles grew and grew. Twenty! Nora rinsed all the soap off. Her hands were clean.

Grandma handed her a cookie. "Crunchy," said Nora, taking a bite. Then she marched around the kitchen with her clean hands held up high. Grandma laughed and gave her the answer she wanted most: "Yes, you may have one more."

Emmett ran into the kitchen. He smelled something sweet. Mom was baking. "Blueberries!" he said. His nose knew.

Then Dad turned on the blender. It roared. It was so loud! Emmett jumped. "Too loud!" he said. He put his hands over his ears. The roar got smaller. The blender went on and on. Then Dad turned it off. Quiet! Emmett took his hands off his ears.

"How did it get quiet so fast?" he asked. "I covered my ears," he said. "My hands made the loud sound little!" He tried again. He clapped his hands over his ears. "Quiet, quiet, quiet," he whispered. He lifted them. He could hear Mom humming. Down came the hands. Quiet again!

"Can you help me?" asked Mom. Emmett looked at the blueberries. He touched one. It was cold and smooth. He tasted one. Sweet! "Yum," said Dad, tasting one too.

After his nap, Emmett heard the vacuum. It was loud and wild. He covered his ears with both hands. The vacuum sound got little. Then Mom began to sweep the floor. The broom went swish, swish. That sound was soft. Emmett took his hands down.

"I have two ears, two eyes, one nose, one tongue, and two hands," he counted. "That is me!"

"And me," said Dad, and he tickled Emmett's tummy. Emmett laughed out loud.

Riley wanted to help Grandma feed the hens. "You can toss the corn," said Grandma. "Count the hens so we know they all come."

Riley looked out at the yard. She counted, "One, two, four." Grandma laughed. "You jumped too far! After two comes three. Try again, slow."

Riley took a big breath. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten hens ran to her. Ten hens pecked the corn. "The words fit!" said Riley.

Then Riley saw something silly. A tiny hen hid under a warm blanket by the door. It was very quiet there. "One more makes eleven," said Grandma. Riley giggled. "Silly hen, you missed counting time."

The little hen fluffed her feathers to dry. Riley gave her a small handful of corn. The tiny hen pecked Riley's shoe. "That tickles!" said Riley. Grandma carried the hen back to the yard, and Riley waved. "Bye-bye, number eleven."

Leah was at the beach with her mom. They walked past the sand to a little pool. Leah wanted to float on her back. But she was scared. "What if I sink?" she asked. "I will be right here," said Miss Kim, the swim teacher.

Leah sat on the pool step. Her mom waved from a chair. Miss Kim held Leah's back with her hands. Leah leaned back into the water. She did not sink. The teacher's hands held her up. Leah looked at the sky. It was blue and wide. "I am floating!" she said. Miss Kim smiled. Her hands stayed under Leah's back. Leah kicked a little. Water splashed her chin.

After the swim, they went back to the sand. Mom had a crunchy snack and a small cake. Leah washed the sand off so she could bathe in the tub later. She closed her eyes and said, "Can we come back tomorrow?" Mom kissed her wet hair. "Yes, tomorrow we float again."

Hazel went out to the backyard with her teddy bear. She wanted to find something for a fairy picnic. She put down her toy truck and a red ball. Then she set out pretend food, a banana, crackers and a little cup of juice.

Under the big tree, she saw something soft. It was small and gray and light. "A feather!" said Hazel. "Birds are animals that have feathers. So a bird was here!" She held it up to her ear. It made no sound at all. It was quiet like a snowflake.

Then she heard a chirp. She looked up. A round little bird sat on the fence. It looked straight at the cracker in her hand. Hazel put the cracker on the grass. The bird flew down. It began to eat. Hazel whispered, "You can come to my fairy picnic too."

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules held his mama's hand. "Why is it so dark?" he asked. "The power is out," said Mama. "No power means no lights."

Jules felt a little scared. But Mama squeezed his hand. "We need the flashlight," she said. They patted the shelf. They patted the table. No flashlight. Then Jules thought of the kitchen. "The drawer!" he said. He planted his feet and walked slow, holding the wall. He felt the drawer handle. He pulled it open. His fingers found the flashlight inside.

"Will it work in the dark?" Jules asked. "Try it and see," said Mama. Jules pressed the button. A bright circle popped onto the wall. "It works!" he said. "The power is out, but the light is on!"

Mama lit a candle way up high, where Jules could not touch. Jules made his hand into a bunny shape in the flashlight beam. Two soft ears grew on the wall. Then something small glowed in the corner. It was his lost toy truck, shining in the light. It had been there all along. "You found my truck!" said Jules. He hugged the flashlight tight. "Dark house, bright light," he said. "That's true."

Victor wanted to build a house for his toy bear. He looked for a square block. He found circles, which rolled away. He found triangles, which looked like little hats. He found a rectangle, long and flat. Where was the square?

Then Victor saw it. But it sat on a corner, all tilted. "That is a new shape," said his sister, Mia. Victor tipped it back down. It had four sides, all the same. It was his square! He stacked it under the rectangle roof.

Mia kissed the bear on its head. "Now bear has a home," she said.

"Next I will fly him to the moon," said Victor. He zoomed the bear round and round, over the square house and the triangle roof. "Zoom, zoom!" said Mia, and she flew her toy rabbit right beside him.

Aiden loves the dog book at school. It has a red dog on the front. Today he wants to hear it again.

Miss Pam sits down with the class. She opens the front of the book. She reads the first page. "Red Dog runs to the park." Aiden listens to every word.

After nap time, Mia's dad comes to read. He lifts the same red dog book. Aiden gets upset for a tiny moment. "That is not Miss Pam," he thinks. "Will the story be new words?"

But Mia's dad opens the front of the book. He reads the first page. "Red Dog runs to the park." The very same words! Aiden claps his hands.

Now Aiden has an idea. He takes the book to his teacher. "Your turn," he says. She smiles and turns to the first page.

"Red Dog runs to the park," she reads.

Aiden nods. "Same words," he says. "Every time."

Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was here! The baby was her little brother, Sam. His crib had a flat, soft blanket. Natalie patted it very gently.

Then Sam began to cry. Loud cries! Natalie put her hands over her ears. "Why is he crying?" she asked. She thought and thought. Maybe he wanted her teddy? She gave him the teddy. Sam kept crying. Maybe he wanted her sticker? She held it up high. Sam kept crying.

Mommy came in. "He is telling us something," Mommy said. "The baby cannot talk yet, so he cries to show he needs something." Mommy gave Sam warm milk. Sam drank and drank. Then the crying stopped! A big smile came on his face.

Natalie clapped her hands. "He talks with crying!" she said. Later, Sam cried again. Natalie ran fast down the hall like a little road. "Mommy! Sam is talking!" she called. Mommy picked Sam up, and Sam grabbed Natalie's finger and held on tight.

Austin sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His mother sat next to him. He heard the door click. He saw a nurse with a small cup. The nurse smiled. "Time for your medicine," she said.

Austin did not want yucky medicine. He saw the pink cup. He smelled it. It smelled like strawberries. He touched the cup. It felt squishy on the sides. The nurse said, "You can pinch your nose closed, if you like."

Austin pinched his nose closed. Then he drank. He opened his eyes wide. The medicine tasted plain, not strong at all! He let go of his nose. He sniffed the air. The strawberry smell came back. He took one more sip with his nose open. That sip tasted strong again.

"Yum," said Austin. His mother laughed. The nurse gave him a sticker. It was a shiny star. Austin pressed it on his hand. Then he yawned a big yawn. He was ready to sleep on the ride home. His mother picked him up and held him close. "Strawberry next time," whispered the nurse.

Hunter wanted to bang his drum. But the baby was asleep.

Bang! Bang! Bang! The drum was loud. The baby woke up and cried.

Dad ran in. "Shh," he said. "Loud and quiet are opposites." He took the baby to rock her.

Hunter sat and thought. He tapped the drum. Tap. Tap. The drum was quiet now. The baby went back to sleep.

Hunter smiled. He tapped fast. Tap-tap-tap! Then he tapped slow. Tap... tap... tap.

Dad came back. "Nice and quiet," he whispered. He gave Hunter a thumbs up.

Outside, the sky looked stormy. Rain hit the window fast. But inside, Hunter's drum stayed soft.

Tap. Tap. The baby slept on.

Dad peeked in again. "My quiet drummer," he whispered. Hunter tapped one more little tap.

Madelyn sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to build a house for her toy sheep. She had blocks of many shapes.

First she tried a triangle block. It wobbled and fell. "That will not fit," she said. Next she tried a circle block. It rolled away. The sheep looked sad in the weak little pile.

Then Madelyn found a square block. She took a piece of string. She laid it along one side. She laid it along the next side, and the next, and the next. All four sides were the same. "Four sides, all the same," she said. She stacked more squares. The wall stood tall and still.

She put on a triangle roof. She made a rectangle door. The sheep went inside. "Now your house will fit you," Madelyn said. The sheep sat down in its square house, safe and snug.

Raphael built a big tower at school. It had ten blocks. Then Ben bumped the table. The tower fell down. All the blocks went crash.

Raphael felt angry. His face got hot. He sat in the corner and did not talk. Miss Kim came over. She knelt down by his chair.

"How do you feel?" she asked.

Raphael thought. Then he said, "I feel sad. My tower fell."

Miss Kim nodded. "I can help you build it again," she said.

Raphael felt excited. "A real big tower?" he asked.

"Yes, a real big one," said Miss Kim. "Maybe we can put a star block on top."

Raphael and Ben built a new tower together. The star block fit just right on top. Ben clapped. Raphael felt happy again.

"I like our tower," said Raphael. "Me too," said Ben.

Everett sat at the dinner table. He looked with his eyes at his carrots. Crunch, crunch, his ears heard the sound. Then the room went dark. The big light went out. "Oh no," said Everett. He could not see his carrots. He could not see his cup. He could not see his teddy bear, who sat in his chair.

Everett touched his plate with his hands. His fingers felt the rough edge. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled warm bread. He took a lick of his cup and his tongue tasted milk. But still, no teddy. "I want Teddy!" he said. He froze and waited.

"I will turn on the lamp," said Grandma. Click. The little lamp made a soft glow. Now Everett could see with his eyes again. There was Teddy, right on the chair. "Found you!" said Everett, and he gave Teddy a big hug.

Lennon sat at the snack table. A jar of crackers sat in front of her. The lid would not come off. She pulled and pulled. Her hands slipped. The lid stayed stuck.

Maybe her teacher knew a trick. "Can you help me, please?" Lennon asked. Her teacher smiled. "Of course I can." She held the jar and turned the lid. Pop! The lid came off.

Lennon picked up a cracker and put it in her mouth. It was crunchy and good. Then she tipped her cup. Milk spilled on the table. "Oh no," she said. "Sorry about that." The teacher brought a towel. Lennon helped wipe it up.

At home time, her dad's phone buzzed in his pocket. She spotted her dad by the door. "Can you help me, please?" she asked again. "Help you with what?" he said. Lennon pointed at her spotted shoe. "My shoe is stuck on my foot." Her dad laughed and bent down. "One shoe, coming off." Pop! The shoe came free too.

Cooper sat in the middle of the back seat. Mama was driving. Cooper wanted his water cup. It was far away on the floor. "Mama, can you help me, please?" he asked. Mama stopped at a red light. She reached back and gave him the cup. "Thank you," said Cooper. "You're welcome," said Mama. Cooper took a big sip. "Why do you say that?" he asked. Mama smiled. "You say it after thank you," she said. Cooper tried it in his head. One: thank you. Two: you're welcome. At the next stop, Cooper dropped his toy. It went under the seat. "Sorry, toy," he said. "Mama, please help me again." She reached back and got it. "Thank you, Mama." "You're welcome, Cooper." He laughed and hugged his toy. The car was quiet now. Cooper looked out the window. "Mama?" he said. "Yes, love?" "I like your words." Mama patted his shoe and drove home.

Gabriella put muffin mix in a bowl. She stirred it round and round. Dad poured the mix into little cups. Then the cups went into the big oven. Dad was the one who touched the hot oven door.

Dad turned a little round knob. It was an old timer, white and shiny. "Now we wait," said Dad. "How long?" asked Gabriella. "Until the timer beeps," said Dad. "The beep tells us it is time to check the muffins."

While they waited, the family played a game. They hid beans under cups. Gabriella watched the cups. She found the red bean twice! Mom laughed. Dad laughed too. Then everyone forgot about muffins. The game was so much fun.

Beep! Beep! Beep! The little timer rang out loud. "The muffins!" said Gabriella. Dad put on big mitts. He opened the oven door. Warm air came out. The muffins were big and gold. Gabriella sniffed the sweet smell. "The beep helped us remember," she said. She bit into a warm muffin. "Mmm," said Gabriella. "Like honey by the river."

Rowan wanted to make cookies. Mom said, "Let's cut shapes in the dough." Rowan picked a square cutter. Press, press. The square cookie had four corners. He picked a triangle cutter. Press, press. The triangle cookie had three corners. Then Rowan picked the circle cutter. He looked for a corner to start on. He looked and looked. "Where is a corner?" he asked. Mom smiled. "A circle is round and has no corners," she said. Rowan touched the edge. It went round and round with no corners anywhere. "No corners!" he said. "No corners," said Mom again.

Rowan pressed the circle into the dough. Press, press. A round cookie sat on the tray. Then a big surprise. Rowan turned the circle cookie sideways. It still looked the same. The square cookie looked different when he turned it. The circle never did. He laughed out loud.

Mom put the tray in the oven. Rowan watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled sweet. Mom hummed a little song while they waited. Rowan hummed too. The cookies came out golden. Rowan found his circle cookie on the plate. He held it up to the window. The round sun was outside. "Look, Mom! The sun has no corners too!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. "Good looking, Rowan." Rowan took a big bite. The cookie was round all the way to the last crumb.

Cooper ran fast to the kitchen. He wanted cold milk for his playroom picnic. He pulled the fridge door open. Brrr! Cold air touched his toes. He could smell the apples inside. Cooper took the milk and ran back. He left the fridge door open.

Dad came in. "The door is open," he said. "Can you make it closed? Open and closed are opposites." Cooper pushed the door shut. Click! Now it was closed.

Back in the playroom, Cooper set up his picnic. His big teddy sat on the big chair. His small mouse sat on the small block. Cooper filled the toy teapot. "Tea is hot," said Dad, holding the cup far from Cooper's little fingers. Cooper touched his own cup instead. It was cold.

Cooper poured slowly, slowly. Then he stirred fast, fast, fast. He looked at the fridge across the room. Its door was closed. "Closed door," said Cooper, and gave teddy a drink.

Isla stood in the bathroom. "Let's play hide and seek," said Mama. Isla wanted to hide in a good spot. She squeezed behind the towel rack. Then she covered her eyes with her hands. Now she could not see the tub. She could not see the sink. She could not see anything at all. Isla smiled. "Mama cannot see me," she thought. She heard the tap drip, drip, drip with her ears. She smelled the soap with her nose. Her tummy felt happy. "I see you, Isla!" said Mama. Isla peeked through her fingers. Mama was looking right at her! Isla took her hands away. Now she could see the mirror and the tidy shelf. "I saw your toes," said Mama, laughing. "Covering your eyes hides them from you, not from me." Isla laughed too. Then she licked her lips and tasted a bit of toothpaste, sweet and minty. She touched the soft towel with her fingers. "My turn to count," said Mama. She covered her eyes. "One, two, three," said Mama. Isla ran to hide. This time she left her eyes open wide.

Jasmine sat at her little table. She was drawing a picture. It was a picture of a party. A party in the grass, with cake and balloons.

Jasmine picked up a gray crayon. She wanted to draw the sky. Then she looked up at the window. The sun was shining big and bright. It was a sunny day. There was not one cloud. And the sky over the roofs was blue. Bright, bright blue.

Jasmine put the gray crayon down. She picked up the blue crayon instead. She drew the sky all blue, up and up and up. "Blue," she said. "Blue, blue, blue." She drew a yellow sun too. Then she drew red balloons. Then she drew green grass for the party.

Jasmine was hungry after all that drawing. Mommy called, "Snack time!" Jasmine marched to the kitchen with her picture. She held it up high. Mommy looked at the blue sky and smiled. "What a sunny day," said Mommy. Jasmine sat down and took a big bite of her apple. Outside the window, the sky stayed blue.

Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. It was warm and noisy. A cook had made toast, and now the toast sat on a cool plate.

Colton wanted to help. Papa gave him a small knife with no sharp edge and some soft butter. Colton dipped the knife in the butter. He spread it on the toast. Slow, slow strokes. The butter made the toast shine.

Then Papa handed him a little cup of milk. Colton poured it into his big cup. Some milk ran over the edge. A little puddle sat on the table.

"What can I do?" Colton asked.

"You can wipe it up with a cloth," said Papa.

Colton took a cloth from the shelf. He wiped the puddle. The table was dry again. He picked up the cup and took a small, careful sip.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything was dark. Kai could not see his toy truck.

"I want my flashlight!" said Kai. He ran to the kitchen. Bump! His leg hit a chair. "Ow!" said Kai.

Dad came fast. Dad held Kai's hand. "In the dark, walk slowly," said Dad. "Hold my hand so nobody trips." Kai held on tight. They took one slow step. Then another slow step. Dad found the flashlight on the shelf and turned it on.

"Now we can have a dark party!" said Dad. They made shadows on the wall. A bunny! A big bird! Kai laughed. "This dark party is pretty fun," said Kai. Then the lights came back on. Kai clapped his hands. "We did it, Dad!"

"I want to do it again tomorrow," said Kai.

Julia woke up and looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. She put on her sun hat. Then she saw clouds come. The sky turned gray. It began to rain.

Julia wanted to jump in puddles. She ran to the door in her sneakers. Mama held her coat for her. "Rain boots," said Mama. Julia put on her yellow rain boots. One boot, two boots. She stomped outside.

The wind blew. It was a windy day too. Her hat flew off her head! Julia held her hat with both hands. She laughed and chased it around the yard.

Then Julia found a big puddle. She stepped right in. Splash! She looked at her boots. Her feet were dry. "My feet are dry," she said. She stepped in again. Splash! Still dry. Boots keep feet dry.

Later the rain stopped. Julia drew pictures inside. She drew a sunny sun, a rainy cloud, a windy tree, and white snow. "Snowy days need mittens," said Mama. Julia drew red mittens.

Mama cut toast into a triangle shape. Julia took a bite. "Tasty," she said. She held up her milk cup. "Toast, milk, boots," said Julia. "Dry feet all day." Then she stomped her boots on the floor, one, two, one, two.

Felix loved the big book about the sea. He loved the fish. He loved the whale. He wanted to know who drew the whale. "Miss Ana, who made this picture?" he asked. Miss Ana smiled. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator," she said. Felix looked at the front of the book. There was a name there. "James Bell," he read, slow and careful. "That name is real writing," said Miss Ana. "The words tell us who did it."

Felix opened the book the right way. He started at the front. He turned one page. Then another page. The whale came last, so he had to wait. Waiting was hard, but Felix kept going. He turned pages one by one until the whale came.

At snack time, Felix had a pretzel. It was salty and crunchy. "I need to show Sam the whale," he said. He found Sam. Sam looked at the front of the book. "Who drew the fish?" Sam asked. Felix pointed at the name. "James Bell," he said. "He is the illustrator. Now you know a surprise too."

Sam turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the whale.

Connor sat at the dinner table. He was very hungry. He wanted his pasta now.

"First, a game," said Mom. She put a big basket by his plate. It was full of little pictures.

Connor tipped the basket over. All the pictures fell out. There were dogs, cats, monkeys, apples, bananas, balls, blocks and more.

"Make three piles," said Dad. "Animals go together. Toys go together. Foods go together."

Connor picked up a monkey picture. He set it with the dog and the cat. Then he found a ball and a block. He patted that pile. "Toys!" he said.

He put apples and bananas in the last pile. His tummy growled loud.

"Good sorting," said Mom. "Now the foods pile helps you. Pasta is a food too."

She set down his warm bowl. Connor wore his biggest smile and picked up his fork.

Jordan runs to the block corner at daycare. Yesterday he built a big tower there. He wants to build it again today.

Jordan stacks one block. He stacks another block. The tower grows tall. Now it is as tall as his tummy.

His friend Milo walks over. "I went to the park tomorrow," says Milo. Milo stops and thinks. "No, not tomorrow. It already happened. I went yesterday."

Jordan looks at his tower. "Yesterday is before today," he says. He taps his blocks. "Yesterday my tower fell down. It went boom."

Jordan pushes the top block a tiny bit. The whole tower wobbles. Then it falls down. Boom! All the blocks are flat on the carpet.

"Again!" says Milo.

"Okay," says Jordan. "But first we clean up. Later we build more."

Miss Kim, the teacher, comes over. "What good builders you are," she says. "It is winter now, so we play inside. Tomorrow we will paint snowflakes."

Jordan stacks the blocks back in the box. He looks out the window. The sky is white and cold.

"Tomorrow," he says. "That is the next day."

"Let's build the tallest one," says Milo.

Jordan grabs a red block. "This one goes first."

Henry went to the park with Mom today. Yesterday it rained, so the swings were wet. Today the sun was out and warm.

Henry wanted to swing high. But a big boy was on the swing now. Henry had to wait. "When will it be my turn?" he asked. Mom pointed to the big clock by the gate. "The clock shows what time it is," she said. The long hand moved a little. Henry watched it. Then the big boy jumped off. "Now it is my turn!" said Henry.

He swung high, high, high. His sweater puffed out like a balloon. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Later we will go home and have a snack." Henry pumped his legs once more. The clock by the gate ticked on.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her father put down a plate of noodles. Zoey was excited. "Noodles are my favorite!" she said.

Then she saw her father's face. His eyes were wet. Tears ran down. Zoey felt scared. "Daddy, why is your face wet?" she asked. "I feel sad today," her father said. "When I feel sad, I cry." Zoey looked at her noodles. Then she had an idea. She ran to her room. She came back with her bunny. The bunny had one bumpy ear from too much love.

"Here, Daddy," she said. "Bunny makes me happy when I feel sad." Her father smiled a little. He held the bunny. Then he laughed. "Bunny tickles my chin," he said. Zoey laughed too. After dinner, they chased each other around the couch, bunny hopping along behind them.

Evelyn sat at the big art table. She was painting a lion. The lion had a round orange face and a long tail.

Now Evelyn wanted grass under the lion. She looked for green paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint. But no green paint anywhere.

"Miss Ana, I need green," said Evelyn. "We can mix two colors," said Miss Ana. "Try your blue and your yellow."

Evelyn put blue on her brush. She put it in a cup. Then she put yellow in too. She stirred with her brush. Round and round she stirred.

The paint turned green! Evelyn clapped her hands. "Look, look!" she said.

She painted green grass all under the lion. Tomás looked over from his seat. "I need green too," he said. "Here," said Evelyn. She showed him her blue cup and her yellow cup.

Tomás mixed his blue and yellow. His paint turned green too. He painted a big green tree.

Evelyn smiled at her lion in the green grass. "Blue and yellow," she said. "It worked!"

Stella marched into daycare with a card in her hand. It was her birthday card from Grandma. On the front, Grandma had written Stella's name.

Stella put the card on the table. Then she looked at her cubby. Her name was there too. "Wait," said Stella. She looked at the card. She looked at the cubby. The letters were the same. S, then T, then the rest. Same letters, same order, both times.

"Sam, come look!" said Stella. Sam came over. He could see his name on his cubby. But he did not have a card. Stella got a pencil. "I will write your name," she said. She copied the letters from Sam's cubby. S, A, M. She wrote them on paper. Sam held the paper next to his cubby. The letters matched.

The room was noisy with kids playing. But Stella sat very still. She turned to the first page of her card and read the pictures front to back. Then she read them again. At the last page she said, "Grandma wrote my name. It looks just like my name on my cubby."

She put the card in her cubby, right under the letters.

Layla was building a tower in her room. The blocks were red and blue and yellow. She had an idea to make it very, very tall.

The sky got dark outside. Layla put on her pajamas. Then she heard a noise. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Layla felt scared. Her tummy felt small and tight.

She did not hide under the bed. She walked to the hall. "Mama, I hear a noise. I am scared," she said. Mama took her hand. "Let's go look together," said Mama. They went slowly. Tap, tap, tap. Mama opened the curtain. A small branch was touching the glass. The wind moved it. The wind made the branch tap.

"Wind," said Layla. She felt happy now. Mama tucked her into bed. The tap, tap, tap sounded different now. It sounded like a little song.

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules could not even see his own hands. "Where did my toys go?" he asked. Dad lit a little candle and said, "Let's sit on the back step while we wait." So they did.

The backyard was very dark at first. Jules saw nothing. He sat still and counted the stars. One, two, three, four. "Is that snow in the sky?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "Those are stars." He counted some more. Then something funny happened. He could see the big tree. Then he could see his red ball. Then he could see his toy fish lying in the grass.

"Is it a real fish?" he asked. "No," said Dad. "It is a toy." Jules laughed. His eyes waited in the dark, and now they could see so much. He patted the tree, then the ball, then the fish. "Hello, dark," he said. "Hello, Jules," said Mom, in her best dark voice.

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there.

"Bunny is lost," said Aubrey. She looked under the blanket. She looked in her cup drawer. No bunny.

Grandma came in. "Let's look together," she said. They looked by the big chair. They looked by the door.

Then Grandma opened a small basket. "This is our lost and found," she said. "We put things we find in here. Then people can get them back."

Aubrey peeked in. There was a hairbrush. There was one glove. There was a shiny spoon.

And there, at the bottom, was bunny!

"Found you!" said Aubrey. She hugged bunny tight.

Then she saw something else. A little red sock sat in the basket. "Grandpa's sock?" asked Aubrey.

Grandpa popped his head in. "My sock! I lost it last week," he said.

Aubrey held it up. "You can get it back," she said. Grandpa laughed and put the sock on his foot.

Then Aubrey shared her cereal with bunny. She gave bunny a bite from her spoon. Bunny liked breakfast, too.

Victoria went to the beach with her mom. The beach had a big pool next to the sand. Victoria wanted to swim there. Her big sister Rosa swam far out in the sea. Victoria wanted to swim far too.

The swim teacher named Miss Kim said, "We start at the shallow end." Victoria stood in the water there. The water came up to her tummy. She could touch the bottom. Rosa stood far away. The water went up to Rosa's shoulders. "That part is the deep end," Rosa called.

Miss Kim held Victoria's hands. Victoria kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. The wind pushed little waves near her cheek. They waited, then she kicked again. She found a slimy leaf in the water and dropped it in the sand.

Victoria walked back to the shallow end. She kicked some more. Her feet lifted up, up, up. "Look, Mom! I'm swimming!" she said.

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had red paint and blue paint. He wanted to paint a big flower for his mom. He was wearing his favorite blue shirt.

Mama came in with a bowl of water. "Let's put on your old shirt first," she said. She pulled a big green shirt over his head. It went down past his elbows.

Mohamed dipped his brush. He made red dots and blue dots. He made a tall green stem. Then a big blue splat went right on his shirt. But it landed on the green shirt, not the blue one. "The paint did not get on me," said Mohamed. He made another dot. That one splashed too. The green shirt caught that one as well.
