Mama held up the painting. The flower had a red middle and blue petals. "I will hang it up," she said. Mohamed looked at his arms. Under the green shirt, his favorite blue shirt was still clean. He smiled and pointed at it. "Look, Mama. Still clean."

Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. It was a big, noisy place. Trucks rumbled by the pots. Ruby picked out little plants. She got tomatoes, carrots and beans.

At home, Dad dug the dirt. Ruby planted every row. Then she had a problem. "Where did the tomatoes go?" she asked. She could not remember. All the rows looked the same. Only tiny green leaf tips showed in the soil.

Then Ruby had an idea. They went back to the garden center. Ruby found small sticks and drew a tomato on one. Dad wrote the word too. They pushed the stick into the dirt by the tomato row. A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot. Ruby made a carrot label. She made a bean label. "Now we know who lives here," she said.

Soon the plants grew tall. Ruby read each label. The tomatoes came up by the tomato stick. The carrots came up by the carrot stick. Ruby watered them and smiled. "Hello, little tomatoes," she said.

Muffins were baking in the oven. Carter wanted to see them. He started to reach for the oven door. "Stop," said Mom. "It is hot." Mom held his hand. They stood back and watched together. The oven light glowed. Warm air moved out of the top. "Where is the cold spot?" Carter wondered. He found it by the door. It felt nice there.

Carter looked out the window. His big sister Lily was on the playground slide. She climbed up, up, up. Then she lay down on her tummy, head first. Carter tapped the glass. Lily sat up. She turned herself around. Her feet pointed down the slide. Whoosh! She went down feet first and landed on her feet.

"Did you see that?" said Carter. Mom smiled. The timer rang. The muffins were done. Mom used her big mitts to move the pan out. Carter smelled them from his safe, cold spot by the door. Then he and Mom sat down, and each ate one warm muffin.

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to play a song all by himself.

Miss Jo showed him a big paper. It had dots and lines on it. "What are those?" Felix asked. "Those are notes," said Miss Jo. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Felix tapped the drum. Miss Jo pointed to a note. He tapped again. She pointed to the next note. He tapped that one too.

Felix felt upset when he missed a note. "Slow down," said Miss Jo. "Try again." So he tried again. And again. A bird sat by the window and seemed to listen. Felix looked at the notes, one by one. He tapped each one. Tap, tap, tap. Then he played them all in a row.

"Look at me!" said Felix. Miss Jo clapped. Felix climbed off his little stool and took a bow. The bird flew up, and Felix tapped one more note.

Milo pushed the library door. The door had a big sign on it. Milo pointed at the sign. "What do those words say?" he asked. His mom read them out. "They say PUSH." Milo pushed, and the door opened. He laughed.

Milo wanted a book about a big red truck. He walked past the busy desks. He walked past a shelf with a label. The label said TRUCKS. "Mom, this says trucks!" said Milo. "Yes, it does," said Mom. "The words tell us what is inside." Milo pulled out a box of books. The box had words too. Those words said TRUCKS as well.

Milo opened a book. He started at the back page. Mom sat down next to him. She turned the book around. She flipped the pages, one by one, from the front. On the first page was a red truck under a tree. "There it is!" said Milo. He put his finger under the words. Mom read them out loud. "Big red truck," she read. A boy ran by, and a puppy began to chase him. Milo stayed on the rug. He turned to page two.

"Read the next words," said Milo.

Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and shiny. His dad held his hand. "I want to swim," said Logan. "But my feet don't touch." He felt worried.

Dad walked into the water with him. It was warm on Logan's toes. "Hold the edge of the pool," said Dad. Logan grabbed the cool wall with both hands. He held on tight. "Now kick your legs," said Dad. Logan kicked and kicked. His legs made big splashes. The water went splash, splash, splash. Droplets flew up and landed on Dad's nose. Dad laughed and wiped his face. "You kicked me!" he said. Logan giggled. His legs felt strong.

A cute rubber duck floated by. It was the color yellow. It bobbed up and down in Logan's splashes. Logan kicked more, and the duck wiggled away. Dad smiled. "Kick, kick, kick," said Logan. He held the wall and kicked all the way to the steps. Dad lifted him out and wrapped him in a big soft towel. "Again tomorrow?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Logan.

Cooper put on his warm coat. Off to the ice rink! Mom and Dad came too. Grandma came too. Even his best friend Ruby came.

The players zoomed on the ice. Their helmets were blue and red. But one man had a striped shirt. He was not on a team. Cooper pointed. "Who is that?" he asked. Dad smiled. "That is the referee," he said. Cooper watched the referee. The referee watched the game. He watched and watched and watched.

Then a blue player pushed a red player. He pushed him right down! The referee blew his whistle. Toot! He held up his arm. The blue player had to sit down. Cooper jumped up and down. "The referee saw it! The referee saw it!" he shouted. Ruby clapped her hands.

After the game, they ate warm pretzels. Cooper held up his arm like the referee. Toot, he said, and laughed. "When I grow big, I will watch the game too. I will be the referee!" Grandma hugged him tight. "Best referee ever," she said.

Grayson ran to the playground. He held Mama's hand. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Grayson kept his hand in hers.

The sun was up. It made the slide hot. Grayson put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot," he said. He pulled his hand back. Mama touched the slide first. "Too hot today," she said. Grayson slid on the cool slide instead. The cool slide felt good on his legs.

Grayson saw a shiny can by the fence. He reached for it. "Wait," said Mama. "We do not touch cans. A grown-up picks them up." Mama picked up the can with a bag. She put it in the bin. Grayson clapped. He liked to help keep the playground clean.

After the playground, they went home for pizza. "A real big slice," said Grayson. He took a bite. Yum.

Then it was bath time. Grayson wanted to jump in. But he remembered the hot slide. He stopped at the tub. "Mama, you check first," he said. Mama put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Grayson touched the water with one toe. Warm, like a hug. He climbed in slowly and smiled. "Warm water," he said. "Just right."

Grandpa came to stay at Jaxon's house. They played in the backyard all week. They made a big pile of leaves. They found a toy snake under the swing. "Is it real?" Jaxon asked. "No, it is pretend," Grandpa said. "I was afraid for a minute!"

Then the week was over. Grandpa put his bag in the car. He waved. The car went down the road. Jaxon felt like crying. "Can I see Grandpa again?" he asked his mom. "Yes," she said. "We can call him on the phone. We can see him on a video call. Or we can send him a letter."

Jaxon got his crayons. He drew Grandpa and the toy snake. Mom put the picture in an envelope. She wrote Grandpa's name on it. Then they walked to the big blue mailbox together. Jaxon pushed the envelope in. It fell down, out of sight. "Go fast, letter," said Jaxon.

Sienna went to Grandpa's house. Then Grandpa said, "Time for your first haircut!" They walked to the salon down the street.

Sienna sat in the big chair. She slid down, down, down. The chair was too big! The hairdresser could not reach her hair. "Hmm," said Sienna. "I think I am too small." Grandpa laughed. "You are just right. The chair is too big."

The hairdresser brought something over. It was a little seat. "A booster seat," she said. "Little ones sit on it so I can reach their hair." Sienna sat on the booster seat. Up, up, up she went. Now she was tall like a mountain!

The hairdresser snipped. Snip, snip, snip. Grandpa made a silly face. "Your curls look tight and bouncy," he said. Sienna looked in the mirror. "I see a big girl!" she said. Grandpa clapped his hands.

Jacob skipped into the kitchen. The table smelled like warm bread. Grandma was setting out bowls. Jacob clapped his hands.

"Soup night!" said Grandma. "First we say the blessing."

Jacob wanted to say it too. He wanted it so much. But he did not know how.

"Watch us," said Grandma. "Then you try."

Daddy stood by the table. Daddy closed his eyes. Daddy bowed his head. Grandpa did it too. His eyes closed. His head went down.

Jacob peeked. One eye open. He saw Grandpa's head bowed low. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut tight. Jacob closed his eye fast.

Grandma said the blessing. Her voice was soft like snow falling.

Now it was Jacob's turn. He squeezed his eyes shut. He bent his little head way down. "Thank you for the soup," he said. "Thank you for Grandma. Thank you for Grandpa. Thank you for Daddy. One, two, three, four!"

Nobody laughed at him. Everybody smiled.

"Jacob said it!" said Grandma.

"Jacob said the whole blessing," said Grandpa.

Jacob looked up. His eyes opened wide. "Again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. "Every soup night."

Jacob sat up tall and picked up his spoon. "I love soup nights," he said.

Lillian was looking for Bunny. Bunny was lost. "Where can Bunny be?" she asked. Bunny was not on the bed. Bunny was not in the toy box. Lillian looked under her shirt on the chair. No Bunny there.

Then she saw something shiny. It was a little toy car. It was her brother Ben's car. Ben was looking sad. He had lost his car. Lillian picked up the car. She wanted to play with it. But it was Ben's. She ran to him. "Here is your car," she said. Ben smiled big. He hugged the car.

"Now I help you," said Ben. They looked together. "Where can Bunny be?" they asked. They looked in the basket. They looked in the hall. Ben peeked under the blanket on the couch. Something soft was there. It was Bunny! Bunny had been sleeping under the warm blanket, not in the cold toy box at all.

Lillian held Bunny close. "Thank you, Ben," she said. Ben rolled his car on the floor. Vroom, vroom. Lillian sat down next to him. She patted Bunny's ears. "Good night, Bunny," she whispered. "No more hiding."

Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was his first pet, a white rabbit. "Hello, Pip," said Oliver. Pip had soft fur and long ears.

At home, Oliver fed Pip a carrot. He cleaned the cage with Dad. Then Oliver ran to the table for his snack. "Wait," said Dad kindly. "Wash your hands first." Oliver looked at his hands. They had rabbit fur and bits of hay on them. He ran back to the sink. He washed with soap and warm water, and Dad helped with the faucet. His hands were clean and nice now.

Oliver sat down and ate his apple slices. "Pip is a good pet," he said. "But my hands needed a wash." Dad smiled and gave Pip a fresh carrot. Pip nibbled it down to the very end, and Oliver laughed.

Florence ran to the shape table at school. She wanted to make a picture for her mom. There were squares and triangles in a big box. There were rectangles too.

Tom held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock is a circle. Look how big it is!" Florence took the button. She held it near the big clock on the wall. Both were round. Both had no corners. "Look, Tom," she said. "Big circle, tiny circle. They are both circles." Tom smiled big. "A tiny circle is still a circle!" he said.

Florence paid her teacher one sticker for some paper. Then she glued the button on top. It became a bird sitting in a paper nest. Around it she put a square house and a red triangle roof. "Mom will love it," she said, and she kept it safe under her arm all the way home.

Charlie woke up and ran to the window. Snow was everywhere. "A snow day!" said Dad. "Let's go out after breakfast."

Charlie put on his boots and his red hat. His mittens had a hole, so one thumb could peek out. They walked to the quiet street. It was empty except for snow.

"I want a snowman," said Charlie. He patted the snow. The ball fell apart. He patted again. It fell apart again. "Try again," said Dad. So Charlie tried again, slow and patient.

Later, the sun came out. The snow felt a little wet now. Charlie patted a big ball. It stuck together! "It's packing!" he said. He rolled it and rolled it.

They made a tall snowman with a carrot nose. Charlie put his ear close to the snowman. "He is quiet," said Charlie. Dad laughed. "Let's make another one tomorrow."

Carter sat on the big soft couch. Grandma and Uncle Ben sat near him. Friends came over too. The big game was on TV. It was ice hockey.

Carter looked for the ball. He did not see one. "Where is the ball?" he asked. Uncle Ben pointed at the ice. "Look at the flat disc," he said. "It is called a puck." The players had long sticks. They hit the puck with the sticks. The puck slid fast across the cold ice.

Carter held his toy stick. He tapped a round coin on the rug. The coin slid under the coffee table, just like the puck. "I hit it like they do!" he said. Grandma laughed and helped him find the coin. On the TV, a player hit the puck into the net. The room cheered. Carter clapped his hands. "Thank you for the puck," he said to Uncle Ben. The clock on the wall showed it was almost bedtime, but Carter watched one more play, his coin warm in his little hand.

Jasper sat very still in the backyard. He wanted to name his five senses. Mama said, "Close your eyes. What can you hear?" Jasper listened. "A bird!" he said. "I hear it with my ears." Then he heard a dog bark. His ears heard that too. Ears were for hearing. He had one sense done.

Next, Jasper opened his eyes. "I see the bright sun," he said. "I see with my eyes." Two senses done. Mama gave him a strawberry. Jasper ate it. "Yum! I taste with my tongue." Three done. Then he touched the warm grass. "I feel with my hands," he said. Four done.

One sense was left. Jasper could not think of it. He sniffed and sniffed. Then he smelled cookies! "Mama, you bake cookies," he said. "I smell with my nose. That is five!" He ran to the kitchen. But the cookies were not done yet. Mama had only just mixed the dough. Jasper laughed. His nose knew before his eyes did. "Smell wins today," said Mama, and she handed him the spoon to lick.

Ruby went to the doctor with her mama. "The doctor will look at you," Mama said. "And I get a sticker after!" said Ruby.

First the doctor looked in Ruby's ears. "You hear with your ears," said the doctor. He rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Ruby heard it with her ears. Then he looked in Ruby's eyes. Ruby saw the light. It was bright! Then Ruby opened her mouth. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Ruby smelled the sticker sheet on his desk. It smelled like strawberries! The doctor touched Ruby's neck. His fingers were warm.

Then the doctor held out an ice cube. "You can touch it," he said. Ruby touched the ice cube. It felt cold! Ruby pulled her hand back fast. "Cold!" she laughed. She touched it again and giggled. Then the doctor said, "All done. What do we do now?" Ruby shouted, "Sticker time!" She picked a shiny red heart and stuck it on her hand.

Joseph ran out to the playground. It was a sunny day. The sun was bright. Joseph made a little face. He squinted and squinted.

"I can't see," said Joseph. His teacher Miss Ana heard him. She held up a sun hat. "Try this," she said. Joseph reached up and put it on. The hat sat over his eyes. The bright sun did not hurt now. He could see the slide. He could see his friend Sam.

The wind blew Sam's coat open. It was a windy day too. "Hold my hand," said Joseph. They walked to the slide together. Sam smiled at him.

"Nice hat," said Sam. Joseph tipped the sun hat down like a bow. Then he ran to the slide, fast, all the way to the top.

Penelope was playing in the backyard. She had three little toy cars. She wanted them to go fast. She pushed the blue car down the path. She pushed the yellow car past the red car. But the cars kept bumping into each other. That was the problem. Her cars needed a way to stop.

Then Penelope looked at the picnic table. There was a red apple and a green apple. Mom had just wiped the table, so it was clean. Penelope picked up both apples. She held up the red apple. "Stop," she said. Dad laughed and parked his toy truck. He held Penelope's hand like they do at the crossing, and they pretended to walk.

Then Penelope held up the green apple. "Green means go," said Dad. The blue car zoomed by. The yellow car zoomed by. When the red apple went up, every car stopped. When the green apple went up, every car went. Penelope made the red car wait a long time. Dad tapped his foot and laughed.

At the end, Penelope rolled the cars off the path. She got the little broom to sweep the crumbs away. The path was clean again. She put the red apple and the green apple back on the table. Then she held up the green apple one more time and shouted, "Go!"

Livia ran to the door in her socks. "Shot day!" she called. "Let's go, let's go!"

At the doctor's office, Mom sat down in a big chair. Livia sat next to her. There were chairs everywhere, and families in every one.

"When is my turn?" Livia asked.

"We wait here," said Mom. "The nurse will call your name at that door."

Livia watched the door. A nurse opened it. "Ben!" she called. A boy hopped up and ran in. The door shut.

"Next will be me!" said Livia.

A baby cried. A man read a book. Livia kicked her feet, fast, fast, fast.

Then the door opened. The nurse looked at her paper. "Livia!" she called.

Livia jumped up. "That is me!"

In the little room, the nurse tapped Livia's arm. "One quick pinch," she said.

Livia squeezed Mom's hand. The nurse pressed a tiny sticker onto her arm.

"All done," said the nurse.

"Already?" Livia laughed. She looked at her arm. There was the sticker, a shiny red star.

"Can we come back next week?" asked Livia.

Mom laughed and gave her a big hug. "Next time we wait in the big chairs again," she said.

"Good," said Livia. "I like waiting. My name always comes."

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts. He kicked the ball to his friend Sam. Then the other team scored. The other team scored again. The game was over. Cooper's team lost. Cooper sat down on the grass. He did not want to talk. His mouth was dry, so he took a big drink of water.

The coach blew the whistle. "Line up, everyone," she said. "We say good game now." Cooper stood at the end of the line. The blue team and the red team made a long line together. Each player walked past and tapped hands. "Good game," said a red shirt boy. "Good game," said Cooper. "Good game," said a girl with a pretty red bow.

Then it was Cooper's turn again at the last red player. It was the boy who had scored. The boy smiled. "Nice kicks," he said. Cooper smiled too. The grumpy feeling went away, like clouds going away. The red team waved. The blue team waved back. Cooper picked up the ball and hugged it all the way to the car. "Good game," he said to the ball.

Today was Hudson's birthday party. His friend Milo came with his mom. Milo looked sad at the door. "I thought we would get lost," Milo said. Hudson held up his card. "See, this is my party invitation. It says the party is here, at the bowling alley. And it says three o'clock. That is when we start!" Milo smiled. "So we came to the right place."

Then Hudson picked a small ball. It was heavy. His dad helped him hold it. Hudson pushed the ball down the lane. The ball rolled and rolled. Then the pins fell down. All of them! "The ball knocked them over," said Hudson. Milo clapped. Then everyone ate cake, and Hudson's mom kept him safe and warm beside her. "Happy birthday, Hudson," said Milo.

Jaxon sat in the family car. He was going to get his very first haircut. "You will look so handsome," said Mom. The sun did shine on Jaxon's hair. Jaxon patted his head. "One, two, three curls," he said. Mom laughed and parked the car.

At the salon, a lady named Rosa put a cape on Jaxon. Then she picked up her scissors. She cut one curl, then two curls, then three curls. Snip, snip, snip. Jaxon sat very still.

Soon Jaxon began to wiggle. He wiggled his shoulders. He rubbed his neck. "My neck feels funny," he said. Rosa saw the tiny bits of cut hair sitting on his neck. She took her soft brush. She brushed one bit away, then two bits, then three bits. The funny feeling went away. Jaxon sat still again.

"There," said Rosa. "One, two, three curls gone." Jaxon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. Mom gave him a thumbs up. "Happy hair day," said Rosa. Jaxon grinned and patted his smooth neck.

Rosalie ran to the art room. "I want to paint today!" she said.

Miss Tam put out three pots. "This is red," she said. "This is blue. This is yellow." Rosalie pointed at each pot. "Red, blue, yellow," she said. She was so happy.

Rosalie dipped her brush in red. She painted a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. Her circle turned purple! She jumped up. "Look! Look! I made purple!" She painted more and more.

When the bell rang, Rosalie wanted to run and play. But Miss Tam said, "Wait. Let's wash the brushes." Rosalie helped. They dipped each brush in water. The water turned pink, then grey. They laid the brushes flat on the tray to dry.

The next day, Ben had left his brush in the yellow pot. He tried to paint, but the brush was stiff and hard. "It won't bend," he said. Rosalie held up her clean, soft brush. "Mine bends! We washed it with water and let it dry."

Then Rosalie mixed yellow and red. Orange! She laughed out loud. "Orange is my favourite!" She painted a big orange sun with a soft, clean brush.

Lena wanted to read a book to Bear. She sat on the small red mat. She picked a book about a duck. She held it up for Bear to see.

"Look, Bear," said Lena. But the duck looked funny. The duck was upside down. All the little words were upside down too.

"Turn it around," said Mia, her friend. Lena turned the book around. Now the duck stood on his feet. Now the words sat flat and neat.

Lena opened the front cover. "This is the front," she said. She turned one page, then the next page. "The duck has a spoon," said Lena. "He eats his soup. Yum."

Mia laughed and kicked her feet. "Read more," she said.

Lena held the book up high. "The end," said Lena. "Now you, Bear." She put the book in Bear's paws. Bear's book was upside down. Lena turned it around for him.

Naomi picked a book for bedtime. She wanted to know who made up the story inside. The cover had words on it. She did not know what they said.

"Who made this story?" she asked Dad.

Dad pointed to the words. "This name is the author," he said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Naomi touched the letters. One by one, she counted them. "Four little letters," she said. "Words that tell a name!"

Dad opened the book at the front. He read page one, then page two. Naomi turned the next page herself. The story grew and grew, like magic from the kitchen making popcorn.

One page was missing! Naomi frowned. "Where did page three go?" Dad looked. The page had stuck to page four. Naomi peeled it apart, slow and careful. There it was, a beautiful picture of a red boat.

Naomi hugged the book. "The author wrote the boat," she said. Dad laughed. "Don't forget the waves," he said. Naomi patted the cover. "Good night, author," she whispered. "Good night, boat."

Florence stood in the backyard with her red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop. Her big brother Sam held the hoop up low. Florence threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. "Try again," said Sam. Florence picked it up. She threw it slowly this time. The beanbag went into the hoop. "Yay!" said Florence. She jumped up and down.

Then Sam brought out a big yellow ball. "Now catch," he said. He rolled it to her gently. Florence held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers. It rolled away under the tree. Florence ran after it. She tried one hand again. The ball fell again.

Sam sat down on the grass. "The wind can blow the ball," he said. "Want to try more?" Florence nodded. This time she held out both hands. She made a big round circle with her arms. Sam rolled the ball. Florence caught it! She did not drop it. "I got it!" she said.

Sam clapped. Their dog Rex woke up from being asleep by the fence. Rex ran over and barked at the ball. Florence laughed. She threw the ball high in the air. It landed right on Rex's head. Rex thought it was a new game. He pushed the ball back to Florence with his nose. Florence got ready with both hands.

Jules was hungry. He wanted bread with honey. Mama got the bread from the top of the shelf. She cut it with the knife. Jules watched from his stool, far away.

The bread went in the toaster. Ping! It popped up. Jules heard the pop with his ears. "The toast is ready!" said Mama. Jules touched the plate. It was warm. His fingers could feel warm.

Jules sniffed the toast with his nose. "Mmm, it smells good," he said. "Where does the smell go in?" Mama smiled. "Your nose has two little openings. They are called nostrils." Jules touched his nose. He felt two soft holes, one and then two.

Jules ran to the mirror. He looked with his eyes. He counted. "One, two! I see my nostrils!" He sniffed again. Sniff, sniff. Could he smell with just one? He covered one nostril. The smell was small. He let go. The smell was big again!

He licked the honey toast with his tongue. Sweet! "Is it too late for more toast?" he asked. "No," said Mama, laughing. She dropped in two more slices. Jules knocked on the counter. Knock, knock, knock. Ping! The toast jumped up high, right past the top of the toaster.

Evan stood by the school gate. It was his first day. He wanted to find the toy trucks fast. So he ran ahead on the path. But he got stuck behind a big red door. It was too heavy to open alone.

His teacher came. She smiled and pushed the door. Light from the sun came in. "Time to walk with us," she said. All the children stood one behind another. They made a long line, like train cars.

Evan found his spot. He held the rope handle. The whole line walked together, slow and steady. Past the slide. Past the swing. At the door to the classroom, everyone stopped. One boy tried to break away and run inside. "Not yet," said the teacher. She opened the door wide.

Evan walked in with his line. There, on the mat, sat the trucks. "I found them!" he said.

Milo ran to Grandma's big chair. Grandma had a cloth bag on her lap.

"We will play a game," said Grandma. "Put your hand in. Do not peek. Tell me what you feel."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. "It is a red ball!"

"Open your eyes wide and look," said Grandma.

Milo pulled out the ball. It was not red. It was blue! He laughed. "I could not tell. My fingers felt the ball. But my fingers did not tell me the color. I had to look with my eyes."

"Try again," said Grandma.

Milo shut his eyes. He put his hand back in the bag. He felt something long and smooth. "A crayon!" he said. "Is it green?"

He looked. The crayon was yellow! "I must look to see," said Milo. "My fingers cannot see colors."

Grandma clapped. Then she yawned a big yawn. "Time for my nap," she said softly.

Milo did not want Grandma to be sleepy. He found her soft blanket. He put it on her lap. "Now try one more ball," he whispered.

Grandma put her hand in the bag. "Round and smooth. Is it yellow?"

"You have to look!" said Milo. Grandma pulled it out. The ball was green!

"My eyes see it," said Grandma. "But first, my nap." She closed her eyes. Milo tiptoed out with his blue ball.

Elizabeth did not want to sleep. She wanted to play all night.

"Can I stay up, Mama?" she asked.

"Just a little longer," said Mama. "Then bath, pajamas, bed."

Elizabeth sat in the warm bath. She counted the bubbles. One, two, three. Mama washed her hair. Then Mama helped her get dressed in soft pajamas. Elizabeth zipped her own sleep sack. Ziiiip!

Mama tucked her in, safe and cozy. "Good night, Elizabeth."

In the morning, Elizabeth woke up. She ran to her blocks. She built a tall tower. She jumped and danced and sang.

The next night, Elizabeth asked, "What if I stay up all night?"

"You can try," said Mama.

Elizabeth stayed up very late. Her eyes got heavy. In the morning, she could not build. She could not jump. She was too tired to play.

"Sleeping at night gives your body rest for the next day," said Mama.

So that night, Elizabeth took her bath. She put on her pajamas. She zipped her sleep sack. One, two, three, good night.

In the morning, she built the tallest tower yet.

Iris put on her red socks at school. She liked getting dressed all by herself. Then it was time for a crunchy snack. Iris ate apple slices. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

After snack, Iris needed the toilet. She went into the little bathroom. She closed the door. She used the toilet. Then she ran out fast to play.

Teacher Mia called, "Iris! Come and look." The toilet water was still there. "You forgot to flush," said Teacher Mia. Iris asked, "What do I do now?" Teacher Mia smiled. "After using the toilet, we flush," she said.

Iris pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled away. "And then we wash our hands," said Teacher Mia. Iris turned on the sink. She washed her hands with soap. Bubbles, bubbles!

Later it was nap time. Iris lay on her little mat. She thought about the whoosh. First flush, then wash. First flush, then wash. "Will we wash after lunch too?" she asked herself. "Yes," she whispered. "Hands get washed a lot."

Her eyes closed slowly, and her red socks peeked out from under the blanket.

Leo planted little seeds in pots on the balcony. He planted lettuce, carrots and one big sunflower. His friend Mia came over to see. "It looks like a tiny farm," she said.

Every morning Leo gave the pots a drink from his orange watering can. Then one hot day, Leo played all day at Mia's house. He forgot to water his plants. When he came home, the lettuce was drooping. Its leaves hung down like sad little ears. "Oh no," said Leo.

Leo ran to get his watering can. He gave the droopy lettuce a big drink. The next morning, the lettuce stood up tall. "Water makes you wake up!" said Leo. Mia laughed. "You are a good plant friend," she said. Leo watered the carrots too, just in case.

Alexis ran to Grandma's house. He ran fast through the yard. His shoes went clap, clap, clap on the porch. Inside there was a new baby. The baby was his new baby sister. She was small as a loaf of bread.

"Can I hold her now?" asked Alexis.

"Yes," said Grandma. "Big brothers wash their hands first."

Alexis looked at his hands. They had dirt on them. One hand had a smudge of mud. The other had grass stains. "My hands are not clean," he said. He held them up to show Grandma. "Look! My hands are all yucky."

Grandma laughed a little laugh. "Come with me," she said. She took him to the sink. She turned on the water. It was warm. Alexis made bubbles with the soap. The bubbles were big and shiny. He popped one on his nose. "Pop!" he said. Grandma said he was a silly boy. She said he was not a mean brother, just a messy one.

Then his hands were clean. They smelled like flowers. Grandma sat him in the big chair. She put a pillow on his lap. Then she set the baby sister on the pillow. The baby made a small sound. It sounded like a tiny sneeze.

"Hello, baby," said Alexis. "I am your big brother. I washed my hands for you." The baby grabbed his finger. Her hand was very small. Alexis smiled so big his cheeks hurt. "Grandma, she likes me!" he said. "She really works at holding on!"

Aaron was at Grandma's house. Grandma was playing a game with him. "Show me your eyes," she said. Aaron pointed to his eyes. "Eyes see!" he said. "Show me your ears." Aaron wiggled his ears. "Ears hear!" Then the phone did ring, ring, ring. Grandma said, "That is the phone. Ears hear the ring." Aaron laughed and clapped.

"Now show me your nose," said Grandma. Aaron pointed to his nose. He sniffed and sniffed. Something smelled sweet. Something smelled warm. "I smell cookies!" said Aaron. "I do not see cookies," he said. He looked left. He looked right. No cookies. Was he wrong? Grandma smiled. "Follow your nose," she said.

Aaron sniffed and walked. He sniffed and walked. His nose led him to the kitchen. There sat Grandma's oven, all warm and shut tight. Grandma opened it with her big glove. Cookies! Aaron had smelled them before he could see them. "My nose knew first!" said Aaron. Grandma gave him a cookie. Aaron sniffed the cookie, then took a big bite. "Noses smell," he said, with crumbs on his chin.

Jasper stood at the painting table at school. He wanted to paint ten balloons. His teacher, Miss May, had hung up a counting song poster. "One, two, three, four, five," the children sang. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," they sang next. Jasper tapped his brush and counted with them. He painted one red balloon, then two blue balloons, then three yellow ones.

Soon he had ten balloons on his paper. Then Miss May asked, "Can you write the number too?" Jasper wrote a 1 for one balloon. He wrote a 3 for three balloons. He wrote a 9 for nine balloons. Then he stopped. Ten felt big. He made a 1. He made a 0 next to it. He looked at Miss May. "Ten uses two numbers," she said with a smile. "A 1 and then a 0."

Jasper wrote 10 under his balloons. His friend Leo leaned over to look. "Ten has a 1 and a 0," said Jasper. Leo clapped his soft little hands. Jasper carried his painting to the wall. It would go home in his bag today. On the way, he passed the toy shelf. A toy truck sat there with a broken wheel. Jasper set his painting down gently. He pushed the truck to the fixing basket for Miss May. Then he picked up his ten balloons again and held them up high. "Ten!" he said. "A 1 and a 0."

Zoe went to the health clinic with her mom. A friendly nurse said, "Time to check you." Zoe stepped onto the big scale. She wiggled her toes. The numbers jumped up and down. "Why do the numbers jump?" Zoe asked. "Because you are moving," said the nurse.

Zoe tried again. She stood very still. She held her arms at her sides. The numbers stopped jumping. The scale showed how much she weighed. "The number stayed put!" Zoe said. "Yes," said the nurse. "Standing still helps."

Then the nurse said, "Now it is time for your shot." Zoe held her mom's hand. She stood still, just like on the scale. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." It was done. It hurt just a little bit.

"Did I do it?" Zoe asked. "You did it," said Mom. The nurse put a fun bandage on Zoe's arm. It had a garden on it, with flowers and a bunny. On the way out, Zoe pushed the door open by herself. "I stood still like a big girl," she said. Mom smiled and said, "You surely did."

Jaxson ran into the kitchen. He was still in his pajamas. He saw the cookie jar up high. "Cookies! Cookies!" he said.

Mom shook her head. "Cookies are not for breakfast," she said. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day. It comes first, before lunch and dinner."

Jaxson pouted. He wanted cookies. But then he heard his tummy rumble. Rumble, rumble. Mom laughed. "Let's pick a breakfast together. You can help."

Jaxson looked in the fridge. He found eggs. Mom cracked them. Jaxson stirred. Mom cooked them on the stove, and Jaxson watched from his chair. He put bread on his plate. He put a banana by it too.

After eating, Jaxson had a bath. The water was warm. Mom washed his hair. Then Jaxson got dressed in his blue shirt. He helped make the kitchen tidy.

That night, Dad read him a story. "What do we call the first meal of the day?" Dad asked. Jaxson grinned. "Breakfast!" he said. "But not cookies!"

Zoe sat in the big waiting room. The chairs were blue and squeaky. She held her bunny tight. The room smelled like soap. A fish swam in a little tank. Zoe tapped the glass, and the fish swam away fast.

A nurse called, "Zoe, it is your turn." Zoe walked in slowly. She saw a small tray with a tiny needle. Her tummy felt tight. "But I am not sick," Zoe said. "Why do I need a shot?" The doctor smiled. "The shot helps protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said. "It helps keep you well, so you can go to your class tomorrow."

Zoe looked at her bunny. "You can have one too, bunny," she whispered. She felt one quick pinch, like a tiny bug kiss. Then it was done. The doctor gave her a special bandage with stars on it.

Zoe picked a sticker from a basket. She chose a shiny red heart. On the way out, she skipped past the fish tank. "Bye, fish!" she said. "I am going back to my class tomorrow."

Xavier was at school. Miss Ana held up a tablet. "We can draw on this," she said. Xavier wanted to draw a red sun.

He tapped the big button. The screen lit up. He clapped his hands. Miss Ana helped him find the drawing app. It had a sticky spot on it from someone's snack. She wiped it clean. Xavier tapped the app. It opened.

Now he needed red. He looked at the little colours on the screen. He tapped a blue dot. His line came out blue. "Not blue," said Xavier. His friend Lily pointed. "Tap the red one." He tapped the red colour. He drew his finger across the screen. A red line came out. He made a big round sun. It was all red.

"Time to put it away," said Miss Ana. Xavier pressed the button. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, all by himself. "Good job, Xavier," said Lily. Xavier smiled and waved at the basket.

Arya went to the library with her dad. She wanted to make a picture there. The craft table had paper and crayons.

Arya picked a paper. "This is a square," she said. It had four sides that matched. Dad nodded. "A square for you," he said.

The boy next to her had a napkin. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He opened his hands. "Look!" he said. It was not a square now. It was long and flat. Arya tilted her head. "It's a rectangle," said the boy.

Arya tried it too. She lined up the edges. She folded her square paper in half. She pressed it flat. Then she held it up. Her square was a rectangle now! "I did it!" she said.

Dad smiled. "Can you spin your rectangle?" he asked. Arya spun it round and round on the table. The boy clapped.

Then Arya looked at the wall. There was a clock like a circle. There was a flag like a triangle. There was a book like a rectangle, with sharp corners.

"I can make shapes," Arya said. She folded her paper again. She held it up to the window. "Look, Dad. A little rectangle."

Dad gave her a spring clip to hang it up. Arya clipped her paper to the shelf. It flapped a little in the air. "My shape stays here," she said. "For everyone to see."

Olivier was at Grandma's house. His little blue car was lost. "Where can it be?" he asked. Grandma said, "Let's look." Olivier looked under the table. No car. He looked in the toy box. No car. He looked by the big chair. No car. Then Olivier saw something. The cat was asleep. The cat's tail was moving. It tapped a basket. Something inside went bump, bump. Olivier peeked in the basket. "My car!" he said. "It fell in here!" After that, Olivier did a new thing. He put the car in the basket every night. Same basket, by his bed. One morning he wanted his car. He looked in the basket. There it was! "Grandma, I found it so fast!" he called. Grandma smiled. "That naughty cat can't hide it now," Olivier said, and drove the car along the floor.

Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. Teacher Anna held up a big card with words. "This is a recipe," she said. "It tells us what to use and what to do, one step at a time."

Max looked at the recipe. Flour, eggs, milk. One cup, two cups, stir, stir. But Max was so excited that he skipped the eggs. He just stirred the flour and milk. His tummy rumbled. Pancakes, pancakes, soon!

Teacher Anna poured the batter onto the pan. Flip, flip. But Max's pancake came out flat. Flat as a rain puddle! Papa giggled. Mama giggled. "Oh no," said Max. "My pancake is sad."

"Let's read the recipe again," said Teacher Anna. They read it one step at a time. Flour, then eggs, then milk. Max cracked the eggs himself. Stir, stir, stir. This time the pancake puffed up big and round. "It's a happy pancake!" said Max. Papa took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "One more, please!"

Joshua went to the park with Mom. He brought his blue ball. But when it was time to play, the ball was gone. Joshua looked under the bench. He looked by the slide. No ball. Joshua felt like crying. "It is hard to lose your ball," said Mom. "Let's look some more."

They walked past the swings. They saw the park helper, Mr. Lee. Mr. Lee held a blue ball. "Is this yours?" he asked. "There is a name tag on it. It says Joshua." Mom had written Joshua's name on the tag at home. Mr. Lee read the name. Then he gave the ball back to Joshua.

Joshua hugged his ball. "Thank you, Mr. Lee!" he said. "Do you want to share it with me?" asked Mr. Lee. Joshua rolled the ball to him. Mr. Lee rolled it back. They played and played. Joshua smiled and held his name tag tight. "My name," he said. "That is me!"

Arthur rode the bus with his mom. Snow was starting to fall outside. Arthur held his hands in his lap. His bunny was not there. Bunny was lost at Grandma's house.

"Where could bunny be?" Arthur wondered. The bus stopped. Grandma was waiting. Arthur ran inside. He zoomed from room to room. He peeked fast in the kitchen. He peeked fast in the bedroom. No bunny anywhere!

Arthur sat down on the rug. Some dirt from his shoe sat there too. He took a big breath. "I will look in one room at a time," he said. He looked all around the kitchen. He looked under the table. No bunny. Then he looked all around the bedroom. He looked under the bed. There was bunny's neat little ear! Arthur pulled bunny out and hugged him tight. "I found you," he whispered.

Alexander wanted Grandpa to read the owl book. It had a big brown owl on the cover. "Please read it now," said Alexander.

Grandpa sat down on the couch. He picked up the book. He squinted at the page. Then he reached for his glasses. He put them on his nose. "Now I can see the words," said Grandpa. "Glasses help me see more clearly."

Alexander wanted to try. "Can I see with them?" he asked. "Just for a minute," said Grandpa. Alexander put on the big glasses. Everything looked funny and blurry. The room looked too big. He took them off fast. His eyes saw clearly again without the glasses. "How curious," said Alexander. "They help you. But not me!"

Then Grandpa began to read. Alexander heard the story with his ears. He smelled popcorn from the kitchen. Mom brought warm popcorn in a bowl. Alexander touched the bumpy kernels with his fingers. He tasted one. It was salty and good.

"Was that owl real?" Alexander asked at the end. "No, but there was one at the zoo," said Grandpa. "Can we go see it?" asked Alexander. Grandpa laughed and put his glasses back on.

Ibrahim woke up. The sun was up too. Mama smiled at him. "Time to brush your teeth," she said. "We brush in the morning." Ibrahim brushed. One, two, three, up and down. His teeth felt good.

At breakfast, Ibrahim ate his egg. Then he played. Then Papa ran the bath. Papa made the water warm with his own hand. Ibrahim got in and splashed. He got dressed all by himself. His sock had a little rip in it. "New socks tomorrow," said Mama.

Night came. The lamp was off. Ibrahim was in bed. Then he sat up. "Mama! My teeth!" He hopped out of bed. He ran to the sink. He brushed and brushed. "We brush before bed too," said Mama. "Good boy, Ibrahim." She tucked him in. She kissed his head. "One kiss," she said. "Two kisses." Ibrahim smiled and closed his eyes.

Eliana and her brother Sam played trains. The trains were loud. They went click clack on the track. Then Sam grabbed the blue train. Eliana grabbed it too. "My turn," said Eliana. Sam let go. Then he got the next turn. That felt fair.

Eliana wished she could keep the blue train all day. But she gave it back. "Your turn," she said. Sam smiled big.

Then it was time for snack. Eliana ran to the kitchen. The toy room stayed messy. Mama was there cutting apples with a safe knife. Eliana watched from her stool.

"Eliana, your trains are still out," said Mama. "Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with." Eliana ran back. She picked up the trains. They felt hard and smooth in her hands. Sam picked up his blocks. Under one block was a red pencil! "Look!" said Eliana. She put it in the cup.

The room was clean. Then they ate sweet apple slices together.

Nathan stood by the little pool at the lake. His teacher was not there yet. The water was blue and cool. Nathan could hear it splash, splash on the side.

A big cow stood in the lake nearby. The cow liked to bathe in the cool water. "Look at the cow," said Nathan's dad. Dad held Nathan's hand. "I want to jump in now," said Nathan. He stepped toward the pool. "Not yet," said Dad kindly. "A grown-up must always watch children when they are in or near water." Nathan stopped and sat down. He put his toes near the edge and waited.

Soon the teacher came. She smiled and said, "I am watching now, Nathan." Then Nathan jumped in. He kicked his legs. The water made little waves. His dad clapped. Nathan felt happy. "I did it," he said, splashing with his hands.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was bunched up close. "That one has more!" said Oliver. He pointed at the long row. "I want the row with more!"

"Count them," said Mom. Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the bunched-up row. "One, two, three, four, five." He sat very still. Both rows had five!

Oliver pushed the close buttons apart. They made a long row too. He counted again. "Still five!" He pushed them back together. He counted again. "Five!" He laughed out loud. "Moving them doesn't change it!"

A bee bumped at the window. Oliver ran to look. "Come back!" he cried. He waved his soft sleeve at the glass. Then he ran back to the table. He spread the buttons out one more time. "Five, five, five!"

Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down three warm bowls of soup. Grandma put down one orange cup. Emmett had his own little spoon.

Grandma smiled at everyone. "Bon appétit," she said. Emmett looked up. "What does that mean?" he asked. "It is what people say in France," said Grandma. "We say it before we eat. It means, have a good meal." Grandma had lived in France when she was young.

Emmett wanted to say it too. He tried. "Bone apple tea," he said. Grandma laughed softly. "Almost," she said. "Bon appétit." Emmett listened. He held his spoon like a pencil, very still. "Bon appétit," he said. Mom clapped. "Perfect!"

Dad came in with bread. Emmett sat up tall. "Bon appétit, Dad," he said. Dad grinned big. "Bon appétit to you, Emmett."

Grandma took a sip of soup. "One bowl, two bowls, three bowls," she said. "And one happy little boy at our table." Emmett dipped his spoon. "Bon appétit," he whispered to his soup.

Zachary sat on the big rug in the living room. The tablet lay on the coffee table. He wanted to draw a red truck on it.

He pressed the little round button. The screen lit up. He tapped the blue square, and the drawing app opened. A white page waited for him. Zachary drew two round wheels. He drew a long red body. He drew a fast truck going down a hill.

Then the screen went black. All his truck was gone. "Oh no," said Zachary. "Where did my truck go? Did I forget to tap something?"

Dad came over and looked. "The tablet ran out of power," he said. "It needs charging now."

Dad plugged the charger into the wall and into the tablet. A small green line showed up on the screen. Zachary watched it. "Is it getting juice?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Power for the tablet."

They set the tablet on the shelf to charge. Zachary put his crayons away too. Later the screen woke up. Zachary opened the app, and there was his red truck. He drew a sun above it. "Hi, truck," he said.

Mila was going on a trip. Her family was going to a campsite with a tent. She put her teddy bear in her little red backpack.

First they had to ride on a big plane. At the airport, Mila saw a long desk. A kind man in a uniform stood there.

Mila put her backpack on a moving belt. The backpack went into a big machine. The machine checks what is inside bags. Then the backpack was gone.

"My teddy!" said Mila. "Where is my teddy?"

Dad held her hand. "Watch the belt," he said.

Mila watched. She watched and watched. Then the backpack came out the other end of the machine. It slid down to her.

Mila opened the bag. Her teddy was still there. She hugged him tight.

"My teddy came out," she said. "The machine gave him back!"

A lady at the desk smiled at Mila. Mila stood tall and proud. She held her teddy all the way to the plane.

Joshua wanted to make a growly bear sound. Miss Amy said, "Try the big piano." Joshua sat near the piano. He pressed a key on the right side. The sound was high, like a little bird. "That is not a bear," said Joshua. He tried the right side again. High, high, high. Still a little bird.

Miss Amy smiled. "Try the other side," she said. Joshua pressed a key on the left side. Boom! A big, low sound came out. "Growl!" said Joshua. He pressed more keys on the left. Low sounds rumbled out. Low, low, low. A car went by outside, and it sounded low too.

Joshua made his bear growl and growl. Then he played the right side again, just to hear the little bird. "Growl," he said. "Tweet," he said. Miss Amy laughed. Joshua played one low key and one high key, over and over, until it was time to stop. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Miss Amy. "Yes," said Joshua. He waved to the piano. "Bye, bear."

Charles rode the big city bus. He held his sleepy bear. The bus went bump. The bear flew out of his hands. "Oh no!" said Charles. "My bear!"

Charles looked down. The bear was gone. It was dark under the seat. Charles could not see anything under there. He got on his knees and peeked. It was just black and shadowy.

The bus driver saw him. She reached up and clicked a little light on her keys. "Here is a flashlight," she said. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots, like under a bed." She gave it to Mom. Mom held it and shined it under the seat.

The light made the dark spot bright. There was the bear! His arm was stuck on a string that hung down. Mom pulled the string aside. Charles reached in and grabbed the bear. He hugged him tight. The bear felt warm and soft. "Thank you," Charles said to the driver. The driver smiled. Charles sat on Mom's lap. He patted the bear's head. "Sleepy time, bear," he said.

Nova sat at the craft table at summer camp. She was drawing a big red apple. One leaf, two leaves, three leaves. She wanted the leaves very, very dark green.

Nova pressed down hard. She pressed harder. Then she pressed her hardest. Snap! The pencil point broke off and flew onto the table.

"Oh no," said Nova. "My point went pop!"

The camp teacher, Sam, came over. "That pencil needs a new point," he said. He sharpened it with his sharpener, slowly and safely.

Nova picked up her pencil again. This time she pressed gently, like a little cat walking. One leaf, two leaves, three leaves. All soft green, all whole.

"My pencil is still alive," said Nova.

Sam laughed. "It likes you better now," he said.

Nova drew a little toy bear next to the apple. She even drew her old red hat. Then she held up her picture.

"Look, everybody!" she said. "One apple, one bear, one hat, and one happy pencil."

Sofia went to the bank with Mama. Sofia carried her own little bag of coins. She put the coins on the counter, one by one. The coins made a small fall into the tray. Ping, ping, ping.

Then it was time to go. Outside the big doors, snowflakes began to float down. Sofia put on her coat by herself. She pulled the zipper tab up, up, up. But the zipper would not close. She pulled again. Still nothing.

"Mama, my zipper is stuck," Sofia said.

Mama did not pull the tab. She held the coat and looked. "See the little box at the bottom?" she said.

Sofia looked down. Yes! There was a tiny box at the bottom of one side. And the other side had a little end. Sofia slid the end into the box. It clicked in. Then she pulled the tab. Zip! The coat closed all the way.

Sofia zipped it down and up again. Zip, zip. Now the wind could not get in.

"Ready?" Mama asked.

Sofia pushed the door open. The snowflakes floated past her warm, zipped-up coat.

Luca stood at the farm with his papa. He had three little seeds in his hand. One seed, two seeds, three seeds. Papa dug a row in the dirt. Luca dropped the seeds in. Papa covered them with soft brown soil.

"Will my seeds grow today?" Luca asked. "No, they need many days," said Papa. So Luca watered the dirt with his small blue can. Then he waited.

Each morning Luca ran to the garden. He saw dirt. He saw dirt. He saw more dirt. A naughty crow flew by, but the seeds stayed hidden and safe. Luca kept on watering. One day, two days, many days.

Then Luca saw something new. Something small and green stood up out of the soil. "Papa, come quick!" he called. Papa came fast. "What is it?" Luca asked. "A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout," said Papa. "A sprout," said Luca. He smiled at the little green sprout. He took a picture of it with Mama's camera, click.

The next day there were two sprouts. Then three sprouts, one for each seed. Luca watered them again. "Grow big, sprouts," he said. "I will fish in the pond while you grow." He sat by the water with Papa, and the sprouts waved in the soft wind.

Amira sat at the big table in math club. She had a little bucket of blocks. "Let's count them," said her friend Tom. Amira touched each block. "One, two, three, four," she said. She had four blocks. Tom had a big pile too. "Who has more?" asked Teacher Nan. Amira looked at both piles. Tom's pile looked big. "Tom has more," she said. She counted his blocks. "One, two, three, four, five." Tom had five. He had more than four.

Then Grandma came in. She had something in her hand. "This one is for you," Grandma said. It was a shiny red block. Amira put it in her bucket. She hoped it would help. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." Now she had five too! "Look, look," said Amira. "I got one more. Now I have five!" Tom put one of his blocks in her bucket too. Amira counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Now she had six!

"Who has more now?" asked Teacher Nan. Tom counted his blocks. He had four. "Amira has more," said Tom. Amira smiled and hugged her bucket. "Ready for more blocks," she said. Grandma laughed and dropped one more block in. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," counted Amira.

Rowan ran to the playground in his blue shirt. The sun felt warm on his face. He heard a kite humming in the wind. It was red, with a long tail. One, two, three ribbons on the tail.

A girl named Mia held the string. Rowan wanted the kite so much. He reached out his hand. Mia pulled the string away. Her face looked scared. Rowan stopped. His tummy felt small and tight.

Then he remembered Grandpa's words. "Say 'May I have a turn?'" Grandpa had said. "It is the polite way to ask." Rowan took a big breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Mia smiled. "Yes! Hold tight like this." She put the string in his hand. The kite pulled and pulled. It tickled his fingers. "Thank you," said Rowan. "You can kick off your shoes if you want," said Mia.

A big boy ran past and bumped Rowan's arm. "Sorry," the big boy said. He helped Rowan hold the string again. One, two, three ribbons danced in the sky. "May I have a turn next?" Mia asked. Rowan laughed and gave her the string.

Mohamed sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Mama, where are we going?" he asked. "To Grandma's house," said Mama. "She will make pancakes." Mohamed loved pancakes. It was his dream to eat a big stack of them. He looked out the window. He saw a red car and an empty truck. "Mama, does Grandma cook pancakes on the stove?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "The stove gets hot." Mohamed thought about that. "Is it hot when it looks cold?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot."

Soon the car stopped. Mohamed held Mama's hand in the parking lot. He stayed close to her, just like a little duck stays close to its mama. At Grandma's house, the kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma stirred the batter. "Is the stove hot now?" Mohamed asked Grandma. "It is hot, but only I touch it," said Grandma. Mohamed kept his hands in his lap. He watched a pancake bubble. He heard it sizzle. Grandma flipped it high in the air. "Wow!" said Mohamed. They sat down to talk and eat. Mohamed took a big bite. "Grandma, the pancake is warm and yummy!" he said. Grandma smiled and poured more batter into the pan.

Weston sat at the dinner table. His plate had yummy noodles. He ate them all up. Now his tummy still wanted more.

The doorbell rang. Ding dong!

Weston slid under the table and hid. It was Mr. Bean from next door. His boots went tap, tap on the floor.

Mom said, "Weston, Mr. Bean is here."

Weston peeked out from under the tablecloth. Mr. Bean waved his big hand.

Weston climbed into his chair. He took a big breath. "Hello, Mr. Bean," he said.

Mr. Bean's face turned into a big smile. "Hello, Weston!" he said. "I heard a little storm under that table."

Weston giggled. "The storm went away," he said.

Then Weston held out his plate. "More noodles, please, Mom."

Mom filled his plate. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you," said Weston.

Mr. Bean sat down too. Mom gave him a bowl. Weston showed him how to twirl noodles with a fork. Mr. Bean made a wobbly nest.

Weston laughed so hard his toes tickled.

One noodle slipped off Weston's fork. It landed on Mr. Bean's shoe.

"Sorry," said Weston.

"That's okay," said Mr. Bean. He picked it up with a napkin.

After dinner, Mr. Bean stood up. "Time to go home," he said. "Goodbye, Weston."

"Bye bye," said Weston. He waved his whole hand, just like Mr. Bean had waved his.

Iris went to Dad's office with him. She saw a big tablet on his desk. "Can I draw?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. He tapped the top button. The screen lit up. "The small pictures are called icons," said Dad. "Tap one and it opens an app."

Iris looked at all the little pictures. She found one with a paintbrush. She tapped the paintbrush icon. The drawing app opened. A white page came up. She drew a red circle. Then she drew a purple monkey with a long tail. The monkey held a sharp yellow banana. She laughed and drew a green hat on him.

Then her picture got too full. "I want a new page," she said. Dad showed her the new page button. Tap, and a clean white page appeared. The old page was safe in the little pictures. She made a new monkey. This one had a rip in his hat. She fixed it with a blue stripe.

When it was time to go home, Dad said, "Now we put it away." He helped her tap the button. The screen went dark. Iris patted the tablet, soft and gentle. "Bye, monkey," she said. "See you next time."

Isabelle went to the hall with Mama and Grandpa. There was a big party there. Many people came. There were songs and a long table with food.

Isabelle saw a food table with little cakes. She let go of Mama's hand. She started to walk to the cakes. The hall was big and full of people. She could not see Mama anymore. She looked left. She looked right. So many legs and coats!

Then Isabelle stopped. She remembered the rule. At a big crowded party, children stay close to their grown-up. She turned around fast. She walked back the way she came. Then she saw Mama's blue coat. "Mama!" she said. She reached up and held Mama's hand.

Grandpa brought her a little cake on a plate. They sat on a chair together. Isabelle ate her cake and held on tight.

Emmett went to the grocery store with Dad. "We need eggs," said Dad. Emmett picked a big white egg. He held it gently all the way to the car.

At home, Emmett wanted to bake a tasty cake. Dad cracked an egg on the bowl. The shell opened, and the egg slid out. "Can I do one?" asked Emmett. Dad helped him tap the egg. The shell cracked open, and the egg fell in. A tiny bit of shell fell in too. It sat in the yellow puddle of egg. Emmett fished it out with a spoon. He tried again, slow and careful. This time no shell fell in.

Dad put the pan in the hot oven. Emmett waited and waited. The kitchen began to smell sweet. At last the cake came out. Emmett and Mom and Dad built a tall slice tower on their plates. Emmett took a big bite. "Tasty," he said.

Kinsley wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. She got her paper and her blue paint. She sat close to Mama at the big table. Mama had a hot mug of cocoa. "Mine is hot," said Mama. "Yours is cold milk." Kinsley touched her own cup. It felt cool and nice.

Then Kinsley dropped her paint brush. It rolled away. It rolled behind the couch. Kinsley went to get it. She looked behind the couch. She saw a little box with holes in the wall. It was an outlet. Her fingers wiggled toward it.

Kinsley stopped. She did not touch it. She ran back to Mama. "There are holes in the wall," she said. "Behind the couch." Mama came right away. "That is an outlet," said Mama. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet. I will get your brush." Mama reached with a grown-up hand and got the brush out.

Kinsley sat down again. She painted big white flakes. "It looks like snow," said Mama. Kinsley smiled. "That is true," she said. "It snows at Grandma's house." She stayed right by Mama and painted until the whole page was full.

Wesley wanted to play a guessing game. He got a cup, a toothbrush, and a towel. He put them in a basket.

"I will guess with my eyes closed," Wesley said. He closed his eyes tight. He did not peek.

Daddy held out the first thing. Wesley touched it with his fingertips. His fingertips said the cup was smooth and cool. "The cup!" he said. He was right.

Next his fingertips felt the toothbrush. It was bumpy on top. The handle was smooth. "The toothbrush!" he said. Right again.

Then the towel. His fingertips said it was soft and fluffy. "The towel!" Wesley laughed.

Wesley heard the water drip in the sink. He smelled the soap, so sweet. Daddy gave him a tiny taste of toothpaste on his finger. It tasted minty, and Wesley made a funny face.

"My fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy," Wesley said.

"You guessed every one," said Daddy.

Wesley held the cup up straight. "My turn to pick for you, Daddy. Close your eyes!"

Paisley wanted a bedtime story. She ran to get her book. She climbed into bed with it.

She opened the book and looked at the page. The words looked all mixed up. The pictures seemed backwards too. "That's funny," she said. The story did not make sense this way.

Paisley turned the book over. Now she saw the front cover. It had a bear on it. She opened the front cover and turned the first page. The words sat in neat little rows. The pictures came in order. The bear found honey, then took a nap.

Papa came in and sat down. "Read it to me," Paisley said. Papa started at the front and turned page after page. Paisley listened and played with her blanket corner.

The last page came. Papa closed the back cover. "The end," he said.

"Again," said Paisley. Papa opened the front cover one more time.

Zayn put on his red shoe. "We need to go to the library," said Mama. "You get your very own card today."

At the library, a lady smiled. She made a card with Zayn's name on it. "My card!" said Zayn. He held it tight. He picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. The lady scanned his card. Zayn took the book home.

The next week, Zayn gave the book back. "Now what?" he asked. He looked at his card. Was it all done? He gave the card to the lady. She scanned it again. "Pick a new book," she said. Zayn gasped. The same card worked again! He ran to the shelf. He chose a book about a sleepy moon.

"Home, moon book," said Zayn. He hugged his card all the way.

Miles ran into the pool changing room. He put his towel in the cubby. His swimming bag had a big owl on it.

"Time to swim!" said Dad.

Miles got in the pool. He kicked and splashed. He practiced and practiced. "Look at me!" he said.

Then it was time to get out. Miles grabbed the side of the pool. He pulled and pulled. His arms slipped. He fell back with a splash.

"Sorry, I can't do it," said Miles.

"Where are the steps?" Dad asked.

"The steps?" said Miles. "Can steps help?"

"Try them and see," said Dad.

Miles swam to the pool steps. He climbed up, up, up. One step. Two steps. Out!

"Easy peasy," said Miles. Then he hopped down and climbed out again.

David climbed the tall steps of the school bus. It was his first day of school. He found a seat by the window. The bus went bump, bump, bump.

At school, everyone went inside. David saw blocks and paints and a big rug. He wanted to play with everything. Then his tummy felt funny. He needed to find the bathroom. Where was it? He looked left. He looked right. He did not see it.

A tall lady walked over. "I am Miss Kim," she said. "I am the teacher." David took a big breath. "Where is the bathroom?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled. "It is right over there," she said. She pointed to a small door. "If you need help at school, you can ask the teacher."

David walked to the door. He pushed it open. He found the bathroom all by himself, well, almost by himself. When he came back, he asked, "Can you teach me the blocks?" "Yes!" said Miss Kim. David built a tall, tall tower. It went up and up and up. Then it fell down with a crash. David laughed and built it again.

Everett sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to feel brave, like a big boy.

The doctor came in. She was a kind man's helper with white shoes. "Everett, can you see my light?" she asked. Everett used his eyes to see it blink. Then she rang a little bell. Everett used his ears to hear it ring. "Good listening," she said.

Next she held out a cotton ball. Everett sniffed it with his nose. "Smells like nothing," he said. Then the doctor put a small wet cloth on his arm. Everett touched it with his fingers. "Cold," he said. "That's your skin doing its job," the doctor said.

Then the doctor gave Everett a lemon slice. Everett thought it would taste sweet, like his orange juice at home. He took a little lick with his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour," he said. "Sour, sour, sour!" The doctor laughed. "Your tongue can taste that a lemon is sour." Everett tried again, a tiny lick. Still sour. He climbed down from the big chair all by himself.

"I used my eyes and my ears and my nose," said Everett. "And my fingers and my tongue too." He gave the doctor a high five. "Same time next year," she said. Everett waved all the way to the door.

Madelyn sat at the table. She wanted juice. "Give me juice!" she said.

Grandpa shook his head. "Try again," he said. Madelyn thought. Then she said, "Juice, please."

Grandpa smiled. "Here you go," he said. He poured the juice. Madelyn drank it. It was cold and sweet.

"Thank you," said Madelyn. Grandpa patted her head. Madelyn felt big.

Then Madelyn ran to the door. The dog was outside. The dog began to bark. A butterfly flew by the window. "Help, Grandpa!" said Madelyn. "I want to see the butterfly!"

Grandpa opened the door. They watched together. The butterfly flew up, up, up. Then it was gone.

Madelyn ran back inside. She bumped the table. Her cup fell. Juice went everywhere.

"Sorry, Grandpa," said Madelyn.

"That is okay," said Grandpa. He wiped the floor. Madelyn helped with her little towel. Soon the floor was clean.

Madelyn yawned. Her eyes closed. She fell asleep in her chair. Grandpa carried her to bed. "Goodnight, Madelyn," he said. The dog barked one soft bark.

Mia ran into the baby store. She held Mama's hand tight. "The baby comes soon!" said Mia. It was windy outside. The door swung shut behind them.

Mia saw cribs. She saw tiny socks. She saw a big shelf of dolls. "Can I pick one?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Mama. Mia chose a doll with a soft round head. Then she saw it. The doll's head tipped way back. It flopped like a sleepy flower.

"Uh oh," said Mia. She put her small hand under the doll's head. The head stayed up. "Look, Mama! I fixed it!" Mama smiled. "A new baby can't hold up his head," said Mama. "So we hold it for him." Mia carried the doll through the whole store. Her hand stayed under the head the whole way.

At home, snow started to fall. Big white flakes came down. Mia had an idea. She put the doll in the new little crib. She tucked a soft blanket around it. Then she tapped the doll's head, very gently. The head rolled to one side. So Mia reached in and cupped it with her hand.

Daddy called from the car. "Time to get Mama! The baby is coming today!" Mia picked up her doll. One hand under the bottom. One hand behind the head. She marched to the door. "I'm ready, baby brother," said Mia. "I will hold your head."

Victoria was home with a cold. Her nose was runny. She sniffed and sniffed at breakfast. One sniff. Two sniffs. Three sniffs.

Mom put down her cup. "You need a tissue, honey." Victoria took one. She blew her little nose. The tissue felt soft. The runny nose felt better.

"Thank you," said Victoria. "My nose was all stuffy before." Mom gave her a hug.

Later, Victoria looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. She saw the big tree sway in the wind. She hoped she could play under the tree soon.

Her nose ran again. Victoria sniffed once. Then she knew just what to do. "Mom, tissue please!" Mom brought the box.

"One tissue for Victoria," said Mom. "Two tissues." Victoria giggled. She put the tissues in the bin all by herself.

"Do you want some warm soup later?" Mom asked.

Victoria nodded. "Yes please. With a spoon."

Edouard sat in the music room at school. Miss Lily played a song on the piano. Everyone had to clap along.

Edouard clapped too fast. Then he clapped too slow. "Why can't I do it?" he asked. Miss Lily smiled. "Try clapping when I nod," she said.

Edouard watched her head. Nod, clap. Nod, clap. Soon his hands went with the beat. The drum in the corner boomed, and his claps fit right in. "It works!" he shouted. Tom laughed and clapped too.

"Can we sing a long song now?" Edouard asked. Miss Lily shook her head. "No, a nursery rhyme," she said. "A nursery rhyme is a short rhyming song for little ones."

So they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Edouard clapped and sang. He did not forget one single word. His brother at home would hear it tonight.

At pick-up time, Edouard sang it to his brother. "Again!" his brother said.

Alexander went to the baby store with Mom. He wanted to pick a toy. He found a soft red ball. "The baby can spin it with me!" he said.

At home, the baby was sleeping. Again. Alexander waited and waited. He watched the baby's small face. "Does the baby sleep all day?" he asked. Mom said, "New babies sleep for much of the day." Alexander set the red ball by the crib.

The baby woke up for a little while. Alexander held out the ball. The baby grabbed it with tiny fingers. Then the baby's eyes closed. Baby was sleeping again. Alexander got his cup and sat close by. "I will wait right here," he said. The soft red ball waited too.

Ava sat at the art table. She wanted to draw a house. But her windows looked lost and wobbly. "My windows won't come out right," she said.

Miss Kim came to help. She took a toy block from the shelf. "Put a sticker on each face," she said. Ava pressed a red sticker on one face. Then another. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six stickers on six faces. Each face was a square, just like her window!

Ava traced a face with her finger. The block felt cool on her skin. Then she traced around the block on her paper. A square came out! "A square window!" she said.

She drew more shapes too. A circle sun. A triangle roof. A rectangle door. Squares one by one, all in a row.

Miss Kim hung the picture on the wall. Ava counted her windows out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

Miss Kim clapped her hands.

Madison ran onto the basketball court. The sun was warm on her arms. The weather was hot and dry. Her team wore blue shirts today.

Coach Maya blew her whistle. "Break time!" she called. All the players ran to the bench. They picked up their water bottles and drank. Madison looked for her bottle. It was not there. She had left it at home.

"Where is my water?" Madison asked. "Can I play without it?"

Coach Maya shook her head gently. "Not on a hot day like this," she said. "Players drink water during breaks." She brought a cool bottle over from her big bag. The bottle felt smooth and cold in Madison's hands. She took big sips. The water was wet and sweet.

Madison went back to the game. She bounced the ball. She aimed at the hoop. The ball went in! Her whole team clapped.

Madison smiled. Next time, she would remember her bottle. "Coach, may I put it in your bag?" she asked.

"Yes," said Coach Maya. "Good thinking, Madison."

Madison dropped the ball into Coach Maya's bag and ran back to the hoop.

Josephine stood at the sand table. She wanted to pour sand into the red cups. But Ben had all the cups. He looked grumpy and held them tight.

Miss Ana came over. "Ben, ask Josephine how old she is," she said. Ben looked at Josephine. "How old are you?" he asked. Josephine held up four fingers. "I am four," she said. Ben held up his fingers too. "I am four too!" he said. He smiled now. He gave her three cups. Josephine poured sand into each one.

Then the whole class sat on the rug. Miss Ana sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," they all sang. Josephine sang too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Her voice was loud and happy. She clapped at the end.

At play time, Ben pointed out the window. "Look, a nest," he said. Two birds sat in it. "How many birds?" Josephine asked. "One, two," said Ben. They counted together. Then Miss Ana called, "Snack time!" Josephine held Ben's hand and walked to the table with him. "I am four," she said again, just to hear it. "And you are four too."

Milan went to the store with his dad. The store had a big book shelf. Milan wanted his favorite book. He could not see it. He only saw a blue cover way up high.

"Dad, can you fetch that blue book?" asked Milan. Dad reached up. The book was too tall. Then it began to slip. Dad caught it just in time. There was no big fall, no crash. The book was safe in Dad's hands.

Dad turned it over. He pointed to the front. "This says The Sleepy Bunny," he said. Milan looked at the words. He traced them with his finger. "That is its name," said Dad. Milan smiled. "The Sleepy Bunny is the book I want!" Dad opened the front cover. Together, they began to read.

It was Ava's first day of school. She held her mama's hand. The room had blocks and paint and a pink table. Ava's tummy felt funny. "Who will play with me?" she asked. "I will stay a little while," said Mama.

At recess, Ava saw the slide. She ran to it. A boy named Sam was at the top. He slid down. Then he ran to go again. Ava stood in front of him. The teacher said, "Sam, we take turns on the slide." Sam walked to the back of the line. Ava got in line too. She waited. Then it was her turn. Whee! Down she went, fast.

After recess, the class ate bread and apples. Ava learned that waiting made the slide fun for everyone. Sam sat next to her. "Want to slide again?" he asked. "Yes!" said Ava. Mama waved from the door.

Beatrice was at Grandma's house. She wanted to draw a picture. Grandma had a soft gray case on the table.

Grandma showed her the tablet. Beatrice pressed her whole hand on the screen. She pressed hard. The screen did nothing. "Hmm," said Beatrice. "Why won't it go?"

"Try one finger," said Grandma. "Just a little tap." Beatrice lifted one finger. She gave the screen a gentle tap. The screen lit up! A tap made it come on.

"What is this?" Beatrice asked. She tapped a green square. The drawing app opened. There was a big white page. She tapped the blue color and drew a ball. Then she drew a broom, like the one Grandma used to sweep the floor.

"All done," said Beatrice. She tapped the top. The page closed. Grandma helped her slide the tablet back into its soft case.

"Bye bye, ball," said Beatrice, and patted the case.

Lucy ran into the playroom. "Look, Teddy!" she said. "A big slide!" The slide was tall. Beside it sat a small red slide for the dolls. Lucy put her friend Teddy at the top of the big slide. "You go first!" she said.

Lucy climbed up. She went up and up, one step, two steps, three steps. Then she sat at the top. "Wheee!" She slid down, fast. Teddy slid down too. "Fast!" laughed Lucy. Then she climbed up again. This time she went down very, very slow, like a sleepy snail. Mom brought warm cocoa. "Careful, it's hot," said Mom. Mom held the cup so nothing would spill. Lucy blew on it. "Now it's cold!" she said, opening her eyes wide.

"Up and down are opposites," said Mom. Lucy looked at the slide. She climbed up. She came down. Up, then down. She tried it again and again. "Teddy, watch me!" she called. She went up the ladder and slid down, fast, fast, fast.

Adam ran to the sandbox. He saw a big red truck. His classmate Mia was holding it. Adam wanted the truck now.

Adam grabbed the truck out of Mia's hands. Mia's face got sad. Her eyes filled with tears. She began to cry. The playground felt noisy with her crying.

Adam looked at Mia's sad face. He gave the truck back. "Here, Mia," he said. "Your turn first." Mia stopped crying. She smiled. "You can have it next," she said.

Mia pushed the truck down the hill. Vroom! Then she rolled it back. "Now you, Adam," she said. Adam took the truck. "Thank you, Mia," he said. He pushed the truck fast. Mia clapped her hands. They took turns all morning. Then they sat together on the bench. "Best friends," said Mia. Adam smiled and rolled the truck to her feet.

Gabriel was building a big block tower at home. His cousin Mia came to play. "My turn?" asked Mia. Gabriel gave her one block. Then one more. They took turns, turn by turn.

Then Gabriel ran fast to get a red block. He bumped the tower with his elbow. Crash! All the blocks fell down. Mia's eyes got big. Her mouth turned down. "My tower," she said.

Gabriel felt something tight in his chest. What could help? He knew a word. "Sorry, Mia," he said. Then he picked up a block. Mia picked up a block too. They built the tower again, taller than before. "This one is ours," said Mia. She gave Gabriel a tight, happy hug until it made him laugh.

"Should we tickle the tower goodnight?" Gabriel whispered. Mia giggled. "Towers don't tickle," she said. "But you do!" And her fingers wiggled toward his tummy.

Norah wants to make pancakes for her family. She pulls her stool to the big shiny counter. "I will cook!" she says. Daddy helps her get the bowl and the spoon.

First she cracks the eggs. Plop, plop. Then Daddy hands her the bag of flour. Norah tips it fast. Whoosh! A big white cloud puffs up. It lands on her nose. It lands on Daddy's nose too. "Achoo!" says Daddy. "You look like a snowman," says Mommy, laughing.

"Let's try again," says Daddy. He pours a new bag of flour slowly. This time there is no cloud. The flour just slides down, soft and quiet. "I can do it slow," says Norah. She takes her turn. Slow, slow, slow. No cloud at all. Mommy mixes the batter, and Daddy cooks the pancakes on the hot pan while Norah watches from her stool.
