At breakfast, everyone has clean noses. "These are the best pancakes," says Mommy. Norah licks her fork. "I made them," she says. "Slowly, slowly, slowly."

Iris sat at the dinner table. She saw a big bowl of grapes. "Can I have three grapes?" she asked. Mom said, "Yes, you can have three grapes."

Iris picked one big grape. "Is this three?" she asked. Mom shook her head. "That is one," Mom said. Iris picked another grape. Now she had two. "Two," she said. She picked one more. "One, two, three!"

Her brother Leo wanted grapes too. "Can I have three?" he asked. Mom gave him three little grapes. Iris looked. His grapes were small. Hers were big. She counted his grapes. "One, two, three," she said. "Leo has three too!"

Then the clock on the wall began to ring. "Wash hands after grapes," said Mom. Iris put her grapes near Leo's plate so he could reach the bowl. Then she ran to wash her hands, singing, "One, two, three!"

Penelope went to the store with Mama. She wanted a new animal toy. "Let's look at the animal bin," said Mama.

Penelope found a little dog. "A dog!" she said. "A dog is an animal." She put it in the cart. Then she found a soft cow. "A cow!" she said. "A cow is an animal too." She put it in the cart too.

Then she saw a small orange fish. Penelope frowned. "This one has no legs," she said. "It cannot be an animal." Mama smiled. "Is a fish an animal?" Penelope asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Penelope hugged the fish. "Hello, animal fish!" she said. The fish went in the cart.

On the way home, Penelope held her three toys. "One dog, one cow, one fish," she said. "Three animals!" She patted them gently. Then she whispered to the fish, "You can hop on my pillow tonight. No legs needed."

Charles left his crayons in the car. The car sat in the sun all day. Now it was time for lunch, and then Charles wanted to draw.

After lunch, Dad got the crayons from the car. Charles peeked into the box. "They look funny," he said. He picked up the orange crayon. It bent like a worm. It was soft and squishy in his hand.

Charles tried to draw with it. The soft crayon made a fat, wet line. It looked different from before. Was it because of the hot car? The sun had made the car hot, and the crayons had gone soft and bendy.

"Can we draw with them anyway?" Charles asked.

"Let's try," said Dad. Charles pressed the orange crayon down. It made a big smudge, like a sunset. He made another one, and another. Soon the whole page was orange.

Charles held up his paper. "My crayons made a hot sun picture," he said. Dad put it on the fridge.

Elias went to the mall with Mom. They walked past the toy store and the big fountain. Then they came to a hair salon. Elias was getting his very first haircut.

"Sit here," said the hairdresser. She put a big cape around his shoulders. It was blue and soft. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell down. The hairs landed on the cape, not on his shirt. Elias giggled. "I look like a superhero," he said. The cape held all the hairs.

After the haircut, the hairdresser took the cape off. She shook it, and all the hairs fell away. Elias looked at his shirt. It was clean. He looked at the floor. The hairs were there. "The cape kept my shirt clean," said Elias. Mom smiled. "You look so big," she said. They walked out past the fountain. Elias waved at his car in the parking lot.

Mohamed's teddy bear, Brown Bear, sat on the floor. He looked sad. His head was tipped over.

"Bear is sick," Mohamed said. "What can I do?"

His mother came close. "You can pretend to take care of him," she said.

Mohamed found a little cup. He held it to Bear's mouth. "Drink your medicine," he said. "Drink it all up."

Then he got a small blanket. He tucked Bear into bed. "Night night, Bear," he whispered.

Mohamed patted Bear's soft head. "Do you feel better now? Yes, you do."

He waited by the bed. His shadow fell over Bear like a hug.

Later, Mohamed found his toy bunny. Bunny looked sleepy. Mohamed smiled. "Don't worry, Bunny. I will take care of you too."

He got the blanket and wrapped Bunny up. "Time for medicine," he said, holding the little cup.

Mother watched from the door. "My Mohamed," she said softly, "you take such good care of your babies."

Mohamed kissed Bear and kissed Bunny. "Sleep tight," he said. "I will check on you after my snack."

Arnaud ran to the story corner. He saw the big red robot book on the shelf. He wanted it now.

"Can we read the robot book now?" he asked.

Teacher Mia smiled. "Not now. Story time is after snack."

"But I want it now," said Arnaud.

"Now means at this very moment," said Teacher Mia. "Now we wash hands. Later we eat. Then the story comes."

Arnaud looked at the clock. He heard the water run. He filled his hands with soap bubbles. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

At the table, Arnaud ate his crackers. He heard a loud bell ring. That was the end of snack!

"Now?" he asked Teacher Mia.

"Now," she said.

Arnaud clapped. Yesterday the robot book was on the shelf all day. Today he waited, and then it happened. Tomorrow he would pick it first again.

Teacher Mia opened the book. The robot on the first page beeped hello.

"Hello, robot," said Arnaud.

Evan ran to the big paper on the grass. He wanted to paint the sky. He dipped his brush in the light blue paint. He made a big sky, soft and pale.

His friend Mia came over with a dark blue crayon. She drew dark blue under his sky. "That is not blue!" said Evan. "It is too dark!"

Mia held her crayon next to his sky. "It is blue too," she said. "Dark blue." Evan looked and looked. The paint was light. The crayon was dark. They put them in a row, lightest first, then darkest. "Both are blue," said Mia. Evan smiled and painted dark blue water under his light blue sky. "Thank you," he said. He gave Mia the polite little bow he did for guests. Then he painted one green leaf and one yellow sun, and Mia laughed and clapped.

Colton wanted to write a note for Grandpa. It would say "GOOD NIGHT." Grandpa was tucking him in, and Colton wanted him to find the note by his bed.

Colton found his smooth blue crayon. He wrote all his letters in a big line. G-O-O-D-N-I-G-H-T. All the letters touched each other. There was no gap at all. They looked like one long, wiggly worm.

Grandpa came in. He picked up the note. He turned it sideways. He held it far away. Then he held it close. "Hmm," said Grandpa. "I cannot read this one."

Colton's tummy felt tight. He looked at Grandpa's storybook on the bed. Grandpa opened the front of the book first. The words sat in little groups on the page. Each group had a space after it. One word. Then a space. Then the next word.

Colton took his crayon again. He wrote GOOD. He lifted his crayon off the paper. Then he wrote NIGHT. The space sat between the two words. He held the note out. "Read it now," he said.

Grandpa smiled big. "GOOD NIGHT," he read. "I can read it now." He put the note on the pillow. He opened Colton's book to the front page. "We start here," he said.

Colton snuggled down. The note would stay by his bed all night. "Read it again tomorrow," he said. Grandpa turned the first page.

Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. There was a Christmas party. In the middle of the hall stood a tall tree. At Christmas, many families decorate a tree, Mama said. Sarah wanted to help.

She held a soft red ornament. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a blue one there too. Then a gold one. Then a boat ornament, white with a little sail. All of them sat on one branch. The branch began to bend. The branch went down, down, down. Plop! The ornaments fell into the soft blanket below.

Sarah picked them up. She looked at the tree. So many branches, all empty. She hung one ornament on this branch. One on that branch. One, two, three, up and up. Papa brought her a stool, and she reached the high branches. The tree began to shine all over.

A little bell chimed somewhere. Sarah turned around. Grandpa was holding a tiny ornament with a bell inside. "Where should this one go?" he asked. Sarah pointed to the very top branch and smiled.

Kinsley sat at the little table in the playroom. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower on it. Kinsley looked in her paint box. She had red paint, blue paint, yellow paint and green paint. But there was no pink paint.

Kinsley made a red flower first. "Too dark," she said. Grandma's flowers were soft and light. Kinsley put her brush in the water jar. The water made a small sound. Swish, swish. She washed the red brush until it was clean.

Then Kinsley had an idea. She put red paint on her paper. She put white paint next to it. She stirred them together with her brush. Round and round she stirred. The red paint turned lighter and lighter. Now it was pink! Kinsley made a happy sound, a high little squeal.

She painted a big pink flower. Then she painted a green stem. She painted blue dots all around it. She painted a yellow sun up high. Mommy came in and looked. "What a pretty pink flower," said Mommy. "Grandma will love it." Kinsley held the card up to show her.

Norah came home with a small cat. The cat was soft and gray. Norah held her teddy bear in one arm. The cat rode in a box.

Then Norah had a worry. "Where will the cat go potty?" she asked. Dad showed her a pan on the floor. "This is a litter box," he said. Norah touched the sand inside. It felt like tiny seeds. Dad let her pour a little more sand in.

The cat sniffed the box. She stepped in. She dug a small hole. Then she covered it up with her paws. Norah clapped her hands. "She used it all by herself!" she said. "What a smart cat." The cat jumped out and rubbed on Norah's leg. It felt warm and soft, like her teddy bear.

At bedtime, Dad tucked Norah in. The cat curled up at the foot of the bed. Norah patted her head. "Good night, cat," she whispered. The cat gave one tiny purr.

Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He wanted to go on the tall slide. But when he looked up, his tummy felt funny. His legs stopped walking.

"Are you scared?" asked Dad. Weston nodded. He felt sad, too. He wanted to slide like the big kids.

Then Dad sat down on the bench. "I was scared of slides once," said Dad. "I was a little boy then." Weston's eyes got wide. "You had scared feelings?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups." Weston thought about that. Grown-ups were so big. But they felt things too.

A girl came down the slide. She laughed and clapped. She looked so happy. Weston held Dad's hand. They climbed the stairs together. Weston sat at the top. His heart went boom, boom. He was excited now, not scared.

Down he went, fast, fast, fast. "Again!" he shouted. Then something surprised him. Dad went down the little slide too. Dad's hair flew up like wings. "Whee!" said Dad. Weston laughed and laughed.

Juliette sat at the art table. She had a brown piece of paper. The paper was a square. It had four sides, all the same. Next to it sat a small circle of glue and a long rectangle of green paper.

Juliette wanted to make a sailboat. "I need two triangles for the sail," she said. She looked in the paper tray. There were no triangles. Only squares, circles and rectangles. She looked again. She waited. Still no triangles.

Her teacher, Miss Ana, came over. "Show me where you want the sail," she said. Juliette pointed to one corner of the brown square. Then she pointed to the corner far, far away from it. "Corner to corner," said Juliette. Miss Ana picked up the scissors. "Scissors are for grown-ups," she said. "I will cut on your line." Snip, snip. The square fell into two pieces. Juliette touched them. Two triangles! She clapped her hands.

Juliette glued the green rectangle down for the boat. Then she glued one triangle on top. Then the other triangle, right beside it. The sail stood tall. At snack time she took a small taste of her cracker, then ran back to look at her boat. "Sail away," she said, and pushed it gently across the table.

Zoey sat in the waiting room with her mom. Today she would get her first real haircut. Her tummy felt a little sour and nervous.

A lady named Mia came out. "Ready, Zoey?" she asked. Zoey shook her head. "The scissors look big," she said.

Mia held up a little comb. "Watch what I do first," she said. She combed a small piece of hair. Then she made one little snip. Zoey leaned forward to see. Mia combed again. Then she snipped again.

"I can count," Zoey said. "One comb, one snip." Mia smiled. "You count with me," she said. Zoey sat up tall in the big chair. One comb, one snip. Two combs, one snip. The hair fell down like soft rain. Soon Zoey's hair was short and neat.

Mom clapped her hands. "You did it," she said. On the way home, they talked about dinner. Zoey looked in the mirror and turned her head. "I like my haircut," she said. "Can we come back and count again?"

Oliver went to the cultural center with Mama and Dad. Tonight there was a big party for Hanukkah. Oliver saw tables with candles. The candles were white and tall and very pretty.

"Can I touch one?" Oliver asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Fire is hot. Only grown-ups light them."

A lady named Ruth stood by a golden candle holder. "This is called a menorah," she said. "We light candles on it for eight nights."

Ruth lit a little helper candle with a match. She used it to light two candles. "We lit one candle last night," she said. "So tonight we light one more."

Oliver counted with his finger. "One, two," he said. "Last night was one. Tonight is two!"

"Right," said Ruth. She smiled at him.

Tomorrow there would be three candles. Oliver had a secret plan. He would count them all the way to eight. He would count slow, so the counting would last.

Mama bought him a warm latke from the food table. It smelled like potatoes and made his tummy feel happy. Oliver ate it while the candles glowed.

"Next year I count again," he said.

Ruth laughed. "Deal," she said.

Violet got to daycare. Her coat was cold from outside. She hung it on her hook. Teacher Mia said, "Snack time is soon." Violet sat down at the little table. She waited. Soon means in a little while, said her friend Ben. Violet tapped her feet. She looked out the window. A bird flew by. Then Teacher Mia rang the bell. Snack time came. It did not take long. Violet got a cup. Teacher Mia poured the milk for her. Violet ate her crackers. Yesterday, she had apples at snack. Today, she had crackers. Tomorrow, Teacher Mia said there would be bananas. After snack, the class went outside to paint. Violet painted a big red circle. "It has to dry," said Teacher Mia. "You can take it home later." Violet played in the sand while she waited. She poured sand from one cup to another. The wind blew a little. Then Teacher Mia called, "Paintings are dry now." Violet ran over. Her red circle was dry and shiny. She held it up. "Now I can take it home," she said. She carried it carefully to her hook, and put it in her cubby for later.

Aubrey wanted to do it herself. Daddy made the toast and set it on her plate. Aubrey took the butter knife. She spread the butter. First one stroke, then another. The butter made a shiny path on the toast. "Look, Daddy, I did it!" she said.

Then came the milk. Aubrey held the cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk splashed onto the table. "Oh no," said Aubrey. Daddy wiped it up. "Try again," he said.

Aubrey looked at the cup. What if it sat down? She set the cup on the table. The cup stayed still. She poured the milk slowly. Not one drop spilled. The milk went up, up, up to the line. Aubrey picked up the cup and took a big drink. "The cup does not wiggle now!" she said. Daddy clapped his hands.

Felix put two slices of soft white bread into the toaster. Miss Ana pushed the lever down. "We buy this bread from the bakery," she said. "Watch now."

The bread popped up. Felix touched one slice with one finger. It was warm. It was brown. It was crunchy. "The bread was white and soft," said Felix. "Now it is brown and crunchy!"

"That is toast," said Miss Ana. "Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy." Felix sniffed the toast. It smelled warm and good.

Now Felix had a job. He took the little knife with the safe round edge. He dipped it into the butter. He spread the butter slowly, one, two, three strokes. The butter melted into the warm toast and went shiny.

Next came the milk. Felix held the cup with one hand. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. He licked a crumb off his thumb. His itchy sweater sleeve rubbed his chin.

He counted his work: one slice of toast, one cup of milk, zero spills. Miss Ana clapped her hands.

"Breakfast time," said Felix, and he took a big crunchy bite.

Evan wanted to paint a pumpkin at daycare. He looked in the paint cup. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. But there was no orange paint. "I need orange for my pumpkin," said Evan.

His friend Mia came over. "Stir red and yellow," she said. "Watch this." Evan got his brush. He put red in the cup. He put yellow in the cup. He stirred it round and round. The paint turned orange! "Neat!" said Evan. He painted his pumpkin orange. It looked just like the one on the shelf.

Then Evan had an idea. He dipped his brush in blue. He stirred it with the yellow. The paint turned green! Mia laughed. "Now we can paint grass too," she said. Evan hurried to get more paper. "Green grass for my pumpkin," he said.

Ruby woke up from her nap at Grandma's house. Her tummy felt empty. "Time to eat," said Grandma. "We will have rice and warm bread."

Grandma put the big bowl on the table. Ruby grabbed her spoon fast. She opened her mouth wide.

"Wait, wait," said Grandma with a smile. "First we say Bismillah. It means in the name of God. Many Muslims say it before they eat."

Ruby put her spoon down. "Bismillah," she said. Grandma clapped. Then Ruby took a big bite of rice.

At dinner, Daddy drove over with a fuzzy blanket for Grandma. Ruby held her spoon and did not eat. "Say it with me," she told Daddy. Daddy laughed and said, "Bismillah." Then Ruby ate her bread all up.

Mason climbed the big school bus. He held his mama's hand. His tummy felt funny, like little wings flapping inside.

"Mama, my tummy is fluttery," he said.

Mama sat next to him by the window. The glass was cool when he touched it. "My tummy felt fluttery on my first day too," she said.

Mason looked up. "Even you?"

"Even me. It is okay to feel that way."

The bus went bump, bump, bump down the road. Mason watched out the window. A dog ran by a fence. The bus stopped, and a girl got on. She held a yellow backpack tight. Her face looked like Mason's tummy felt.

Mason patted the seat next to him. "You can sit here," he said. "My tummy is fluttery too."

The girl sat down. "My mama said that is okay," she said.

The bus stopped at the school. The driver smiled. "Here we are, friends," she said. Mason slid off the seat and waited while the doors folded open.

His tummy still fluttered a little. But now his mouth was smiling too. He took the girl's hand, and they walked up the steps together, into their classroom, where blocks sat in a happy red row by the window.

Amelia ran to the art room. Today she wore her new pink shirt. "No paint on it!" she said.

Her teacher held up a big red apron. "Put this on first," she said. "An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Amelia put her arms in. The apron went swish.

Then came the fun. "This is red," said Amelia. "This is yellow. This is blue." She knew all three. "Good work!" said her teacher.

Amelia wanted to mix. She dabbed red. She dabbed yellow. She stirred with her brush. The paint turned orange! "Ooh!" she said. She flicked her brush. A red dot flew. It landed on the apron, not her shirt. Amelia grinned and painted a big orange sun. "My favorite," she said.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name all by himself. Miss Jo gave him a fat pencil and some paper.

Ryan held the pencil in his fist. Miss Jo showed him how to pinch it near the tip. "Like this," she said. Ryan tried it. The pencil felt better now.

He began his R at the right side of the page. He wrote R, then Y, then A. But then there was no room left. The N ran off the paper. Ryan frowned. His mouth turned sour.

He looked at the paper. He thought for a moment. Then he flipped it over and started at the left side. He wrote R, Y, A, N. This time every letter fit.

"I did it!" said Ryan.

Miss Jo clapped her hands. "Would you like a sticker?" she asked.

Ryan grinned and pointed at his name. "Can we write it again?"

Grayson woke up and saw white outside. "Snow!" he shouted. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day."

Grayson wanted to play with his friend Sam. But first he wanted his red toy plane. It was lost! He had dropped it outside yesterday.

Mom put on his boots and coat. They stepped into the soft, fresh snow. Grayson looked down. His boots made marks in the snow. "Look, Mom! My feet make footprints!"

Then he saw more footprints. They were little ones. They went across the yard. "Maybe they know where my plane is," said Grayson. He followed the bumpy little footprints. Step, step, step. They went next door, to Sam's door!

Sam opened the door. He held the red plane. "You dropped it. I was bringing it back!" Grayson clapped his hands. "My footprints found you!" he said. "Come play in the snow," said Sam. And they did.

Felix was starting his first day of school. He wore his new backpack. It had a picture of a bear on it. "That is a backpack," said his mom. "It is a bag you carry on your back." Felix stood up straight in the playground.

But Felix could not run. His backpack was too heavy. He wanted to play on the wooden swing. He tried to walk fast. His back hurt a little. He sat down on a bench.

Then he opened his backpack. He looked inside. He had packed three toy cars and a big teddy bear. Felix took them out. He put them in his mom's bag. Now his backpack was light. Felix ran to the swing. He went up and down, up and down. A girl named Mia ran next to him. "Your backpack is small," she said. Felix laughed. "It is light now. And it still goes on my back."

Isabella went to Miss Jo's music room. She saw a shiny drum and a little stool with a cat on it. The cat had a long tail. "Hello, cat," said Isabella. She wanted to sing the whole rhyming song by herself.

First they tried it fast. "One, two, three, fast as can be!" The words got all tangled up. "Muddle-muddle-moo," said Isabella, and she laughed. The cat jumped off the stool.

"Let's try it slow," said Miss Jo. "One, two, slow and low." Isabella clapped her hands on her knees. Clap, clap, clap. The claps made a steady beat. The words came out just right, one by one. "I can do it slow!" said Isabella.

Then Miss Jo asked, "Fast or slow now?" Isabella grinned. "Slow first!" She sang it slow and clapped along. Then she tried it fast, and this time the words did not tangle. The cat came back and tapped its tail, one, two, one, two, right on the beat.

Zachary walked into the school computer lab. His teacher, Ms. Bell, smiled at him. "Today you will learn the tablet," she said. Zachary felt a little worried. "It looks big," he said. "I will stay right here," said Ms. Bell.

Zachary pressed the round button. The screen lit up! He pressed his finger on the drawing app. It opened. He drew a green pond with a fat blue frog. "Look!" he said. His friend Maya set her juice cup right beside the tablet. "Juice goes on the far table," said Ms. Bell. "Tablets are kept away from water and drinks." Maya carried her cup to the other table. Zachary was careful to keep his hands dry too.

Then it was time to go. Zachary pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the soft blue basket. "All done," he said. Ms. Bell clapped. "You did it all by yourself." Zachary ran to line up, still smiling at the dark screen in the basket.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Elizabeth ran to the guest bedroom. The bed was empty. There was no pillow on it. There was no blanket on it. Grandpa could not sleep like that.

Elizabeth went to the linen closet. She counted what she found. "One pillow, two pillows, three pillows," she said. She chose the softest one. It was big and white. She hugged it all the way to the guest room.

Next she looked for a blanket. She found her old blue blanket. It was warm and soft. She laid it on the bed. She tucked the edges in tight, like a little nest. "There," she said. "One bed, one pillow, one blanket, all ready for Grandpa."

That night Grandpa climbed into the bed. He patted the pillow. He pulled the blanket up to his chin. "This is the best bed," he said. "Did you make it ready for me?"

"Yes," said Elizabeth. "I got your sleeping spot all ready." Grandpa gave her a hug. She loved the smell of his sweater. "Good night, Grandpa," she said. "Sleep tight."

Jasmine wanted to run to the swings. The sun was shiny and bright. "Stop," said Mom. "Let me put on your sunscreen." "Why?" asked Jasmine. Mom rubbed the cream on her nose and her neck and her arms. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Jasmine took Mom's hand and they walked to the swings. The wind blew. "It is windy today," said Jasmine. Her hair flew up like a flag. She held her hat with one hand. Big clouds came. Drip, drop. Rain fell on the slide. Mom opened an umbrella. "Rainy days need umbrellas," said Jasmine. They sat under it and watched the puddles grow. Then the rain stopped. Jasmine looked at her arms. No red spots. No sunburn at all. "The sunscreen worked," she said. Mom smiled. "Sunny, rainy, windy," said Jasmine. "Every day needs something different." She ran back to the swings and pumped her legs high, up into the shiny sun.

Mohamed wanted his turtle book at bedtime. He ran to get it. He held it out to Dad. "Read this one!"

Dad opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He read the words out loud. "Little turtle grew and grew." Mohamed looked at the black marks under the picture. "What are those little marks, Dad?"

"Those are words," said Dad. "I read the words. They tell the story." Dad's finger slid along the marks. The words came out of his mouth, one by one. Mohamed watched the finger. Then the words came again. He tapped the marks himself. Nothing came out of his mouth.

Then they came to a page with just a turtle. It was a big green turtle. There were no black marks on it at all. Mohamed pointed at it. "Read this page, Dad!"

Dad looked at the page. He turned his head this way and that. Then he shook his head. "There are no words here, Mohamed. There is nothing written on this page to read."

Mohamed leaned close. He looked and looked. The page felt smooth under his hand. No marks anywhere. Just the turtle, fast asleep in the sand. Mohamed sat very still and thought about that.

Dad turned to the last page. More little marks! Dad read them. "The dizzy turtle spun and spun, then slept." Mohamed giggled. He turned the book around in his hands. He looked at the marks upside down. They looked funny that way.

"Now you hold it," said Dad. "Turn the pages from the front, like this." Mohamed turned the pages, front to back, all by himself. He stopped at the big green turtle. He tapped the empty page. "No words here," he said. Dad smiled and kissed his head. Mohamed hugged the book tight to his chest.

The morning was sunny. Samuel put on his sun hat. He ran to the backyard to build a sand castle. Then the wind came. It was windy! His hat blew off. "Come back, hat!" he called. He put on his little jacket for the wind.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Samuel ran out to save his castle. The rain fell on his head and his shirt. He was all wet! He ran back to the door. "Mom, why am I wet?" he asked. "No raincoat," said Mom. "A raincoat helps keep your body dry." She helped him put it on. It was red with a happy hood.

Samuel went out again. The rain fell on the raincoat. He stayed dry! Dry, dry, dry. He touched his shirt under the coat. Not wet at all. Later the rain stopped. "Will we see snow today?" he asked. "No, just rain," said Mom with a smile. Samuel patted his quiet, dry castle and waved to the sky. "Bye bye, rain."

Naomi wanted to win the shape game. Mama had hidden shapes all over the playroom. "Find a circle," said Mama. Naomi found a round ball. It rolled when she pushed it. Soft and smooth.

"Now find a triangle," said Mama. Naomi held up a toy roof. It had three sides and pointy corners. "Triangle!" she said.

"Last one. Find a rectangle." Naomi looked and looked. She saw the play kitchen. She saw a toy fork on the little table. She was thirsty, so she took a sip from her cup.

Then she saw the door. She touched the side. One, two, three, four sides. She touched each corner. One, two, three, four square corners. "The door is a rectangle!" said Naomi. Mama clapped. Naomi laughed and patted the door.

Wyatt stood at the bus stop with Grandma. The sun was out. It was sunny. "My shadow is big," said Wyatt. He zipped his jacket up, up, up.

Then the wind came. It blew his hat right off. "Come back, hat!" laughed Wyatt. Grandma caught it. "It is windy," she said. The wind made the leaves spin and spin.

Dark clouds rolled in. Rain began to fall. Plop, plop on Wyatt's boots. Then he heard a big rumble. Thunder! Grandma said, "When you hear thunder, go indoors." Wyatt grabbed her hand. "Indoors, indoors!" They ran to the cafe next to the bus stop. They watched the rain from the warm window. "Good thinking," said Grandma. Wyatt munched his snack and smiled. "I listened to the thunder."

Sarah was at Grandma's house. Ten red apples sat in a big bowl. Sarah wanted to count them all by herself.

She started at the left side. One, two, three. She went slowly. Four, five, six. Grandma waited. Seven, eight, nine, ten. "Ten apples!" said Sarah.

Grandma poured milk into two cups. "Now let's count them again," she said. "Start at the other end this time."

Sarah started at the right side. One, two, three. She took her time. The cat watched from the chair. Four, five, six. Seven, eight, nine, ten.

Sarah put her hands on her cheeks. "Ten again! Ten both ways!" Grandma smiled and put one apple in each cup. "Ten again," said Sarah.

Then Grandma held up two plates. Cookies on one. Crackers on the other. "Which plate has more?"

Sarah counted the cookies. One, two, three, four, five. She counted the crackers. One, two, three. "The cookies!" she said. "The cookies have more!"

Grandma gave her a cookie. The dirty bowl went to the sink. Sarah ate her cookie and counted her bites. One, two, three. She laughed. "I can count anything!"

Brielle got to school early. Teacher Mia put a pencil on her desk. "You can write your name," said Teacher Mia.

Brielle picked up the pencil. She held it tight and walked to the table. The point was up in the air. It waved near Leo's arm. "Careful," said Teacher Mia. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down."

Brielle turned the pencil around. The point went down, near the floor. She walked all the way to her chair. Nobody got poked. Then she held the pencil the way Teacher Mia showed her. She made a B. She made an R. Her letters were wiggly, but they were her letters. "Look, I wrote Brielle!" she said. Leo clapped for her.

Charlotte went to the library with her dad. On a big table there were three signs. One said "Animals." One said "Toys." One said "Foods."

Charlotte picked up a toy car and put it under "Toys." Then she found a soft bear and put it under "Animals." "What goes under Foods?" she wondered.

She found a basket of picture cards. There was an apple card. There was a bread card. And there was a carrot card. Charlotte put the carrot under "Toys." It looked silly next to the teddy bear!

A boy named Sam ran over. "Hey!" he did not yell. "Carrots are foods," he said. "Like apples and bread." Charlotte looked at the carrot. Then she looked at the apple. Then the bread.

She picked up the carrot and moved it. She put it under "Foods" with the apple and the bread. Sam clapped. Charlotte spun the wheel on the toy car. Round and round it went.

"Can we eat a book?" Charlotte asked her dad. Dad laughed. "No, books are not foods." Charlotte held the apple card up high. "This one is!"

Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair bounced as she looked around. She saw a poster of a dog on the wall. She saw a jar of stickers by the sink.

"Today you get a shot," said Mom.

Mila shook her head. She thought a shot would be big. She thought it would hurt for a long time. She hid her arm behind her back.

The nurse came in with a small tray. On the tray was a very thin needle. It was small like a tiny straw. Mila looked at it. It did not look big at all.

"It is a quick poke in the arm," said the nurse. "Then it is done."

Mila held Mom's hand. She pulled up her sleeve. The nurse touched her arm. Mila felt one small poke, quick as that.

"All done!" said the nurse.

Mila looked at her arm. There was a tiny round bandage on it. She had waited for something big. But it was just one quick poke.

The nurse did not hurry away. She sat down and smiled. "You can pick a sticker now," she said.

Mila picked a sticker of a yellow dog. She put it on her sleeve, right over the bandage. Then she waved her arm in the air.

"My arm is quick and brave," said Mila.

Lennon went to the store with Mama. Yesterday, Lennon had a cough. Today, her cough was just a tiny squeak, like a weak little mouse. So today they could go out.

Lennon saw a stuffed mouse on the shelf. It was gray and soft. "I want to hold it now," she said. Mama picked it up and turned it over. "This is for Mia," said Mama. "It is her birthday present. We give it to her tomorrow." Lennon hugged the mouse. She did not want to put it down. "Not now?" she whispered. "Not now," said Mama. "First we sleep. Then it will be tomorrow."

They bought the mouse and put it in the bag. At home, Lennon ate soup. Then she slept and slept. When she woke up, the sun was in a new place in the sky. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. Mama smiled and lifted her up. "Yes. Today is the day after yesterday. Come on, let's go." Lennon carried the bag to Mia's house all by herself. Mia opened the door. Lennon held out the mouse. "Happy birthday, Mia," she said.

Ayla sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted to feel brave, but she felt a little mad about the wait. A balloon floated near the ceiling. She saw it with her eyes. "Look, Mommy," she said. A baby cried, and Ayla heard it with her ears. The room smelled like soap. She noticed that with her nose. The doctor looked in Ayla's mouth. "Say ahh," she said. Ayla tasted the wooden stick, just a little. Then the doctor held Ayla's hand. "Squeeze my fingers," she said. Ayla felt the squeeze with her fingers. Then the doctor said, "Shoes off, please. Let me see your toes." Ayla took off her shoes and socks.

After the visit, Mommy walked Ayla home. In the backyard, Ayla took off her shoes again. She stepped on the grass. "It tickles, Mommy!" she said. "My feet feel it too!" Mommy laughed and took off her own shoes. They stood in the soft grass together. "Wiggle your toes," said Mommy. Ayla wiggled them. The grass tickled and tickled.

Mateo ran into Grandma's house. "Where is the baby?" he asked. Grandma pointed to the soft chair. Papa sat there, holding a tiny bundle. It was the new baby. It was Mateo's baby sister.

"I want to hold her!" said Mateo. He reached up on his tippy toes. The baby was too far away. He jumped. Still too far. "You can hold her," said Papa, "but you have to sit down on the couch. And I will sit right beside you and help."

Mateo sat on the couch. Papa sat next to him. Papa placed the baby in Mateo's arms. "Hello, baby," Mateo whispered. The baby made a little mouth, like a fish. Mateo laughed. Her hand popped out of the blanket and tickled his chin, so small and warm.

"She is squeezing my finger!" Mateo said. Grandma brought a glass of water for Papa. "Big brother, you are doing a good job," she said. The baby yawned a great big yawn. Her eyes closed. Mateo held still, very still, like a stone. Papa smiled and whispered, "She likes your arms." Mateo grinned and looked down at his sleeping sister. "Stay right there," he told her softly.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She was putting on her swimsuit. Today she would learn to swim. "I hope I can do it," she said. Mom held her hand. They walked out to the pool. The water was big and blue.

Leah saw a tall chair by the water. A man sat up in it. "Why does he sit so high?" Leah asked Mom. "Look and see," said Mom. Leah watched. From up high, the man could see every swimmer. Then a boy splashed too far out. The man blew his whistle. He climbed down fast. He helped the boy back to the wall. "He saw him from up there!" said Leah. She waved at the man. He waved back.

Leah got in the water. She kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. She was quiet and careful. The man in the tall chair watched her too. "I did it!" Leah called. Then, splash, a drop of water went right in her eye. The man saw it happen. He was already walking over. "Here is a towel," he said. Leah smiled. He really did watch everyone.

Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He had a blue beanbag in his hand. He wanted it to land in the hoop.

Hudson threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a soft sound. "Oh no," said Hudson. "How will I get it in?"

His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. She picked up her own beanbag. "Watch me," she said. "This is an underhand toss." Her arm swung from low down. It swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed into the hoop. Hudson's mouth opened wide.

"I want to try that!" he said. He held his beanbag low. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up and over. Plip. It landed in the hoop. "I did it!" said Hudson. Miss Kim clapped.

Then she rolled him a big yellow ball. Hudson held out both hands. The ball bounced off his chest. He ran after it. "Messy try!" he laughed. He tried again with both hands open wide. This time the ball landed right in them. Hudson hugged the ball tight.

"Again, please!" he said.

Asher ran to the big red slide. He was so excited. "My turn, my turn!" he said. He climbed up the steps. Then a big boy pushed past him. Asher fell down on his bottom. His face felt hot. His hands made tight fists. He was angry.

Asher stomped off the slide. He wanted to yell. His grandma sat on the bench. "Come here, Asher," she said. "Let's try slow, big breaths." Asher sat next to her. Grandma took a slow breath in. Asher copied her. He blew the air out, slow and long. They did it again. In and out, like a big balloon.

Asher unclenched his fists. His body felt calm now. "I feel better," he said. He looked back at the slide. The big boy had gone to the swings. "You can go up now," said Grandma.

Asher climbed the steps again. He saw the whole playground from the top. He slid down fast and laughed. "I did it!" he said. Grandma clapped her hands in a big circle. "Hooray for Asher!"

Adam wanted a story about a storm. He ran to his room with his big book. "Daddy, read this one!"

Daddy sat on the bed. Adam snuggled close. The lamp made a warm, soft circle of light.

Adam pointed at the page. "What does it say?" He put his finger on the right side of the page. He slid his finger to the left.

Daddy smiled. He took Adam's hand. "Start here," he said. He set Adam's finger on the left side. Then he moved it along, slow and smooth. "The words go this way."

Adam tried it himself. Left to right, just like Daddy. Then Daddy read the words out loud. The words said "A big storm is coming." Adam gasped. The marks on the page had told Daddy what to say!

"It knows the storm story," said Adam. "The little marks talk to you?"

"Yes," said Daddy. "They talk to whoever reads them."

Adam turned one page. Then another page. The story went on and on. He found the stinky skunk at the end, after the storm. Then they came to the last page.

"The end," said Daddy. He closed the book.

Adam yawned. "Don't forget the storm book tomorrow," he said. He hugged it tight to his chest.

Ethan ran up to the bookmobile. The door was open wide. He wanted his very own library card.

Inside, the shelves were tall, tall, tall. The books were big and thick. Ethan could not reach them at all. He stood on his tiptoes. His fingers touched only air.

Then he saw something. A little corner with a tiny rug. The rug was squishy under his feet. Small shelves stood there, just his size. Every book had big, bright pictures.

"This is the children's area," said the driver. "The books here are just for young kids like you."

Ethan grabbed a book about trucks. He hugged it tight. The driver gave him a shiny new card.

"Can I take the truck book home?" Ethan asked.

"You sure can," said the driver. She put the book in a bag. The bag covered it up like a blanket.

Ethan held the bag all the way home. "Truck book, meet my lunch," he said. He set them side by side on the table.

Maya ran to the park with her teddy bear, Ben. She saw her friend Leo by the big tree. Leo had a stick in his hand.

"I am flying a plane," said Leo. He held up his flat piece of bark. It was not a plane at all. Maya looked hard. Then Leo ran in a circle. "Zoom, zoom!" he said. The bark went up and down in his hand.

Maya laughed. "I know what to do," she said. She put Ben on a flat rock. The rock was her house now. She made a bed with leaves. "Shh, Ben is sleeping," she said. Leo tapped the rock with his stick. Maya said, "Knock, knock! Who is it?" Leo said, "It is the pilot!" Maya clapped.

Then a real wind came. It blew the leaves off Ben's bed. Maya gasped. "My house is losing its roof!" Leo held his bark over Ben. "Now it is a roof," he said. The wind stopped. The leaves lay flat on the grass.

"I love this game," said Maya. "The bark is a plane. The rock is a house. None of it is real. But we play like it is!" Leo smiled and flew his plane round and round. Maya hugged Ben tight. "Time for dinner, Ben," she said. "Knock, knock on our rock house."

Isaiah sat in the school library with his teacher, Ms. Rao. He wanted to find his own name in a book. But he could not read the letters yet.

"Let's start with the first letter," said Ms. Rao. "I. It says i, like in igloo." Isaiah looked at the big black letters on the page. Then he found a card with his name. But the first letter was small. "That is not right," said Isaiah. Ms. Rao smiled. "Your name starts with a capital I," she said. She took out a red crayon. Isaiah drew a big capital I over the small one. Now it said Isaiah, just right.

He held the card up high. The lamp made the letters shine. "I did it," said Isaiah. Ms. Rao clapped. "Now let's find the S," she said. Isaiah turned the page. "S says sss," he said, like a snake. "Yes," said Ms. Rao. Isaiah laughed and pointed at the next letter. "That one is A!"

Bennett was going to be a big brother. Grandma was knitting a small blue sock. Grandpa was painting a small white crib. Bennett wanted to help too.

"Can I pick a gift for the baby?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Let's go to the baby store." At the store, Bennett saw soft blankets. He saw tiny hats. Then he saw a big stack of diapers, tall as a tower.

A boy next to him pointed at the tower. "Why so many diapers?" he asked his mom. "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet," she said. Bennett listened. He looked at the tower again. So babies need diapers, he thought. One after another after another.

Bennett picked out a pack of diapers. He picked a little pencil and a pad of paper too. At home, he asked Grandpa to cut the paper into small cards. Grandpa cut the cards slowly. Bennett waited. Then Bennett drew on each card. One card had a diaper. One card had a bottle. One card had a sock.

At last the baby came home. Mama laid him on the soft rug. Bennett gave him his cards, one by one. The baby grabbed the diaper card in his little hand. "That one is for you," said Bennett. "You will need it first."

Emmett sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all.

"One, two," he said. Then he stopped. What came next? He made a mad face. He could not remember.

Big sister Mia sat next to him. She sang a little song. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door."

Emmett listened. The song was teaching him! "Three, four," he said. "Shut the door!"

He pushed one pea with his spoon. One pea went into the pile. He sang, "Five, six, pick up sticks."

Then Mom smiled. "Look at your peas, Emmett."

The peas made a round line. Red sauce was under them. It looked just like a rainbow!

Emmett sang on. "Seven, eight, lay them straight."

He laid the peas in a straight row. "Nine, ten," he sang. "A big fat hen!"

Mia laughed. Emmett ate the rainbow, one pea at a time.

James wanted to be a rocket ship. He found a big box in the playroom. "This is my rocket," he said.

Dad came to play. "Rockets need a countdown," said Dad. "We count ten, nine, eight, all the way down to one."

"Ten, nine, eight," said James. "Seven, six, five." He patted the box. It made a boom sound. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" James jumped up high.

"Can I count too?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You can do it again." James counted again, quick and loud. "Ten, nine, eight!" One jump on one. "I did it!" said James.

He sat down after his flight. He picked up his puzzle. He put in one piece, then two pieces, then three. "Rockets go up," said James. "And then they come back home." He gave his rocket box a soft pat. "Blast off tomorrow too?" asked James. Dad smiled and said, "Yes, we can count down again."

Aurora waited by the school gate. Grandma was late. Aurora's tummy felt small and tight. She held her teacher's hand.

Then Grandma came around the corner, smiling. "Sorry, sweet pea. The car was slow today." Aurora ran to her and hugged her legs.

At home, Grandma made a warm snack. Aurora ate cheese and apple slices. Then Grandma said it was bath time. Aurora took off her socks and her dress. Grandma ran the bath, and the water was warm and foamy.

Aurora rubbed the soap with water on her hands. Bubbles grew on her fingers. "Look, Grandma! Bubbles!" She patted them on her chin. Now she had a thick white soap beard. Grandma laughed and laughed. Aurora giggled too.

After the bath, Grandma helped her dry off with a big soft towel. Aurora put on her striped pajamas. She brushed her teeth with Grandma's help.

Then came a surprise. Under her pillow was a small paper star. "You put it there last night," Grandma said. Aurora smiled and held it tight. She snuggled into bed.

"Night night, Aurora," said Grandma.

"Night night, bubbles," said Aurora.

Carter went to the store with Mom. He wanted to find a squishy ball. "Stay with me," said Mom. Carter held her hand.

They walked past the bread. Then Carter saw a shelf way down the aisle. He let go of Mom's hand and skipped to the end. He looked back. He could not see Mom. He could not see her anywhere.

Carter stood very still. Then he walked back up the aisle. He passed the bread again. There was Mom! "I could not see you," said Carter. "I came back so you could see me." Mom hugged him.

They found the squishy ball. At the checkout, Carter watched Mom tap the computer screen. He held the bag. He held Mom's hand all the way to the car.

"Next time I will stay close," said Carter.

Josephine sat at the art table. She had a red crayon, a blue one, a yellow one, and a green one. She wanted to draw snow. Big soft snow, like outside her window.

She drew snow with the white crayon on white paper. She looked and looked. She could not see it. "Oh no," said Josephine. "My snow is hiding."

Then she had an idea. She took a blue paper. She drew white dots on the blue paper. They showed up! The snow was white, just like the snow outside. "Look, Ben," she said. "White snow on blue."

Ben smiled. "I want snow too," he said. Josephine did not want to be mean. So she shared her blue paper with him. He drew white snow too.

The teacher gave them a hug. "Snow pictures," she said. Josephine touched her drawing. It felt bumpy and waxy. Her white snow shone on the blue. "More snow," said Josephine, and she drew one more big white dot.

Nova put on her clean blue dress. The morning was bright and warm. Today was Eid, and there was a big festival on her street.

Mama said, "We say 'Eid Mubarak' to greet people today." Nova practiced the words in the car. "Eid Mubarak. Eid Mubarak."

At the festival, Nova smelled sweet cookies and warm bread. She heard drums. Then Auntie Salma came near the food table. Nova wanted to say hello the right way. She took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak, Auntie Salma!" Auntie Salma's face turned into a big smile. She opened her arms wide and gave Nova a hug. "Eid Mubarak to you too, little one!"

Nova tried it again on Uncle Yusuf. "Eid Mubarak!" He laughed and gave her a shiny coin. Nova gasped. The coin smelled like metal and lemons.

Every time she said the words, someone smiled back. Nova kept walking down the street. "Eid Mubarak," she called to Grandpa Omar. "Eid Mubarak!"

Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint grass. The green pot was empty. Mia wanted green too. She looked grumpy.

"I need green," said Mia. "All gone."

Hayden looked at his paints. He had a red pot, a blue pot, and a yellow pot. No green. He dipped his brush in blue. He put blue on the paper. Then he dipped his brush in yellow. He put yellow right on top.

"Look!" said Hayden. The paint turned green. Green like grass. Green like the leaves outside.

Mia clapped her hands. "Green! Thank you!"

"Blue and yellow make green," said Mia. She mixed some too.

Hayden painted tall green grass. Mia painted a green frog. Then Hayden added a yellow sun. "One sun," he said. "The sun will shine on the grass."

Mia put her frog in the grass. Hayden put a blue puddle by the frog. "Splash," said Mia.

The teacher hung both paintings on the wall. "My grass," said Hayden, pointing up. "My frog," said Mia, pointing too.

Paisley put on her little apron. The chef said, "You can wear it today." In the restaurant kitchen, the toast was ready. A grown-up had made it warm.

Paisley wanted to butter the toast all by herself. She took the knife. It was a safe, soft knife. She dipped it in the butter. She spread the butter on the warm toast. The butter went shiny. Then it melted away. Paisley looked and looked. "My butter is lost!" she said. The chef smiled. "Look again," he said. Paisley tipped the toast to the light. The butter was still there. It was shiny and wet and soft. Warm toast made the butter melt.

Next came the milk. Paisley held the cup with two hands. She poured slow, slow, slow. One drip ran down the side. But the cup did not spill over. "I did it!" said Paisley. The chef clapped his hands.

Outside the window, a tree moved in the wind. Paisley ate her warm, shiny toast. "More milk, please," she said.

Clara ran to the dress-up corner at school. Today was scarf day! She wanted to be a sleepy ocean queen with a long, wavy scarf.

She found a blue scarf. She held it up. It was so little! It went up to her elbow and stopped. "Oh no," said Clara. "This scarf is short!"

Milo came by with his scarf. His scarf went down, down, down to his shoes. "My scarf is long," said Milo.

"Long and short are opposites," said Milo.

Clara wanted a long scarf too. She looked in the box. She found a red scarf. She held it up high. Down it went, past her knees! Long!

"Look, Milo!" said Clara. She spun around fast, then slow. The scarf flapped like ocean waves. "Now I can be the ocean queen!"

"Is the ocean cold?" asked Milo.

"Pretend cold," said Clara. "Brrr!"

Milo laughed. Clara wrapped the long scarf round and round. Then she yawned a big yawn. The sleepy ocean queen lay down on the rug.

"Goodnight, ocean," said Milo.

"Goodnight," said Clara.

Violet stood by the pool. The pool was next to the big lake. Violet held her mama's hand. She wanted to swim like the big kids. But she did not want to put her face near the water.

A swim teacher named Ben knelt down. "I am your new teacher," he said. "Want to blow bubbles?" Ben put his mouth in the water. He blew out. Bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop. Violet watched the bubbles. They tickled the top of the water.

"My turn," said Violet. She held the wall. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out. Big bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! Violet laughed and laughed. Her face was wet, and it was fine. The light made the bubbles shine. "Look, Mama!" she said. She blew more bubbles. Then she kicked her feet, and Ben held her tummy. "I am swimming!" said Violet. "Again!"

Amelia put her toy mouse in the box. Tommy took the toy mouse out. Amelia put it back in. Tommy pulled it out again.

"In and out are opposites," said Miss Jo. Amelia looked at the box. How odd, she thought. What goes in can come right out.

She tried it with a small red ball. In went the ball. Out came the ball. Then she tried a big teddy bear. It was too big. Only small toys fit inside.

At snack time, Amelia got cold milk. Tommy's soup was hot, so Miss Jo blew on it for him. Amelia did not touch the hot bowl. She watched Miss Jo help, from her seat.

After snack, a mouse ran across the floor. It ran so fast! Amelia tiptoed. Tiptoeing was slow. The fast mouse hid under the shelf. Could it come back out? She waited. Out it popped, quick as that.

Then it was tidy-up time. Amelia had an idea. If toys go in the box, maybe the mouse goes in its hole. She peeked at the little hole in the wall. The mouse peeked back at her.

"Hello, little mouse," she whispered. "Is that your house?"

The mouse twitched its nose. Then it popped back into its hole, tail and all.

Weston was at a big festival with his grandma. There were flags and drums and food everywhere. A long table had warm bread on it. Weston's tummy made a loud growl. "Feed me," it seemed to say.

Weston reached for the bread. Then he saw everyone sitting still. Their hands were folded, not eating. Grandma held up one finger. "We wait," she whispered. "First comes the blessing." An old man sang the blessing out loud. His voice went up and down. Weston waited, though the bread smelled so good.

Then the singing stopped. Everyone smiled and picked up bread at last. Weston took a big bite. It was warm and a little salty. "Yum," he said. "The blessing made it taste better," he whispered. Grandma laughed and gave him one more piece.

The wind blew hard outside Sienna's window. It howled and howled. Then all the lights went out. The whole apartment went dark.

"Oh no," said Sienna. "The dark!" Mommy held her hand. "The big wind knocked out the power," said Mommy. "The lights cannot work now." Daddy lit a little lantern. Mommy put a plastic cup of water on the table. Sienna's hands were wet from washing, so Mommy dried them with a towel.

They sat together on the big sofa. The lantern made a warm yellow circle. Sienna made shadows on the wall. The wind kept howling outside. Sienna was not scared. Mommy and Daddy were right there. Then the lights came back on, all at once. Sienna clapped her hands. "Hello, lights!" she said.

Lincoln was at Grandma's house. His new baby sister was here too. Her name was May. Grandma had made bread. Lincoln could smell it. "Can I hold the baby?" he asked. "Yes, sit on the big pillow," said Grandma. May's hand was so small. Her cheeks were soft and squishy.

At night, Lincoln slept in the little bed. He heard a cry. "Is it morning?" he asked. Grandma shook her head. "It is still night," she said. "The baby is hungry. She drinks milk many times, day and night." Mom sat in the chair and fed May. Lincoln watched from his bed. May drank and drank. Then she went back to sleep.

The next night, May cried again. "It is milk time," said Lincoln. Grandma smiled. "Yes, it is." Lincoln counted the feedings he had heard. One at bedtime. One in the dark. One when the sky turned pink. He patted May's blanket, soft and slow. "Drink your milk, baby," he whispered. "I will be here in the morning."

Nicholas had a new book. It had a bear on the front. He wanted Dad to read it, but Dad was still in the bath.

So Nicholas ran to Mom. "Can you read it?" he asked. Mom opened the book. She turned the pages from the front to the back. She read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey."

Then Dad came in, all warm and dry. "Read it too," said Nicholas. Dad sat down. He opened the book the same way. He turned the pages one by one. He read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey."

Nicholas blinked. Dad read the same words as Mom! "Do it again," he said. Dad read it once more. "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey." The words did not change. They were the same every time.

Nicholas tried it himself. He held the book upside down. The pictures looked wrong. He turned it around and started at the front. The bear was there, waiting for his honey.

"Now I know the bear's words," said Nicholas. He hugged the book tight.

Eloise sat on the rug in her bedroom. Her teddy bear sat on the little table by the bed. Eloise wanted to hug him. She reached out her arms.

Then she stopped. Teddy's mouth looked down, not up. His eyebrows made a frown. Eloise froze. "Teddy looks sad," she said. She picked him up and patted his back. "I will hug you." She turned his mouth up into a smile. Now Teddy looked happy. Eloise clapped. She felt so excited she jumped up and down.

The door creaked open. Eloise felt scared. She hid behind the bed. Then she heard a soft laugh. It was Mama. Mama's eyes were smiling. Her face was happy. Eloise laughed too. She ran to Mama with Teddy. "Teddy was sad. I made him smile." Mama kissed Eloise's head. "You did, sweet girl." Eloise hugged Teddy tight. Teddy smiled all night long.

Harrison went to the library with his grandma. There was a big rug on the floor. On the rug were three piles. One pile was animals. One pile was toys. One pile was foods.

Harrison picked up a black toy dog. He put it in the animal pile. Then he sat still. He looked at the toy dog. He looked at a picture of a real dog on the wall.

"Is the toy dog an animal?" he asked.
"No," said Miss Kim. "A toy dog is not alive."
"A toy dog is a toy," said Harrison.

He moved it to the toy pile. Then he sorted a red apple, a ball, and a toy cat. "A toy cat is a toy," he said. "Not alive."

Miss Kim made a happy sound. "Your sorting works now," she said.

Harrison clapped his hands. "I did it all by myself!"

Anna climbed the school bus. She held her lunchbox tight. It had a plane on it. Anna loved that plane.

She sat by a boy named Sam. Sam held a lunchbox too. It had a plane on it too. "Hey, same plane!" said Sam. They laughed.

At school, the lunchboxes went on one big shelf. After lunch, Anna grabbed a box. But it was not hers. It felt too heavy. Sam opened his box and frowned. "My apple is gone," he said. "I got an apple I did not want," said Anna.

The teacher came over. "Look inside the lid," she said. Anna opened her box. There was writing on the lid. It said ANNA. Sam opened the other box. It said SAM. "That is my name!" said Anna. They swapped boxes. Anna got her own snack back. "Our names found our lunchboxes," said Anna. "Smart names," said Sam. They sat down to eat, and Anna smiled at her plane.

Myles sat on his bed. He had a fresh new book. He opened the front cover first. The pages turned one by one.

"I love this bear," said Myles. He tapped the big picture. "Who drew him?"

Myles looked at the picture. He chewed his thumb while he thought. He wanted to know. He ran to Mom.

"Who drew my bear?" he asked.

Mom opened the front of the book. She pointed to some small black marks. "Those little marks are words," she said. "Words can tell us things."

Myles leaned in close. Mom read, "It says the name of the illustrator."

"What is that?" asked Myles.

"A person who draws the pictures for a book," said Mom.

"The illustrator drew my bear!" said Myles. He ran back to his bed.

He opened the front again. He turned each page the right way. He found the bear. He found the illustrator's name too.

"The illustrator drew the dog! The illustrator drew the moon!"

Myles hugged the book. Tomorrow he would ask about a new one. "Who drew this?" he said, and pointed at the moon.

Luca stood by the bus stop with Mama. The sun came out. The sky was blue. "Sunny day," said Mama. Luca wore his yellow hat.

But then the wind blew. The wind blew his hat. Luca held his hat with both hands. "Windy now," said Mama. She zipped up his jacket.

Then the rain came. Drip, drop, drip. Mama opened a big umbrella. Luca stood under it. The rain fell and fell.

The bus came. They rode to the playground. "I want to swing," said Luca. He ran to the swings. He stopped. There was water on the ground. A big puddle sat right under the swing.

Luca looked at the sky. The rain was gone now. He looked down. The puddle was still there. "Mama! Look! Rain makes puddles on the ground," said Luca. "Yes it does," said Mama. She laughed.

Luca put on his red boots. He was ready. He gave a little spring and landed in the puddle. Splash! Water went up and up. His boots were wet. His socks were dry. "Again!" said Luca.

After splashing, they sat on the bench. Mama gave him a banana. Luca took a big bite and began to chew. "Winter will come soon," said Mama. "Then we need snow pants and mittens." "Snow!" said Luca. He pointed his banana at the sky. "Maybe tomorrow!"

Sofia was going on a big trip. The family would sleep at a campsite. She helped put her bag in the car. "I want to sit in my seat now," she said.

Sofia climbed in fast. She held her teddy bear tight. Papa sat down and looked at her. "Where is your click?" he asked. Sofia looked around. Her car seat had straps. The straps were loose. She pushed the buckle in. Click!

"Why did we wait for that sound?" Sofia asked. "The car seat keeps you safe when we drive," said Mama. Sofia patted the buckle with her hand. Then the car started. The trees went by. Sofia pretended her teddy was buckled too. She held him up high. Click, she said softly, and smiled at the window.

Iris went to the pharmacy with Mom. Iris rubbed her hands on her pants. They felt sticky from lunch. "I want clean hands," said Iris. Mom smiled. "The pharmacist is smart about clean hands. Let's ask."

The pharmacist knelt down. She showed Iris a little bottle of soap. "We sell this soap right here," she said. "Wash for twenty seconds. Count it out." Iris wanted to try right away.

But the sink in the pharmacy bathroom was too tall. Iris stood on her toes. She could not reach the water. The pharmacist brought a step stool and stayed close by her side. Iris climbed up. The water ran over her hands! She pumped the soap. "One, two, three," she counted, all the way to twenty. The bubbles swirled down the drain. Iris held her hands up to the sun coming through the window. They were clean and shiny. "Twenty seconds!" she cheered, waving her soapy-sweet hands at Mom.

Henry sat in his car seat. The car went up a big hill. Then it went down a small hill. "Up and down," said Henry. The wind whooshed past the window. It was a windy day. Outside, a big truck went fast. A little blue car went slow. The sun made the seat feel hot. Henry's cup was empty. Not one drop was left. "I'm thirsty," said Henry. Dad stopped the car at a little shop. They went in to pay for some cold water. Dad held the big bottle. It was cold in his hands. The sun outside was hot. Henry found a small cup on the counter. It was empty. Dad poured the water in. The water came fast. "Stop!" said Henry. The cup was full, all the way to the top. One more drop would spill. Dad poured the next cup slow. Henry watched the water rise. He said, "Stop!" just in time. Not one drop spilled. Dad smiled. They walked back to the car. Henry held his full cup with two hands. He drank it all down. Now the cup was empty again. The car drove on, slow and steady, over the next big hill.

Daniel went to the park with Grandma. He wanted to splash in the big puddle by the bench. He took off one shoe. He put in his toe. Splash! The water was cold. Then Daniel saw something shiny in the grass. It was a little lighter. It did not belong to anyone at the park. Daniel did not pick it up. He kept his hands behind his back. He walked to Grandma. "I found a little lighter," he said. Grandma looked at it. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," she said. She picked it up and put it in her pocket. "Good job telling me." Daniel went back to the puddle. He put in his whole foot. Splash! Splash! The sun went down. It was getting late. "One more splash," said Grandma, "then we go home."

Jake was getting better from his cold. He sat on his bed with a box of tissues. His nose was runny. He pulled out a soft tissue. Then he blew his nose. Toot! He dropped the tissue on the floor.

Mom came in. She picked up the tissue. "Used tissues go in the bin," she said. She pointed at the little bin by the door. Jake looked at the bin. Could he get a tissue in from far away? He wanted to try.

Jake blew his nose again. He held the tissue up high. He aimed. He dropped it. It fell in! "Yay!" said Jake. He laughed and clapped. His shy little cat peeked out from under the bed. Then Jake blew his nose once more. He fixed his aim and dropped the tissue. In it went. Mom smiled and said, "Good shot, Jake."

Grayson put on Papa's big boot. It went clomp, clomp on the floor. "I am a giant!" he said. His teddy bear was the giant's baby. Grayson made soup for the baby in the pretend kitchen. He stirred it with a spoon. The pot went crash. Cups rolled under the table. Plates sat upside down on the rug.

Then Grayson could not find the red spoon. "Where did it go?" he asked. Papa peeked under the chair. "Here it is," said Papa. Grayson reached for it. But wait. The kitchen was a big mess. He could not cook more giant soup here.

So Grayson put each cup back on the shelf. The plates went into the little sink. The pot went on the stove, all alone. "All clean," said Grayson. Then he spelled out his bear's name, B-E-A-R, and tucked the baby into bed. "Night night," said Grayson. "Sleep tight, little bear."

Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name.

"First you hold it like this," said the woman. She was his mama. She showed him how to hold the pencil. Gabriel tried it too.

He made a G. He made an A. Then he made a big wobbly B. It leaned over like a sleepy duck. Gabriel frowned. "My B is all wrong," he said.

"Try the pink eraser," said Mama. Gabriel turned the pencil around. He rubbed the wobbly B. He rubbed and rubbed. The wobbly B was gone! The paper was clean again.

"Now I can try again," said Gabriel. He held the pencil tight. He made a new B. It stood up tall. He made R, I, E, L.

"Look, Mama! GABRIEL!" he shouted. He jumped up and did a happy stomp. Then he sat back down. "Now I want to write it big!"

Bennett ran into the music room. He wanted to clap and sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by himself. He tried it fast. He tried it slow. His claps went everywhere. The song went one way. His hands went another way. It did not sound right at all.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Try this," she said. "Clap at the same time as the beat." Bennett put down his yellow cup of milk. He hid his hands under his legs and listened first. The song went clap, clap, clap. Then he let his hands out. He clapped when the song clapped. His hands and the music landed together, like two friends jumping at the same time.

"Now the song!" said Miss Rosa. Bennett sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He did not stop clapping. Miss Rosa clapped too. Then everyone in the room clapped with them, all at the same time. Bennett sang louder. "How I wonder what you are!"

Oliver sat at the dinner table. He kicked his feet under his chair. One brown sock fell off his foot. It landed on the floor.

"One sock," said Oliver. He counted it. "One."

Mama came over. "A sock needs its partner," she said. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks."

Oliver looked under the table. He saw his brown foot. He saw the sock on the floor. He counted again. "One, two, three," he said, pointing at the chair legs. "Four, five, six." He kept going slow. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Can you fetch the sock?" asked Mama.

"I can fetch it," said Oliver. He climbed down. He picked up the sock. He looked for the other one. He looked left. He looked right. There it was, under his high chair.

He pulled it out. He put on one sock. He put on the other sock.

"Now I have a pair," said Oliver. "Two socks!"

Mama smiled. "Two socks for two feet," she said.

Oliver wiggled his toes. Both socks were on. He sat back down at the table. He tapped his socks together. "One, two," he said. "A pair."

Evan was playing in the backyard. He had a big box of blocks. He wanted to build a tower on his little desk. But first, he wanted to sort them.

Evan picked up a red block. "Red," he said. He put it in a pile. Then a blue block. Then another red block. "One red, two red, three red," he said. His red pile grew tall. The blue pile grew too. Now all the blocks were sorted by color.

Then his big sister Mia came out. "I can sort them a different way," she said. She put all the big blocks in one pile. She put all the little blocks in another pile. Evan's mouth fell open. The same blocks! Now they were sorted by size!

"Let me try," said Evan. He found some round blocks. He put them in one pile. He put the square blocks in another pile. "Sorted by shape!" he said. Mia clapped. Then they built one big tower together. It was Evan's favorite kind of tower, red and blue, big and little, round and square, all the way up to the sky.

Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to learn her five senses. Grandpa said, "Let's find them one by one."

First Isabelle saw a shiny red apple on a tree. "I used my eyes," she said. Then she touched a soft sheep. "I used my hands." Next she heard a loud cow. "Moo! I used my ears." She smelled bread. Grandpa was going to bake it later. "I used my nose," she said. "One sense left," said Grandpa.

Grandpa picked two apples. One was sweet. One was sour. "Guess with your tongue," he said. Isabelle took a little bite of the first apple. "Sweet!" she said. Then she tried the other one. Her face went squinty. "Sour!" she said, and she laughed.

Grandpa gave her a small gift. It was a shiny apple for her pocket. "My tongue knew," said Isabelle. She patted her pocket all the way home.

Josephine wanted to make a bed for the class bunny. She found a big box on the shelf. She pulled it. The box did not move. She pulled again. Still it stayed. "This box is heavy," said Ben. "It is too heavy for me."

Miss Dana came to help. "Heavy and light are opposites," she said. Together they pushed the big box down. It went slow, slow, slow. Then Josephine found a small pillow. It was light! She lifted it up high. She carried it fast across the room. She put it in the box so the bunny could sleep.

At snack time, Josephine drank cold milk. She touched the warm cup with her hands. The bunny snuggled into the pillow bed. Josephine gave the bunny a soft kiss on its head. "Sleep tight," she said.

Alexis sat at the big table. His friend Milo came to dinner. Milo brought a little red car. It was heavy for such a small car.

Milo zoomed the car on the table. Alexis wanted a turn now. His hand went out fast. Grandma put her hand on his. "Milo is first," she said softly.

Alexis wanted to grab it. That felt hard. Grandma said, "Try three slow breaths." Alexis took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His hand felt calm. Milo rolled the car to him. "Your turn," said Milo.

Alexis zoomed the car to Milo's cup. Then he rolled it back. They took turns, back and forth, all through dinner. After dinner, Alexis helped wash his hands at the sink. Water ran over his ear as he leaned down. He laughed and gave Milo one more turn with the red car.

Jacob stood in the bathroom. He looked at his face in the mirror with his eyes. He saw a boy with toothpaste on his chin.

Then his nose knew something. A yummy smell came in under the door. "Sniff, sniff," said Jacob. "I smell dinner! Is it soup?" His tummy made a little growl. He did not want to miss one drop.

Daddy came to the door. "You smelled it before you saw it," said Daddy. "Good nose! Come and listen." Jacob used his ears. He heard the pot bubble on the stove. Daddy stirred it with a big spoon. The man in the kitchen was Daddy, and he was safe.

At the table, Jacob touched his warm bowl with his fingers. He took a taste with his tongue. "Soup!" said Jacob. "My nose was right." Daddy smiled and gave him bread. The kitchen smelled good, and Jacob was warm and happy. "More bread, please," said Jacob.

Ivy went to the library with Dad. There was a new tablet on the little table. Ivy wanted to draw a cat on it. But the screen was dark and still.

Dad showed her the small button on the side. "Press that," he said. Ivy pressed it. The screen lit up, bright and pretty. She pressed the drawing app. It opened with a pop. Ivy drew a cat with green ears. She drew summer sun, too. "Your cat looks silly," said Dad. "That is the plan," said Ivy.

Soon it was time to go. Ivy remembered the small button. She pressed it once. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the table. "All done," said Ivy. Dad gave her a big grin. "Bye-bye, green-eared cat," said Ivy.

Jaxon sat on the big red cushion. Dad put the game on TV. Aunt Mia and Grandpa came too. Popcorn jumped in the bowl, warm and salty.

The blue team ran and ran. The red team ran too. "The blue team runs more," said Jaxon. "They win!" Grandpa laughed. "Look at the score," he said. Jaxon stood up and looked. The red team had more points. The red team was winning!

Jaxon watched more. A red player kicked the ball. It went in the net. The red score went up by one. "The ball went in," Jaxon shouted. "Now the number is bigger!" He marched around the couch like a little turtle in a hurry, arms and legs going fast.

The game ended. The red team had more points at the end. The TV said the red team won. The blue team had run a lot, but that was not what counted. Jaxon held up the popcorn bowl like a prize. "More points means you win," he said. Grandpa clapped. Aunt Mia cheered. Dad said, "Snack time, everyone!" Jaxon ran to the kitchen, not lost at all, right behind him.

Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread and fresh butter. They bought a big carton of milk too. At the bread stand, a lady sliced the bread flat on a wooden board. Dad said, "I will teach you to butter toast today." Ezra said, "Can I do it all by myself?" Dad said, "Yes, you can."

They sat at a little table. Dad put butter on Ezra's knife-safe spoon. Ezra spread the butter. The butter made the toast shiny. "I did it!" said Ezra. Then Ezra tried to pour milk from the big carton. It was too heavy. Milk nearly spilled. "Why is it so hard?" Ezra asked. Dad said, "The carton is too big for your hands."

Dad poured some milk into a small jug. Ezra held the little jug. He tipped it slowly. Milk went into his cup. Not one drop spilled. Ezra poured more milk into Dad's cup too. "Small jug, small hands," said Ezra. He drank his milk and ate his toast down to the last flat crumb. "Can we get juice next time?" asked Ezra. Dad laughed and said, "Yes, and a small jug to pour it from."

Leah went to the library with her mom. There was a playroom in the back. Leah wanted to find the toy box, but it was empty. "Where did all the toys go?" she asked.

Her friend Ben was putting toys away on the wrong shelf. He had put a ball next to the books. Leah picked it up. "A ball is a toy," she said. "It goes in the toy box." She dropped it in. Thump!

Ben found a doll under the chair. He handed it to Leah. Dolls are toys too. In it went. Then Leah saw blocks by the door. Blocks are toys. In they went, one by one. Soon the toy box was full.

But then Leah heard a funny sound. Something was snoring in the toy box! She peeked inside. A fat orange cat was asleep on the doll. The cat twitched its nose. Leah gave it a soft pat. "The cat is not a toy," she whispered. "But it can stay." The cat purred and purred.

Sienna wanted to make a paper sun at camp. She found red paper and yellow paper. She wanted to cut long points for the sun's rays.

She saw the big scissors on the table. The big scissors had sharp, shiny points. "Can I use those?" she asked.

Camp Leader Joe shook his head. "Those are for me," he said. "Here are your safety scissors. They have rounded tips. I will watch while you cut."

The safety scissors were small and blue. Sienna held them. Snip, snip, snip. The yellow paper fell into long strips. "I did it!" she said. "The scissors make the paper fall!"

"Snip, snip, snip," she sang. Soon the sun had many rays. But one ray was too long. It looked like a dirty old sock.

"You can rip it shorter," said Joe. Sienna pulled the paper. Riiiip! The ray was short now. She put all the rays in her bag to carry home.

Then Joe held up a surprise. "Look what I cut with the big scissors," he said. It was a tiny paper crown. "For the sun artist," he said.

Sienna put it on her head. "My sun is boss of the sky now," she said.

Jasper wanted to sort his toys. He had a big problem. His toy box was all mixed up.

He put all the toy cars in one pile. He put all the stuffed animals in another pile. The animals were bear, bunny and duck. Then Jasper saw something silly. A banana sat with the toy cars!

"Guess what I found," he told his sister, Mia. "A banana with my cars."

Mia laughed. "That is the odd one out," she said. "It does not belong there."

Jasper picked up the banana with gentle hands. He carried it to the kitchen. He gave it to Dad for snack time. Dad cut it into little round slices.

Jasper ran back to his toys. All the cars were together now. Only cars. No bananas.

"Odd one out," said Jasper. "Found you."

Lea sat at the big art table. Her teacher, Miss Jo, put out paper stars, glitter, and a full bottle of glue. "I will make a crown," said Lea. Miss Jo smiled. "A crown for a queen," she said.

Lea counted her stars. One, two, three, four, five. She put glue on each star. She stuck them on a long paper strip. Then she grabbed the crown to try it on. The stars slid off. The paper ends slid apart too. Lea's lip wobbled. "My crown is broken," she said.

Miss Jo sat down next to her. "The glue is still wet," she said. "Wet glue needs time to dry. Then the pieces hold together." Lea sniffed the glue. It smelled funny and sharp. She touched one dot of glue with her finger. It felt cold and slippery. Miss Jo set the crown on the shelf. "Let's wait," she said.

Lea drew pictures while they waited. One sun. One cat. One baby in a stroller. Then Miss Jo said, "Touch it now." Lea poked the glue. It felt hard and dry. She picked up the crown. The stars stayed on. The ends stayed stuck. Lea put the crown on her head. "It worked," she said. Miss Jo clapped her hands. "A queen with a fine crown," she said.

Ellie stood on her tiptoes at Grandma's house. The big challah bread sat on the table. Everyone was coming for dinner.

Grandpa picked up the bread. "Time for the Hamotzi," he said. Ellie wanted to say it too. She wanted it very much.
