"I can do it," said Ellie. Grandpa smiled. "Let's practice," he said. They practiced under the big tree. They practiced in the kitchen. Ellie got mixed up. She tried again. She got mixed up a different way. "Keep trying," said Grandpa. So Ellie kept trying. Practice, practice, practice.

Now everyone sat down. Aunt Sara held the baby. Cousins wiggled in their seats. Grandma put the warm bread in Grandpa's hands. Grandpa looked at Ellie.

"You say it with me," he said.

Ellie took a big breath. She said the blessing. Grandpa's voice went up, and Ellie's voice went up too. Then both voices came down together. Everyone at the table said "Amen."

The bread was cut and passed around. Ellie took her piece and bit it. "I said the Hamotzi," she said. Grandma kissed the top of her head.

Sofia sat in the family car. She held her favorite toy bunny. "Are we going to the doctor?" she asked. Mom smiled. "We are going to a special doctor," she said.

Sofia hurried out of the car. The office door said DENTIST. A kind man in a blue coat waved. "Hello, Sofia!" he said. "Open wide, please." Sofia opened her mouth. He looked and looked. But he did not look at her ears. He did not look at her toes. He only looked at her teeth!

"You only check teeth?" Sofia asked. The man laughed. "Yes! A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth." Then he gave her a little mirror. Sofia held it up. She saw her own teeth shine back. "Hello, teeth!" she said. "Nice to meet you!"

Rehmat wanted to play the shouting game with her big brother. He said a word, and she had to shout back the opposite. "Opposites are two words as different as they can be," he said. Then he began.

"Big!" he shouted. Rehmat looked around the playroom. She pointed at the big teddy bear. Then she held up a small sock. "Small!" she shouted. Her brother laughed and clapped.

"Fast!" he said. Rehmat ran fast across the room. Then she walked slow, slow, slow, like a sleepy turtle. The game got tricky. "Hot!" he said. Rehmat pointed at the kitchen. "Daddy's tea is hot," she said. Her daddy waved and held the cup far away, so she would not touch. "Cold!" she shouted next, and hugged the cold window glass.

Rehmat got one wrong. Her brother said "Up," and she shouted "Cat." She felt grumpy and sat on the floor. "Big and small are different," her brother said. "Up and down are different too. You almost had it." Rehmat stood up. "Down!" she shouted. He gave her a gold star letter, her very own S. She held it tight and smiled. "Again!" she said.

Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to bake cookies for the whole family. Grandma said, "Yes! Let's bake."

Parker poured the sugar. He stirred the eggs. Grandma let him drop the dough onto the pan. The pan looked full and bumpy, like a nest of little round stones.

"Now the pan goes in the oven," said Grandma. Parker reached for the oven door. Grandma held his hand. "A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven," she said. "You can watch from here." Grandma slid the pan in all by herself. Parker sat on his blue stool and waited. Soon the kitchen smelled sweet.

Grandma pulled the pan out. The round dough had turned into real cookies! Parker saw that. The oven made them warm and done. "You waited so nicely," Grandma said. Parker carried the plate to the table. Mom took a bite and smiled. Dad took two. Parker pointed at the oven. "The oven did that," he said. Grandma laughed and gave him the biggest cookie.

Weston was in the backyard. He wanted to make soup for Bear. He found a round bucket and a small stick. He put in a pinecone, two leaves, and a little rock. Then he stirred and stirred. "Soup is ready!" he said.

He held the spoon up to his mouth. He tipped it in. "Stop right there," said Mom. She knelt down next to him. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth." Weston looked at the pinecone soup. He was sorry. He did not want a real pinecone in his tummy.

He tried again. He held the spoon near his lips and made a big slurp sound. "Sluuurp!" Nothing went in his mouth. Mom clapped. Bear got a sip too, right on his fuzzy nose. Then Weston set his soup on the square patio stone. He patted Bear's head and said, "All done. Time for naps."

Nova stood by the wooden table at the community hall. Big pots of soup sat at one end. Nova was hungry. She wanted to eat right now.

Grandma held Nova's hand. "First we say the blessing," Grandma said. "Then we eat." Everyone at the table held hands. They bowed their heads. Nova looked at the soup. She looked at the bread. When could she eat?

Grandma spoke softly. "We thank you for this food. We thank you for our family." Nova waited. She squeezed Grandma's hand. Still they did not eat. Then everyone said one word together. "Amen." Right after that, the spoons went up, and the bread began to pass down the table.

Nova ate her soup. It was warm and good. Then a lady brought out a present, a box of little cakes. "Ooh," said Nova. Before the cakes, everyone held hands again. Nova watched carefully this time. She waited for the soft words. She waited and waited. Then came the word. "Amen," said everyone, and Nova said it too. She reached for a cake, and Grandma smiled.

Everett turned four today. He was at Grandma's house. The cake sat on the big table. Grandma put in four little candles. Then she lit them with a match. Everett watched from his chair.

"Now we sing," said Grandma. Everyone began to sing. "Happy birthday to Everett," they sang. His name was in the song! He hid his smiling face behind his hands. "Sing it again," he said. "Please sing it again."

So they sang it again. "Happy birthday to Everett." He peeked through his fingers. His name was in the song both times. He was not mad at all. He blew out the candles. Grandma cut the cake. Everyone clapped. Then Everett asked, "Can we drive home and sing it again in the car?" And Grandma laughed and said, "Yes, we can."

Elijah wanted to play hide-and-seek at school. But he could not find anyone to count for him.

Miss Kim smiled. "I will be the seeker," she said. "You go hide, Elijah."

Elijah hid behind the toy horse. It was big and brown. He made himself tiny behind it.

Then Mia said, "I want to seek too." Miss Kim said, "We both will."

Mia covered her eyes. She counted very fast. "One two three four five!"

Elijah peeked out. His shoes were showing! He pulled them in.

The other kids called out, "Too fast, Mia! Count slowly. We need time to hide."

Mia counted again, slow and soft. "One... two... three..." Elijah held his breath and froze like a stone. He heard grass sounds outside the window. He heard a buzzing bee.

"Eight... nine... ten. Ready or not!" Mia opened her eyes.

She found Ben first. Then she found Sam. But she walked right past the toy horse. Elijah waited, still as still.

Then his tummy giggled. He giggled too. "You found me!" he laughed.

"My turn next," said Elijah. "Everyone hide. I will count to ten, nice and slow." He covered his eyes. "One... two... three..."

Bennett ran in from Grandma's backyard. He wanted to stir the pancake batter. The bowl sat on the big kitchen table. It smelled sweet like vanilla.

"First, the sink," said Grandma. She pointed to it. "Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food." Bennett looked at his hands. They had dirt on them from digging. He went to the sink. Grandma turned on the water. It ran warm over his fingers. He rubbed the soap until it made white bubbles.

Then Grandma held the bowl for him. Bennett stirred the batter round and round. The flour and milk mixed into something smooth and tan. He dipped one finger in to taste it. Grandma laughed. "That batter has raw egg," she said. "No tasting yet."

Grandpa poured the batter into the pan. The pan was hot, so Bennett stood far away on his stool. Soon the batter bubbled in little dots. Grandpa flipped each pancake high. One went so high that Bennett felt dizzy watching it. It landed right back in the pan.

The pancakes came to the table warm and golden. Bennett ate three. Grandpa ate five. Grandma put one more on Bennett's plate, and it was shaped like a heart.

Audrey ran into the pharmacy on a sunny day. Today she would get a shot. She was very excited. Then she saw the big table in the little room. Her tummy felt funny.

"I don't want to sit up there," said Audrey. The table was too big. Her feet could not touch the floor. Mom sat down on the chair instead. "Come sit on my lap," said Mom. Audrey climbed up. Mom held her in a big hug.

The nurse came in with a tiny tray. "Ready?" she asked. "Ready!" said Audrey. Mom's arms were warm and snug. Audrey took a deep breath. "You can squeeze my hand," said Mom. Audrey squeezed. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done!

"That was fast," said Audrey. "It did not hurt much." The nurse poured a little juice from a small cup for her. Audrey drank it all. Mom picked her up high. "What a big girl," said Mom. Audrey held up her bandage and showed the whole pharmacy.

"It's my bandage," she said. "See you next day!"

Peyton sat at Grandma's big table. She had red paint and a fat brush. She painted a big red sun. Then she wanted to play outside. She left the brush in the paint cup.

The next day, Peyton came back to the room. She picked up her brush. The brush felt hard. It would not bend at all. "Oh no," said Peyton. "My brush is all stiff."

Grandma held the brush under the tap. The warm water was too hot, so Grandma turned it to cool. She let Peyton watch. They put the brush in the water and swished it. The red paint came out. The brush turned soft again.

"Now we know," said Grandma. "After painting, we rinse the brush." Peyton got a fresh cup of water. She painted a blue fish. Then she rinsed her brush right away. The brush stayed soft.

Jaxson sat at the dinner table. Daddy set down a big pot. It was soup night!

Jaxson felt excited. He loved soup night. He tapped his spoon on his bowl. Tap, tap, tap!

His sister Mia sat next to him. She covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked sad.

Jaxson stopped tapping. He looked at his spoon. Then he looked at Mia. Hmm, could they feel different about the same sound?

"I love the tap," Jaxson said. "You don't like it?"

"No," said Mia. "It scares me."

Daddy smiled. "Maybe you two like different things."

Jaxson put his spoon down. He wanted Mia to feel happy. He picked up his doll from the chair. "Want to feed the doll?" he asked.

Mia smiled big. "Yes!" She held the doll and made it dance over the bowl. The doll dipped in the air. Mia laughed and laughed.

"Slurp, slurp," said the doll. Now Mia was happy too.

Jaxson watched her. Same table, same soup. But he loved the tapping, and she loved the doll. He wondered what else they might like differently.

"Mia," he said, "do you like carrots?"

"No!" said Mia, with a grumpy face.

"I love carrots!" said Jaxson. He took a big bite.

Mia giggled and fed the doll one more slurp.

Rowan went to the big hall with Mama and Grandma. There were red lanterns on the walls. There was music and lots of people. Rowan held Mama's hand tight.

A girl named Mei walked up to Rowan. She was holding a small red envelope. "Look," said Mei. "It is for Lunar New Year. Many children get red envelopes. There is money inside." Rowan looked at the envelope. It was shiny and flat.

Then Grandma gave Rowan a red envelope too. Rowan wanted to open it right away. His fingers pulled at the corner. Mei shook her head. "Say thank you first," she said. Rowan stopped. He looked up at Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma," he said. Grandma smiled big. "You are welcome, Rowan." Then Rowan opened the envelope. Inside was a shiny coin. It caught the light and glowed.

At the table, Daddy poured warm tea for everyone. Rowan took one small cookie from the plate. The lanterns swayed above them. Mei waved from across the room. Rowan held up his coin so she could see it shine.

Audrey sat in the school library. She wanted to write her name. But the K kept coming out wrong. It looked funny every time. Audrey frowned at her paper.

The librarian gave her a bumpy card. The letter K was raised up on it. Audrey put her finger on the card. She traced the shape, top to bottom, then out and out again. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it one more time.

Then she picked up her pencil. Her arm moved slow and careful. She wrote the K. This time it was right! Audrey made the K sound, "k, k, k." She wrote A, U, D, R, E, Y too. Her whole name sat on the paper, just right. Audrey held it up high. "Look what I can do!"

Sadie ran to the playground with her dad. The sun was out and the slide was hot. "Careful, it is hot," Dad said. He put his hand on the slide first. Sadie touched it after, just a little. It felt warm like tea. She waited for the shady side to play on.

Then Sadie saw a boy on a bike. He zoomed down the path. He wore a big helmet on his head. Sadie wanted to ride her bike too. She ran to it and jumped on. "Wait," Dad said. "Where is your helmet?" Sadie stopped. She looked at the boy again. He had his helmet on his head.

Sadie walked back to the car. Her helmet sat inside. It was red with a star. She put it on. It felt snug over her nose strap. Then she pedaled off down the path. Her ride was short and fun. A dog ran beside her, and its ears flapped up and down.

Sadie rode past the swings. She stopped by Dad. "I had my helmet," she said. Dad smiled and held up a water bottle. The water was cold on Sadie's tongue. The boy on the bike rode by again. He waved, and Sadie waved back. "Race you to the tree," he called.

Aubrey stood in the school computer lab. Her teacher said, "We will use the tablets today." Aubrey looked at the little shelf. The tablets sat in a row, one, two, three.

"Press the round button," said her teacher. Aubrey pressed it. The screen lit up. She pressed it again. The picture came back. "I made it wake up!" she said.

She tapped the drawing app. She picked blue. Then she picked yellow. The two colors mixed on the screen. Blue and yellow made green. "One, two, three colors!" said Aubrey. She drew a big green frog.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey set her tablet on the soft couch. Ben came running. He was going to sit down. "Stop!" said the teacher. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place." Aubrey picked it up fast. She carried it to the shelf. One, two, three tablets in a row again. "My frog can rest here," said Aubrey. She patted the shelf and skipped to the door.

Alexander wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. Mom was cooking noodles on the stove. The kitchen was warm and sunny. Alexander tiptoed closer to peek inside. The pot made a cloud of steam. It went up, up, up. Alexander put his hand near the steam. Mom caught his hand right away. "Steam is hot," she said. "It can burn. Stay back." Alexander stepped back three big steps. He held Mom's apron and stayed close.

From far away, he still could see the bubbles. They popped and jumped in the water. Alexander clapped his hands. He saw the steam touch the sunny window. The window got foggy and wet. One little bubble went pop very loud. Alexander laughed. Then he ran to get his pencil. He drew the bubbles and the steam cloud on paper.

Dad came in and looked at the drawing. "You drew the steam too!" Dad said. Alexander pointed at the foggy window. The steam mark was still there. Dad gave him a high five. "Can I watch again tomorrow?" Alexander asked. Mom smiled and said, "Yes, from three big steps back." Alexander nodded. He held up his drawing so everyone could see the big steam cloud.

Josephine ran into the library with her mama. She wanted the counting book with the big red cover. "It is here somewhere," she said. A lady sang in the story room. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. Josephine tapped her toes to it.

Then Josephine saw a door. A big number sat on the door. The number looked like half a circle, with a straight line on top. Josephine held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." She looked at the door. She looked at her hand. The same! "Five," she said. "That means five!"

"That is room five," said the librarian. "Your counting song is in there today." Josephine pushed the door open wide. Inside, kids sat on a rug. The lady kept singing. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Josephine sat down fast. She held up all ten fingers. "I know those words," she said. "Sing it again!"

Julia walked into the band room. She saw a big piano. The piano had white keys and black keys. "Can I play it?" she asked. Mr. Bean nodded. "Sit here," he said.

Julia put her finger on a white key. It made a soft sound. She pressed a black key. It made a new sound. She wanted to make a song, but she felt upset. The white keys and the black keys mixed together. Her tune went all jumpy.

Then Julia had an idea. She used only her right hand on the black keys. She skipped over the white ones. Press, press, press. The black keys made sounds that fit together. It sounded like raindrops on the roof. Julia played it again. Press, press, press.

"That is a nice tune," said Mr. Bean. "What is its name?" Julia thought hard. "Raindrops," she said. "Its name is Raindrops." She gave the piano a little hug. Then she played her song one more time.

Evan ran to Grandma's house. On the wall hung big letters. A, B, C, all the way to Z. "I know that one!" said Evan. "A!"

Then Grandma opened a book. Evan looked at the page. He saw a little round shape. It looked new. It looked shy, hiding in the corner.

"That is not A," said Evan. "That is a different letter!"

Grandma smiled. "That is the same A," she said. "It is a small letter."

"Big A, small a," said Evan. "Same letter!"

"Yes!" said Grandma. "Letters can be big or small."

Evan jumped up and down. He said the letter sound. "Ah, ah, ah!" A feather drifted off the shelf. It made Evan giggle.

"Now the B!" said Evan. He began to climb onto the chair.

"Wait, I will hold you," said Grandma. She held his hand.

"B!" said Evan. "Big B, small b, same letter, buh, buh, buh!"

Grandma laughed. "My smart boy."

Matthew held his mama's hand. The bookmobile was big and blue. It had wheels like a truck.

Inside, a lady smiled at Matthew. "Hello! Are you here for a library card?" Matthew nodded. He wanted a card so much. The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave him a little card with his name on it. Matthew picked a book about a red truck.

The next week, they went back. "Time to bring your book back," said Mama. Matthew hugged the book tight. "My book," he said. He did not want to let it go.

Mama pointed to a small door on the side of the bookmobile. "That is the return slot," she said. "We drop books there to bring them back." Matthew looked at the little door. He pushed his book in. The book slid down, out of sight.

Matthew felt his eyes get hot. Then he heard a soft thump inside. The lady opened the door from the inside. She held up his book! "Here it is, safe and sound," she said. Matthew laughed. The slot had taken the book to her!

He waved at the book. "Bye bye, truck book!" he sang. Then he picked a new one, about a big yellow bus. His smile was loose and happy all the way home.

Henry walked into his classroom. He held his daddy's hand. His bag felt heavy on his back. He saw blocks, paints, and a little red chair.

"I don't know anyone," said Henry. "Will school be fun alone?"

"Maybe you will find out," said Daddy with a smile.

At play time, Henry saw a boy by the window. The boy stood all alone. He held one green truck. Henry stood alone too, by the blocks. Two alone boys, and no friends yet.

Then Henry had an idea. He walked over to the truck boy. "My name is Henry," he said. "What is your name?"

"Sam," said the boy. "Want to touch my truck? It can carry the doctor car!"

"Two trucks," said Henry. "Yes!"

Henry and Sam pushed the trucks on the rug. Sam laughed when Henry made a loud truck noise. Henry laughed too. The teacher smiled at them.

At nap time, Henry waved at Sam. Sam waved back.

"Did school be fun alone?" Daddy asked later.

"No," said Henry. "It was fun with Sam!"

"Who is Sam?" asked Daddy.

"My friend," said Henry. "I asked him his name, and now we are friends forever!"

Henry showed Daddy his heavy bag. "Sam wants to come play on Saturday," he said. "Can he, can he?"

Daddy nodded. Henry cheered so loud that the doctor across the street looked up and waved. Henry waved back with both hands.

Art class was sunny and bright. Myles sat at the little table. He wanted to paint a boat, but he did not know how to make one.

Miss Ada gave him a paper with shapes. "Look at these," she said. There was a circle, a square, a triangle, and a rectangle. Myles touched the triangle. It felt pointy on his finger.

At snack time, Miss Ada cut Myles's sandwich. Each piece was a triangle. Myles counted the corners before he took a bite. One, two, three. "It has three corners," he said. His friend Poppy counted the sides of her piece. One, two, three. "Three sides too," she said.

Myles looked at his triangle sandwich. Then he looked at the paper. The triangle was pointy, just like a boat sail! He picked up his brush. He painted a square for the boat. He painted a triangle for the sail. He painted a big circle for the sun above it.

Miss Ada held the painting up. "What a fine sunny boat," she said. Myles hopped up from his chair. He clapped his hands. "I made a boat with shapes," he said. "My sail has three corners!" Poppy leaned over to look at the little white sail. "Mine will have three too," she said, picking up her brush.

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All clean," he said. "Now you can pick a sticker and a snack."

Grace chose a red sticker. Then she saw apple slices on a tray. Her tummy made a hungry sound. "Wash your hands first," said the nurse. "Use soap. Wash for twenty seconds. That is a long wash."

Grace ran to the little sink. She made bubbles fast. She rinsed fast. "Done!" she said. The nurse shook her head. "That was too quick," she said. Grace frowned. Twenty seconds felt so long. How would she know?

Then Grace remembered camp. At camp they sang a song at the sink. The nurse smiled. "Sing it," she said. Grace sang while she scrubbed. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She scrubbed and sang. The song helped her keep going. When the song ended, she was done.

"Twenty seconds!" said the nurse. Grace looked at her hands. The bubbles had washed away. Where did the sticky jam hide? It was gone now. "My hands feel fuzzy clean," Grace said. She took an apple slice and crunched it. "Can we sing the song at home too?" she asked. "Every time," said Mom. Grace skipped to the door, still humming.

Ibrahim ran to Maya's house. Maya had a tablet on the table. It was flat and shiny and blue. "Can we use the tablet?" Ibrahim asked Maya's grandpa.

"Yes, you may," said Grandpa. "Children ask a grown-up first. Good asking!" Grandpa tapped the button. The screen lit up like a little window. "Now you try," he said. Ibrahim pressed the button. The light came on! He laughed. His finger made the light.

"Open the drawing app," said Maya. Ibrahim tapped the green square. It opened with a pop. He drew a big sun. He drew a purple cat. The cat had three legs. "Silly cat!" said Maya. They laughed so hard the table shook.

Then the sun went down in the sky. Time to go home. Ibrahim pressed the button. The screen went dark. He slid the tablet into its soft case. "I put it away," he said. "Bye bye, purple cat." Grandpa smiled and waved. "Come learn more tomorrow," he called. "I will bring the cat a fourth leg!"

Jayden was at home with Mom. "We need a present for Grandma," Mom said. They put on shoes and went to the store.

The store was big and bright. Jayden held Mom's hand. He saw a thin ribbon. He saw a candle. He did not touch it. Mom said, "Only grown-ups touch candles." There was tea in a pot. Steam rose up. "That is hot," Mom said. Jayden looked with his eyes only.

Then Jayden saw a teddy bear. It was soft and brown. He let go of Mom's hand. He hugged the bear. When he looked up, Mom was not there. Jayden felt worried. He saw a lady at the checkout. She had a kind face. "I can't find my grown-up," Jayden said. "Let's find your mom," the lady said. She stood with him and called out.

Mom came fast. She hugged Jayden tight. "You told the store lady. That was good," Mom said. They bought the teddy bear for Grandma. At home, Grandma opened her present. She smiled and smiled. The ice cream cake began to melt, so everyone ate fast. Jayden licked his spoon. "Cold!" he said. Grandma laughed and held his hand.

Joshua went to his friend Mia's house. Mia had set up a little shop. It had a table and a door made from a cardboard box.

"I am the shopkeeper," said Mia. She stood behind the table. "You be the shopper."

Joshua did not know what to do. He just stood there. Mia waited. She did not pick anything for him.

Then Joshua picked up a toy apple. He gave Mia a button for money. Mia put the button in a cup. "Thank you," she said.

The shop had a little pot, too. Joshua asked, "Can I stir the pot?" Mia said yes. He stirred and stirred with a wooden spoon. Round and round went the soup.

After that, Joshua wanted a turn behind the table. They swapped. Now Mia was the shopper. Joshua waited for her to choose. She chose a toy banana. She gave him a leaf for money.

Then came a surprise. The leaf had a tiny ladybug on it. The ladybug crawled onto Joshua's hand. "Look!" he said.

They played shop all morning. The baby doll got tired and slept in a shoe box bed. Joshua stirred more soup. The door of the shop went open and shut, open and shut.

Then Joshua held out his hand. "Hello, ladybug," he said. "Do you want one apple?"

Charlotte was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Charlotte wanted to draw on it. She tapped the screen. The screen stayed dark. She tapped it again. Still dark.

Mia's mom came over. "Here is the charger," she said. "I will plug it into the wall." Charlotte watched. The charger went into the wall plug. The cord went into the tablet. A little picture came on the screen.

"Now you can try," said Mia's mom. Charlotte pressed the round button. The screen lit up. She had made that happen. She tapped the drawing app. She drew a big green hill. She drew a yellow sun on top. "I hear the sun," said Mia, laughing at the silly idea. Charlotte laughed too.

Soon the tablet said it was tired. Charlotte drew one last picture. It was a small cat. Then she gave the tablet to Mia's mom. "All done," said Charlotte. The tablet went on the shelf, nice and safe.

Sarah ran to the library play corner. There was a big red basket. There were tiny shirts in it. There were tiny socks in it. There was a tiny hat, too.

"Those are all clothes," said Miss Jo. "Clothes go in the basket."

Sarah grabbed the sock. She put it with the toy animals. She put it with the toy cars. Then she laughed and picked it up again. She dropped it in the basket with the shirt and the hat. All the clothes were together now.

Then Sarah found a book with a big picture of a puppy. The puppy had a rough, scratchy coat. Sarah could almost bend the soft page as she turned it.

"Again!" said Sarah. She pulled the clothes out one by one. Shirt. Sock. Hat. Then she sorted them all back in.

"Look, Miss Jo! Clothes!"

Miss Jo clapped. "Good sorting, Sarah."

Sarah hugged the book and grinned. "Puppy next!"

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big pencil and a paper. Max wanted to write his name all by himself. His brother could write his name, but Max was still young. Max tried to make an M. It came out wobbly and crooked. He tried again. It looked like a squiggle worm. Max frowned at the paper.

Grandma slid a new paper to him. It had the letters M A X on it. Each letter was made of little dots. "Trace the dots," said Grandma. Max put his pencil on the first dot. He drew a line to the next dot. Then the next one. The dots made an M. A real M. Max made a happy sound.

He traced the A and the X too. Then he found a dry spot on the paper. He wrote M A X with no dots. He looked at it. Was that his name? He held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma! I wrote Max!"

"You did," said Grandma. She clapped her hands. Max turned the paper over. There was a blank side. Maybe he could write it again. He picked up his pencil and began.

Nicholas was at Grandma's house. He wanted to play with his cousin Mia. But Mia sat with her bear and did not look up. Nicholas tried to hand her a block. Mia did not take it. He tried to sit next to her. She just hugged her bear.

"What do you like to play?" Nicholas asked. "House," said Mia. "How do we start?" he asked. Mia smiled big. "Just say let's pretend," she said. "Let's pretend we have a house!" said Nicholas. Mia jumped up. Now the game began!

Mia made the bear a bed from a box. Nicholas fed the bear a pretend bottle. The bear got grumpy and cried. "He needs a hug," said Mia. Nicholas counted one, two, three pats. The bear went to sleep. "Let's pretend the bear is a baby dog," said Nicholas. Mia laughed. "Woof, woof," she said.

Willow wanted to play firefighter at school. But her friend Sam said, "You can't be a firefighter. You are just Willow."

Willow frowned. Then she saw the dress-up box. She pulled out a big red hat. She put it on her head. "Look at me!" she said. "I am a firefighter now!"

Sam's eyes went wide. "A firefighter!" he said. "Help! My teddy bear is stuck up high!"

Willow ran over on her fast feet. She stood on her tiptoes. She reached up with both hands. She grabbed the teddy bear. "I got him!" she said. She held him close and patted his head. "There, there. You are safe now."

Sam clapped. "Thank you, firefighter!" Willow's hat stayed on her head. She felt very awake and very proud. "Firefighters keep teddy bears safe," she said.

Then Sam dug in the box too. He found a shiny silver hat. He put it on. "Now I am a firefighter too!" he said.

Two firefighters ran off to find the next teddy bear in trouble.

Gianna saw the blocks at the party. A boy named Sam grabbed them first. Gianna wanted them too. Her hand reached out, but she stopped.

"Can I have a turn?" she asked.

"You can have them next," said Sam.

Gianna waited. It was hard to wait. She watched Sam stack one block. Then another. The tower was thin and wobbly.

"Is waiting done yet?" she asked herself. "Not yet. I can wait a little more."

Sam looked at her sad face. "Do you want to help me?" he asked.

Gianna nodded. "We can build one big tower together," said Sam.

Gianna put a red block on top. Sam put a blue one. Back and forth they went. The tower grew tall.

"Wow," said Gianna. "One tower. Two kids. We both played!"

"Want to knock it down?" asked Sam.

They counted, "One, two, three!" and pushed it over together. The blocks went crash, and they both laughed and laughed.

Olivia went to the garden center with Gran. The sun was bright. "The sun can burn your nose," said Gran. So Olivia wore her big hat.

A truck beeped outside. It was very loud. Olivia held Gran's hand. Then it was quiet again.

Olivia picked little seeds. They were tiny and hard. They felt like small beads in her palm. They smelled like dirt. She found a pot and some brown soil. She made three little holes. She dropped the seeds in. She patted the soil down on top.

Gran checked the weather on her phone. "No rain today," she said. "The seeds need water to start growing." Olivia filled her small watering can. She tipped it over the pot. The soil turned dark and damp.

The next morning, Olivia ran to the pot. She saw only dirt. No sprout. Her tummy felt tight. "Where is my plant?" she asked. Gran patted her back. "Keep watering," said Gran. "A sprout does not come up right away."

So Olivia watered the pot each day. She watched and waited. On the fifth morning, something green poked up. It was small and curly. "It came!" Olivia shouted. Gran smiled and clapped. Olivia touched one soft leaf, very gently, with one finger.

Maverick sat on Grandma's soft rug. He held his toy pig. "Time for bed, pig," he said. He tucked the pig under a little blanket.

Then his cousin Poppy came in. "The pig is sick," said Poppy. "No," said Maverick. "The pig is just sleepy." They both looked at the pig.

"How about a sleepy pig with a sniffle?" said Poppy. "Yes!" said Maverick. He patted the pig gently. Poppy got a tiny toy cup. She held it to the pig's snout. "Drink this," she said. "It will help."

Grandma sat in her big chair nearby. The kettle whistled in the kitchen. The room smelled like warm bread. Grandma gave them each a small cup of milk.

"May the pig have a cookie?" asked Maverick. "That would be very polite," said Grandma, smiling. Poppy swung the pig in a happy dance. "All better!" she said.

Maverick hugged the pig tight. "Night night, pig," he whispered.

Emma was at the campsite with Dad. She wanted to make pancakes for the family. Dad said, "Let's pour the sugar from the bag." Emma tipped the bag. Sugar rushed out. Too much sugar went in the bowl!

Dad helped her pour it back. Then he held up a little cup. "This is a measuring cup," he said. "It helps us put in the right amount." Emma scooped sugar into the cup. She filled it up. She poured it in. Just right!

She did the same with a spoon. One small spoon of salt. Not too much, not too little. Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot grill. Emma stayed back from the sharp edge of the table and watched.

A green frog hopped near the tent. It sat very still. Emma whispered, "Hello, frog."

The pancakes were ready. Emma took a taste. "Yum!" she said. Dad gave her a big hug.

Anna had a little toy robot. It could puff out air. Anna pushed the button. Whirr! Wind touched her face. She heard the whirr with her ears. She felt the wind on her cheeks.

Then Anna saw dust in the air. Some dust flew toward her eyes. She blinked fast. The dust landed on her eyelashes. It did not go in her eyes.

Anna ran to Mama. "What are these little hairs?" she asked. Mama said, "Those are your eyelashes." Anna blinked again. "Eyelashes stopped the dust!" she said. "Did the dust go in?" asked Mama. "No! My eyelashes caught it."

Anna sniffed a snack with her nose. Cookies! She touched one. It was warm. She took a little bite. Yum! "My eyes are happy," said Anna. "No dust, no sad eyes, no tears." Then she pressed the robot button one more time. Whirr, blink, blink!

Jake wanted to play house with his gray robot toy. His friend Mia came into the playroom. "I want to be the parent," said Mia. "I want to be the parent too," said Jake. They both held the same toy pot. Neither one would let go.

Then Mia had an idea. "We can pick roles," she said. "I will be the parent now. You can be the baby." Jake sat in the little chair like a baby. Mia fed him a pretend bottle. Then Mia patted the robot. "You are the baby's robot," she said.

After that, Mia said, "Now let's switch. You be the parent." Jake stood up tall. He rocked the robot in his arms. He gave the robot a soft blanket. "Time for bed," Jake said in a big parent voice. Mia giggled and clapped her hands.

Then they put all the toys away together. The pot went back on the shelf. The blanket went in the basket. "Same game tomorrow?" asked Mia. Jake nodded and hugged his robot. "You can be the parent first," he said.

Austin went to the playground with his dad. The sun was hot on his face. He found a big slide and a small slide. He went down the small one. Then he went down the big one. "You were fast on that one," said Dad. Austin saw a boy going slow on a little toy horse. The boy rocked back and forth, back and forth.

Then Austin saw a puddle. He did not go alone. Dad stood right there. Austin jumped in the puddle. Splash! His socks got wet. The water was cold on his toes.

"My socks are all wet," said Austin.

"Wet and dry are opposites," said Dad. He pulled dry socks from the bag. The wet socks went in. The dry socks went on. Austin touched his toes. They were warm again. "Fast, fast, fast," he said, and ran to the swings.

Nova went to her friend Milo's house. It was early, right after breakfast. In the playroom, Milo had a big cardboard box.

"I want it to be a car," said Milo. "Vroom, vroom!"

"No, a boat," said Nova. "Row, row!"

They both pulled the box. It tipped over. They both sat down hard.

Milo's mom came in. "Maybe you can take turns," she said.

First it was a car. Milo sat in the box. Nova pushed it a little. "Beep beep!" she said. Then Nova crawled in too. They drove to the kitchen for pretend gas.

Then it was a boat. Nova rowed with a wooden spoon. Milo held a teddy bear. "Teddy is sleepy," said Milo. They rocked the box slow and soft. Teddy closed his eyes.

Then Nova had an idea. "Now let's make it a house," she said. They turned the box on its side. It had a door and a little window.

Teddy peeked out of the window. "Hello!" said Nova, in a tiny bear voice.

The doorbell rang. It was the real mail truck. Nova gasped. "A bus for teddy!" she said. She waved at the window.

"Tomorrow," said Milo, "our box can be a rocket."

"Yes," said Nova. "Zoom, zoom!"

A puppet show was coming to daycare. Liam was so excited. His tummy felt jumpy. His feet wanted to bounce. He bounced and bounced. He wanted to shout, too.

"Look at me!" Liam shouted. He bumped the toy box. Blocks fell out with a noisy crash. Mia began to cry. She felt sad. Liam felt bad. Teacher Amy knelt down. "It's okay," she said softly. She helped Mia pat the blocks back into the box. Liam helped too.

"Waiting is hard," said Teacher Amy. "When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout." Liam sat on his hands. He took a big breath. He patted his knees, slow and slow. His feet got still.

The puppet show began. A red dragon danced! Liam clapped and laughed. The dragon landed right on his lap. "Hello, dragon," said Liam.

Emile ran into art class. He wanted to draw a big sun today. He sat down all alone at the little table. He picked up his yellow crayon. First he drew the sun's rays. Those were easy lines. But the round part was hard. His circle came out wobbly. It looked like a squished egg. He tried again. It was still wobbly. Emile frowned at his paper.

Then he saw Mia. She had a round cup on her paper. She was drawing all around the bottom of it. She lifted the cup up. "Look, a circle!" she said. Emile jumped up. "I want to try that!"

He found a cup too. He held it down on his paper. He drew all around the bottom. He lifted the cup away. There it was, a perfect circle! Emile laughed out loud. He colored the circle yellow. Now his sun had a good round face. He drew a square house next to it. He drew a triangle roof on top. He drew a rectangle door.

"Teacher, look!" said Emile. The teacher took a photo of the sun with her phone. "What a big beautiful sun," she said. "I will play suns all day," said Emile. He grabbed another cup and drew one more circle.

Eva went to the playground with her grandma. The sun was hot on the slide. The bench in the shade was cold. Eva touched the bench with one finger. "Cold," she said. She stayed close to grandma the whole time.

At the picnic table, Eva saw something shiny. It was a little box with red and white dots inside. The dots looked like candy. Eva wanted to touch them. She counted, "One, two, three dots." Then she remembered. She did not touch. "Grandma, come and see," she called.

Grandma came right away. She looked at the dots. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine," grandma said. "Even if it looks like candy." Grandma picked up the box and put it high in her bag. Eva went back to the slide. She slid down, one, two, three times. "Good watching, Eva," said grandma. Eva held grandma's hand all the way home.

Zoe sat at the paint table. She wanted to make a green leaf for her tree painting. Green was her favourite colour of all.

She put yellow paint on her brush. Then she put blue on the same brush. She brushed it on the paper. But the green came out muddy and brown. "Oh no," said Zoe. "My leaf looks like mud."

Her friend Mia looked over. "Rinse your brush," Mia said. Zoe dipped her brush in the water cup. She swished it around. The water turned grey. She wiped the brush on a paper towel.

Now Zoe put yellow on the clean brush. Then she put blue. She brushed the paper. Bright green! Like a magic dragon, green and shiny. Zoe laughed and painted a big green leaf, then another, then ten more.

"Look," said Zoe politely to her teacher. "My tree has leaves." The teacher smiled. Zoe held up her brush. "Next, red and yellow," she said. "I will make dragon fire."

Sebastian stood in the backyard. He had a red beanbag. He wanted to throw it into the hoop. The hoop lay on the grass like a circle. He threw the beanbag. It landed far away in the flowers.

Sebastian frowned. He tried again. The beanbag missed the circle again. "I can't do it," he said. His dad was busy raking leaves nearby. "Try one more time," said Dad, soft and kind.

Sebastian picked up the beanbag. He threw it again. It missed. He tried again. And again. Then the beanbag went up, up, and down. It landed right inside the hoop. Sebastian jumped. "It went in!" he said.

Then Dad rolled a big blue ball to him. Sebastian held out both hands. The ball bounced off his fingers. Dad rolled it again. Sebastian missed. But he kept trying, again and again. Soon the ball came right into his arms. He held it tight with both hands. "Look, Dad!" he called. "I caught it!"

Ivy went to the playground on a summer day. She wanted to slide ten times. She loved the slide.

A boy named Sam stood at the bottom. He was counting the swings. "One, two, four," said Sam. His big sister shook her head. "Four does not come next," she said. "The counting words always go in the same order. One, two, three, four." Sam tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He laughed and clapped.

Ivy was careful as she climbed the slide ladder. She slid down fast. "One!" she said. She slid again. "Two!" She slid and slid. "Three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine..." Her juice cup tipped over. It did not spill, because her mama had closed the lid tight. Ivy slid one more time. "Ten!" she called. "Ten slides!" Sam cheered from the swings. "Now me!" he said. "One, two, three, four..."

Olivier went to the garden with Papa. He had tiny carrot seeds in his hand. He wanted to grow big carrots for a snack.

Olivier made a little hole. He dropped a seed in. He patted the soft brown soil on top. "Grow, little seed," he said. Papa gave him a cookie to eat while they waited and watered.

Days went by. Green leaves popped up. But one leaf was not a carrot. "Can I pull it out?" Olivier asked. Papa nodded. Olivier pulled. Out came a weed with long stringy tails. He stared. "What are those wiggly bits?"

"Roots," said Papa. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Olivier looked down at his carrots. "Your roots are under there," he said. He watered the soil. Maybe the roots could feel the wet. A pink worm wiggled by his shoe. Olivier waved. "Hello, worm. Say hi to my roots."

Eliana wanted Grandma to read the purple book. But there were so many books. "Which one is mine?" she asked. Grandma pointed to a stack. "One has your name inside," she said.

Eliana opened a book. She turned the pages the right way, front to back. On the first page she saw little black marks. "What are those?" she asked. "Those are words," said Grandma. "They say your name." Eliana looked hard. E, then L, then more letters. "Eliana," she read. Then she saw her name on a birthday card on the table. E, then L, then the same letters again. Same letters, same order, both times!

A tiny ladybug began to crawl across the page. It stopped right on the E. "Even the ladybug likes my name," said Eliana. She ran to the big map on the wall. "Does the map say Eliana too?" Grandma laughed. "No, the map says places." So Eliana pointed to the purple book. "Read this one, Grandma. It has words too." Grandma opened it, and Eliana turned the very first page.

Isaac sat in the waiting room with his father. He held his favorite blue truck. Today Isaac was getting a shot. His tummy felt funny about it.

A doctor came in. A tube hung around her neck. "What is that?" Isaac asked. "A stethoscope," said the doctor. "It listens to your heart beating." She put the little ends in Isaac's ears. She put the other end on his chest. Thump, thump! Isaac heard his own heart. It beat fast, like a drum. He took a big breath. The sound got calm and slow.

Then it was shot time. Isaac squeezed his truck. His father held his hand. Quick poke, one tear, all done. "All done, brave boy," said the doctor. She put a bandage on his arm. Isaac pressed his hand to his chest. He could feel his heart go thump, thump. "Still beating," he told his truck. His father picked him up and they walked out. "Ice cream next," his father said.

Elena looked out the window and gasped. Snow! Lots and lots of snow! "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day!" Elena put on her boots and her red coat. She ran out to the sidewalk.

Then her boot slid sideways. Whoosh! Elena sat down in the snow. She felt grumpy. She stood up and tried again. She ran, and she fell again. "Why do I keep falling?" she asked. Mama smiled. "The ice is slippery," she said. "Try walking slowly."

Elena took one small step. Then another small step. She did not fall! Slow steps, slow steps, all the way down the street. She let her mittens wave at Mama. At the corner, Dad was scraping ice with a hammer, tap, tap, tap. "Look at me, Dad!" Elena called. "Slow and careful, slow and careful!" She walked all the way to him without one single fall.

Matteo put on his new shoes. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. He held Mama's hand all the way.

The classroom was big. Many children ran and played. Matteo hid behind Mama's coat. His foot did not want to move.

A lady with a red sweater came near. "Hello," she said. "I am Miss Ana. I am your teacher. A teacher looks after the children in the class. I help them too."

Matteo peeked out. "Miss Ana?" he said, very small. "Yes, that is me," she said. She waited. She did not rush him.

Matteo let go of the coat. He took one step. Then another. "Hello, Miss Ana," he said. Miss Ana smiled. "Would you like to see the blocks?" Matteo nodded, and he walked with her to the blocks.

Jasper had a special red car. He took it to the school playground. Now the car was gone. "Where is my car?" Jasper said. His teacher Miss Ana came close. "We will find it," she said. "Don't worry."

Jasper looked and looked. One look at the sandbox. No car. Two looks at the slide. No car. Three looks at the climbing bars. No car.

Then Jasper saw the little playhouse. It had a small couch and a small bed inside. The car had wheels. Wheels can roll. Jasper got down low. He peeked under the small couch. There it was! The red car had rolled under the couch. Jasper reached in and grabbed it.

Miss Ana smiled. Jasper held the car up high. "Found you!" he said. Then he put a green leaf on top of it, like a little blanket. "Now you can rest."

William wanted the fast red car. Ben had it. Maya wanted it too. Teacher Sam said, "Make a line." William stood by the door. Maya stood behind him. Ben stood behind Maya. "A line means staying in your place until it is your turn," said Sam. William wiggled his feet. He waited. He watched Ben roll the car. Zoom, zoom. Then Maya got her turn. She rolled it fast to the wall. Then it was William's turn. He held the red car. He rolled it far. The car went under the shelf. "I will get it," said Sam. She shut the little door and reached in. She gave the car back. Then it was Ben's turn again. William sat down to wait. Soon Sam called, "Time to wash hands for dinner." William stood up. He said, "My turn again tomorrow!" Ben nodded. "Yes, your turn," said Ben. Then they all ran to wash hands.

Florence ran into the backyard. Grandma followed with a pink hat for her.

"Let's play a guessing game," said Grandma. "You have five senses. Guess one!"

" Eyes!" said Florence. She pointed at her eyes.

"Good. Eyes see," said Grandma. "Now look at the flowers."

Florence looked. She saw a pink rose. "My eyes see the rose!" she said.

Then Florence looked up at the sky. She wanted to see the sun. She began to turn her face up to it.

"Stop," said Grandma. She put her hand over Florence's eyes. "Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes."

Florence blinked. "Okay," she said. "I will not look."

She pointed at her ears. "Ears hear!" she said. Grandma clapped. Florence heard the clap.

"Nose smells," said Florence. She sniffed the rose. "Mmm!"

Then a bee buzzed by. Florence touched a fuzzy leaf. "Hands feel the leaf!" she said.

"One more," said Grandma. "Which body part is left?"

Florence thought. Then she giggled and pointed at her mouth. "Mouth tastes! That was fun!"

Grandma laughed. "All five senses. Now let's go find a snack for that tasting mouth."

Connor ran to the big sandbox at the playground. He had the only blue truck there. He pushed it up and down the sand. "Vroom," he said.

Then Mia came. She sat down next to him. She had no truck at all. She watched Connor play. Her hands sat still in the sand.

Connor stopped his truck. He looked at Mia. Then he looked at his truck. He held it out. "You can use it too," he said. "That is sharing."

Mia smiled big. "Thank you," she said. She took the truck and made a long road in the sand. Connor patted the sand flat with his hands. It was hard work, and he patted it again and again.

Then Mia gave the truck back. "Now you," she said. Connor drove it over the new road. One turn for him. One turn for her. The sun was warm. The sand smelled like summer.

Mia asked, "Can we do this again tomorrow?" Connor nodded. "Yes. Come early," he said. "I will bring my truck and two shovels."

Sophie ran to the soccer field with her team. The coach had a red cone in her hand. "Time to warm up!" said Coach. "What is warm up?" Sophie asked. "We run and we stretch first," said Coach.

Sophie wanted to kick the ball right away. She looked at the gray sky and stomped her little foot. "But I want to play now," she said. Coach smiled a soft smile. "Come run with us, Sophie."

Sophie ran around the cone with her friends. They reached up high and touched their toes. Her legs felt fast and ready. Grandpa waved from the bench by the tree.

The game began. Sophie ran after the ball. Her feet felt quick and strong. She kicked the ball to her friend Mia. Mia kicked it into the net. The team cheered, but nobody fell down or had to cry. Grandpa clapped his hands. Sophie ran to him and hugged his knees. "Grandpa, we warmed up first," she said. "And then we played our best game!"

Olivier sat in the doctor's waiting room. He was not late. Mommy had brought him on time. He looked at a picture of a plane on the wall with his eyes. He heard music playing with his ears.

Then the doctor's office door opened. Behind it, a big machine started to hum. It got very loud. Olivier did not like the loud sound. He covered his ears with his hands. The loud sound got quieter. He took his hands away. It was loud again. He put his hands back. Quiet again.

"Loud, quiet, loud, quiet," said Olivier.

"You found a trick," said Mommy with a smile.

Soon the big machine stopped. The waiting room was calm. The nurse called them in. "Open your mouth," said the doctor. Olivier stuck out his tongue. He touched a sticker with his finger. It felt bumpy. It smelled like strawberries.

The doctor gave him a paper to draw on. Olivier drew a plane and two big hands over two little ears.

Zayn was four. He was going on a big trip. The whole family rode a ferry across the water. Zayn held the rail with both hands. The wind made his hair flap. The ferry went up and down on the waves. "Look, Mama," said Zayn. "The boat makes the water splash!" The waves rolled and rolled behind them.

On the ferry there was a little cafe. Papa stirred sugar into his tea with a spoon. Zayn drank his milk. Then he played with a tiny packet. Inside was one seed, all alone. "How did a seed get in here?" asked Zayn. Nobody knew. Mama put the seed in her pocket, safe.

At the beach, Zayn ran in the sand. His shoes came off. His feet got sandy and stinky. He giggled and put his shoes back on. Then it was time to go home.

The next day, Mama said, "We unpack our bags now." Zayn opened his little bag. He pulled out his shirt. He pulled out his socks. Then he shook his shoes. Sand fell out onto the floor. "The beach is still in my shoes!" he laughed. Papa laughed too. Zayn put his shirt in the drawer. He put the socks in the basket. The shoes went by the door. His bag was empty at last. "All done," said Zayn, and he clapped his hands.

Hannah stood in the big school gym. Her teacher put a small beanbag in her hand. "Throw it in the hoop," said Teacher Joe. Hannah threw it. The beanbag flew past the hoop and landed on the floor. "Oh well," said Hannah. She tried again. This time she threw it slowly. The beanbag went in the hoop. "I did it!" said Hannah.

Then Teacher Joe rolled a big ball to her. The ball hit her legs and stopped. "Why did the ball fall down?" Hannah asked. "My hands were in my pockets." Teacher Joe smiled. "Try holding your arms out," he said. "Keep your hands open."

The ball rolled to Hannah again. Her arms were out. Her hands were open. The big ball went right into her hands. "I caught it!" she shouted. Her friend Ben clapped. "Now me," said Ben. He held his arms out too.

Asher sat at the big craft table at the library. He wanted to make a butterfly. But his butterfly had only one wing, and it looked sad.

Asher painted one wing with red paint. He painted dots too. His tummy felt hungry, but he wanted to finish first. The paint was wet and shiny.

Then Asher folded the paper in half. He pressed it down with his hands. He did not scratch the paint. He opened the paper slowly.

"Wow!" said Asher. The paint had printed on the other half. Now the butterfly had two wings. The wings matched, red with dots on both sides.

"Look, look!" Asher said. A girl named Mia came over. Her butterfly had one wing too. Her face looked sad like his had.

"Fold it," said Asher. "Fold it while the paint is wet." Mia folded her paper. She opened it. Two blue wings, both the same!

"Now we each have a butterfly," said Mia. The librarian smiled and hung them by the window. The sun made the red and blue wings shine like a rainbow.

"Two wings are better than one," said Asher. He clapped his painty hands together.

William sat in his little car seat. "Big world, little car," said Daddy. William looked out the window. He saw one cow. Then two horses. Then a dog on a porch. William tapped the glass. The dog wagged its tail. Tap, tap, wag, wag. William laughed. "Big world, little car," he said.

William had an itchy tag in his shirt. Daddy reached back and fixed it. "All soft now," said Daddy. William cuddled his toy bear. The bear did not fall. William held him tight.

Soon the car stopped. "We are at the library," said Daddy. "I want a book with animals," said William. "Animal books live together on one shelf," said the librarian. "The books are in groups, so we can find them." She pointed. There was a shelf of animal books. There was a shelf of toy books. There was a shelf of food books.

William picked a big book. It had a cow on it. It had a horse on it. It even had the dog. Daddy put the book on the table. William sat on the little chair and turned the pages.

At home, Daddy read to William. "One cow," said Daddy. "Two horses," said William. "Big world, little book," said Daddy. William hugged his bear and tapped the page. The cow in the picture stood still, but William waved anyway. "Hello, cow," he said.

Evelyn ran to the park with Dad. She carried her blue bunny in her arms. First they went down the slide. Then they played in the sand. Then they sat on the big rock for a snack.

After the snack, Evelyn looked for bunny. Bunny was gone! She wanted to run far away to look. She took one step, then two steps, then three steps.

Then she stopped. "Dad!" she called. "Bunny is lost. Come look with me." Dad took her hand. "Good job telling me," he said.

They looked together. One, the slide. Two, the sand. Three, the big rock. Evelyn peeked behind the rock. There sat bunny, all sandy and safe.

Evelyn hugged bunny tight. "No more running off alone," she said. Dad smiled. "We find things together."

Then Evelyn put bunny in her pocket, so bunny could not fall. They walked home, counting the trees. One, two, three. Bunny peeked out and saw the blue sky.

Noah ran to soccer practice. Coach Sam had a big red ball. All the kids wanted it. Noah got there first. He hugged the ball tight.

"My turn," said Noah. He held it all to himself. His friend Leo had no ball at all. Leo sat on the grass. His face looked sad. Noah looked at Leo. Then he looked at the big red ball. He wanted to kick it, but a kick needs two friends.

Noah rolled the ball to Leo. "You can use it too," said Noah. "This is sharing." Leo smiled big. Leo kicked the ball back. Noah kicked it to Leo again. The ball went back and forth, back and forth.

Soon more kids came over. They made a line for turns. Noah waited. He did not grab. When his turn came, Coach Sam gave him a thumbs up. Noah laughed and kicked the ball far. It flew like a bird over the green grass.

After practice, Mom came to get Noah. She held his hand. "I like playing with Leo," said Noah. Mom kissed his head. The sun went down slowly, like an ocean of orange light in the sky. "Can we come back tomorrow?" asked Noah. Mom said, "Yes, we can."

Snow fell all night. Rehmat looked out the kitchen window. "No school today," said Mama. "A snow day!" Rehmat ate her toast. She was hungry for more. Mama gave her a second slice.

Then Rehmat saw Papa by the door. He had a big shovel. He pushed the snow off the path. Swipe, swipe, swipe. Rehmat put on her boots. "Can I help too?" she asked. Papa gave her a small shovel. She pushed one little pile of snow. Then another pile. Then one more. One, two, three.

The path turned brown and clear. Papa said, "Now we can walk without slipping." Just then, the mail carrier came up the path. His boots went tap, tap, tap on the clear ground. He did not slip one bit. "Is that for us?" Rehmat asked. He handed her a small package. Inside was a tiny toy sled. Rehmat laughed and held it up high. "Snow again tomorrow, please!" she said.

Charles sat at the dinner table. He wanted the blueberry cake. Mama put it on the shelf. "You can have cake later," she said.

Charles ate his carrots. Then he asked, "Is it later yet?"

"Not yet," said Mama. "Eat your rice first."

Charles ate his rice. He picked up his spoon. He looked at the shelf. "Is it later now?"

Daddy smiled. "Later means some time after now," he said. "Not right away."

Charles wiggled his toe under the table. He took a tiny bite of bread. He looked at the window. The sky turned pink. His plate was empty.

"Now?" he asked.

"Yes, now it is later," said Mama.

She cut a small piece of cake. Charles took a bite. It was sweet and good.

"Tomorrow we can have cake again," said Daddy.

"What is tomorrow?" asked Charles.

"It is the day after today," said Daddy. "Yesterday we had no cake. Today we have cake."

Charles licked his fork. "I like today," he said. Mama laughed and kissed his head.

Raphael was playing house at daycare. He stirred a big red pot. The pot had a thick blue sock inside. "This is soup," he said. His friend Mia had a baby doll. Mia ran fast and the doll fell down. Boom. The doll hit the floor. Mia began to cry. "The baby fell!" she said. Raphael stopped stirring. He looked at the doll. Would the doll cry too? He waited. The doll did not cry. The doll did not feel the bump at all. Dolls cannot really feel, he thought. But maybe the doll could feel a hug, just pretend.

Raphael picked up the doll. "Here comes a hug," he said. He held the doll close. He patted the doll's back, soft and slow. Then he made a little voice. "I am okay now," the doll said. Mia wiped her eyes. She looked at the doll. "Baby is fine?" she asked. "Baby is fine," said Raphael. He gave the doll to Mia. Mia hugged the doll too. Then she hugged Raphael.

"Thank you," said Mia. Raphael ran back to his pot. He took out the thick sock. He put it on the doll's foot. One sock on, one foot bare. "Baby needs a shoe," said Raphael. Mia laughed. She got a small cup. She fed the doll pretend soup, spoon by spoon. The doll got a full tummy, just pretend. Outside the window, a bird went hop, hop, hop. Raphael pointed at it. "Look," he said. "Maybe the bird wants soup too."

David woke up and saw white everywhere. The sky was gray and soft. "No school today," said Mom. "Snow day!"

David wanted to sled. But the big hill was far away. The road was too deep with snow.

They stood at the window. They waited. David watched and watched.

Then a big truck came. It had a big scoop in front. Mom said, "Look, a snowplow." The snowplow pushed the snow off the road. The road turned black and clear.

"Now we can drive," said Mom.

They drove to the hill. David went down, down, down. He climbed up again. He was careful on the icy step.

"Daddy, watch me!" he called.

Daddy waved. David zoomed down like a little fish in the sea, fast and free.

Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. She saw the big round swing. She wanted to swing high.

Three kids were playing a game near the slide. It was a waiting game. They counted to ten. Then the next kid slid down. Elizabeth asked to play too. A boy named Sam said yes.

Sam slid down first. Then it was Elizabeth's turn. But Sam ran back up fast. "My turn again," he said. The other kids shook their heads. "That is not fair," one girl said. They all stopped playing. They sat on the bench.

Sam looked at the bench. He came back down. "Okay," he said. "We all take turns." The kids came back. Elizabeth found her spot in the line. She counted to ten out loud. Then she slid down, fast and far. "Yay!" she said.

After the game, Dad had a snack ready. It was a little round cake. Elizabeth broke it in two. She gave half to Sam. "Thank you," he said. Then they ran back to the slide, hand in hand.

Emily sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. She looked out the window. She saw a cow. "A cow is an animal," said Mommy. Then Emily saw a dog. The dog was an animal too. At the red light, a little feather floated down. It landed on the car window. "Mommy, look! A soft little feather."

"Who lost it?" asked Emily. "A bird," said Mommy. "Birds have feathers." Emily gasped. "A bird lost its feather! Can we find the bird?" "The bird flew away," said Mommy. "But the feather can be yours." Emily held the feather. It was soft and gray. She tickled her own nose. "Ah-choo!" she said, and they both laughed.

At the next stop, Emily saw a spider on a leaf. "Hello, spider," she said. "Do you have feathers? No, no. You are not a bird." The car went on. Emily saw a toy store with a big teddy bear. She saw a food truck with bananas. Then a small bird flew right by the window. "It's a bird!" said Emily. She held up her feather and waved it. The bird flapped its wings and flew over the trees. Emily kept the feather safe in her little pocket. "Good night, bird," she whispered. "Thanks for my soft gray feather."

Grandpa was coming on the train. Bennett wanted to see the train first. He stood on his toes at the platform. He leaned out far to look. Dad held his hand. "Stand back from the edge," said Dad. "We wait until the train stops." Bennett stepped back behind the yellow line. The big train came in. It stopped. The doors opened. Grandpa stepped out with his bag. "Bennett!" he said. They hugged for a long time.

Grandpa said, "Let us try the market today." At the market, they smelled fresh bread. Bennett helped Grandpa pick red apples. They saw a little turtle in a tank. The turtle was slow. Bennett waved at it. Grandpa bought bread, apples, and one small toy turtle for Bennett. They walked home holding hands. "Train tomorrow too?" asked Bennett. "Yes," laughed Grandpa.

It was Ayla's first day of school. She ran into the big cafeteria. It had long tables and lots of chairs. She counted them. "One, two, three tables!" she said. Then her tummy made a sound. Rumble, rumble. Ayla was hungry. She wanted lunch right now.

"I want to eat," she told her teacher. "We eat at snack time," said the teacher. "Snack time comes after our morning song." So Ayla waited. She sang the morning song. She painted a cat. She built a tower. One block, two blocks, three blocks, four! Then the bell rang. "Snack time!" everyone shouted.

The class walked to the cafeteria. Ayla sat at table one. She opened her bag. Inside was a surprise. A cookie shaped like a star! "I know that star," she said with a big smile. She took a bite. Her tummy felt happy. "Can we come back for lunch?" she asked. "Yes," said the teacher. "A school day has a time for lunch too." Ayla grinned. "I love school days."

Sarah sat at the big table. She had paper and paints. Mom sat next to her. Sarah dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She painted a big sun. Then she painted a green garden. The garden had little flowers in it.

Sarah wanted to hold her picture up. She grabbed the paper with her hand. Her fingers pressed on the sun. "Oh no," said Sarah. The yellow sun had a smudge. It looked smeary and yucky. Sarah's lip went down. "My sun is messy," she said.

Mom looked at the paper. "The paint was still wet," said Mom. "Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries." Sarah touched the paper again, very gently. Her finger came away yellow. She saw the wet smear on her skin.

"Let's make a new sun," said Mom. Sarah painted a new sun. This time she put her hands in her lap. She looked at the paint. It was shiny and wet. She waited. She sang a little song while she waited. The paint got dull and dry.

Then Sarah picked up the paper. The sun was clean. No smudge at all. The garden was dry too. "I waited!" said Sarah. Mom clapped her hands. "Let's put it on the wall," said Mom. Sarah carried her picture slowly, with two careful hands.

Billie waited at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day, so Billie wore her sun hat. Then gray clouds came. "Is it going to rain?" Billie asked. "Yes," said her mother. She opened a big umbrella.

Rain went tap, tap, tap on top. Billie held her mother's hand. Then the rain stopped. The wind began to blow. "Look at the trees!" said Billie. The trees swayed back and forth. Leaves blew all around the bus stop.

Billie let go of the umbrella handle. She chased a red leaf. It blew left. It blew right. She chased it across the yard. The leaf went round and round. Billie laughed and laughed. Her hat blew off too! She grabbed her hat and held it tight.

"Why do the leaves run away?" Billie asked. "The wind pushes them," said her mother. Billie caught the red leaf at last. She held it up high. Just then snow began to fall. Billie's mother zipped her thick coat up to her chin. "The bus is coming!" said Billie. She waved her leaf at the big yellow bus.

Maeve sat on the big city bus. She held Mama's hand. "My bunny is gone," said Maeve.

Mama looked under the seat. Maeve looked in her bag. No bunny. The bus went bounce, bounce, bounce. Maeve began to cry a little.

"Think," said Mama. "Where did you see bunny last?"

Maeve thought hard. "I had bunny at the window!" she said. "I showed bunny the cars."

Maeve looked at the window seat. There was bunny, sitting straight up by the glass. The sun was on her soft ears.

"Bunny was watching the cars," said Maeve. She gave bunny a big hug.

"You found her," said Mama.

"Yes! I remembered the last place," said Maeve. She waved bunny's paw at a red car going by. Bunny caught the light on her nose, and Maeve giggled all the way home.

Ryan got to daycare and looked out the window. Gray clouds sat over the playground. Little bits of snow began to fall. Miss Amy wore her red sweater and rang the bell.

"Let's count the blocks," said Miss Amy. Ryan counted with his friends. "One, two, three." Then more blocks. "Four, five, six." The pile grew. "Seven, eight, nine." Miss Amy put down one more block. "Ten!"

Ryan wanted to write ten on his paper. He made a nine. That was not ten. He made a one. That was not ten either. He frowned at his paper.

Then he saw the big number card on the wall. Ten had two numbers. There was a 1 first. Then a 0. Ryan wrote a 1. He wrote a 0 right after it. "I made ten!" he said.

Miss Amy smiled. Ryan held up his paper. Outside, the snow fell on the swings.

Lily woke up on her mat. The room was dark and quiet. "Is it night?" she whispered. She wanted her mommy.

Miss Kay came over. She opened the curtain. The sun came in. It was bright. "It is day," said Miss Kay. "Day and night are opposites." Lily looked out. One sun, one big blue sky. Not night at all. She felt better.

It was time to go outside. Lily put on her shoes. She found her cubby. It had a letter L on it. "L is for Lily," she said. Outside, the sun felt hot on her hands. Then she sat in the shade. The shade felt cold. "Hot sun, cold shade," she said.

Lily wanted the big swing. But Ben was on it. He went fast, fast, fast. Lily waited on the small swing. She went slow, slow, slow. Then she saw a snail on the wall. Its trail was slimy. "Yuck," she said, and she wiped her hand on her dress. Ben jumped off the big swing. "Your turn, Lily!" he did shout. Lily ran. One, two, three, she climbed up. "Push me slow," she said. "Then push me fast."

Madison went to the library with her mom. She found a box of toy monkeys. There were ten little monkeys in the box. Madison counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten monkeys sat on the table.

Then she heard a song. A boy was singing in the corner. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Madison picked five monkeys. She put them on a book about a park. She sang too. "One fell off and bumped his head." She tipped one monkey over. Now she saw four monkeys standing. "Where did one go?" she asked. "It fell down," she said. She sang again. One more monkey fell. Now there were three.

Madison stopped and had to think. Each time she sang, one monkey fell. Each time, the number got one smaller. Three monkeys, then two, then one. She sang the last verse. The last monkey fell. Zero monkeys were standing. All five were lying down. "It gets one smaller each time," she whispered.

She set the five monkeys up again. She sang the song again from the start. One monkey fell, then another. She laughed at the pile. A library helper walked by. "That song is my favorite too," the helper said. Madison pointed at her monkeys. "Watch," she said. "One falls, and one less is left." She pushed the next monkey over.

Charlotte was playing blocks with her brother Sam. Grandma came in with a small bag. "This is for you, Charlotte," she said.

Inside was a new cup. It had a yellow bee on it. Charlotte held it up high. "My bee cup!" she said. Grandma smiled and went to paint at her table.

Sam looked at the cup too. Charlotte let him hold it. "Your turn," she said. "Now my turn." They took turns, back and forth. Then Grandma fell asleep in her chair. She was tired.

Charlotte looked at Grandma. She had not said her words yet. She ran back to the chair. She tapped Grandma's hand softly. Grandma opened her eyes.

"Thank you for my cup, Grandma," said Charlotte.

Grandma hugged her tight. "You are welcome, sweet girl," she said. Charlotte held her bee cup all the way to snack time.

Sarah stood in the bathroom. She wanted to wash her hands all by herself. "Can I do it?" she asked her dad. "Yes," said Dad. "I will turn the water for you."

Dad turned the red tap a tiny bit. The water ran warm. Dad held his own hand under it first. "Warm is good," he said. "Hot water can hurt. Only a grown-up touches the taps." Sarah watched the warm water. She put her hands in. The soap got bubbly. She rubbed and rubbed.

Then they heard a noise outside. A big truck went by. "The park!" said Sarah. She could see the swings from the window. "Can we go?" "Yes," said Dad. They walked to the door. Sarah reached up. She held her dad's hand. The road was in front of them. Sarah stopped at the edge. They looked left. They looked right. Then they walked across together.

At the park, Sarah ran to the swing. "I held your hand on the road," she said. Dad smiled. "You did," he said. "Now swing high, Sarah!" Sarah pumped her legs. The swing went up and up. "Watch me, Dad!" she called.

Emilia woke up from her nap. She was not asleep anymore. She wanted a bath right away.

Mama was in the kitchen. She filled a cup with water for Emilia to drink. Emilia tugged Mama's shirt. "Bath now, please!"

Mama turned on the bath water. Emilia tried to climb in fast. "Wait," said Mama. She held Emilia's hand. "A grown-up checks the bath water first. We make sure it is not too hot."

Mama put her hand in the water. Steam went up, up, up. "Too hot," said Mama. She added some cold water. She checked again with her hand. "Now it is just right."

Emilia put in her little foot. The water felt warm and nice. She splashed and laughed. Later Mama helped her get dressed in soft pajamas.

Then Daddy called on the phone. "Bath time went well?" he asked.

"Yes," said Emilia. "Mama checked the water with her hand."

After that, they ate bread and honey. Then Mama helped Emilia sweep crumbs from the floor. Emilia held the little broom with both hands.

She swept the crumbs into a small pile. "I did it!" said Emilia. Mama clapped.

Elijah sat in the big waiting chair. His feet did not touch the floor. He was waiting for his very first haircut. "I don't want one," he whispered to Dad. "My hair might fall off and never come back."

Dad laughed a little. "Come and sit with me. We can watch." A man sat in the salon chair. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down, dark bits on the bright floor. Then a boy got up from the chair. His hair was short now. "See," said Dad. "Look at that lady there. Her hair was cut last month. It is growing back already."

Elijah looked. The lady had little soft hairs on her head. New hairs! So hair comes back. "Okay," said Elijah. "My turn. But save the bits for the birds." The hairdresser smiled and held the broom. "The birds can have them," she said. Elijah climbed up into the big chair, way up high. Snip, snip. He watched his own dark bits fall. Then he made a tiny haircut for his teddy, too, snipping with two fingers, snip snip snip.

Zoey wanted to tell Grandma her age. Grandma was coming today. Mom asked, "How old are you, Zoey?" Zoey held up her fingers. She looked at her hand. She did not know the word.

So Zoey tried. She held up one finger. "One!" she said. Mom shook her head and smiled. "Not one," said Mom. Zoey held up two fingers. "Two!" Mom shook her head again. "Keep trying," said Mom. "Take your time." Zoey tried three. Three little fingers went up in the air. "Three!" she said.

"Yes!" said Mom. "You are three." Zoey laughed and jumped. Then the door opened. Grandma came in with a big hug. "How old are you now?" Grandma asked. Zoey held up three fingers, nice and tall. "I am three!" she said. Grandma clapped. "Three is a special age," said Grandma. "Let us eat a snack and draw a picture together." Zoey sat at the table. She drew one circle, two circles, three. "One, two, three," she counted. Then she counted her grapes too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Grandma counted with her, slow and easy, all the way to the end.

Grace held her dad's hand in the school hallway. The floor was shiny and squeaky. Squeak, squeak, went her shoes. A boy stood by the big doors. He had come on the school bus, and he was the last one in the line. "I stood up on the bus," he said. "I wanted to wave at the street." "What happened?" asked Grace. "The driver said, sit down, please. On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats." Grace laughed. "Then you could not wave?" "Not one bit," said the boy. He waved his hand at her now, fast and silly. Grace tried to wave back. But then she heard her teacher say, "Walking feet in the hallway!" Grace froze like a statue. Then she walked, very slowly, and waved with just her fingers. "Sneaky wave," whispered the boy. "The sneakest," said Grace.

Milan was at the park with his dad. He saw a red berry basket on the picnic mat. "Can I taste one?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "They are sweet strawberries."

Milan picked one up. His eyes saw the bright red. His hands felt the bumpy little seeds. His nose smelled something sweet. His ears heard a bird singing in the tree.

Milan pinched his nose closed. Then he took a bite. He blinked. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. He let go of his nose. Sniff! Now the sweet taste came back, strong again.

"Wow," he said. "My nose was closed and the taste went away!" He tried it again, just to know for sure. The taste got small again.

"How lucky I have a nose," said Milan. He took a big sniff of the basket. "My nose works like an elephant's big nose, right Dad?"

Dad laughed. "An elephant's nose can do even more. It can spray water!"

Milan held the last strawberry. He smelled it first. Then he ate it up.

Maria went to Miss Kim's music studio. She saw a big drum on the floor. "Can I play it?" Maria asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. "Let's build a song together. You tap, and I tap too."

Maria tapped the drum. Boom! Boom! The room felt loud and hot from all the drumming. Miss Kim played a lion song, loud and strong. Maria tapped along. The song went fast, then slow, then it stopped.

Mama and Miss Kim clapped their hands. Clap, clap, clap! Maria just stood there. She looked at Miss Kim. Miss Kim bent down low at her waist. Maria did the same thing. She bent down low, too. Clap, clap, clap went Mama's hands again. Maria smiled big. Every time they clapped, she bowed again. Bow, clap. Bow, clap. "Again!" said Maria, and she bowed one more time.

Ivy had to wait for the doctor. She held her teddy on her lap. Then teddy fell down. He slipped under the big coat on the chair. The room was dark there. Ivy looked and looked. She could not see teddy.

"Let's be a team," said Nurse Ann. First Ivy used her eyes to look. Her ears heard the paper crinkle. Her nose smelled soap. She touched the soft coat with her hands. Still no teddy. "It is hard to see in the dark," said Nurse Ann. She reached up and turned on the light. The bright light made the dark corner bright. There was teddy!

"Now I can see him with my eyes," said Ivy. She hugged teddy tight. He was not grumpy at all. The doctor came in. He looked in Ivy's ears. He looked in her mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Ivy laughed. "Ahh," she said.

Kayden ran onto the big green field. "The game is starting!" he shouted. Mom held his hand. Grandpa carried a red blanket. The sun was warm on Kayden's face. The weather was good for a game.

The players kicked the ball. Everybody cheered. Kayden clapped his hands. "Go, go, go!" he yelled. One team kicked the ball into the net. Boom! The crowd jumped up. Then the other team kicked the ball in too. Boom! Kayden stomped his feet with joy.

The whistle blew. The game was over. Kayden tugged Mom's sleeve. "Who won?" he asked. Mom looked at the big board. Both numbers were the same. Two and two. "Nobody won today," she said. "The same score is called a tie."
