"A tie!" said Kayden. He held up two fingers on each hand. "Same, same!" He laughed. Grandpa picked him up high. Kayden dreamed of kicking the ball in the net himself one day. "Kick it far!" he called to the players leaving the field.

Isaac ran to the backyard with a big basket. "Today I cook soup!" he said. Daddy had carrots from the market. Isaac pulled one out. It had dirt all over it. "Yuck!" said Isaac. "Can we eat dirty carrots?"

"No," said Daddy. "Cooks rinse dirt off carrots first." Isaac ran to the sink. He turned the water on. He scrubbed the carrot with his hands. The dirt washed away. The water turned brown, then clear. "Look!" said Isaac. "The carrot is clean and orange now!"

He rinsed every carrot, one by one. He rinsed a potato too. Then Daddy cut them up. Daddy put the pot on the stove. Isaac watched from his chair. Soon the soup went pop, pop, pop. "Mmm," said Mommy at the table. "My name for this soup is Isaac's Special." Isaac grinned big. "I rinsed it myself!"

Luke put on his red shoes. Today he would get his very own library card! He ran into the storytime room. It had round rugs and big soft mats. Miss Kim smiled at him.

"Here is your card, Luke," she said. Luke held it with two hands. It was his! Now he could take a book home.

Luke found a book about a tiny seed that grows into a big sunflower. He loved it. But he put it back on the wrong shelf. Miss Kim turned the book. "See the label on the spine," she said. "It shows where the book belongs." The label had letters on it. Luke looked at the other books. They had labels too! He pushed his book next to the matching ones. It fit just right.

"Good job, Luke," said Miss Kim. Luke checked out his book. He hugged it all the way home. "Let's read it now!" he said.

Violet was on the little swim team. The pool was blue and cool. It smelled like sunscreen. "Kick, kick, kick," said the water in her ears.

Today was the relay race. Violet stood in the middle of the deck. She did not know where to stand. She looked left. She looked right. The other kids were in lines. Violet wondered where her line was.

"Coach Kim," she said. "Where do I stand?" Coach Kim smiled. "Come with me. I teach the team and help you learn the game." Coach Kim pointed to the wall. "Stand here, next to the ladder. When your friend taps your hand, you jump in and swim fast."

Violet stood by the ladder. She waited. The water went splish, splash, splish. Her friend Ada swam close. Ada tapped Violet's hand. Violet jumped in. She kicked her legs. She paddled her arms. She touched the other side!

"Where do I stand?" asked her friend Milo. He looked confused, just like she had. Violet pointed to the ladder. "Coach Kim teaches the team," she said. "She shows us where to go. Stand here, and tap my hand when I swim back." Milo smiled and got ready.

Everly stood at the big desk in the library. She wanted her very own library card. The librarian smiled and typed on her computer. "Here it is," she said. "Your first card, Everly."

Everly held the card with two hands. It had her name on it. Then she heard a loud voice from the other room. "Storytime!" the librarian called out. Children ran to sit on the rug. Everly hid behind her mommy's legs.

"What is storytime?" Everly asked. Mommy said, "Let's go see." The librarian sat in a small chair. She opened a big funny book. "Achoo!" she read, and made a silly face. All the children laughed. Everly peeked. Then she sat right down on the rug too.

After the story, Everly picked a book about a bunny. She gave the librarian her new card. The librarian stamped the book. "Bye-bye, bunny book," Everly said, and hugged it tight.

Mackenzie turned four today. Her whole family came to the bowling alley. Grandma, Dad, and her friend Zoe were there too.

Dad blew up a big red balloon. He puffed and puffed until it was round. "This one is for you," he said. Mackenzie held the string tight.

The party store balloons on the wall floated up high. They sat near the ceiling all day. Mackenzie looked at them. Then she looked at her red balloon. She wanted to see it fly up too.

She let go of the string. "Fly, balloon, fly!" she said. "Fly, balloon, fly!" But the balloon did not fly up. It went down, down, down. It landed softly on the floor by her party shoes.

Zoe picked it up and handed it back. "It likes the floor," said Zoe. Mackenzie laughed. She let go again. Down it went, down, down, down, right onto the bowling lane.

The red balloon rolled slowly into the gutter. A man came and helped get it out. Then Dad gave Mackenzie a balloon from the party store. That one floated up, up, up.

"Happy birthday, Mackenzie!" said Grandma. Mackenzie munched a salty pretzel. Then she rolled her ball down the lane and watched every pin fall down.

Zayn stood on the baseball diamond. He wanted to hit the ball far. The sun was bright. His teammate Mia was up first. She swung the bat. She missed the ball.

Mia's face looked sad. But then the whole team clapped. "Try again, Mia!" they called. Mia smiled. She swung again, and she hit the ball! It went deep into the grass. Everyone cheered loud.

Then it was Zayn's turn. He swung the bat. He missed too. "Do you feel sad now?" Mia asked him. "No," said Zayn. "I hear you cheering!" The team clapped for him. Zayn took a big breath. He swung again. Crack! The ball flew. Mia jumped up and down. "Run, Zayn, run!"

Emily wanted her bedtime story. She ran to the bookshelf. But Daddy was still in the kitchen.

Emily looked at the book by herself. The cover had words on it. She pointed at the letters. "Cat," she said slowly. The picture showed a cat. The words said cat too.

She opened the front of the book. "This way," she whispered. She turned one page. Then another page. She hummed a little song and waited for Daddy.

Daddy came in with warm milk. "Read the words," said Emily. Daddy read them. The words told about a curly cat with soft fur.

"Words tell us things," said Emily. "Like the sign at the store says STOP." Daddy smiled. "Yes. Words are on boxes and signs too."

Emily looked at the milk box. There were little words on it. She pointed at them. Then she snuggled down and turned to the last page. "Good night, curly cat," she said.

Beatrice woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said Mama. "Snow day!"

Beatrice put on her red coat. She put on her puffy mittens. She ran to the big sledding hill. Dad pulled the sled up, up, up. Then down they went, fast and bumpy. Beatrice laughed and laughed.

Then Beatrice lay down in the snow. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. She stood up to look. "Oh no!" Her boot made a big smudge on her snow shape. "Try again," said Dad. "You lie down and sweep, then I help you up." So Beatrice lay in a different spot. She swept her arms and legs. Dad pulled her hands, and she popped up without touching the snow. There it was! "It looks like an angel!" said Beatrice. "A snow angel," said Dad. Beatrice flopped down again right away. "I need ten more!"

Rowan's basket fell over in the backyard. All his picture cards spilled out on the grass. Rowan wanted to find his dog card, but there were so many cards. "Too many," he said. Dad sat down next to him. "We can make piles," Dad said. Rowan put the dog card down. Then he put the cat card on top of it. Then the bird card. "These are all animals," Dad said. Rowan found more animal cards. A fish. A cow. The animal pile grew big. Then Rowan found a ball card. It was not an animal. He started a new pile for toys. The ball went there. The drum went there. The kite went there too. Rowan found a picture of an apple. "Apple is a food," he said. He made a third pile for foods. The bread card went there. The banana card went there. The cheese card went there. Now the grass had three neat piles. Rowan looked at the animal pile. He found his dog card right away. "Woof," said Rowan, holding it up high. Dad laughed and clapped. Then Dad brought out a frozen pop from the house. He handed it to Rowan. Rowan sat on the warm grass and licked it. "Best pile day ever," said Dad.

Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She looked around with her eyes. She saw a poster on the wall. It had a happy face on it.

Then Everly heard a sound. Beep, beep! It came from down the hall. She used her ears to hear it. The room smelled like soap, and she smelled it with her nose. The nurse gave her a sticker that felt bumpy. Everly touched it with her fingers.

Now it was time for her checkup. "Open wide," said the doctor. Everly opened her mouth. The doctor looked at her tongue. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Everly said, "Ahh!" She could taste a little yucky taste in her mouth.

Then the doctor said, "Time for one small poke." Everly did not want a poke. She squeezed her eyes shut tight. Now she could not see the doctor. Now she could not see her mama. She could not see anything at all!

But the doctor still saw Everly. The poke came anyway. It was quick. It was small. "All done," said the doctor. Everly opened her eyes. She could see again! Her mama held out a cookie from her bag. Everly took a bite. It tasted sweet. "That was fast," said Everly. "Can I read the poster now?" The doctor laughed and pointed to the happy face.

Livia could not find her spotted bunny at daycare. "Where did you go, Bunny?" she asked. Miss Ana helped her look. They peeked under the table. No bunny. They looked in the toy box. No bunny. Livia felt like crying a little. "It is okay to feel sad," said Miss Ana. "We will keep looking."

Then Livia saw Tommy's big coat on the hook. The coat had a pocket. The pocket was bumpy and round. She reached in and pulled out her bunny. "My bunny was inside the pocket!" she said. Tommy laughed. "I put my snacks in there," he said. "Maybe Bunny wanted a snack too."

Miss Ana smiled. "Livia, will you speak at circle time and tell everyone?" Livia hugged Bunny tight. "Yes! Bunny was hiding in the coat, inside the pocket!" Then Bunny got a turn on the slide, right before snack time.

Anna had a little drum. It sat in the school band room. Miss Polly said, "Play the bumpy song today." Anna tried. Boing, boom, splat. The song came out wrong. Anna frowned. "I'm afraid I can't do it," she said. "It's too hard." Tom laughed, not mean, just a little. "My song was hard too," he said. "Now watch me!" He played his song all the way through. Anna wanted to know how he did it. "I just played a little bit every day," said Tom. So Anna played her drum a little bit. Then she stopped and had a cookie. The next day she played a little bit again. Boing, boom. The next day, boom, boom, ting. Every day she played some more. One morning Anna sat at her drum. She took a big breath. Boom, boom, ting, boom! The song came out right, all the way to the end. Tom clapped. Miss Polly clapped. Anna bowed and hit one last boom.

Jaxon ran to the park. He saw a big red truck in the sand. It was not his truck. It was Ben's truck.

Jaxon wanted it so much. He grabbed the truck fast. Ben began to cry. His face went sad and red.

Jaxon looked at Ben. He looked at the truck. Maybe the truck was Ben's very own? Jaxon gave the truck back. "Can I have a turn?" he asked.

Ben wiped his eyes. "Yes," said Ben. "Can I have my turtle after?" Jaxon nodded. First Jaxon pushed the truck. The wheels went round and round. Then he gave it to Ben. Ben made the turtle splash in a puddle. The water went splash, splash, splash. Then Ben handed the turtle to Jaxon.

A big kid ran up. He reached for the truck with one strong hand. "Ask first," said Ben. The big kid stopped. "Can I play too?" he asked. "Yes!" said Jaxon.

They all sat in the sand. Truck, turtle, truck, turtle, round and round. Jaxon smiled. "This is a good game," he said. "Ask, and then take a turn."

Jayden was at the park for his birthday. There was a big cake on the table. Mom set candles on top. Jayden counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then he stopped. He looked at Mom. "Am I four this year?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "You are five now. One candle for each year."

So Jayden knew what to do. "We need one more candle!" Mom smiled and put it on. Now there were five candles, all the same size. Dad lit them with a match, far from Jayden's hands.

A little wind blew by. One flame wiggled. Then all the flames bent the same way. "Quick, make a wish!" said Dad. Jayden closed his eyes. "I wish for this same cake next year," he said. Then he blew, and the candles went out. "Did my wish go into the smoke?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "Maybe it spells yes in the sky."

Peyton ran to the park with Dad. She wanted a cold drink, but her cup was warm. "Yuck," said Peyton. "Warm water is no fun."

Dad had a bag with ice. He put one ice cube in her hand. Peyton yelled, "Cold, cold, cold!" She dropped it fast. It fell into her cup with a plop. The ice cube felt cold when she touched it. That was the trick!

Peyton looked with her eyes. She saw the little ice bobbing. She heard it go clink, clink with her ears. She smelled the sweet apple juice Dad poured in. She took a sip and tasted it with her tongue. "Yum!" she said. She touched the cold cup with her fingers. "More ice, please!" said Peyton. Dad laughed and dropped in two more.

Maeva went to the store with Dad. She wanted a book about fish. "Can we find one?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. They walked past one cart, two carts, three carts. The store smelled like bread. Maeva heard a clock tick, tick, tick near the wall.

She found a little red book. It had a fish on it. Dad read the words out loud. "Fish can swim in the deep blue sea." Maeva looked at the letters. Dad pointed. "These are the words. They say what I read."

Maeva held the book upside down. She giggled. The fish looked upside down too! The words were all wrong. Dad laughed. "Turn it around." Maeva turned it. Now the fish swam right side up. She opened the front cover first. "Read it again," she said. Dad began, "Once there was a little fish..."

Athena ran to her cubby at daycare. Her bunny toy was not there. She looked under her coat. No bunny. She looked in the toy box. No bunny.

It was winter, so Athena wore her big boots. She searched the reading corner. She lifted the crunchy leaves in the craft bowl. No bunny anywhere. Athena sat down. Her eyes felt hot. She wanted to give up.

Then her big sister came in. Her dad came in too. "Can you help me look?" Athena asked. "Yes," they said. Now three people were searching, not one. Dad looked behind the shelf. Sister looked under the table. Athena looked in the dress-up bin.

Sister lifted a red cape. "Bunny!" she called. Bunny had been hiding under the cape all day. Athena hugged bunny tight. Dad helped her cut a piece of tape. She taped bunny's ear back on.

"More lookers found him fast," Athena said. She waved bye to her teacher. "Come on, bunny. Home time."

Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted a stuffed animal. "Pick one!" said Mama.

First they walked past the toys. Balls and trucks sat on a long shelf. Then they saw the animal shelf. A dog! A cow! Isaiah hugged a soft dog. "This is an animal," he said. Mama smiled.

Next they passed the fish tank. A little fish swam round and round. "Fish is not an animal," said Isaiah. "It has no legs!" A big boy leaned close to the glass. "Fish are animals too," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Isaiah's eyes got big. "Wow! The fish is an animal!"

Isaiah ran back to the shelf. He could not forget that fish. He picked the dog in one hand. Then he pointed at a fish toy. "Mama! Can I have an animal that swims?"

Mama laughed. "You can have both." She put the dog and the fish in the cart. Isaiah waved at the fish tank. "Bye, animal!" Then they went to get juice, and Isaiah held his fish all the way home.

Grandma's car pulled into the driveway. Amira ran to meet her. Grandma opened the trunk. A big pink suitcase sat inside. "Can I pull it?" asked Amira. "Yes, you can pull it," said Grandma. Amira pulled and pulled. The wheels rumbled on the ground. "What is inside?" she asked. "My clothes," said Grandma. "Guests pack their clothes and things in a suitcase."

Amira thought about that. She looked at the suitcase. How many shirts were in there? How many socks? Grandma unzipped it right there on the grass. Out came one shirt, two shirts, three shirts. Out came a warm scarf and a soft hat. "Why do you bring so much?" asked Amira. "I am staying a whole week," said Grandma.

That night, Amira had an idea. She found her own little bag. She packed one shirt, two shirts, three shirts. She packed her toy sheep. She wanted to be a guest too. In the morning, she rolled her bag to Grandma's room. "Look! I am a guest!" she said. Grandma laughed and clapped. Then she patted the bed. "Come in, little guest. There is room for you and your sheep." Amira climbed up next to her, bag and all.

Leah sat in her car seat. One, two, three toys sat next to her. She had a bear, a bunny and a small red car.

The car went over a deep bump. Leah's bear flew up. The bear came down and hit her baby brother's foot. He began to cry.

"I am sorry," Leah said. "It was a mistake."

Baby brother looked at her. He stopped crying. His face got soft again.

"Can you help me, Mom?" Leah asked. "Please reach the bear?"

Mom smiled in the mirror. She handed the bear back.

"Thank you," said Leah.

Then she made a silly joke. "The bear wanted to swing on the roof!"

Baby brother laughed. The car went on. One, two, three toys, all safe now.

Owen ran into daycare on a windy morning. His hat almost blew off. He had big news. It was his cat's birthday today.

Miss Ada was talking to Ben. "Ben, please pass me the tape," she said. Owen tugged her sleeve. "Miss Ada! Miss Ada!" She held up one hand. "Wait, Owen. I am still talking."

Owen closed his mouth. He watched. Ben gave her the tape. She stuck the paper sun on the wall. Then she stopped. There was a quiet pause.

"Now I am done," said Miss Ada. "You may talk, Owen."

Owen took a big breath. "Today is my cat's birthday!" he said.

"A cat birthday! Thank you for telling me," said Miss Ada. "Can you help me make a card?"

Owen nodded hard. He drew a cat with a party hat. He whispered to the cat in the picture, "Happy birthday."

At snack time, Mia talked about her new shoes. Owen waited. He watched her lips until they stopped. Then he said, "Nice shoes, Mia."

She smiled. "Thank you," she said. Owen smiled too.

Mya stood at the school gate. She held her mama's hand very tight. The gate was huge and red. Behind it, kids ran and laughed.

"Can I run in now?" Mya asked.

"First we wait for the bell," said Mama.

They waited. Ding! The bell rang. The gate opened. Mya ran in.

Inside, the teacher smiled. "Hello, Mya! Sit on the blue mat."

Mya sat down. Then she jumped up. She wanted to run to the toy horse in the corner. It looked so fun!

A boy tugged her sleeve. "We sit on the mat now," he said. "That is a class rule. Everyone follows the rules."

"Rules?" said Mya. "What are rules?"

"Things we all do," said the boy. "Like this one. Sit and listen."

Mya sat back down. The teacher read the rules one by one. One, two, three. Mya counted them on her fingers.

Later, it was play time. Mya ran to the horse. She hugged it and made it gallop. Neigh!

Then the bell rang again. Mya kept playing.

The boy ran over. "Bell means clean up!" he said. "Rule number three!"

Mya put the horse on the shelf. "Rules are not so bad," she said. "Now can we line up?"

"Yes!" said the boy. "You go first."

Ryan ran into the music studio. A big guitar sat on a stand. "Can I play it?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled. "Yes, you can try."

Ryan patted the guitar like a drum. Tap, tap, tap. The guitar made no song. "Why is it quiet?" he asked. Miss Kim said, "Try the strings." She showed him how to strum. Then she said, "You can pluck them too, one by one."

Ryan passed his fingers over the strings. Pluck, pluck. Then he strummed them all at once. Boom! A big, happy sound filled the room. "It sings!" Ryan laughed. His tummy felt warm. He strummed again and again. Miss Kim clapped. "You are a guitar player now, Ryan." Ryan stood tall and proud. "Listen to my song!" he said.

Zayn was a small boy in a big hotel room. He wanted to play plane. "This chair is my seat," he said. Dad sat near him. Dad took the belt from his bathrobe. "Buckle up for takeoff," said Dad. Zayn slid the belt through the loop. Click! "I am buckled," said Zayn. "Buckle up for takeoff," said Dad again. Zayn laughed. "Buckle up for takeoff!"

Then it was time to fly home. On the real plane, Zayn sat by the window. He buckled his seat belt all by himself. Click! The plane began to move. Zayn wanted to stand up. He wanted to look out the window standing tall. "Sit down, buckle up," said Dad. "The plane is taking off." So Zayn sat. The plane went fast. Then the plane went up, up, up! Zayn peeked out the window from his seat. "I can see clouds!" he said. "I am buckled like everyone."

Later the plane came down. "Landing," said Dad. "Buckle up for landing." Zayn held his belt. "Buckle up for landing," he said. The plane touched the ground softly. Zayn looked out the window and waved. "Bye bye, plane," he said.

Arnaud could not sleep. He wanted his favorite cow toy. It was not in his bed. He looked under his pillow. He looked under his blanket. No cow.

Arnaud felt sad. His mouth turned down. Then he heard a bump. It came from the toy box. Arnaud felt a little scared. He held his blanket tight.

Daddy came in. "Let us look," Daddy said. Daddy opened the toy box. Out jumped the cat! The cat had been sleeping on the soft cow.

Arnaud felt surprised. Then he felt excited. "Cow!" he said. He hugged his cow tight. His face made a big smile.

Daddy said, "Look at that happy face." Arnaud ran to the mirror by the door. He made a big smile again. He saw a happy boy looking back.

Then Arnaud made a sad mouth. The boy in the mirror looked sad too. Arnaud giggled. He made an angry face. He made a scared face. The mirror boy copied them all.

Arnaud got back into bed. He held his cow. Daddy tucked him in. "Happy face," Arnaud said softly. He smiled at the ceiling. Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Evelyn woke up in her bed. She heard a spoon in a bowl. She ran to the table. Mama and Papa were there, eating eggs.

"Good morning, Evelyn," said Mama.

Evelyn climbed into her chair. "Good morning," she said back. She ate her eggs too. Morning was the time when they woke up and ate breakfast. Then it was time for the park.

At the park, the sun was wide and bright. Evelyn ran to the swing. But a boy was on it.

"Can I have a turn later?" Evelyn asked.

"Yes," said the boy. "Later, when I count to ten."

Evelyn waited. The boy counted slowly. One, two, three. He counted all the way to ten. Then he jumped off.

"Now it is my turn," said Evelyn.

Mama pushed her high. Evelyn held on tight.

"Yesterday I could not swing," said Evelyn. "Yesterday the swing was wet."

"Today it is dry," said Mama. "Today you can swing."

"And tomorrow?" asked Evelyn.

"Tomorrow we can come back," said Mama.

After the swing, they sat on the grass. Evelyn found a dandelion. It was gone to seed, all white and round.

"Make a wish," said Mama. "Then blow."

Evelyn took a big breath. She blew. The little seeds flew up and away. They floated over the sandbox. They floated past the big tree.

Evelyn looked at the empty stem. "My wish is gone," she said.

"It is not gone," said Mama. "It went with the seeds."

Evelyn smiled. She put the stem in Mama's hand.

"Put it in my pocket," said Mama. "It can be my present."

They walked home slowly. The sun was going down.

"Good night, park," said Evelyn. She waved her hand.

Jules ran to the garden with a little bag of seeds. "Peas!" he said. "I will plant peas!" Grandma made a row in the dirt. Jules dropped the seeds in, one by one. He patted the soil down. Then he watered the seeds. "Grow, grow," said Jules.

Every day Jules came back. Little green leaves popped up. The leaves got bigger. Tall vines climbed up a stick. A fat frog sat by the water can. Jules looked and looked. But where were his peas? He saw no peas at all. "I want peas for my snack," said Jules. He frowned at the vines.

Then Jules saw something long and green. It hung on the plant. "What is that?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "That is a pod," she said. "Pick it." Jules picked the pod. He squeezed it. Pop! It opened in his hand. Inside was a row of little round peas, all in a line!

"Peas!" Jules shouted. "They were hiding in the pod!" He picked more pods, pop, pop, pop. He counted five peas in one. Grandma said they could eat them at home. Jules held his pods tight. "Best garden ever," he said. A red ladybug flew up and landed on a pod. Jules laughed. "You can't have my peas," he said. "They are mine!"

Beatrice went to the mall with her dad. They found the hair salon. Beatrice wanted a haircut, but she also felt a little scared. The scissors looked big and sharp. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, said, "I will be very careful." Miss Jo held the scissors herself. Beatrice sat very still in the big chair.

Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They stuck to Beatrice's sweater. "Not a bad haircut," her dad said with a smile. Beatrice looked in the big wall mirror. She could see her bangs. She could see her short hair by her ears. But she could not see the back of her head. "I want to see the back," said Beatrice.

Miss Jo did not say anything. She picked up a little mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice's head. Now Beatrice could see the back of her hair in the big mirror. "I see it! It is so short and cute!" said Beatrice. She turned her head slowly. She looked one more time. Then she stuck out her hand for the key-shaped balloon her dad had bought. "Let's go show everyone," she said.

Elijah went to the store with his mom. He wanted a book about a big red truck. He skipped down the book aisle. There were so many books.

He found a truck book. He opened it at the back. Mom said, "Start at the front." He turned to the first page. The words told about the truck. Mom read them out loud. The words made the story. Elijah turned each page, one by one, all the way to the back.

Then he had a question. "Who made up the truck story?" he asked. The store lady smiled. She pointed to the front of the book. "See this name?" she said. "That is the author. The author is the person who wrote the words." Elijah looked at the name. He said it out loud. On the way home, he held the book tight and said, "Maybe I will write a book about my dream. A dream about a cute puppy."

Leah sat on the classroom rug. Miss Polo held up big letter cards. Each letter had a sound. "B says buh," said Leah. "Buh, buh, bear!"

Then Miss Polo mixed all the cards in a pile. "Can you put them in order?" she asked. Leah picked up the letter M. She looked at the pile. Where did M go? It was hard. There were so many letters.

Her friend Tom grabbed a card and put it way at the end. "No, Tom!" laughed Leah. "That one goes in the middle." Tom stuck out his tongue. "How do you know?"

Then Leah had an idea. She began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She tapped a card each time. "H, I, J, K." She tapped and tapped. "L, M! There!" Leah slipped M into its spot, right after L and before N. The song told her where it went!

Tom clapped his hands. "Sing it again!" he said. So they sang the alphabet song together, all the way to Z. Miss Polo smiled at the door. "Now you know your letters, Leah."

Leah hugged the M card. "M says muh," she said. "Muh, muh, me!"

Abigail was staying at Grandma's house. It was time to sleep. Grandma said, "Pick two socks from the basket." The room was very dark. Abigail could not see the socks well. She felt two socks with her hands. They felt the same to her. She put them on and went to sleep.

In the morning, the sun came in the window. Abigail looked down at her feet. She saw one red sock and one green sock. She laughed and laughed. "Grandma, come see!" she called. Grandma looked and smiled. "You found a trick of the dark," said Grandma.

The next night, the room was dark again. Abigail had a good idea. She carried the basket to the door. The friendly hall light helped her see. She picked two blue socks. In the morning, both socks were blue. Abigail jumped like she was on a hill of soft grass. "The light helped me," she said. Then she ran to show Grandma her two blue feet.

Elena woke up at Grandma's house. The kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma was baking cookies. Elena wanted one so much.

"May I have a cookie, please?" Elena asked. Grandma smiled and gave her a warm cookie. "Thank you," Elena said. The cookie was soft and yummy.

Then Grandma said, "Put on your shoes. We will go to the park before it gets late." The air was cool and fresh outside. At the park, a boy was digging in the sand. His shovel fell. Elena picked it up for him.

"Gracias," the boy said. Elena blinked. She did not know that word. "It means thank you," Grandma said softly. "Other languages have their own words for it." So thank you was not the same everywhere.

Elena tried the new word. "Gracias!" she said. The boy laughed and dug a big hole. Then he poured water in. "Look, it can swim," he said, floating his little boat on top. Elena clapped her hands.

On the walk home, Elena stepped on Grandma's toe by mistake. "Sorry," she said. "That's all right," said Grandma. At the door, Elena asked, "Can you help me with my coat, please?" Grandma helped her.

Then Grandma gave her one more cookie, right before dinner, just because. Elena held it in both hands. "Gracias," she said. Grandma hugged her tight.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. She held her soft bunny. The car went bump, bump over the road.

"Is the library today?" Kinsley asked. "No, we went yesterday," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done." Kinsley thought about yesterday. Yesterday she got a book with a red truck in it.

"Is today the library?" she asked again. Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is now. We are driving there now." Kinsley looked out the window. Now she saw a cow. Now she saw a big red barn. Now the car went over a bridge.

At the library, Kinsley climbed the little steps to the book shelf. She picked a book about a juicy orange. "Can we read it later?" she asked. "Yes, later at home," said Mom.

"And tomorrow we can come back," said Mom. Kinsley hugged her book. Tomorrow was not here yet. Today was here, and now the cow went moo outside the window.

Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose was red. He wanted to play, but he felt slow and small.

Grandma set out some warm soup. Henry took a sip. Then his nose tickled. "Ah... ah... CHOO!" He sneezed right into his hand.

Grandma gave him a tissue. She wiped his hand. "Watch me," she said. She lifted her arm. She put her nose in her elbow. "When you cough or sneeze, you cover it with your elbow."

Henry tried. He lifted his little arm. He made a cough in his elbow. "I did it!" he said. Grandma clapped.

Then his nose tickled again. Henry moved fast. He put his nose in his elbow. "Ah-CHOO!" This time his hand stayed clean. Grandma smiled big.

Outside the window, the sky was cloudy. Henry drank more soup. Then he coughed once more, soft and small, right into his elbow. "Good job," said Grandma. Henry giggled and held up his arm.

Jules was at home in the kitchen. He had a cold. His nose was red. He sat in his big chair.

Grandma was cooking. "Pancakes today," she said. Jules loved pancakes. He wanted one very much.

But his throat felt scratchy. It hurt a little. He closed his mouth. He thought, if I say nothing, I can still have pancakes. So he stayed quiet.

Grandma set down the pan. "Jules, you look small today," she said. Jules dug his spoon into his yogurt. He did not eat. He looked at his plate.

Then he remembered. "Grandma, my throat hurts," he said. It was a small voice, but she heard.

Grandma put her hand on his head. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Now I can help you." She made him warm milk with honey. She gave him a soft blanket. Jules sipped slowly. The warm milk felt good in his throat. His heart felt warm too.

Then Grandma put one small pancake on his plate. "When your throat is ready," she said. Jules smiled a tiny smile. He touched the pancake with one finger. "Soon," he whispered, and hugged his blanket tight.

Harper ran to the farm gate. Grandma waved her over. "Time for a game!" she said. "We name our five senses."

Grandma held up a red apple. "Eyes see," Harper said. "I see the apple!" Grandma rang a big bell. "Ears hear!" Harper shouted. She touched a soft sheep. "Hands feel. The sheep is so soft and beautiful!" Then Grandma gave her a warm cookie from the oven. Grandma had done the hot baking herself. Harper took a tiny bite. "My tongue tastes it. Yum!"

"One sense left," said Grandma. "Use your nose." Harper sniffed the cookie. "Mmm, I smell it!" Then she pinched her nose shut with her fingers. She sniffed again. Nothing! She let go and sniffed. The sweet smell came back! "Grandma, come quick!" Harper cried. "Pinch your nose and peek at the cookie smell. It hides!" Grandma laughed and pinched her nose too. "You're right," she said. "I can't smell a thing."

Layla was at Grandma's house. It was morning. Grandma was baking bread. Layla wanted to help name her five senses. Grandma held up one hand.

"One, eyes. I see the bread," said Layla. "Two, ears. I hear it hum in the oven." Her dad took the bread out with big gloves. "Three, nose. I smell it. Yum!" said Layla. "Four, tongue. I taste a warm bite." Then she stopped. She looked at her thumb. "What about five? Did I forget one?"

She thought hard. Then she touched the soft bread with her finger. "Touching! That is five!" Grandma laughed. Layla counted again on her fingers. "See, hear, smell, taste, touch. Five senses. Five fingers."

Grandma said, "My favorite sense today is smelling." Layla giggled. She sniffed the bread one more time. "Mine too," she said, and took another little bite.

Matthew wanted to play tea party at daycare. But the teapot was empty. There was no real tea in it. Matthew felt sad.

His friend Mia ran over with her bear. "Pour the tea," she said. Matthew tipped the empty pot. He made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug." Nothing came out, but the cups were full of pretend tea. Mia clapped her hands.

"Careful," said Mia. "It's pretend hot!" She blew on her cup. Matthew blew on his cup too. Then he took a big pretend sip. "Yum," he said. Mia gave some pretend tea to her bear. The bear drank it all up.

Miss Beth came to see. She sat in a tall chair at the little table. Matthew poured her a cup. "Would you like a cookie too?" he asked. Miss Beth smiled and said, "Yes, please." Matthew passed her the empty plate. "These are pretend cookies," he said. Miss Beth took a big pretend bite. "Delicious," she said. "May I have one more?" Matthew tipped the pot again. "Glug, glug," he said. "I will remember you like two."

Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a sock on each foot and a warm blanket on his lap. His nose was red and his throat felt scratchy. He coughed one small cough.

"I want to run outside," said Arthur. He slid his feet to the floor. "Not yet," said Mama. "You have a cold. First we rest here. Then your body can get better." Arthur frowned. His face felt sour and grumpy.

Mama brought his favourite book. Arthur looked at the pictures. He found a cat, a moon, and a red boat. "Where is the frog?" he asked. He turned the page. There it was! Arthur let out a happy sound. He drank a little water from his cup.

He rested his head on the pillow. His eyes got heavy. He slept for a long time. When he woke up, he sniffed the air. Soup! His nose could smell again. He sat up tall. "My body feels better," said Arthur. He hugged the soft blanket tight. "Can we read the frog book one more time?"

Grandpa turned on the big game. Oliver sat on the rug at Grandpa's house. Everyone wore blue shirts. Uncle Max wore blue. Aunt Bea wore blue too. Oliver looked down at his red shirt.

"You have no blue shirt," said Grandpa. "Fans wear their team's colors. That shows who they cheer for."

Oliver wanted to cheer for the blue team. He looked in his bag. No blue shirt. He looked in Grandpa's drawer. Grandpa held up a big blue sweater. It was warm and soft.

Oliver put it on. It went down to his feet. Everyone laughed in a kind way. The blue team ran fast. They kicked the ball. Goal!

"Who are you cheering for?" asked Aunt Bea.

Oliver pointed at the sweater. "This team!"

Victor woke up on his birthday. "A party today!" he shouted. Mom blew up red balloons. Dad hung a big paper chain. Soon Grandma came. Then Ben came. Then Aunt Lily came with a box.

The box was covered in shiny blue paper. Victor could not see inside it. He shook the box. Thump, thump. He squeezed it. It was not scary at all. It was fun! "What is in it?" he asked. "You have to open it," said Grandma. Victor pulled the paper off. Rip, rip! There was a little red truck!

"Now I know," said Victor. "The paper hides the present!" He hugged the box. "Cake time!" called Mom. She cut the cake with a big knife, and everyone sang. Victor held up his new truck. "Beep, beep!" he said.

Brielle was at school. It was play time outside. There was a big hoop on the ground. There were little beanbags in a basket. Brielle wanted to throw a beanbag into the hoop.

She picked up a beanbag. She held it with both hands. She threw it. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed in the grass. "Oh no," said Brielle. She got the beanbag. She stood closer to the hoop this time. She threw it again. The beanbag went in! "I did it!" said Brielle. She clapped her hands.

Then Miss Kim, the teacher, rolled a big ball to her. "Now try to catch," said Miss Kim. The ball came and came. Brielle shut her eyes. The ball bumped her arm and rolled away. "I missed it," said Brielle. Her friend Tom shut his eyes too when the ball came. He missed it also. Tom looked sad. His face was not angry, just sad. Brielle patted him on the back.

Miss Kim rolled the ball again. This time Brielle watched the ball. She watched it all the way to her hands. She kept her eyes open. She caught the big ball with both hands! "I caught it!" she said.

A woman at the fence was watching the children. She smiled and waved. Brielle waved back. "Watch the ball, Tom," said Brielle. "Watch it all the way to your hands." Tom watched the ball. He kept his eyes open. He caught it! "Yay, Tom!" said Brielle. They threw the beanbags and caught the ball until the bell rang.

Natalie ran to the baseball field. She wore her red team shirt. It was her turn to hit the ball. She picked up the bat fast.

"Stop, Natalie!" called Coach Ben. "Come get your helmet."

Natalie trotted back. Coach Ben put the helmet on her head. It was blue and a little big. He made the strap snug.

"Now you can hit," said Coach Ben. "The helmet keeps your head safe."

Natalie felt the helmet with one hand. It was hard, like a shell. An ant crawled near her shoe. She watched it for a second, then stepped up to the plate.

She swung once. She missed. She swung again. Miss again. Her friend Milo shouted, "You can do it, Natalie!" Natalie felt a little shy. But she took a deep breath.

The ball came again. Natalie swung hard. Clunk! The ball flew over the grass. "Run, Natalie, run!" said Coach Ben. She dropped the bat and ran to first base. She was safe!

Milo clapped and clapped. "Next time I hit, I will wear my helmet too," he said.

"Good," said Natalie, smiling under her big blue helmet.

Maya stood at the big school door. Her mama held her hand. The hallway was long and empty. "Where is my class?" Maya asked.

A teacher came out. "This way, Maya," she said. "We walk in a line." The children stood one behind the other. Maya saw the line. Each child stood in front of another child. Maya ran ahead to be first. But then she could not see her teacher. She stopped and looked back.

"Come find your spot," the teacher said. Maya walked back. She stood behind a boy with red shoes. Now she could see her teacher. The line moved together, one child after another, all the way down the hall. The teacher smiled at Maya. Maya caught mama's wave at the door.

Inside the room, there was a sandbox. Maya sat down and let the sand run through her fingers. "I like school," she said. The teacher said, "Tomorrow we will walk in our line again." Maya nodded. She patted the sand flat and made a little hill.

Clean-up time came to Natalie's room at daycare. The blocks were in one messy pile on the floor. Miss Jo held up a basket. "We are sorting by color," she said. "All the red ones go together."

Natalie picked up a red block. She put it in the red pile. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Then a green pile. Soon the sun did shine through the window. The colors looked bright on the rug.

Natalie counted her piles. But one block looked wrong. A yellow block sat in the blue pile. "Who put you there?" she asked the block. The block did not answer. Natalie picked it up. She put it with the yellow blocks. Now every block sat with blocks just like it. Sam clapped from the toy corner. He held his doctor kit. "All better," he said. Natalie smiled and set the last basket on the shelf.

Jack waited at the airport. He held a big sign with a heart on it. "There he is!" said Mom. Grandpa waved and walked fast. Jack ran to him and hugged his legs.

At home, Grandpa took out a card game. "I want to go first!" said Jack. He grabbed all the cards. "My turn, my turn, my turn," he said. "But then I never get a turn," said Grandpa. Grandpa looked sad, like an ant with no crumbs. Jack stopped. "You can go first this time," said Jack. So they took turns. Jack went first, then Grandpa went first. They counted, "One turn for you, one turn for me."

They played the game all week. On Friday, Grandpa had to fly home. "Same game next time?" said Grandpa. "Yes," said Jack. "You can go first."

Wesley stood in the pet store. He was very tall for four, but he still held Mama's hand. A small brown puppy looked up at him.

"Can we take him home?" Wesley asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "He is yours."

At home, Mama put food in the puppy's bowl. The puppy began to eat. Wesley wanted to play. He reached for the ball.

"He is eating," said Mama. "We leave him alone now."

Wesley sat on the floor and waited. The puppy crunched and crunched. Soon the bowl was empty. Wesley rolled the ball, and the puppy ran after it in a big circle. Wesley laughed.

Then the puppy yawned. He curled up on his soft bed and closed his eyes. Wesley wanted to pet him. He stopped his hand.

"He is sleeping," Wesley whispered. "I will leave him alone."

He sat very still and watched. The puppy's tail twitched. His paws wiggled. He was running in a dream!

After a while, the puppy woke up. He found Wesley's shoe and gave it a happy chew. "Hey," Wesley said with a giggle. "That's my shoe, not a toy!"

Mama helped him trade the shoe for the ball. Wesley threw it, and the puppy brought it back. "Good boy," said Wesley.

That night, the puppy slept in his bed. Wesley gave him one soft pat on the head. "Good night, puppy," he said. The puppy licked his hand once, just a small good-night kiss.

Mateo sat on a thick carpet at the library. He had a big book of letters. His mama sat next to him.

"A says ah," said Mateo. He patted the letter A on the page. He turned more pages. "B says buh. C says kuh." He kept going. He got all the way to P. "P says puh." He clapped his hands. "All done, Mama!"

A girl sat close by. She was singing a song. "Q, R, S, T, U," she sang. Mateo leaned in and listened. He looked at his book. There were more pages. He turned one.

"V says vuh," said Mateo. "W, X, Y." He went slow. He waited and looked at the letters. The girl sang on.

She sang one more letter. "Z!" said the girl. Mateo turned the last page. There it was. The big letter Z sat at the end.

"Z is the last one," said Mateo. "A is first, and Z is last." He patted the Z, soft and slow.

The girl smiled. "Sing it with me," she said.

"A, B, C," sang Mateo. He sang all the way to the end. "X, Y, Z!"

Violet went to the library with her grandma. She wanted a book about a boat. She looked on the low shelf, where the little books hide. Her fingers found a blue book with a boat on the front.

She sat down on the soft rug. She opened the book. But the pages felt wrong. The pictures came in a jumble. A fish came first. Then a storm. Then a little boy at home. "That is all mixed up," said Violet.

Grandma sat close by. "Turn it over," she said. Violet turned the book over. Now the boat picture was at the front. This cover was the front cover. She opened it there.

The first page showed the little boy. Then he got in the boat. Then the fish came. Then the storm. Page by page, the story went in order. Violet turned each page slowly. The paper felt smooth and cool. She heard a page make a tiny flip sound.

At the end, the boy got home safe. That page was near the back cover. Violet patted the back cover and smiled. "It ends at the back," she said. Grandma laughed softly and patted Violet's head. "One more book?" she asked. Violet ran her hand along the shelf, back at the front cover where books begin.

Wesley got to school early. Miss Ana had a surprise. "We will bake bread today," she said. She held the warm pan. Wesley touched the pan. "Ouch, no," said Miss Ana. "Hot pans are for grown-ups." Wesley pulled his hand back.

The bread sat on the wood table. Wesley saw the bread. It was brown and round. He heard it crackle. Then he smelled it. "Yum," said Wesley. "My nose smells it!" Miss Ana gave him a small mirror. "Look at your nose," she said. Wesley looked. He saw two little holes. "What are these?" he asked. "They are called nostrils," said Miss Ana. "Two nostrils!" Wesley shouted. He took a big sniff through both of them. The bread smell came in strong.

Miss Ana cut one slice. She gave Wesley a small piece. He tasted it. "Sweet," said Wesley. "My tongue knows!" He wiggled his toes in his shoes. "My feet can't taste," he said. Miss Ana laughed. "No, feet just walk," she said. Wesley hugged her leg. "My arms hug," he said. Then he took another sniff. Two nostrils, one big smell.

Sienna sat in her car seat. She hugged her brown teddy. But Bunny was gone. "Bunny is lost," she said. Her tummy felt worried.

Mama turned around from the front seat. "Don't worry. We will find Bunny," she said. "First we go home. Then we retrace our steps."

"What is that?" asked Sienna.

"It means going back to each place we went, in order," said Mama.

The car stopped at home. Sienna ran to the porch. She looked by the door. No Bunny. Next, they drove to the shop. Sienna looked at the bread shelf. No Bunny. Last, they drove to the park.

Sienna walked back along the path. First she stopped at the swings. She looked under the seat. No Bunny. Then she stopped at the slide. There, at the bottom, was Bunny! Sienna picked her up.

"Retracing worked!" said Sienna. She hugged Bunny tight. "Thank you, Mama," she said.

Back in the car, the warm sun came in. The lamp post glowed outside. Bunny sat beside teddy on the seat. Sienna closed her eyes. "Home soon," she whispered. Mama smiled and drove on.

Thomas stood by the big door. The hall was full of people. They were all smiling and talking. He held his grandma's hand tight.

Drums started to boom. People began to dance. Thomas hid behind grandma's coat. "Look," said grandma. "Music and dancing go together. They are part of the party."

Thomas peeked out. His uncle twirled by like a big spinning top. His cousin hopped like a bunny. Thomas giggled. He wished he could dance too.

The music got faster. Grandma held out her hand. "Want to try?" she asked. Thomas took one small step. Then another. Soon his feet were hopping too! He spun and bumped into uncle's big belly. "Oof!" said uncle, laughing. "You squashed me!"

The drums boomed on. Thomas danced and danced until it was late. On the walk home, his feet kept hopping on the street. "Stop dancing, sleepy boy," grandma said. But his toes ticked like a little clock, all the way home.

Stella looked out the window. The sky had been stormy last night. Now the backyard was all white. "No school today!" said Dad. "A snow day surprise!"

Stella put on her boots and her red coat. Dad pulled the sled out of the shed. There was a little hill by the fence. Stella wanted to go down fast. She lay on her tummy. "Head first!" she said.

"Not like that," said Dad. He helped her sit up. "Face the way you are going. Hold on here." He stood at the bottom of the hill. Stella touched the sled with both mittens. Down she went, sitting up, facing forward. Whee!

"I want to try again!" she said. Dad watched from his spot. She slid down five more times. Then Stella made a snow cow. It had a carrot for a nose. "Moo," said Dad. Stella laughed and laughed. "One more sled ride," she said. "Watch me, Dad!"

Theodore stood in the gym at school. Miss Polly put a hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in," she said. Theodore threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. He threw it again. This time it went in. The hoop did not move, but the beanbag stayed. Theodore laughed. One throw made the beanbag land.

Then Miss Polly rolled a big red ball to him. He held out his hands. The ball hit them and bounced out. It rolled away across the floor. Miss Polly rolled it back. Again it bounced out. Theodore wanted to hold it so much. This time he caught it and hugged it to his chest. The ball stayed right there. He did not let go.

"You did it!" said Miss Polly. She clapped. Theodore spun around with the ball still tucked in his arms. Later they sat for a snack. He wore his blue hat and ate crunchy carrots. The big red ball sat by his feet. He hugged it one more time before he went home.

Axel sat at the big table. He wanted to paint a picture of the sky. He picked up a gray crayon first. He drew a big gray sky. Then he looked out the window.

The sun was shining. The sky outside was not gray. The sky was blue. "Mama, look!" said Axel. "The sky is blue today." Mama smiled and nodded. Axel put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He drew a new blue sky. It looked just like the real one.

Then Axel wanted to build the rest of his picture. He painted a yellow sun in the corner. He painted green grass at the bottom. He painted a red ball on the grass. Every part was a different color.

Mama hung the picture on the wall. Axel stood back and looked at it. "Blue sky, sunny day," he said softly. Mama clapped her hands. Axel clapped too.

Chloe went to the store with Grandma. She wanted a red balloon. The store was out of red ones. "We can look again next week," said Grandma. Chloe held Grandma's hand. A big pig statue stood by the door. It was too heavy to move. Chloe patted its nose.

Outside, they waited at the street. A tall light hung over the road. It turned red. All the cars stopped. "Red means stop," said Chloe. The light turned green. The cars all went. "Green means go!" she called.

Back home, Chloe found a yellow crayon. She drew the tall light. She drew a green one, and cars going. She drew a red one, and cars stopping. Then she drew a blue sky over it all. Chloe hung her picture by the door. "Now we can practice," she said.

Nathan went to the park with his dad. They were bringing home a baby guinea pig. Nathan wanted to carry her around. He held her with one hand and stood up tall.

"Sit down on the grass," said Dad. "Hold her with two hands." Nathan sat down. He cupped his two hands under her. The guinea pig felt warm and soft.

Nathan tried to stand. She wiggled. Nathan sat right back down. "Two hands, sitting down," said Dad. Nathan held her with two hands, sitting down. The guinea pig made a little squeak. That was the surprise. She licked his thumb.

"She likes me," said Nathan. Dad smiled. At home, Nathan helped clean her bowl. He held her again, with two hands, sitting down on the floor.

Charles sat at the little table at school. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name all by himself. "C for Charles!" he said.

He pressed down the pencil. Then his paper slipped away. His C went wiggly and long. "Oh no!" said Charles. His teacher came over. "Try your other hand," she said. Charles put his other hand flat on the paper. He held it still.

Now he drew the C. The paper did not slip. The C was round and neat. Then he made an H, an A, and more letters. He wrote C-H-A-R-L-E-S! Charles jumped up. He ran to show his friend. "Look! I wrote my whole name!" he said. His friend clapped and clapped.

Elijah sat in a small room at the vet. A puppy sat in a box beside him. The puppy was tiny and brown. "Is he mine now?" Elijah asked. "Yes," said Mom. "He is your first pet."

The vet smiled. She clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. "There," she said. "The leash." Elijah held the leash with both hands. It felt smooth and long.

Then a bird flew by the door. The puppy wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash was clipped to his collar. And Elijah held on tight. So the puppy stayed close to Elijah. "Look, Mom!" said Elijah. "The leash keeps him close to me!"

At home, the puppy's tummy made a little growl. "Is he hungry?" Elijah wondered. Mom said yes. Elijah filled the bowl. The puppy ate it all up. Then he got sleepy, not grumpy at all. He curled up on his blanket.

"Can we walk him tomorrow?" Elijah asked. Mom laughed. "Yes. And you can hold the leash." Elijah patted the puppy's soft head. "Good night, puppy," he whispered.

Rosalie went to Grandma's house. Lots of cars sat outside. "Why so many cars?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "It is a special holiday. Families gather together to celebrate." Rosalie looked and looked. Aunties and uncles walked in the door. Then came her cousin Leo! She had not seen Leo for a long, long time. "Leo!" she called. They hugged and jumped.

Inside, Grandma set out little clay lamps. Grandma lit them with a match. Rosalie watched from far away. The lamps made the room glow.

"Look," said Rosalie. "The lamps are round like a wheel." Grandma laughed. "Yes, little and round."

Rosalie held Leo's hand. They walked past the lamps together.

"More lamps, more light," said Rosalie. Leo clapped.

Austin went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big orange carrot on the shelf. The carrot looked like a rocket ship. "Zoom, zoom," said Austin.

But a lady with a cart stood in the way. Austin tried to squeeze past. His tummy bumped the cart. "Oops," said Austin. "Sorry, cart!"

Mama bent down. "Say excuse me," she said. "Excuse me," said Austin. The lady smiled and moved her cart. The aisle was open! Austin walked right through.

He reached up on tiptoe. The carrot was too high. "Please, help," said Austin. Mama handed him the carrot. "Thank you," said Austin.

At home, Mama cut the carrot for snack. Austin took a crunchy bite. Then he put the frozen peas in his toy cart. "Excuse me," he told the cat. The cat moved one paw. Austin rolled his cart past, all the way to the moon.

Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp glowed soft and yellow. Daddy set down three bowls of soup. "Now we eat," said Daddy. Sophia spooned up one bite, two bites, three bites.

"I went to the park tomorrow," said Sophia.

Daddy looked up. "Tomorrow?" he asked. "Tomorrow is the day that comes next."

Sophia shook her head. "No. I already went. I went yesterday." Yesterday was the day before today. Yesterday she had slid down the big slide. Yesterday was all done.

"Mmm, yesterday you went to the park," said Daddy. "Today we eat soup. Tomorrow we can go again."

"Tomorrow," said Sophia. She held up one finger. "One more sleep?"

"One more sleep," said Daddy. "Now we eat. Later we wash our messy faces."

Sophia ate one more bite, then two. "Now it is later," she said. Her face was messy with soup.

Daddy laughed. He wiped her cheek with a soft cloth. "Now it is clean," he said.

Sophia looked at her bowl. All gone. "Tomorrow, park," she said. "After one more sleep."

"Yes," said Daddy. "One more sleep, and then the slide."

Olivia sat at the wooden table. She had red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. Mama had a question for her. "Can you paint a sunny day?" Olivia nodded fast. A sunny day! She could not wait.

She painted the sun first. Red and yellow made orange when she stirred them. "Orange like a pumpkin!" she said. Then she painted the sky blue. Big swipes of blue all across the paper.

Olivia held up her paper. She frowned. The sky was too dark. It did not look like morning at all. It looked like night. She wanted a light, bright sky. She almost cried, but she did not.

Then she saw the white paint pot. She scooped some white with her brush. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round she stirred. She stopped and looked. The blue was lighter now! It was a soft morning blue. Olivia gasped. White paint made the blue lighter!

She painted a big light sky. Then she painted green grass. She mixed yellow and blue in a cup. Round and round. Green! Olivia held up her paper high. "Look, Mama! Sun, sky, grass!" Mama clapped. "What a sunny day," said Mama. Olivia dipped her brush again. "Now I will paint pink flowers!"

Mya was in the playroom. She wanted to build a tower. Her brother Sam had the blocks. "Can I have three blocks?" she asked.

Sam gave her one big block. Then he gave her two little blocks. Mya looked at her pile. "That is only one big one," she said. "I want three."

Sam counted with her. "One, two, three," he said, tapping each block. "Three blocks. Big or little, three is three." Mya tapped them too. One, two, three. Three blocks, just like Sam said. She felt lucky to have such a nice brother.

Now she had her blocks. But she wanted more. "Can I have five?" she asked. Sam gave her five little blocks. Mya counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." Five blocks. It worked again!

Mya stacked her blocks up high. "Ten blocks in my tower," she said. She counted them from the bottom. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The tower stood tall. Then it wobbled. "Oops," said Mya. Sam laughed and held it steady. "Good job," he said. Mya put one more block on top, very slowly.

Blake's teddy, Brown, felt hot. He was sick, and he would not smile.

"I will be your doctor," Blake said. She held a spoon of pretend medicine to his mouth. "Drink this." Brown drank it all up. Then Blake got her old blanket. She tucked Brown into bed, just like Mama does for her. She patted his head. "Sleep now, little bear."

Brown slept for a long time. Blake waited. Then Brown blinked his eyes. Blake gave him a pretend sandwich and a pretend cup of tea. "Eat and grow strong," she said. Brown grew strong. He jumped out of bed and danced on the rug.

"My job is done," said Doctor Blake. She put her toys in a neat row. Brown sat on the pillow and waved his paw. "Same time tomorrow," Blake whispered.

Jacob ran to the playground. He ran fast. His baby sister Lily went slow. She rode in her wagon.

Jacob saw a big slide and a small slide. He took the big one. The sun felt hot. Lily's juice box was cold. She drank it all up.

Then it was naptime for Lily. She laid in the wagon under a tree. But Ben was there. Ben banged his drum. He banged it loud. Lily woke up and cried.

"Can you make it quiet?" Jacob asked.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Ben. "Watch this."

Ben tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. So quiet. So soft. Lily closed her eyes. She fell asleep.

"Shh," said Jacob. He gave Ben a pretend gift, a big green leaf.

"Ooh," said Ben. "Is it smelly?"

"It's a grassy smell," said Jacob.

They giggled, very, very quietly.

Jake ran to the window at school. It was raining. Big drops went tap, tap, tap.

"No park today," said his friend Mia. Her face looked sad. Her mouth turned down.

Jake felt sad too. He wanted the swings. He wanted the slide.

Then Miss Lily clapped her hands. "We can build a fort inside!" she said.

Jake felt excited. His tummy went flutter, flutter. He got a clean blanket from the shelf. Mia got another one. They put the blankets over two chairs. It made a little house.

"Come in," said Jake. Mia crawled inside. It was soft and warm. It smelled like soap and grandma's hugs.

"My turn to spell a word," said Mia. She spelled C-A-T on the fort wall with her finger.

Jake laughed. His sad feeling was gone. Now he felt happy.

"See," said Mia, smiling wide. "I'm happy now."

Jake smiled back and pulled the blanket snug.

Edouard loved the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. It came to his street every Tuesday.

Edouard ran to the steps. He saw his friend Pia show a small card. The man at the desk scanned it. Then Pia took a book home.

"I want a card too," said Edouard. "Can I get one today?"

He tried to sign up all by himself. The man shook his head. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," he said.

Edouard looked around. There was Grandma, waiting by the steps. He begged her, "Please come with me!"

Grandma followed him to the desk. She wrote her name. Edouard wrote his own name too. His letters wiggled like little worms. The man smiled and gave him a shiny new card.

Edouard picked a book about diggers. He held the card up high. "Look what my name did!" he said. Grandma laughed as the digger book fell open in his hands.

Sara ran to the park with her bunny. She hugged him tight. "We will play all day!" she said.

Then Sara saw the swings. She ran so fast. She pumped her legs. She went up high. But when she jumped off, her hands were empty. Her bunny was gone!

Sara looked in the sandbox. One, two, three scoops. No bunny. A dog barked at her. "Woof, woof!" Sara looked behind the bench. She looked by the water cup fountain. Still no bunny.

A park lady with a thin red scarf came over. "Try the lost and found," she said. "People put things they find there. Then the owners can get them back."

Sara ran to the little green box. She opened the lid. One mitten. One hat. One bunny!

"Bunny!" Sara shouted. She hugged him soft and warm. "Now we swing together." And she held him tight, up and up, all the way home.

Mia was thirsty after helping Mama shop. She wanted cold milk. The big fridge was closed. "Closed means shut tight," said Mama. Mia pulled the door. Now it was open! She got her small cup. She drank the milk fast, like a bunny. Then she put the cup down slow, like a turtle.

Mama was at the stove. The stove was hot, so Mama held the pan. Mia stayed far away. "Is the fridge open or shut?" Mama asked. Mia looked. The door was open. Could the door be open and shut? No, it was one or the other. Open and shut were opposites, Mama said.

Mia pushed the door. Click. It was shut now. "I closed it!" she said. The fridge hummed its happy hum. One door, shut tight. "Good job," said Mama. "Do you want warm oatmeal too?" Mia nodded and watched the pot bubble.

At school, Miss Dana held up a big cloth bag. "It is a feely bag," she said. "You put your hand in. You touch. You guess." Scarlett wanted to go first. It was her favorite game.

Scarlett put her hand in the bag. The thing inside felt round and smooth. "A ball!" she said. She rolled it in her fingers. Then she shouted, "A red ball!" Miss Dana smiled. "Now pull it out and look." Scarlett pulled it out. The ball was blue! Everyone laughed, even Scarlett. "My fingers told me it was a ball," she said. "My fingers did not tell me the color."

Next came Ben. He patted the bag. He felt something soft. "A sock! Is it green?" He pulled it out. The sock was yellow. "Close try," said Scarlett. "You must use your eyes for colors."

Then Scarlett felt again. Something small and bumpy. "Is it a crayon?" she asked. Miss Dana nodded. "What color do you see?" Scarlett looked. The crayon was green, her favorite color. On the wall, Miss Dana pointed to a sign with green on it. "Green like the grass," said Scarlett. "I saw it with my eyes!"

Zoe rode in the car with Daddy. The road was long and the sky was cloudy. "We are going to meet the baby," said Daddy.

At the hospital, Mommy sat in a big bed. A tiny baby was in her arms. "This is your new brother," said Mommy. Zoe looked at the baby. He was so small. Everyone looked at the baby. Nobody looked at Zoe. She wanted to hide under the chair.

Then the baby made a little cry. "Oh," said Mommy. "He needs a clean diaper." Daddy looked in the bag. He could not find it. "Zoe, can you help?" he asked. "Big sisters can fetch things."

Zoe ran to the bag. She found the clean diaper. She brought it to Daddy. "Thank you, Zoe," said Mommy. "Now can you find a soft blanket?"

Zoe found a blue blanket. She carried it to the bed. Daddy put the diaper on the baby. Then he wrapped the baby in the blanket. The baby stopped crying. He opened his little eyes.

"Sit here," said Mommy. Zoe sat next to her. Mommy laid the baby in Zoe's arms. Zoe held him very softly. "Hello, baby," said Zoe. The baby held her finger.

Elena stood by her bedroom window. It was windy outside. The tree waved its leaves. On her table was a little toy pond with a small duck floating on it.

Elena wanted the duck. She reached up on her toes. Her teddy bear sat on the edge of the table. Oops. The teddy fell down. He landed on the floor, face down.

Elena felt scared. She ran over. She picked teddy up. His head drooped. He looked sad. Elena patted his soft ears. Then she held him close and asked, "Are you okay?"

Teddy did not answer. But Elena asked again, soft and slow. "Are you okay, teddy?" She gave him a hug. His head popped up. Now he looked happy again. Elena smiled a big smile. She felt excited.

"Mama!" she called. "I asked teddy if he was okay!" Mama came in. "That was kind," said Mama. Elena sat teddy on the pillow. She kissed his nose.

Then Elena pointed at the duck. "Can I send the duck across the pond?" Mama blew on the water, gently. The duck sailed to the other side.

Elena clapped her hands. "Again!" she said.

Mason was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to write his name all by himself. Grandpa gave him a big pencil. "Hold it like this," Grandpa said. He turned the pencil in Mason's small hand. The cat sat on the table to watch.

Mason tried the letter M. It came out wiggly. "Why is it so hard?" he asked. "Try it again and see," said Grandpa. So Mason wrote M, then M, then M. Each M looked better. "M, A, S, O, N," he said, naming the letters. He wrote his whole name. Then he wrote it again. The letters came out neat.

The next day, Mason wrote his name again. It was easy now. He was not afraid of the big M anymore. "Look, Grandpa! I did it five times!" Grandpa laughed. "Put it on the fridge," he said. Mason clapped his hands and picked up the pencil one more time.

Owen got to the playground early. The sun felt warm on his face. He wanted to go on the big red swing. But a big kid was on it. Owen waited and waited. He sat on a bench with his little pillow from the car. He did not say anything. He just frowned. Dad looked at him. Dad did not know what was wrong. Then Owen said, "I feel sad. I want the red swing." Dad smiled. "Now I can help you," Dad said. Dad asked the big kid to take turns. The big kid said yes! Owen clapped his hands. The swing went up high. The wind whooshed past his ears. "I feel happy!" Owen shouted. Dad laughed and gave him a big push.

Matteo put on his swim shorts. He ran to the pool door. "Wait!" Dad called. "We take a shower first."

Matteo stopped. "A shower?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." Matteo looked at the little shower by the wall. The water was warm. It made his hair thick and wet.

Then Matteo saw a girl run past. She jumped up and down. "I want the pool!" she shouted. A lifeguard held up one hand. "Shower first," the lifeguard said. The girl looked at the shower. The water went splish, splish. She ran under it and laughed.

"Your turn," said Dad. Matteo stood under the warm water. It ran down his nose. "Now the pool?" he asked. "Now the pool," said Dad. Matteo walked to the steps. He kicked his legs in the blue water. "I did it!" he shouted. "I showered, and then I swam!" Dad clapped his hands. "Look at you, Matteo!" said Dad. "Look at you go!"

Layla woke up in her big girl bed. Her heart was happy. Today she would wear her new dress.

She jumped out of bed. She ran to her mirror. "Oh no," said Layla. Her hair looked like a bird's nest. It was all puffy and wild.

"I can't wear my dress like this," she said. She found her brush on the shelf. She touched her hair. There were little knots in it. She pulled the brush fast. "Ow!" she said. That hurt.

Layla thought for a minute. She tried again. She brushed slowly, one small bit at a time. The knots came out, one by one. Soon her hair was smooth and shiny. "It worked!" she said.

Mama came in with her yellow dress. "You brushed your own hair," said Mama. "May I ask how it got so pretty?" "I brushed it slow," said Layla. "The slow way wins."

After her bath that night, Mama helped her put on pajamas. Layla was tired but still awake. She put the brush by her bed. "For my morning nest," she said. She patted her smooth hair and closed her eyes.

Evan ran to the block corner. He wanted the big red blocks. He was the last one there. Mia had them first.

"My turn!" Evan shouted. His voice was very loud.

Then he heard a small sound. It went "wah, wah." The teacher's baby was sleeping in a little bed by the window. The teacher put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she whispered. "The baby is sleeping. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice."

Evan made his voice tiny. "My turn?" he whispered. Mia nodded. "You can have some blocks. I will share." Evan dug into the bin. He found a long stick block. He held it up. "Look what I found," he whispered. Mia smiled and took a quiet turn with it too.

The baby kept sleeping. The room was soft and calm. Evan whispered, "Is the baby still asleep?" Mia peeked with him. "Yes," she said. "We were quiet."

The baby woke up and blinked. The teacher said, "Time for snack now." Evan whispered, "The baby can come too."

Wyatt wants to go down the big slide at school. But the slide is tall. His feet feel small on the ground. He runs to his friend Mia. "Watch me," Mia says. She climbs up the ladder. Up, up, up she goes. Then she slides down, down, down. "Up and down are opposites," Mia says with a smile.

Wyatt looks at the ladder. He puts one hand on a rail. Then the other hand. He takes a step up. Then one more. His knees feel a little weak. Mia waits at the bottom. "You can do it," she says. Wyatt climbs up some more. Now he is at the top!

He sits down on the slide. He takes a big breath. Whoosh! He goes down, down, down. His tummy tickles. He lands in the soft sand. "I did it!" Wyatt says. Mia claps her hands. Then they build a little hill in the sand together. Wyatt slides his hand down the small hill. "Fast," he says. He climbs up again for another turn.

Alice wants to make soup for dinner. She wants to make it all by herself. "I will be the cook," she says. Dad will help a little bit.

First, Dad fills the big pot with water. Alice drops in three carrots. Plop, plop, plop. She adds a potato shaped like a square. "A square potato," says Alice. "How funny." Dad laughs too.

Then Dad cuts the onion. He cuts it into little bits. Suddenly Dad's eyes water. Tears run down his face. Alice stops. "Dad, are you sad?" she asks. "Do you need a hug?" Dad wipes his eyes. "No, no," he says. "The onion makes my eyes sting. Onions can do that. Watch." He cuts one more bit, and his eyes water again.

Alice giggles. "Dad is crying onion tears," she says. "Onion tears, onion tears!" She brings him a towel for his face. Then she stirs the soup from her safe spot, far from the hot pot. Dad lifts her up so she can see. The soup bubbles. It smells warm and good.

At dinner, Mom takes one bite. "Mmm," says Mom. "Who made this?" Alice puffs up tall. "The cook did. But the onion made Dad cry first." Dad winks and pretends to cry again. Alice laughs so hard that milk almost comes out of her nose. Then she gives the soup one more stir with her big spoon, like a real cook.

Nathan stood on the ferry with his big brother, Sam. The water went splash, splash against the boat. Nathan held his little blue bag. "One bag for me," he said. "Two bags for Sam. Three bags for Mama." Mama counted the bags too.

Nathan opened his bag. He pulled out his swimsuit. "I will swim at the mountain," he said. Sam laughed. "No, Nathan. Look out the window." Nathan looked. The mountains far away were white with snow. Snow, snow, and more snow.

Mama knelt down. "We pack clothes that fit the weather where we are going," she said. "Snowy weather needs warm clothes, not a swimsuit." Nathan put the swimsuit back. He found his black mittens instead. One mitten, two mittens. He put them on. The wool felt soft and warm on his hands.

That night, Nathan had a dream. He dreamed he built a big snowman wearing his very own swimsuit. He laughed in his sleep. In the morning, the ferry blew its loud horn. "To the snow!" Nathan shouted, waving his black mittens out over the rails.

Leon was playing store on the kitchen floor. His toys sat in one big line. His teddy bear was the first shopper. "I want to buy things," said Bear, in a growly voice.

Mom gave Leon a basket of things from the kitchen. Inside were an apple, some bread, and one fresh carrot. Leon picked up the carrot. He put it with the toy cars. "Cars do not eat carrots," said Bear. Leon giggled and put the carrot next to the apple. Then the bread went there too.

"Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Bear. Leon clapped. Bear paid with a shiny button. Then Bear bit the carrot, and juice went drip, drip, drip all over the floor. "Bear!" laughed Leon. "You made a carrot river!" He grabbed a towel and followed the drip all the way to the rug.

Lea sat on the city bus next to her mom. She held her new library card in both hands. It had her name on it. On her lap was a book about a big orange cat.

The bus went bump, bump, down the street. Lea felt the seat shake under her. She found a crayon in her pocket. She put the crayon point on the cat page. She wanted to give the cat snowy white whiskers.

Her mom saw the crayon. "Wait," said Mom. "That book belongs to the library. Many other kids share it too. We take care not to draw in it or tear it." Lea pulled the crayon back fast. She looked at the cat. Other kids would want to see those pages too.

Mom pulled some paper from her bag. Lea drew her own cat on the paper. She gave it snowy whiskers and a big smile. The bus went bump, bump, and Lea kept drawing.

At their stop, Mom took Lea's hand. Lea carried the library book under her arm, nice and safe. "Home now," said Mom. Lea said, "Bye bye, bus. Bye bye, cat."

Rose wanted Grandpa to read her book. But the sky was cloudy, so the room was dim. "I can't see the words," Grandpa said. He put on his glasses. Then he could read. Rose wanted to see the glasses too.

She touched them with her fingers. They felt cool and smooth. She heard a little click when they closed. Grandpa let her look. "Do they help you see?" he asked. Rose put them on. The book looked big and funny. "No," she said. "My eyes see fine." Grandpa laughed softly.

He took the glasses back. He read the story. Rose smelled cookies in the oven. Mom brought one over. Rose tasted the sweet cookie. She touched the warm plate. "Read it again," said Rose. Grandpa smiled and turned the page.

Felix went to the library with his grandma. The librarian had set out big mats and three boxes. One box had a picture of animals. One box had a picture of toys. One box had a picture of foods. "Can you sort these for me?" the librarian asked. Felix nodded his head yes.

He picked up a card with an apple on it. Apples are food. He put it in the food box. He picked up a card with a bear on it. A bear is an animal. It went in the animal box. Then he found a card with a little black dog on it. A dog is an animal, he thought. He put it in the animal box.

Then he looked again. The dog was soft and stuffed. It did not bark. It did not wiggle. It was not alive. "Is this dog a toy?" Felix asked. Grandma smiled. "Look close," she said. Felix held the card up. "Yes, it is a toy," he said. He moved it to the toy box.

"Good sorting," said the librarian. She showed Felix a stamp of a gold star. She pressed it on his hand. Felix laughed and waved the stamp goodbye. "See you next time," he said.

Charlie got a new bunny. He carried the cage to the backyard. "Hello, bunny!" he said. He opened the cage door. He put out a bowl of water.

The bunny did not hop out. The bunny hid in the back of the cage. Charlie waited. Still the bunny hid. Charlie felt sad. He wanted to pet his bunny so much.

Mom came out with a chair. "Sit here," she said. "The bunny needs time. A new pet hides at first." Charlie sat down. He sat very still. He looked at the clouds. He looked at the flowers.

Then the bunny's nose came out. Then one ear. Then the whole bunny! It hopped into the grass. Charlie giggled. He let the bunny sniff his shoe. "You are safe here," Charlie whispered. Mom took a photo with her phone. Charlie filled the water bowl again, just in case.

Hunter ran into the backyard. He wanted to go down his little slide. The slide sat by the grass. Hunter climbed up the steps. He lay down on his tummy. His head went first. That felt wrong. His tummy did not like it. Hunter turned himself around. Now his feet went first. Down he went, whee, into the soft grass.

Dad was cooking at the grill. Hunter could smell the warm corn. "The grill is hot," said Dad. "I will hold the food. You stay close to me." Hunter stayed by Dad's feet. He did not touch the grill.

After lunch, Hunter built with his red block. He stacked it high. Then he made a messy pile of leaves for his toy truck. The truck went down the leaf pile, feet first, just like Hunter on the slide. Hunter clapped his hands. "Again," he said.

Sienna sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. Her tummy felt stormy. "I don't like shots," she whispered. "The needle might hurt."

The nurse came in with a little tray. A small needle lay on it. Sienna pointed. "Can I hold the needle? I want to see it."

The nurse smiled. "Only I touch the needle," she said. "That is my job, not yours. But you can hold my sticker sheet."

Sienna took the sticker sheet. It had a flower sticker on top. "I will hold this," she said.

"Good," said the nurse. "Now look at your flower." Sienna looked. The nurse gave the shot so fast. "All done!"

"Wait. That was it?" said Sienna. "It did not hurt much!" She put the flower sticker on her arm.

Afterward, Mom took Sienna to the ice cream shop. Sienna got a pink cone. She licked it and smiled.

The nurse had a needle, and Sienna had a sticker. That was just right.

Leo ran to the play corner at school. Mia and Sam were already there. "The floor is a river!" said Mia. She hopped onto a cushion. "This is my rock."

Leo stopped at the edge. He wanted to play house across the river. But how could he cross? He put one foot on the floor. "No!" cried Sam. "You will splash in the water!"

Leo looked around. He saw three cushions. One, two, three. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three!" Then he jumped. One cushion. Two cushions. Three cushions. He made it to the other side.

"You did it!" said Mia. She handed him a doll. "The baby is sick. Can you help?"

Leo patted the doll. He wrapped her in a small blanket. "My sister does this at home," he said. "She rocks the baby so soft."

"It is not a real baby," said Sam. "We are just pretending. But we act like it is real!"
