"Yes!" said Leo. He took his turn to rock the doll. He sang a little song.

Then Mia said, "Time to cook dinner!" She turned a pretend knob on the toy stove. Leo clapped. "Dinner on a rock in a river!" he said. "Best house ever!"

James ran into writing club. "I want to write my name today!" he said. Ms. Rosa smiled. She gave him a fat pencil and showed him how to hold it. "Pinch it like this," she said. "Now pick your letters."

James looked at his name card. J, A, M, E, S. Ms. Rosa had put the letters in two trays. One tray was full of straight letters. A went in. M went in. E went in. The other tray had curvy letters. J went there. S went there too.

"That one pops right in the curvy tray," said James. He laughed.

Then he wrote. Straight lines for A. Curves for S. His letters made a word. "JAMES! I did it!" he shouted. "My name popped onto the paper!"

Kayden ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. But first, his hands needed a wash. "Soap, water, rub," said Mama. Kayden counted, "One, two, three." He kept rubbing the soap. "Ten, eleven, twelve." Bubbles grew on his hands. "Nineteen, twenty!" Kayden pulled his hands out of the sink. The water did not stop there. It went drip, drip, drip. A drop would fall on his shirt. A drop would fall on the floor. "Where do the drips go?" Kayden wondered. He shook his hands. More drips fell! Then he saw it. A soft white towel hung by the sink. Kayden dried one hand. Then he dried the other hand. All the drips went away. His hands were clean and dry. "Last step," said Kayden. Then he sat down and took a big bite of lunch.

Wyatt dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped in a carrot seed. Mom helped him pat the soil down straight and flat. Every day he came back with his spoon and gave the seed a tiny drink of water.

One morning, green leaves popped up. Wyatt smiled wide. But then he saw more green leaves, in a spot where he had not planted anything. Hmm, he thought. What is this little plant doing here?

He grabbed the funny plant and pulled. "Wait," said Mom. She held his hand. "That one is a carrot. It grows where we planted it. The other one grows where we do not want it. That one is called a weed." Wyatt looked at both plants. One grew in his hole. One grew on the path. He let go of the carrot. He pulled the weed instead, all by himself.

Weeks later, Mom dug up a big orange carrot. She washed it at the sink. Wyatt took a bite and chewed happily. "It grew from my seed," he said. "It grew in the right spot!"

Lillian ran to the toy box. She wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She found a block with four flat sides. "A square!" she said.

Lillian stacked the square on top. Then it slipped. It turned on its side. Now one corner pointed up. Her brother Ben peeked in. "That is a new shape," he said. "No it isn't," said Lillian. She grabbed the block. She gave it a turn. The corner went down. The flat side sat on the floor. "Look! It is the same square," she said. Ben clapped. "The square was hiding!"

Lillian used the square for the door. She found two triangles for the roof. A circle became a window. A long rectangle made a bed. The silly snake slid right in. "Home at last," said Ben. Lillian smiled and rang a little bell.

Owen sat in the waiting room. He held his teddy bear tight. "Your turn," said the nurse. Owen took a big step into the small room. Dad gave him a hug first. The nurse said, "This is quick." Owen looked at his teddy. Then he felt a tiny pinch in his arm. "All done!" said the nurse. "That was fast," said Owen. He got a nice bandage with a star on it.

In the car, Owen rubbed his arm. "It feels sore," he said. "Will it stay sore?" he asked. Dad said, "The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while. It will feel better soon." Owen nodded. He held his teddy's paw.

At home, Owen played with his blocks. He built a tall tower. Then he looked at his arm. The star bandage was still there. He touched it softly. "Not sore now," he said. He smiled at Dad. "Want a hug?" asked Dad. "Yes," said Owen. He ran over fast.

Lena woke up in her bedroom. Today was the day. Mom had said, "Today we go to the store." Yesterday they had not gone. Yesterday it rained. Tomorrow would be too late, because tomorrow the store would be closed.

"Now?" Lena asked. "Can we go now?" Mom was still brushing her hair. "Not yet," said Mom. "We go later."

Lena did not like later. Later felt very long. She asked again. "Now?" Then the clock on her bedroom wall made its loud tick sound. Mom pointed to it. "Look," she said. "The clock shows what time it is." Lena looked at the little hands. "When the short hand points to the nine, then we go," said Mom.

Lena watched the clock. Tick, tick, tick. The short hand moved a tiny bit. She got dressed while she watched. She put on her shoes. She found her red hat. She watched some more. Then the short hand was at the nine. "It is nine!" she shouted. "It is time now!" Mom laughed and took her hand.

At the store, Lena picked out apples. She put them in the bag all by herself. "Thank you," she said to the man at the counter. Mom smiled. "We can come back tomorrow too," said Mom. Lena held up the apples. "When the clock says it is time," she said.

Athena put on her warm coat. She put on her red boots. It was snowy at the park. The snow was white and soft. "Snowy day, snowy day!" said Athena. She scooped up a big snowball. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Grandma said, "Put it in your pocket, then." Athena held the cold snowball tight.

At home, Athena took out her snowball. She set it in a glass. "Now I will look at it every day," she said. She went to draw a picture. The sun came out. It was sunny in the window.

Later, Athena came back. She looked in the glass. "Oh no!" she cried. "My snowball is gone. Now it is just water." The warm room had melted it. Snow melts into water where it is warm. "Don't worry," said Grandma. "We can make a new one. And we can grow a paper snowball that stays." Athena smiled. "Snowy day, snowy day," she said, and hugged Grandma tight.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two," she said. Then she stopped. "Oh no," she said. "I forgot what comes next." Her lip wobbled and she looked upset.

Mom smiled. "Sing your shoe song," she said. "The one from the car."

Aubrey sang. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." She peeked at her plate. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." She pushed a pea with her spoon. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!"

"Look, Mom! I counted to ten!" said Aubrey. "The song helped me remember."

"Yes it did," said Mom. "Now let's count your carrots."

Aubrey pointed at the carrots. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Dad tapped his spoon to the beat. Aubrey giggled and kept going, all the way to ten again.

After dinner, they drew a big hen. Mom drew a river by the hen. Aubrey drew ten little sticks beside it.

"One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang, and added one more stick.

Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had a soft pillow and a big book. The book was full of letters. Charlie pointed at a curvy letter. "What is that one?" she asked.

"That is S," said Dad. "S says sss." Charlie made the sound too. "Sss," she said. "Sss like a snake!" Dad smiled and nodded.

Charlie went on a hunt. She wanted more sss things. She found her sock. "Sock starts with S!" she said. She found a small bag of sand. "Sand starts with S too!" Then she saw sun light on the rug. "Sun! Sss!" Charlie laughed. "Sun, sock and sand. All S!" She hugged the book like a feather had landed on her. "Stinky socks," Dad said with a giggle. Charlie giggled too. "Sss!" she said.

Ava packed her little red bag. She was going to the beach with Mommy and Daddy. Grandma waved from her door. "Bring me a shell!" she said.

The car drove a long, long way. Ava watched trees go by. Then her tummy felt funny. "I need the potty," she said. Daddy said, "We can stop soon. There is a place ahead." Ava asked, "What place?" Mommy said, "A rest stop." The car turned in. Ava held Mommy's hand and used the potty. Then she stretched her arms up high. "Look how tall!" she said.

Back in the car, the drive felt short now. Soon Ava saw blue water. A white boat did float on the waves. Ava ran to the sand with Daddy. She found a pink shell. "This one is for Grandma," she said.

Ivy went to the library with Dad. She got her very first library card. It had her name on it. She picked a big book about a worm. The worm was long and wiggly. "I want to keep this book forever," Ivy said.

The librarian stamped a paper. "This book goes back on your due date," she said. "That is the day it has to come back." Dad read the paper. "Your due date is Saturday," he said. Ivy held the book tight. "But I love the worm book." Dad said, "You can love it, and then bring it back."

At home, Ivy read the worm book three times. She read it to her teddy bear. She read it in her dry, sunny window seat. Saturday came. Ivy put the book in her bag. She carried it to the desk all by herself. Then she saw the shelf. "Can I take this one now?" she asked. The librarian smiled and stamped a new paper. "A new due date," she said. Ivy hugged the new book. "See you on Saturday," she told the worm book on the shelf.

Raphael stood in the pool changing room with his dad. His swim shorts had a tight waist. Dad helped pull them up. "Swim time!" said Raphael. He ran to the door.

Dad caught his hand. "Walk, please. Wet floors are slippery," said Dad. "So we walk near the pool." Raphael looked down. The floor was shiny and wet. It even smelled like pool water. He tried one big step. His foot slid a little. Whoops!

"I see it," said Raphael. "Wet floor, slippery feet!" He walked slowly, one step at a time. His feet stayed under him. At the door, a small surprise waited. His friend Mia was there, holding a rubber duck. "Want to play a walking game?" she asked. "Who walks slowest wins?" Raphael laughed and walked with her all the way to the pool.

Sofia sat at the big table. She had paper and crayons. Her mom had a bag of letter cards. Sofia pulled one out. "S," she said. "S makes the sss sound, like a snake."

Mom smiled. "Now find S somewhere in the house." Sofia looked and looked. She stopped at her lunch box. There was her name on it. S-o-f-i-a. "There is my S!" she said.

"Write your name," said Mom. Sofia wrote it slowly. She made a small s first. It looked little and shy next to the other letters. Mom wrote Sofia's name on her own paper. Mom's S was big and tall. "Your S is a capital letter," Mom said. "A name starts with a big one." Sofia looked at her small s. Then she looked at Mom's big one.

Sofia rubbed out her small s. She drew a big capital S. She sat back and looked at her name. It stood up tall. "Sofia," she read out loud. "S makes sss. And my S is the big one." She held the paper up to the window so the sun could see it too.

Aaron stood in the pool changing room. He pulled on his swim shorts all by himself. Then he sat on the bench and looked at his toes. "Will the water be too big for me?" he asked. Dad smiled. "The teacher will be there," he said. "Her name is Miss Jo."

The pool room was huge and bright. Blue water made wavy lights on the wall, like someone used paint to draw them. Aaron held Dad's hand tight. Miss Jo said, "Time to float on your back." Aaron shook his head. "I will sink!" Miss Jo put her hands under his back. Her hands held him up, just like that. He did not sink. He lay on the water and looked at the ceiling.

"I'm floating!" Aaron called. Then a small surprise came. A splash of water jumped up and made the wall light wiggle. Aaron laughed. Dad waved from the side. "Can we come again tomorrow?" Aaron asked. Miss Jo said, "Yes, we sure can."

Liam looked out the window. The sky was gray. Big drops fell on the glass.

"Is it rainy today?" Liam asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Rainy and windy. See the tree move?"

The tree bent and swayed. The leaves shook.

Liam put on his boots. He put on his coat. Mom took the umbrella. It was red with yellow dots.

They walked to the car. The rain went tap, tap, tap. Mom held the umbrella over both of them.

Liam put out his hand. His hand stayed dry. The rain hit the umbrella instead.

"The umbrella keeps the rain off my head," Liam said.

"It does," said Mom. "It keeps mine dry too."

At school, Liam looked at the snow pictures on the wall. "Snow is cold," he said. "I wear my mittens in snow."

Mom smiled. "One day it will snow. Then we will wear hats and mittens."

Liam drank his juice from his cup. He sat up straight for story time.

"When will it be sunny again?" he asked.

"Soon," said Mom. "Then we wear our sun hats."

Liam waved. "Bye, Mom. Stay dry!"

Mom opened the red umbrella and walked home through the rain.

Sara ran to the little orange kitchen at the playground. "Time to make soup!" she said. She stirred leaves and pebbles in a pot. Her bear sat in a chair with a bib on. "One spoon for you, bear," said Sara. "Two spoons for baby doll. Three spoons for me." The soup smelled like leaves and sunshine.

Then Ben came over. "Can I play house too?" he asked. "You can be the dad," said Sara. Ben fed the bear a pebble pie. They laughed and made a big mess. Cups were everywhere. Leaves were on the floor.

Then Sara's mom called, "Time to go home!" Sara looked around. "Our pretend game is done," said Ben. "So the toys get put away." Sara picked up the cups. Ben put the pebbles in a bag. One, two, three, four cups. The bear went in the stroller. The kitchen was clean again. "Goodbye, little house!" said Sara. She waved at the orange pot all the way to the gate.

Emilia went to the library. She wanted her favorite book. It had a bear on the cover. Emilia looked on the shelf. She found books about cats. She found books about trucks. No bear book. Her feet tapped the floor. She wanted to kick a little, but she took a big breath instead.

The librarian knelt down. "Tell me the book's name," she said. "The name on the front is called the title." Emilia looked at a cover. There were little words there. "The words say the name?" she asked. The librarian nodded. "Yes. The words mean something."

Emilia found the bear book. The title said Bear Gets Sleepy. She opened the front cover first. She turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back. "I read the words," she said. The librarian smiled. "You found your book." Emilia hugged it tight. "Bear Gets Sleepy," she read. "That is its name."

Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. It was soup day! She wanted to make the best soup ever. Her friend Leo was already there, holding a big plastic pot.

"Let's make soup!" said Amelia. She put in a pinecone, a leaf and two round play dough balls. Then she stirred with a long wooden spoon. The soup smelled like nothing at all, but that was okay. It was pretend soup.

Amelia lifted the spoon to her mouth. She wanted to taste it. "Stop!" said Miss Kim, the teacher, coming over fast. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat." Amelia looked at the spoon. Oh! She held it near her lips and made a big slurping sound. "Sluuurp!"

Leo peeked into the pot with wide eyes. "More soup please!" he said, holding out his arm. Amelia ladled out a pretend scoop. Leo pretended to slurp too. "Yum!" he said. They both laughed and clapped.

Then Teddy the bear got a pretend bowl. Amelia fed him one tiny pretend bite. "Good job, Teddy," she said. Miss Kim gave them both a thumbs up, and Amelia stirred the pot again, faster and faster, because soup day was the best day ever.

Clara got to school and saw the snow. Big snowflakes fell. They fell fast, then they fell slow. Clara wanted to play outside. But her scarf was too short. The cold wind got in. "Brrr," said Clara.

Her friend Mia had a very long scarf. It wrapped twice around her neck. Mia said, "Mine is long. Yours is short. Long and short are opposites." Clara touched Mia's long scarf. It was soft and warm. Her own scarf felt small in her hand.

The teacher, Miss Pam, came to help. She found a big box of yarn. Clara picked red yarn. Miss Pam helped her sew. Clara worked slow and careful. First it was short. Then it got longer. Then it was very long. "I did it!" said Clara.

Outside, the snow squeaked under her boots. Clara's new scarf wrapped twice, just like Mia's. A naughty snowball flew by. It was Tom, playing a joke. Clara laughed. Then she helped sweep snow off the slide, fast, fast, fast. The slide shined. "My turn!" she called.

Lucy wanted to draw the snow. She got her doll to watch. She looked in her crayon box. "I see red, yellow, green," she said. "But where is the sky color?"

She held up a dark blue crayon. "Is this blue? It looks so dark."

Her brother Ben grabbed a pale one. "No, this one is blue. Yours is not."

Lucy lined up the crayons on the table. Light blue. Middle blue. Dark blue, like the deep night sky. "One, two, three blues!" she said.

Ben picked up the dark one. "It is blue too," he said. "Dark blue and light blue. Both are called blue."

Lucy smiled. She drew soft white snow. She drew a light blue sky up high. She drew dark blue water down low.

"Two blues, one picture," said Lucy. Her doll got a blue hat too.

Logan had a violin. It was small and shiny. He wanted to play a song for his cat.

Mom held out a long stick. "This is the bow," she said. Logan grabbed the bow. He held it the wrong way. He poked the violin with the fat end.

"Squeak!" went the violin. The cat ran under the chair. Logan made a sad face. "That was a bad sound," he said. "This is hard."

Mom sat close to him. She turned the bow in his hand. "Now pull it across the strings," she said. "Slow and smooth."

Logan pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang. It made a long, pretty note. Logan pulled again. Another sweet note filled the room.

The cat came out from under the chair. It sat down near Logan. Its tail swished to the music.

Logan played one more note. The cat purred. Mom clapped her hands. "Play it again," she said.

Logan laughed and pulled the bow across the strings one more time.

Aurora was three. Today she went to the dentist for the first time. In the waiting room there was a big fish tank and a chair that spun like a wheel. A young boy sat next to her. He held a blue toothbrush. Aurora held her green one.

The nurse said, "You can both show me how you brush." Aurora put down her green toothbrush. Then she picked up a toothbrush to brush. But it was the blue one! The boy laughed. "That is mine!" he said.

Aurora looked at the blue brush. Then she looked at the green one on the chair. She put the blue one in his hand. She took her green one back. Each person had their own toothbrush now.

The nurse said, "Ready, Aurora?" Aurora hopped up onto the big chair. It spun her around, whee, like a wheel. She opened her mouth wide and brushed her big toy teeth with her green toothbrush.

"Did I do it right?" she asked.

"Yes!" said the boy, and he clapped.

Isabella ran to the rug at school. "Story now!" she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "Not now, Isabella. Now means this very moment. The story is after snack."

Isabella looked at the clock. The big hand was not at snack yet. So she waited. First she ate her apple. Then she drank her milk. Then the clock showed snack was done.

"Now?" she asked.

"Now!" said Miss Kim. She opened the big book up high so all could see.

Isabella clapped. "Yesterday we had the bear story," she said. "Today we have the dog story!"

"That's right," said Miss Kim. "And tomorrow you can pick the book."

Isabella looked at her friend Leo. "Tomorrow I will pick the dinosaur book," she told him.

"After school, I will tell my mom at dinner," said Leo.

Isabella sat up tall. She had waited, and the story came.

Miss Kim turned the first page. "Once there was a little brown dog," she read.

Leon was at Grandma's house. Snowy flakes fell outside the window. Today Leon would help make bread.

Grandma let him pour the flour. She added water. Leon mixed it with a spoon. Then he touched it with his hands. The dough stuck to his fingers. It felt gooey and lumpy.

"Oh no," said Leon. "The bread is ruined. It is all sticky."

Grandma laughed softly. "It is not ruined," she said. "Watch me." She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

"Can I try?" asked Leon.

"Yes," said Grandma. "This is how cooks do it."

Leon pushed the dough. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his hands. The dough turned smooth and soft. It made a funny squishy noise.

Grandma put the bread in the oven. Leon stood far back, because the oven was hot. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and good.

"Grandma," said Leon, "did I make this?"

"You did," said Grandma. She cut a slice. Leon took a big warm bite.

"Mmm," said Leon. "Push and fold!"

Gabriel went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm. Ducks sat by the pond and fish in the water. Gabriel had a red beanbag and a big blue ball.

There was a hoop on the grass. Gabriel wanted to throw the beanbag in. He tossed it. It hit the rim and fell out. He tried again, slower. The beanbag went in. "I did it!" said Gabriel.

Then his little friend Mia came to play. Gabriel threw the big ball to her. He threw it hard and fast. It flew past her hands and bumped her arm. Mia sat down on the grass.

"Oops," said Gabriel. He picked up the ball. He walked closer. He tossed it slow and soft. Mia held out both hands. The ball landed right in them. She laughed. "Again!" she said. Gabriel smiled and gave the ball a gentle toss.

Wyatt wanted to zoom his rocket ship. He had a small red rocket made of paper. But the rocket would not fly. It just sat on the rug.

Dad sat down next to him. "Rockets need a countdown," Dad said. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown." Wyatt patted the soft rug. He was ready to try.

"Ten, nine, eight," said Wyatt. A little bug crawled by. "Seven, six, five," he said. His tummy felt jumpy like jelly. "Four, three, two, one." He took a big breath. "Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up high. He threw the rocket into the air. It zoomed over the couch and landed on the rug. "Again!" said Wyatt. Dad laughed and held up ten fingers. "Ten," said Wyatt, and he started the countdown once more.

Elizabeth had a big box of blocks. She wanted to make a rainbow on her floor.

First she picked all the red blocks. Then she picked all the blue ones. Soon she had a red pile and a blue pile and a yellow pile. "Look, Mommy!" she said. "The colors go together!"

Then her big brother Sam came in. He sat down with her. He picked up a red block, a blue block, and a yellow block. "These are all little," he said. He put them in one pile. Then he found a red one, a blue one, and a yellow one that were all big. He put those in another pile.

Elizabeth blinked. "But the colors are all mixed!" she said. Sam laughed, gently. "You sorted by color. I sorted by size."

Elizabeth tried it too. She found all the little blocks and stacked them. Then she found all the big blocks. Her tower grew tall. But there were also square blocks and round blocks. "Those are square," she said. "Those are round."

Mommy came to look. "You sorted them three ways," she said. "Colors, sizes, and shapes." She gave Elizabeth a kiss on her head.

Outside, a truck rumbled down the street. Elizabeth waved at it. Then she picked up a round block and set it on top of her tower. It stayed. "Big round one," she said.

Alexander sat on the little red chair. The music room had drums, a piano, and a big basket of shakers. On the wall hung a small guitar with a pig sticker on it. Alexander wanted to play that guitar.

Miss Rosa took it down for him. "You can play it today," she said. Alexander pulled the strings. Plunk. Plonk. He pulled them again. It sounded funny. It did not sound like the song they sang. Alexander frowned at the pig sticker. "It sounds wrong," he said.

"Let me fix it," said Miss Rosa. She held the guitar and turned the little pegs at the top. Turn, turn, turn. "This is called tuning," she said. Then she pulled a string. Ding. It sounded clear and sweet.

Miss Rosa gave the guitar back. Alexander pulled the strings. Ding. Ding. Ding. He sang their hello song, and the guitar sang too. He tapped his itchy sweater sleeve to the beat. Then he played one more note, very soft, for the pig.

Jake wanted to play a game. "I will find all my senses," he said. His mom said, "That is a nice game."

Jake put his hands over his eyes. It was dark. He could not see the sun. He opened his eyes. "I see with my eyes!" he said. "I see the sun and the tree."

Jake found a flower. He sniffed it with his nose. "I smell with my nose," he said. He touched the grass. "I feel with my hands." A bird sang. "I hear with my ears." His mom gave him a berry. Jake ate it. "I taste with my mouth."

Then Jake got dirt on his face. His mom helped him wipe it off. "Five senses," said Jake. He held up five fingers. "Eyes, nose, hands, ears, mouth!"

His mom clapped. "You did it, Jake."

Jake covered his eyes again. "Now I see nothing!" Then he peeked. "Now I see you!"

Matthew went to the store with Mama. He held her hand. "Can we buy new socks?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "You need a pair."

Matthew looked at the sock shelf. There were red socks and blue socks. He picked up one red sock. "Where is its friend?" he wondered. "A pair means two," said Mama. "Like a pair of socks."

So Matthew looked again. He found the other red sock hiding under a blue one. He put the two socks together. "One, two," he said. "Now it is a pair!" Mama smiled.

The store had a big lamp by the shoe hats. The lamp made a warm glow on the floor. Matthew counted the shoes under it. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Can I count more?" "Count them all," said Mama.

They walked past the fruit. "What would you like?" asked Mama. "Apples," said Matthew. He put them in the bag, one at a time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He stopped and looked in the bag. "How many is that?" "Seven," said Mama. Matthew carried the bag to the man at the desk. "Hello," said the man. "Apples for you?" "Seven apples," said Matthew. "And a pair of socks!"

Aurora sat on the big clean rug. The whole family was watching the game. Aunt Rosa brought a bag of popcorn. The popcorn was warm and salty.

On the TV, tall players ran fast. One player threw the ball up high. The ball went through the hoop. The crowd cheered loud. "The ball went in the hoop!" said Dad. Everyone clapped and jumped. Aurora clapped too. She wanted to try that.

Aurora found her soft red ball. She looked around the room. She saw the laundry basket on the floor. She stood back a little. She threw the ball up. It hit the rim and fell out. She tried again. This time the ball went through the basket. "I scored!" Aurora said. She stirred her popcorn with her fingers and smiled. Dad gave her a big high five.

Elijah wanted to write his name. He had a sticky marker and some paper. He knew his name started with E. But he could not remember how to make it.

He drew a tall line. He drew some little lines. "That does not look right," he said. Mom came to sit by him.

Mom had a card. The letter E was on it. The E was bumpy, like tiny hills. "You can trace it," Mom said. "Use your finger as a tool." Elijah put his finger on the bumpy E. He went down, down the tall line. Then across, across, across.

The bumps tickled his finger. He giggled. He traced it again. Down, across, across, across.

Then he picked up his marker. He drew a tall line on his paper. Then he drew one line across. Then another. Then one more. He looked at his letter.

"That is E!" he said. He wrote E, l, i, j, a, h. Some letters were wiggly. But the E was just right.

Mom clapped her hands. Elijah traced the bumpy E one more time. "Tickle, tickle," he said, and laughed.

Ellie went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find her favorite book. It was a book about a bunny. But the bunny book was not on the shelf.

Ellie looked by the fish tank. No bunny book. She looked by the big pillows. No bunny book. Then she heard music. It came from the playroom.

A boy named Sam was cleaning up. "Blocks, dolls and balls," he said. He put each toy in the toy box. "Blocks, dolls and balls. Blocks, dolls and balls." Ellie watched him. She picked up a ball. She put it in the box too. Sam smiled. Then Ellie saw something under the chair. It was a red book. It had a bunny on the cover!

"You found it," said Sam. Ellie hugged the book. She sat on a big pillow. Her dad read to her. Ellie got sleepy. She closed her eyes, just for a little bit. "Blocks, dolls and balls," she whispered. "And one bunny book."

Ella sat on her bed with a big book. She opened the front cover first. On the first page, she saw little black marks. "What are those?" she asked. Grandpa said, "Those are words. They tell a story." Grandpa read them out loud. Ella listened.

Then Ella wanted to write words too. She got paper and paint. With her brush, she painted letters. She painted them all touching, like a long train. HITHISISELLA. She gave the paper to Grandpa. Grandpa looked and looked. He turned the paper around. "I can't read this yet," he said. Outside the window, the sky was cloudy, so they had lots of time.

Ella looked at her book again. She saw little gaps between the words. "The words have spaces," she said. "Can I try that?" Grandpa nodded. Ella painted her letters again, slowly. This time she put a space between each word. HI THIS IS ELLA. Grandpa smiled big. He read it out loud, word by word. "You did it," he said. Ella held her paper up to the cloudy window and said, "Read it one more time."

Maeva held a small clay lamp in her hands. "It is called a diya," Mama said. It was the festival of Diwali, and the street was full of people. There were sweets, drums, and bright paper flags.

Maeva wanted the diyas to shine, but hers was dark inside. "Why won't my lamp glow?" she asked. "The flame has to come from somewhere," Mama said. Mama used a match, because matches are for grown-ups. She touched the little flame to Maeva's diya. A soft light grew.

Maeva set the diya down in a slow, careful line with the others. One by one, each lit diya helped light the next. The whole row began to glow. "Now the street is smiling," said Maeva. She slipped her hand into Mama's warm hand and watched the little flames flicker.

Luka sat on the park bench with his grandma. Grandma had a little bag of snacks.

"Let's play a game," said Grandma. "We have five senses. Can you name one?"

"Eyes!" said Luka. He pointed at his eyes. "I see with my eyes."

"Yes," said Grandma. "I see that big rainbow kite." Luka looked up. The kite flew high.

"Next one?" asked Luka. "Ears! I hear with my ears." A dog barked. Luka heard it.

Then Grandma opened her bag. She cut a strawberry with her safe little knife. She gave Luka a tiny piece. Luka put it in his mouth. He did not chew yet. It tasted sweet.

"Now try this," said Grandma. She gave him a small slice of lemon. Luka tasted it. His mouth went tight. "Sour!" he said. "It is sour!"

"Which body part tasted it?" asked Grandma.

Luka stuck out his tongue. "My tongue! We taste with our tongue."

"That's right," said Grandma. She clapped.

Luka ate the sweet strawberry next. Then he touched the bench. It felt hard and warm. "Hands!" he said. "I touch with my hands." He smelled the lemon peel. "And my nose smells it!"

Grandma laughed. "You did it. All five senses."

Luka jumped off the bench. "Nose, tongue, eyes, ears, hands!" he sang. Then he ran to look at the rainbow kite again.

Athena went to the park with Dad. Under a big tree, she set out her toy cars. "Red car, blue car, green car," she said. Then she saw something yellow. It was long and round at the ends. It was a banana! The banana sat right in the row of cars.

"You are the odd one out," Athena told the banana. Dad smiled. "Yes, the odd one out is the thing that does not belong," he said. Athena put the banana in the picnic basket with the apples and the bread. Now the cars were all cars again.

Athena let her round red balloon float up above the tree. It bobbed in the wind. Then she sat down and shared the banana with Dad, slice by slice. "Goodbye, odd one," she whispered. "You belong with us."

Abigail wanted to draw a big round sun. She sat at the little table and looked at the tablet. The screen was dark. She tapped the dark screen with her finger. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. The screen stayed dark.

Her teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Press this little button," Miss Kim said. Abigail pressed the button. The screen lit up. It was bright and full of colors. Abigail smiled. She tapped the drawing app and drew a big round sun. Then she drew a bird. She gave it wings so it could fly.

A boy named Sam sat down next to her. His screen was dark too. He tapped it and tapped it. "Press your button," Abigail said. Sam pressed his button. His screen lit up. "You did it," Abigail said. When they were done, Miss Kim helped them put the tablets away. "All done," said Abigail, and she patted the tablet gently, like a sleepy pet.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. She splashed in the little tub. Splash, splash! Now her arms were wet. Now her dress was wet. Even her hair was wet. Drip, drip, drip went the water on the floor.

Max ran past her. He was dripping too. "Look, I am a wet dog!" he said. He shook like a puppy. Water flew everywhere. Miss Ana laughed. "You two need towels," she said.

Penelope wanted to go color at the table. But she was too wet. Her paper would get soggy. Then Miss Ana held out a big blue towel. Penelope rubbed her arms. Rub, rub. The towel made her arms dry! She rubbed her legs too. Now her dress was not dripping. Max came back for a towel as well. "Warm and dry," he said.

Penelope sat down at the table. She picked up a red crayon. Max sat next to her. "That was a kind towel," he said. Penelope giggled and began to color a big red apple.

Charlie stood at the gate. It was her first day of school. The playground was big. Kids ran and laughed. Charlie held her red bag tight.

A boy hopped like a silly frog. A girl found a worm by the fence. Charlie wanted to play too. But then her tummy felt funny. She needed the bathroom. She did not know where it was.

She looked around. She waited. She looked some more. The sun was warm. Her ice pop from home began to melt in her hand. She still did not know where to go.

Then she saw the teacher. The teacher smiled. Charlie walked over slowly. "Can you help me find the bathroom?" she asked. "Yes, I can," said the teacher. "Come with me." The teacher held her hand. They walked together. Charlie felt better already.

Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. It would have one big flower on it. A pink flower, like the fairy flowers in his dreams.

But there was no pink paint. Felix looked in the cup. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No pink anywhere. "No pink," he said. His tummy felt a little scared. Would Grandma still like a red flower?

Miss Pia came over. "What is wrong?" she asked. "No pink," said Felix. "I need pink for Grandma." Miss Pia smiled. "Try the white paint," she said.

Felix dipped his brush in the red. He painted a big red dot. Then he dipped his brush in the white. He stirred and stirred. "Stir, stir, stir," he said. The red dot grew soft and pale. It was pink! Real pink! "Pink!" shouted Felix. "Pink, pink, pink!"

He painted a big pink flower on the card. Then he added a green stem and a yellow sun. He hoped Grandma would love it. At pick-up time, Felix held the card up high. "Look, Grandma! A pink flower, just for you!"

Ava sat in her car seat. Mom was driving to Grandma's house. Ava had two bags. One bag held her toys. One bag held her clothes.

Ava looked out the window. She saw cows in a field. "Cows are animals," she said. "Yes," said Mom. "Just like the ducks we saw."

Ava was hungry. Mom gave her a banana from the food bag. Bananas, crackers and juice were all foods.

Then Ava looked in her toy bag. She found something soft. It was a sock! Ava laughed. She held it up. "A sock is not a toy," she said.

"That's right," said Mom. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Ava put the sock in the clothes bag. Then she found her teddy bear. Teddy could sleep on the soft sock.

At Grandma's house, Grandma gave Mom money for the food bags. "Thank you, you are so kind," Mom said. Ava carried her teddy inside. The sock was under teddy's arm, like a little blanket.

Gianna stood at the big window. She watched the planes come in. One plane, two planes, three planes. Mom held her hand tight.

A door opened. Out came Grandma with her little blue bag. Gianna ran to her. Grandma hugged her and Mom at the same time.

"Wait," said Gianna. "Grandma, you hugged Mom too. Why?"

Mom smiled. "Grandma is my mom."

Gianna's eyes got big. Grandma was a mom too? "Grandma is Mom's mom?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "A grandma is a parent of your mom or your dad."

Gianna thought about that. "So Grandpa is Dad's dad?"

"He is," said Grandma. "You are a smart fish."

Gianna giggled. She had one more question. "Grandma, do you make pancakes?"

"I do," said Grandma. "All week long."

Gianna counted on her fingers. One day, two days, all the way to seven. Grandma would stay for seven days!

They walked to the car. Gianna held one hand of each of them, Mom's hand and Grandma's hand, all the way.

Elizabeth had a new coat. It had big red buttons. Her old coat had a zipper, but this one did not.

At school, Elizabeth tried to zip it. She pulled and pulled. Nothing happened. There was no zipper at all.

Her teacher knelt down. "Look," she said. She held the coat open. Little holes ran down the front.

Elizabeth pushed the first button. It went right through its hole. The coat closed a little bit. She pushed the next button. Click, through the hole. The coat closed some more.

"Fast buttons!" said her friend Tom. He laughed and showed his tooth, the one that was wiggly.

One by one, every button went through its hole. The coat was all closed. It was warm and snug.

Elizabeth ran to the mirror. "I did it," she said. "All by myself."

Madelyn had on her party dress. It was red with white dots. She wanted to sleep in it. "I wish to wear my dress to bed," she said.

Daddy shook his head. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said. Madelyn pouted. Then she looked at her soft pajamas. They had wild monkeys on them. She touched the dress. It was stiff. She touched the pajamas. They were soft and cozy.

"I will try the monkeys," she said. Daddy helped her pull off the dress. She wiggled into the pajamas. She ate her apple slice first. Then she brushed her teeth. She climbed into bed. The soft monkeys hugged her arms. Her eyes closed fast.

"Goodnight, monkeys," she whispered.

Henri ran up the steps to Grandma's house. Today was a big day. His new baby sister was here! He wanted to hold her more than anything. But Mom said he had to sit very still on the couch. That felt hard.

Henri sat. He made his body as still as a frozen pond. Grandma put the baby on his lap. The baby was so small. Her hand opened and closed. Henri did not know what to do. Then Mom said, "Try putting your finger in her hand."

Henri put one finger in the baby's little hand. Her tiny fingers closed around it. She held on tight! Henri laughed out loud. "She likes me!" he said. He wiggled his finger a little. The baby held tighter. She made a small sound, like a happy worm squishing through the dirt.

"Can we do it again?" Henri asked. Grandma smiled. "She can follow you anywhere with that finger," she said. Henri walked his finger through the air, slow and low. The baby's eyes followed it too. At supper, Henri saved a spot on the couch for her. He held up his finger and waited, as still as a stone.

Mateo sat at the art table. He had a cracker in his hand. "Is this a square?" he asked his teacher.

"Let's find out," she said. She gave him a piece of string. Mateo laid the string along one side of the cracker. Then he laid it on the next side. It fit just the same. Side three matched too. Side four matched too. All four sides were the same. "It's a square!" said Mateo.

Next to him, a baby in a stroller watched from the doorway. The baby's big sister was painting. Mateo poured some purple paint into her cup. "Thank you," she said.

Then Mateo dipped his sponge in the purple paint. He pressed it down. It made a square print. He turned the sponge and pressed again. The square sat beside a circle and a triangle on the paper.

The baby clapped her hands. Mateo held up his purple painting. "Four sides, all the same!" he said. The baby kicked her feet and laughed.

Paisley wants to play the pretend shop at school. But Ben is already there. Ben stands behind a little box. "I am the shopkeeper," says Ben. "You can be the shopper."

Paisley wants to be the shopkeeper too. She takes the box. Ben frowns. Then she gives it back. "Okay, I shop," she says.

Ben holds up a toy banana. Paisley picks it out. She gives him a leaf for money. Ben smiles big. "Thank you, shopper!"

Paisley digs in her pocket. She finds a stinky sock. "Yuck," says Ben. "No socks in my shop." Paisley laughs and puts it away.

Then it is Paisley's turn. She stands behind the box. Ben walks down the pretend road. He shops now. "One banana, please," says Ben.

Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. He held her hand. The sun was warm on his toe through his sandal. "Where is the sun going?" he asked.

A big cloud moved in the sky. The cloud hid the sun. Now the sky was gray. Harrison's toe felt cool. "The sun went away," he said. "The cloud is in front of it." The wind began to blow. It blew Mama's scarf. It ruffled Harrison's hair. "Windy day," said Mama. She zipped his jacket up high.

Rain began to fall. Drop, drop, drop. Mama opened the umbrella. It went pop over their heads. "Can the sun come back?" Harrison asked. "Watch the cloud," said Mama.

They watched and waited. The bus came. The cloud moved away, slow and soft. The sun came out again. The rain stopped. Everything looked bright and shiny. Harrison smiled his sweet smile. He waved at the sun. "Hello again!" he called. The bus door opened with a hiss, and Harrison stepped up, holding Mama's hand.

Henri sat in the big waiting room. He held his doll tight. Today he would get his very first haircut. He wanted to look like Papa, but he was scared of the scissors.

"Mama, what if the hair spills everywhere?" he asked. Mama smiled. "The lady is very gentle," she said. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it."

Henri's turn came. He sat up tall on the booster seat. The lady snipped one little curl near his ear. She held it out to Mama. Mama put the curl in a small white envelope. "Why do you keep it?" Henri asked. "So we can remember this day," Mama said.

Henri looked in the mirror. His hair was short like Papa's. He made a silly face, and the lady laughed. He waved his doll at the mirror. "We look handsome," he told the doll. On the way out, Henri held the envelope all the way home.

Leah turned three today. Her party was in the backyard. Grandma hung balloons on the fence. Friends sat near the picnic table.

Dad carried out the cake. It had three candles. Leah wanted to light them herself. She reached for the matches.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job."

Leah put her foot down with a little stomp. Then Dad lit one candle. A small flame popped up. Leah watched it flicker. Then he lit the next one, and the next. All three candles glowed.

"Now you get the big job," said Dad. "Make a wish and blow!"

Leah closed her eyes. She took a big breath. She blew out all three candles at once.

Everyone clapped. Leah hopped up and down. Mom cut the cake, and Leah got the first big piece.

"Happy birthday, Leah!" everyone said.

Leah smiled with frosting on her chin.

Beatrice went to the store with Mama and baby Sam. She put apples in the cart. Sam took the apples out. Beatrice put them in again. Sam pulled them out again. "Sam, you are being silly," said Beatrice. Did Sam want the cart empty?

Mama smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. Beatrice put a big melon in the cart. It was too big for Sam's hands. It stayed in! Beatrice put a small plum in too. Sam took the small plum out. Out it came, fast. Beatrice laughed.

Then they passed the bakery. The bread was hot. Mama picked it up with a cloth, slow and careful. "Hot bread can hurt," said Mama. Beatrice touched the cold milk carton instead. It felt nice.

At the checkout, Beatrice had her answer. Sam just liked taking things out. So she gave him a soft bun to hold. Sam held it. Nothing went in. Nothing came out. The cart rolled away, full.

Sofia wanted to make a book about her five senses. "I know eyes see," she said. "Ears hear. A nose smells. A tongue tastes." She drew them all. But one page was empty. She did not know the fifth sense yet.

Mama was in the kitchen. "Can you help me?" she asked. She put a bowl of warm oats on the table. Sofia did not touch it. "It is warm," Mama said. "Only Mama touches warm things." Sofia watched from her chair. She blew on the oats, fast fast fast, and the steam went away.

Then Mama gave her a cold spoon. Sofia held it in her fingers. The spoon felt cold. Her fingertips told her that. "We feel things by touching them with our skin," said Mama. "Like our fingertips." Sofia touched the spoon again. Cold! She touched her soft sleeve. Soft! She touched the smooth table. Smooth!

Sofia drew two hands on the empty page. "Hands feel," she said. "That is five!" She ran to the window. The moon was coming up. She touched the glass with one fingertip. It felt cool and smooth. "Good night, moon," she said. "My hands know you are there."

Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. White flakes were falling down. "It's snowy!" said his teacher, Miss Kim. "Snow pants day!" Grayson wiggled into his snow pants. He zipped up his big coat. He put on his hat. "Where are your mittens, Grayson?" Miss Kim asked. Grayson looked in his bag. No mittens! "I forgot them," he said. He felt shy about it. "You can go out anyway," said Miss Kim. "We will find a way."

Outside, the snow was deep and soft. Grayson stomped in it. Crunch, crunch! His friend Mia had red mittens. She made a snowball and threw it. "Catch, Grayson!" Grayson caught it with his bare hands. The snowball was cold. Very cold! "Brrr!" he said. His hands hurt. They turned pink. He dropped the snowball fast.

Mia looked at Grayson's cold hands. "Here," she said. She pulled off one red mitten. "Try this." Grayson put it on. Soon his hand felt warm again. "Mittens keep hands warm on a snowy day!" he said. Then Mia gave him the other mitten too. Together they made a big snowman. They glued on a paper sign that said HI. The wind blew their hats sideways. "Windy!" laughed Grayson. Inside, cocoa waited on the table. Miss Kim held the cups, one by one. Grayson wrapped both warm hands around his.

Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. "Dad, can you pass the bread, please?" she asked. Dad passed her the bread. "Thank you," said Wren. Dad smiled a big smile. Then he gave her some apple slices too. "Thank you," said Wren again. Dad smiled again. Wren saw that. One little word made Dad's face light up. That was fun to see.

Then Wren reached for her cup. Oops. The cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. "Sorry, Mom," said Wren. Mom wiped the milk with a towel. "That's okay," said Mom. "Can I help?" asked Wren. "Yes, you can bring me the towel basket." Wren ran to get it. She was not lazy about it one bit. Mom wiped the table and it was dry again.

After dinner, Mom brought out a little hat. It was a tiny party hat, just for fun. Mom put it on Wren's head. "Thank you, Mom!" said Wren. Mom clapped her hands. Wren tapped the hat with one finger. The hat wiggled. Wren laughed. "Do it again," she said.

Livia looked in her toy box. "Where is Bunny?" she said. Bunny was gone. Livia wanted Bunny very much.

She looked under her bed. No Bunny. She peeked behind the curtain. No Bunny. "Bunny is not far away," said Mama. "Let's look together." They looked in the living room. They looked by the big chair.

Then Livia saw something. It was a small blue car. It was not her toy. It belonged to her brother, Sam. Sam was looking for his car. His face was sad. Livia picked up the car. She ran to Sam. "Here is your car," she said. Sam smiled big. "You gave it back!" he said. "Thank you, Livia." He gave her a hug.

Then Sam said, "Come with me." He led her to the sofa. He lifted the blanket. There sat Bunny! "I saw Bunny there," said Sam. "I wanted to give Bunny back to you."

Livia hugged Bunny tight. Bunny's soft ears were the best color in the world. "Thank you, Sam," she said. "You gave Bunny back to me." Sam held his blue car. Livia held Bunny. They sat together on the sofa. "Now we both have our toys," said Livia. Sam laughed and rolled his car along the arm of the chair.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. On Monday, Sienna and Grandma went to the market. It smelled like apples and warm bread. "Dad loved this market," said Grandma.

Sienna stopped walking. "Dad was a boy?" she asked. She could only see Dad now, tall and big. Grandma laughed. "Yes, he was little once. He was just four, like you."

They sat by the fruit stand. Grandma told about Dad's first bike. It was red, and he painted a blue star on it. He fell off far from home, and he cried. Then he got back on and rode all the way home. Sienna giggled. "Dad cried?"

"He did," said Grandma. They bought a big red apple. On Tuesday, Dad came to pick them up. "Guess what," said Sienna. "You had a bike and a star!"

Dad looked at Grandma. Grandma smiled and tapped the kitchen clock. "Time for dinner," she said. "And more stories tomorrow." Sienna took a big, crunchy bite of her apple.

Emilia sat at the big table. Mom put warm toast in front of her. Mom also put a small cup and a jug of milk. "You can do it yourself today," said Mom. Emilia wanted to do it herself. She wanted to butter her own toast and pour her own milk.

Mom gave her a knife. Mom held the knife with her, safe and slow. Emilia poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast got a hole in it. Butter went everywhere in little bits. "That is tricky," said Emilia. "Try the flat side," said Mom. Emilia turned the knife over. She laid the flat side on the butter. She pushed it across the bread. The butter spread out. The toast looked smooth and shiny.

"Now the milk," said Mom. Emilia picked up the jug with two hands. She poured slowly. Milk went into the cup. One little drop ran down the side. She stopped and waited. Then she poured a tiny bit more. Not one drop spilled on the table.

Emilia ate her toast. An ant walked across the floor far away. "Look, Mom, I did it," said Emilia. "We can talk about it at snack time too," said Mom. Emilia took a big sip of milk.

Anthony rode the bus with Mama. He held his little red bunny. Then the bus went bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands. "Oh no," said Anthony. "Bunny is lost!"

Anthony looked under the seat. He looked in Mama's bag. Where could bunny be? A lady next to them smiled. "Look by your shoe," she said. There was bunny! The bump had made him fall. Anthony hugged him tight.

At home, Anthony found a basket. He put the basket by his bed. "This is bunny's nest," he said. Each night, bunny went in the basket. Each morning, Anthony knew just where to look. "It worked again!" he said. Was that true? He peeked in. Yes! Bunny sat there, clean and soft. "Night night, bunny," said Anthony.

Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the very first time. "I want to be brave," said Florence. "We can go slow," said Mama.

At the dentist, a kind woman looked in Florence's mouth. "Open big," she said. Florence opened. The dentist looked and looked. Then she gave Florence a little mirror. Florence saw her own teeth. "Big smile," said the dentist. Florence smiled at herself.

On the bus home, a boy sat near Florence. He had apple slices. He bit one with his front teeth. Then he chomped it with his back teeth. The apple got small and small. "He bites first, then he chews," said Florence. Mama nodded.

At home, Florence ate fish for lunch. She bit a piece with her front teeth. Then she chewed it with her back teeth. "The fish tastes good," said Florence. She took another bite, and chewed it all up. "All done," said Mama. Florence held up her empty plate.

Leah ran to the big tree at the playground. Her friend Mia was already there.

"Let's play hide-and-seek," said Mia. "You count. We hide."

Leah put her hands over her eyes. "One, two, three, four!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around.

Mia was still standing in the open. So was their friend Sam.

"We didn't have time to hide," said Mia. "Please count slowly."

Leah hid her eyes again. "One... two... three... four... five... six... seven... eight... nine... ten." She counted slow like a snail.

Mia ran behind the slide. Sam got under the bench. Leah heard little feet on the wood chips.

She looked around. She saw Sam's shoes in a line under the bench. "Found you, Sam!"

Then she saw a happy face peeking around the slide. "Found you too, Mia!"

"Now you hide," said Mia. "I will count to ten. Slowly."

Arthur ran to Grandpa's garden. "We will plant seeds today!" said Grandpa. Arthur dug little holes in the dirt. He put tomato seeds in one row. He put carrot seeds in the middle row.

The next day, Arthur forgot his spot. "Where are my tomatoes?" he asked. Grandpa held up a stick with a tomato picture on it. He pushed it into the dirt. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," said Grandpa. Arthur clapped his hands.

Arthur made more labels with Grandpa. He drew a yellow tomato on one. He drew a long orange carrot on another. He pushed each label into the dirt, and the wind made them wiggle. Arthur watched his rows every morning. Soon tiny green leaves popped up next to every label. "Look, Grandpa! The labels found my plants!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week! Juliette clapped her hands. She put on her red hat. "Let's go to the market, Grandpa!" she said. Grandpa smiled big. Off they went.

The market was loud and busy. There were apples and bread and flowers. Juliette helped pick a big green apple. "This one!" she said. Grandpa put it in the bag. They waved to the apple man. What a fun day!

At home, Grandpa took a warm bath. Juliette waited outside the door. Then Grandpa called, "Oh no! Where are the towels?" He peeked out, dripping. Juliette heard him. A problem! Grandpa was a guest. Guests don't know where things are.

Juliette ran down the hall. She opened the tall cupboard. The towels were stacked inside, soft and white. "Here, Grandpa!" she called. Grandpa took a big towel. "Thank you, my host!" he said. Juliette felt proud. She was a good host.

The next morning, Grandpa couldn't find the bathroom. Juliette showed him the door. At night, he couldn't find his slippers. Juliette pointed to the mat. "My host knows where things are," said Grandpa. Juliette grinned under her hat. Then she took his hand and said, "Come on, Grandpa. I will show you everything!"

Owen ran to the park with Dad. He felt so excited. The swings were free at last.

Then a big dog ran up. It barked very loud. Owen felt scared. The dog looked big as a horse. Would it bite him? Owen wanted to cry.

He ran to Dad and held his hand tight. "Dad, I am scared of that dog," Owen said. "Can you help me?"

"Yes, I can help you," Dad said. "Stay right here by me."

Dad stood with Owen. The dog's owner came and called a name. "Biscuit, come here!" The dog ran to her. It wagged its tail. It did not bite anyone.

"See? Her name is Biscuit," Dad said. "She just wanted to play."

Owen watched Biscuit sniff a smelly old shoe. He laughed. That was a happy sound. Then a boy fell off the slide. He looked sad, and his sister looked angry about her dropped ice cream. So many feelings in one park, Owen thought.

Then Biscuit brought the smelly shoe back and dropped it at Owen's feet. "Thank you, Biscuit," Owen said. "But that is your shoe, not mine."

Penelope loved the guinea pig at school. His name was Pip. Yesterday Pip hid in his little house. Today Pip sat on the top of his hay. His food bowl was low and almost empty. "Can I feed Pip?" Penelope asked. "Soon," said Miss Amy. "First we walk to the rug for story time." Penelope sat down. She did not want to wait. She looked at the clock. The big hand moved a little bit. "Is it soon now?" she asked. "Soon means in a little while," said Miss Amy. "Not a long wait." Miss Amy read one book. Then she clapped her hands. "Story time is done. Now you may feed Pip." Penelope got the hay. She put some in the bowl. Pip ran over and began to eat. Tomorrow she would feed him again. "That was not a long wait," said Penelope. Pip made a happy squeak.

Jasmine ran to Dad with her new book. "Please read this to me!" she said. Dad sat on her bed. He opened the front of the book. He began at the first page. He read the words out loud, one by one. Jasmine looked at his finger. It moved along the little black marks. The marks told him what to say!

Jasmine turned a page. This page had no marks at all. It only showed a big rainbow in the sky. "Read this part too!" she said. Dad looked at the page. "There are no words here," he said. "There is nothing written on this page to read." So they just looked at the rainbow together.

"Can words be on the last page?" Jasmine asked. Dad turned to the back. "Yes, look," he said. There were words at the end too. Jasmine smiled. "Tomorrow can I read the words?" she asked. "You can try," said Dad. "I will help you." Jasmine hugged the book tight. "Good night, words," she said. Dad turned off the light. "Sweet dreams," he said, "my true little reader."

Henry sat at the little red table. There was white paper in front of him. There were paint cups too.

"Today we paint pumpkins," said Miss Ana. She held up a big pumpkin. It was orange.

Henry looked in his paint cups. Red. Yellow. Blue. One, two, three. He counted them again. No orange cup. His tummy felt tight.

"I need orange," Henry said. "My pumpkin needs orange."

His friend Mia had orange paint. But Mia was using all of hers. Henry did not want to grab it. He sat and thought.

Then he looked at his brush. Red on one side. Yellow on the tip. He dipped the red brush in the yellow cup. He stirred it round and round.

The paint turned orange!

Henry stared. He touched the paint with his finger. The paint felt cool, like a tickle on his skin.

He painted a big round pumpkin. Then he painted another one. "Red and yellow made orange," he said to Mia.

"I need orange too," said Mia. Her face looked sad.

Henry pushed his orange cup across the table. "Here," he said. "You can share mine."

Mia smiled. She painted a small pumpkin next to Henry's big one. Then she put her brush down on the white paper like a pillow for it to rest.

Miss Ana came to look. "What nice orange pumpkins," she said.

Henry held up his painting. "I made orange!" he said. "Come and see!"

Max wanted the red truck. Ben had the red truck. Max grabbed for it. Miss Ana put her hand out. "We wait," she said. Max sat on the pillow. The pillow was itchy. He wiggled and waited.

Then Ben held out the truck. "Your turn," said Ben. Max took it. He remembered something. "Thank you, Ben," he said. Ben smiled big. Ben gave him a hug.

Max pushed the truck across the rug. It went far. It went under the doll house. A tiny mouse toy was hiding there! "Look!" said Max. Ben laughed. "You found him," said Ben. "My turn now," said Max, holding out the truck.

Riley sat on the blue rug at school. Miss Kim held up a big card. It had a big A on it. "A says ah," said Miss Kim. "Ah, ah, apple," said Riley.

Then Miss Kim opened a book. Riley pointed at a small word. "That little one is not A," said Riley. "A is big. That one is small." Miss Kim smiled. She put the card next to the book. The small a sat under the big A. Riley looked and looked. She waited. Then she put her finger on both letters. "Same letter," said Riley. "Big A. Small a. Both say ah."

Riley went to the wall. The wall had big letters all across it. She found the small a in her book again. She held the book up high. The small a sat under the big A on the wall. "Ah," said Riley. "Ah, ah, apple."

At dinner that night, Riley saw a box on the table. "That is a big A," she said. "And that is a small a. Same letter." She tapped the box two times. "Ah, ah," she said, and took a big bite of her apple.

David waited by the gate at school pickup. He wore his green hat. His tummy made a little growl. "Lunch soon," said Mama. "First we go home."

At home, David ate his sandwich. Then he played in the sand. His socks got sandy. His pants got muddy too. Mama said, "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed." David looked at the big basket.

David made a game. He held his sandy sock. He tossed it. It went in the basket. "Goal!" said David. He tossed the other sock. It went in too. Then his muddy pants went in. Mama smiled. She took the basket to the washing machine. Soon the clothes would be clean. David got dressed in soft blue pajamas. "Bath first," said Mama, and she turned on the warm water.

Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted to go to Mia's house. "Can we go now?" she asked. "Now it is dinner time," said Mom. "You slept last night. That was yesterday." Sadie looked at her plate. Yesterday she had peas. Today she had carrots. The carrots were orange. What a nice color!

"But I want to go today," said Sadie. "Today is now," said Dad. "Tomorrow comes after today. Tomorrow is the day after today." Sadie counted on her fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. Three days! "What comes after tomorrow?" she asked. "Another tomorrow," said Dad with a smile. Sadie laughed.

"After I sleep, it will be tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Then you wake up. Then we go to Mia's house." Sadie ate her carrots. One, two, three carrots. She would sleep, and then it would be tomorrow. She felt happy. "Tonight I will sleep fast," said Sadie. Dad gave her a big hug. "Sleep first," he said. "Mia tomorrow."

Charlie was so excited. Today he would write his name! He grabbed a pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The letters came out big and wiggly. "Yucky," said Charlie. "That is not my name."

Miss Amy sat down next to him. "Watch me," she said. She pinched the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then she let it rest on her middle finger. She wrote Charlie's name, C-H-A-R-L-I-E, one letter at a time.

Charlie tried it. Thumb, first finger, middle finger. Pinch and rest. He lifted the pencil and made a C. Then an H. Then A, R, L, I, E. Seven letters!

"Look, Miss Amy!" said Charlie. "That says Charlie!"

He held up his paper like a flag on a road. "Can I do it again?"

Jayden sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. The paper pumpkin had no color yet. Grandma gave him a plate with paint on it. "Look," she said. "Red, blue, yellow, green."

Jayden looked and looked. He wanted orange for his pumpkin. He saw no orange paint. He said, "I need orange. One, two, three, four paints. No orange anywhere."

"Try two paints together," said Grandma.

Jayden put his brush in the red. He put his brush in the yellow. He stirred them on the plate. Red and yellow made orange! "Orange!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow made orange!"

He painted his pumpkin all orange. The stem he painted green. Then he used blue for the sky behind it. "My pumpkin looks so good," said Jayden. "Not bad at all!"

Grandma smiled and clapped. Jayden held up his wet painting. "Red and yellow," he said. "One more time, tomorrow!"

Amira was going to a new place. Mama held her hand in the big hall. "We look for door five," said Mama. Amira wanted to find it first.

They walked past door 1. Then door 2. Then door 3. Amira counted on her fingers. "One, two, three," she said. Her sock began to scratch her heel, so she stopped to wiggle her foot.

Then Amira saw a sign. It said 5. She held up her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Mama, look! It is five!"

"Yes," said Mama with a smile. "That means five." She knocked on door 5.

Grandpa opened the door. "You found me!" he said. He gave Amira a big hug. "Come and see my world of buttons," he said. He had jars of buttons, all colors.

Amira counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten buttons in the red jar. Grandpa clapped.

Aurora sat at the dinner table. Something smelled good. Her nose knew it first. "What is that smell?" she asked. "Soup," said Mom. Aurora heard it bubble. Her ears heard the pot pop and puff.

Dad put three things by her plate. "Close your eyes and guess," he said. "Use your fingers." Aurora shut her eyes tight. Her fingertips touched something bumpy. "A pinecone!" Next her fingertips felt something soft. "A feather!" Last came something smooth and cool. "A rock!" Dad said, "Yes! Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy."

"How do they know?" asked Aurora. She touched the pinecone again. The bumpy bumps tickled her fingers. "They just know," she said.

Mom set the soup in the middle of the table. Aurora dipped her spoon. Her tongue tasted carrots. She painted a carrot mark on her bread with the tip of the spoon. "My mouth knows carrots," she said, and she touched the pinecone one more time, just to feel the bumps again.

Camille put on her warm coat. She was going to the hockey rink with Dad. There was a game on the ice, but today the rink had a fun corner for little kids. A red hoop lay on the floor. A big soft ball sat in a basket. Camille wanted to win a sticker.

First she tried the beanbag. She threw it from far away. It missed the hoop. It landed on the cold floor. She ran and got it. She threw it again. It missed again.

"Can I try from here?" Camille asked.
"Sure," said Dad. "Try it!"

Camille took three little steps. Now she stood close to the hoop. She tossed the beanbag. It went in! The beanbag sank right into the middle of the red hoop.

"It went in!" she shouted. She jumped up and down.

Then Dad rolled her the big ball. She held out both hands. The ball was soft and pretty and blue. She squeezed it to her chest like a blanket. "I caught it!" she said.

Dad clapped his hands. "You did it, Camille!"

A helper gave Camille a shiny star sticker. Camille stuck it on her coat. She ran back to the hoop with the beanbag. "Watch me!" she said. She stood close and tossed. In it went again!

Jasmine wanted tea for her bear. She found two cups on the playroom shelf. One cup was big. One cup was small. The small cup had nothing in it. The big cup had nothing in it too.

Daddy brought a pot of warm water. It was not hot like tea for grown-ups. It was just warm, like a bath. Daddy poured slow, slow, slow. The small cup filled up. Jasmine held her bear's cup. It was empty, so empty. She poured too fast. Water ran over the top. "Oh no," said Jasmine. Daddy gave her a towel. She wiped the little puddle.

Jasmine tried again. This time she poured slow. She watched the water climb. She stopped before the top. Now the cup was full. "Look, Bear," she said. "Your cup is full now." She took a tiny pretend sip. "Yummy," she said. "Just a little sour, like lemon tea." Then she tickled Bear with a string from her pocket, fast, fast, fast, and Bear got a big hug, slow and cozy.

Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish, birds, and one small kitten. The kitten was gray with white paws. It looked at Quinn. "Can we take it home?" Quinn asked. "Yes," said Dad. "It will be your first pet."

Dad got a box with holes for the kitten to ride in. He got food in a little bag. He got two small bowls too. "One for food," said Dad. "One for water." At home, Dad put the bowls on the floor. The kitten drank some water. Then it went to sleep.

The next morning, Quinn ran to see the kitten. The kitten was at its water bowl. The bowl was empty. The kitten looked up at Quinn. It looked sad. "Dad!" Quinn called. "The water is all gone!"

Dad came with Quinn to the sink. He held the bowl under the tap. Fresh, clean water filled it up. Quinn helped Dad carry it back. She could not reach the floor from up high, so Dad set it down. The kitten drank and drank. Then it rubbed on Quinn's leg and purred. "Fresh water every day," said Dad. "That is your job, Quinn." Quinn smiled and petted the kitten's soft head.

Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels. "Look," said Mama. "One cow. Two horses. Three ducks." Felix saw them all in the green field. "Ducks say quack," said Felix. Then his tummy made a little rumble. Mama gave him a banana from the food bag. It was yellow and soft.

Soon the car stopped. They were at the library. "I want a book about animals," said Felix. "Like the ducks and the cow." A kind librarian heard him. "Come with me," she said. She walked to a shelf. "Here are all the animal books, in a group." Felix touched the spines. One, two, three, four books. He picked a big one with a cow on the front.

Mama found toy books on another shelf. "Toys are in a group too," she said. Felix hugged his cow book. On the bumpy ride home, he turned the pages. The last page showed a duck. Under the duck was a tiny frog. "A surprise!" said Felix. He laughed all the way home.

Alice pushed her baby doll in one little swing. She wanted her friend Max to push the other swing. But Max was on the steps. He was counting them so he could jump down. "One, two, four," said Max. Alice stopped pushing. "You went one, two, four," she said. "Is that right?" she asked herself. She sang her counting song in her head. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." "Three," said Alice. "Three comes before four."

Max tried again. He stepped on each step and said each word. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He had counted all ten steps. He jumped down with a soft bump onto the wood chips. Alice clapped. Max ran to the swing. Alice pushed one swing and Max sat in the other. "Dream swings," said Alice. "Side by side." Max touched the wet slide. "It feels slimy," he said, and wiped his hand on his shirt. They swung high together, counting one, two, three.

Hayden went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a cat. He looked at shelf one. He looked at shelf two. No cat book. He looked at shelf three. Still no cat book.

The librarian came over. "Can I help you?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Hayden. "I want a cat book." The librarian found one with a cloudy blue cover. "Would you like a sticker, too?" she asked. "No, thank you," said Hayden. The librarian smiled a big smile.

Then Hayden saw his friend Mia. Mia offered him a cracker. Hayden did not like crackers. "Yuck!" he shouted. Mia's face looked sad. Hayden tried again. "No, thank you," he said softly. Mia smiled and ate the cracker herself. Hayden held his cat book tight. "Thank you," he told the librarian. She waved as he walked out the door.

Brooks had a cough. Mom said, "Let's get your medicine." They went to the pharmacy down the street.

The pharmacy had bright lights. There were bandages and soap and little bottles on shelves. Brooks saw a big bottle of cough medicine on the counter. He reached up his hands.

The pharmacist shook her head gently. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," she said. Brooks put his hands down. He waited by Mom's coat.

Mom picked up the bottle. She read the label slowly. Then she filled the small cup. She poured it carefully. The medicine was purple. Brooks looked at it.

"Show me how you drink it," Mom said. Brooks took the little cup from her hand. He sipped the purple medicine. It tasted like grapes.

They walked home in the soft light of night. Mom said, "That was your last spoonful." Brooks yawned. At home, his cough was quieter. His teddy sat by his bed. Mom tucked the blanket up to his chin.

"Night night, bear," Brooks whispered. He closed his eyes.

Louis stood at the little table. The toast sat on his plate. He held the butter knife. The teacher had given him soft butter. Louis spread it slow. He pushed the knife across the bread. The butter made the toast shiny. "Look at me," said Louis.

Next came the milk. The carton was big for his hands. He tipped it over his cup. Milk came out fast. A drop ran down his hand. Louis took a breath and tipped it slower. The milk went in, not one drop on the table. His friend Mia clapped. "Good pouring," she said.

Louis set the milk on the table. He started to run off to play. Then he stopped. He looked at the milk. "The milk goes back in the fridge," said Mia, "to keep it cold." Louis picked up the carton. He carried it to the fridge, one careful step at a time. He put it on the shelf and shut the door. "Far from warm, nice and cold," he said. Then he ran back to chase Mia around the table, laughing, his toast waiting on his plate.

Connor wanted to build a big tower in the playroom. He pulled a heavy box of blocks. He pulled and pulled. The box would not move. "Why won't you go?" he asked. The box was heavy.

Then he saw a feather pillow on the chair. He picked it up. Up it came, so easy! "Heavy and light are opposites," said his sister, popping her head in the door.

Connor wondered about the blocks. Maybe he could take some out. He used a small tool, a toy shovel, to scoop blocks out. The box got lighter. Now he could pull it! He stacked the blocks fast. The tower grew tall. Then it fell down slow, block by block. "Again!" said Connor. He put the pillow on top, so soft and light, and started once more.

Asher ran to the swing at the park. "Stay close to me," said Mommy. So Asher swung right next to her. The sun made the slide hot to touch. A big kid touched it and pulled his hand back fast. "Hot," said Mommy. "Let a grown-up check first." She put her hand on the slide. "Still hot. We will come back."

Soon it was time to go home. Asher was hot too. Mommy said, "Let's bring your juice for the walk." Asher sipped his cold juice. It was sweet and cool. The cold juice made his hot day feel better.

At home, Daddy ran the bath. Asher wanted to jump right in. "Wait," said Daddy. Daddy put his hand in the water. "A grown-up checks first. Warm, not hot. All good." Asher touched the water with one little toe. It was warm like a hug. He splashed and laughed. Then a rubber duck popped up from under the bubbles. "Quack!" said Asher, and he was happy.

Isaiah sat in his car seat. The car went fast. Then the car went slow. "Mama, why did we go slow?" he asked. "A big truck was in front of us," said Mama. "Now it is gone."

Mama smiled at him. "Let's play the opposite game," she said. "I say a word. You shout its opposite. Two words as different as they can be are opposites, like big and small." "Yes!" said Isaiah. "Start!"

Mama said, "Big." "Small!" said Isaiah. He won that one. Mama said, "Fast." "Slow!" said Isaiah. He laughed. His voice sounded loud in the little car.

Mama said, "Hot." Isaiah thought hard. He looked out the window. He saw a cup of ice in his hand. The ice was so cold on his fingers. "Cold!" he shouted. "You win again," said Mama. Then she stopped the car. She held his cup of warm cocoa, and blew on it. "This is hot," she said. "So sip it slow." Isaiah touched his cup with just one fingertip. The ice in his other hand stayed cold. "Ice is cold," he said. "Cocoa is hot. Opposites!" Mama buckled his seat belt again. "Ready to play more?" she asked. Isaiah grinned. "Go!"

Raphael was at the dentist. The friendly nurse gave him a sticker. Then Raphael had to use the toilet. He hurried out fast. He wanted his snack.

The nurse stood by the little sink. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet," she said. Raphael looked at his hands. They looked clean. But he went back anyway.

He pushed the soap pump. Bubbles! He rubbed and rubbed. The nurse helped him count to twenty. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. The water washed the bubbles away.

Then Raphael sat in the middle of the big chair. He opened his crackers. He ate them with clean hands. The dentist peeked in and smiled. "Nice brushing too," she said. Raphael skipped to the door with his sticker.

Eva rode the school bus. It was her first day of school. She held her pink backpack on her lap. The bus went bump, bump, bump. "One stop, two stops, three stops," said the driver. "Yours is next." Eva got off with her teacher.

Outside, the playground had a big slide. Eva wanted to go down it. She ran to the steps. But other children stood in a line. One, two, three, four children waited. Eva tried to go up first. A boy said, "We take turns on the slide." So Eva went to the back.

Each child went down. Whee! One gone, two gone, three gone, four gone. Then it was Eva's turn. She slid down fast. The wind tickled her nose. A girl named Mia ran to the back. "Your turn now," Eva said, and she ran too.

Arlo sat at the big table. He had paper and washable markers. He drew a red sun. He drew a green garden. One, two, three flowers in the garden.

Then the blue marker slipped. It drew a long blue line on his hand. "Oh no," said Arlo. "My hand is blue." He looked and looked. Would it stay blue forever? "I guess I will try water," he said.

Mama helped him at the sink. She turned on the water. Arlo rubbed his hand with soap. The soap felt slippery. He rubbed and rubbed. The blue line went away. All gone! Arlo held up his clean hand. "Washable markers wash off with soap and water," he said. Then he went back to the table. He drew one, two, three more flowers. "This time I will be careful," said Arlo. He smiled at his clean, wet hand.

Snow fell at school today. Avery looked out the window. The snow was white. "I will draw the snow," she said.

She got white paper. She drew with her white crayon. She looked and looked. She could not see the snow. "Where did it go?" she said. Her friend Mia came over. "Try blue paper," said Mia. Avery got blue paper. She was careful with the glue pot so it would not spill. She drew with her white crayon. Now the snow showed up. White on blue!

Avery drew a red hat. She drew a green tree. She drew a yellow sun. She drew her pet dog, too. He was brown with white snow on his nose. "Look," said Avery. "My snow is white, like real snow." Mia clapped her hands. The two friends hung their pictures by the window. Outside, more white snow fell down, down, down.

Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her tummy felt fluttery, like small wings inside.

Mom knelt down next to her. "My tummy felt that way too, on my first day," Mom said. "Feeling nervous is okay."

Elizabeth held Mom's hand. Then she saw a boy by the cubbies. His backpack had a stuck zipper. He pulled and pulled. It would not move.

Elizabeth walked over. "Can I help?" she asked. The boy nodded. She held the backpack still. He pulled the zipper again. This time it slid open. A slimy toy frog jumped out and landed on the floor. They both laughed.

"I am Sam," the boy said. "I am Elizabeth." The teacher rang a soft bell. Time for a story on the rug.

Elizabeth sat next to Sam. Her tummy felt calm now. Mom waved from the door.

"Thank you for my frog," Sam whispered.

"Thank you for sitting with me," said Elizabeth. She opened the book about frogs and turned the first page.
