Beau sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Look!" said Mom. "A cow!" "An animal!" said Beau. He saw a dog too. Another animal!

It was windy outside. The trees waved their leaves. Beau saw a store with apples. "Food!" he said. He saw a shop with balls and bears. "Toys!" said Beau. "Yes, toys," said Mom. She laughed.

Then the window was open a little. The wind blew something in. It landed on Beau's lap. It was soft. It was a feather! "Mom! Look!" said Beau. He held it up. Mom peeked in the mirror. "A bird lost that," she said. "Birds are animals that have feathers." Beau looked out the window. A bird flew by! It had feathers too. Beau waved his feather at it. "Bye, bird!" he called. "Bye!"

Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Myles went to the airport with Dad to get her. They waited by the big doors. "Families wait here to meet people coming off a plane," said Dad. The doors opened. A man walked out. "Grandma!" yelled Myles. It was not Grandma. It was a tall man with a hat. The doors opened again. "Grandma!" It was not Grandma. It was a lady with a dog in a bag. Dad laughed. "You keep looking, Myles." The doors opened one more time. "Grandma!" It was Grandma! She gave Myles a big hug.

The next day, they went to the park. Myles ran to the swings, but the gate was closed. "Closed!" said Myles. Grandma showed him a little latch. She pushed it up, and the gate swung open. Myles ran in and did a big spring from his toes, up into the air. "Look at me!" he said. Grandma clapped and said, "Again, please!"

Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the table. Nora wanted to draw on it, but she did not know how to start. "Watch," said Mia. Mia pressed one small button. The screen lit up. Nora pressed it too. The screen lit up again.

Mia tapped a little picture of a paint pot. A drawing app opened. Nora put her finger on the screen and slid it across. A purple line followed her finger! She moved her finger again and again. Soon she had a long squiggly line. It looked like a snake. "My snake!" said Nora. She gave it a messy tongue.

A bell rang. It was time for a snack. Nora pressed the button and the screen went dark. She set the tablet down next to Mia's book. "All done," she said. Then she ran to the table, and behind her the tablet sat quiet and neat, with a snake hidden inside.

Paisley walks to the bookmobile with her dad. It is a big blue bus full of books. Paisley wants one book very much. It is about a little red fox.

The librarian smiles at Paisley. "You can have your very own library card," she says. Paisley holds the card with two hands. It has her name on it. Paisley feels a big, happy feeling inside.

Paisley hugs the fox book to her chest. Then she sees the door of the bookmobile. "I have to put it back now," she says. Her face goes sad.

The librarian shakes her head. "No, you can take it home," she says. "Your card lets you borrow it. You can read it at home. Then you bring it back next week."

"My card lets me take the fox home?" Paisley asks. "Yes," says the librarian. "That is what a card does."

Paisley holds the card up high. "Take it home! Take it home!" she says. The card is a little rough on the edges. Paisley likes that. It feels real.

At home, Paisley puts the card in her pocket. She sits with Dad on the soft couch. They read about the little red fox. The fox finds his mom in the end.

Paisley pats her pocket. "Good card," she says. "We go back next week."

Lennon went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. It was Diwali day. Little lamps sat in rows on a long table. Each lamp was small and clay. Each lamp needed a flame.

"I want to light one," said Lennon. She reached for a match on the table. Mama held her hand. "Grown-ups light the flames," said Mama. "You can pick a lamp for me." Lennon looked down the row. She chose a fat lamp with a red stripe. "This one, Mama." Mama lit it with the match. The wick made a small flame. It flickered and glowed.

The flame sent warm light onto Lennon's face. Then Mama put the lamp in the window. "The wrong place would be under the paper stars," said Papa. He moved a paper star far away. Lennon watched her lamp shine. "I picked it," she said. Mama smiled and held her hand. The little flame danced in the glass.

Lucy went to the park with her dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Lucy wore her sun hat to keep the sun off her face.

Then the leaves began to move. The trees went swish, swish. "It is windy," said Dad. The wind blew hard. Lucy's hat flew right off her head!

"Oh no," said Lucy. "My hat is gone!" She ran after it on the grass. The hat rolled and tumbled. Dad ran too. He caught it by the swing.

Dad put the hat back on Lucy's head. He tied the strap under her chin. "There," he said. "Now the wind can't take it again."

Lucy patted the hat to keep it on. "Good hat," she said. A kind boy gave her a daisy from the dirt by the fence. Lucy smelled it. The wind blew her hair, but the hat stayed put.

Hailey sat at a little table in the cafe. Mom gave her a pencil and a paper napkin. "You can write your name," Mom said. Hailey wanted to write her name so much.

She held the pencil tight. She pressed down hard. Snap! The black tip broke off. The pencil had no point now. "My pencil broke," Hailey said. Mom got a new pencil from her bag. "Try again," she said. "Press soft this time."

Hailey held the pencil with soft fingers. She pressed gently. The tip stayed whole. She made a big H. Then a round a. Then i, l, e, y. There it was. Hailey! The letters were a little crooked, but Mom said they were not ugly at all. Mom kissed the top of Hailey's head. Hailey kissed the paper, right beside her name. Then she painted a small red heart under the H, with her crayon. "Now everyone knows this is mine," Hailey said.

Lily wants to draw a big yellow cat. Her teacher hands her a tablet. Lily takes it with one hand. The tablet tips and slips. It almost falls to the floor. Her teacher catches it just in time.

"Try again," says her teacher. "One, two, hands." Lily holds the tablet with one hand. It wobbles. Lily holds the tablet with two hands. Now it sits still and safe in her arms. She smiles and carries it to the little table.

Lily presses the round button. The screen lights up. She taps the blue square and the drawing app opens. She moves her finger on the screen. A straight line appears, then a tail, then two pointy ears. She draws a stick for the cat to scratch. The cat needs one, two, three whiskers. Lily counts them out loud.

The bell rings. Time to go. Lily presses the button and the screen goes dark. "One, two, hands," she says. She carries the tablet with two hands and sets it in the basket. "Bye, yellow cat," says Lily.

Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted to buy apples for a snack.

Mom said, "Let's count the apples." Sarah put them in the bag, one by one. "One, two, three," she said. She found one more. "Four, five, six, seven." Two more made it nine. Then Mom held up one last apple. "Ten!" said Sarah. Ten apples in the bag.

At the sign, Sarah saw numbers. The sign said 10 beside the apples. Sarah frowned. "Why does ten have a 1 and a 0? Little numbers have just one number." Mom said, "I guess that is how ten is written. A 1, then a 0." Sarah traced the numbers with her finger. First a 1. Then a round 0. "Ten," she read. She smiled big.

On the way home, they passed the cracker boxes. Sarah spotted a triangle on one box. "Look, Mom. A triangle cracker! So cute." Mom laughed. At home, Mom washed the apples. Sarah counted them again, all the way to ten. Then she bit into the biggest one. "Ten apples make one good snack," said Mom. Sarah nodded, munching happily.

Ibrahim sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. He looked out of the window. He saw a big blue river. Some ducks sat by the water. "Look, ducks!" he said.

Ibrahim felt hungry. "Can I have my snack, please?" he asked. Dad reached back. He passed the little bag of crackers. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. Dad smiled at him in the mirror.

The bag had a tight top. Ibrahim pulled it. He pulled and pulled. His hands hurt a bit. The top would not open. His face went hot and cross. Then he took a big breath. He said, "Dad, it is too hard. Can you help me, please?"

Dad pulled over and stopped the car. He turned around and opened the tight top. It made a pop sound. "Here you go," said Dad. "Thank you, Dad," said Ibrahim. He ate a cracker and watched the ducks fly over the river. "This was a good early morning ride," said Dad. Ibrahim gave Dad a cracker too. "One for you," he said.

Lydia stood on the baseball diamond. Daddy brought a purple hoop and a big red ball.

"Throw the beanbag in," said Daddy.

Lydia threw the beanbag. She thought it would bounce. It went flop. It lay still on the grass.

She picked it up. She threw it again. Flop. It fell flat and stayed down. She patted it with her hand.

"It doesn't bounce," said Lydia.

Then Lydia threw the big red ball. Bounce, bounce, bounce! The ball hopped high. But it rolled away from her hands.

"Try again," said Daddy. "Use both hands."

Lydia held out both hands. She waited. Daddy rolled the ball to her. She caught it. She hugged it tight.

Now Lydia looked at the beanbag. It would not roll away. She held it up. She let go. Flop. It fell right down into the purple hoop.

"I did it!" said Lydia.

Daddy clapped. "One more time," he said.

Lydia brought the beanbag back. She held it high. She let go. Flop. In it went, soft as a sleepy cat.

Charlie ran to the table with muddy hands. "Bath first, then supper," said Mom.

"Why?" asked Charlie.

"Muddy hands make muddy bread," said Mom. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Charlie looked at her hands. They were very muddy. She had been digging at school all day. She had made a big mud pie.

So Charlie went to the sink. Mom turned on the water. Charlie washed and washed. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

Then Charlie sat at the table. Mom had baked bread, and it smelled good. Charlie picked up a piece. Her bread stayed clean.

"Look, Mom! No mud on it," said Charlie.

"You are a smart girl," said Mom.

After supper, Charlie put on her soft pajamas. She yawned a big yawn.

"Can mud pie be my breakfast?" she asked.

Mom laughed. "No, silly. Mud is for digging, not for eating."

Mom tucked Charlie into bed. Charlie closed her eyes. Her clean hands rested on the blanket.

"Goodnight, mud pie maker," Mom whispered.

Addison went to the library for story time. The librarian, Miss Ana, held up a book. "Today's story is about shapes," she said. Addison clapped her hands.

After the story, Miss Ana put out paper shapes on the big table. There was a square. There was a triangle. There was a long rectangle. And there was a circle, round like a pancake.

"Let's make a shape house," said Miss Ana. "I will cut the shapes for you, because scissors are sharp." Addison picked up the circle. "This can be the sun," she said.

Miss Ana handed Addison the square. "You can glue this one," she said. Addison pressed the square onto the paper. Then she pressed the triangle on top, like a roof. The rectangle made a door. She scratched the glue with her finger to make it stick.

Addison looked at the circle again. She turned it over. She turned it around. "Miss Ana," she said, "I want to cut this one too, but I can't find the corner to start."

Miss Ana smiled. "That is because a circle is round and has no corners," she said.

Addison felt the edge with her finger. Round and round her finger went. "It just keeps going!" she said. She giggled. "Silly circle."

Miss Ana cut slow, careful snips around the sun. Then Addison glued it high in the sky. Her shape house had a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and one round, no-corner sun.

"Your house needs a mean old cat," said her friend Ben. "A mean triangle cat!"

"Here, kitty kitty," said Addison.

James was painting at school. He wanted to paint green grass. He looked in the green paint pot. It was empty.

"My grass needs green," said James. He sat and thought. Then he saw a blue pot and a yellow pot.

He put blue paint on his brush. Then he put yellow paint on it too. He mixed them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Look, look!" said James.

His friend Mia came over. "Green," she said. "What is its name?" "Grass," said James. He painted tall grass and short grass. All of it was green.

Outside, the wind blew cold. The water cup felt almost frozen on his fingers. Miss Bell said, "Let's hang the paintings up to dry." They waited and waited. The paint dried slowly. Then James saw his green grass, hanging on the wall. "Blue and yellow," he said with a big smile.

Athena wanted to help cook. Her mama said, "You can wash the apples." Athena ran fast to the sink. The water splashed up. Splash, splash! Her socks got wet. Her curly hair got little drops on it too.

"Wet socks feel squishy," said Athena. She looked down at her feet. The big puddle was on the floor. The small puddle was on her sock. Mama came over slow and careful. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mama. "You need dry socks now." Athena sat on her little chair. She pulled off one wet sock. She pulled off the other wet sock. Her feet were cold and drippy.

Mama brought warm, dry socks from the basket. Athena pushed her toes in. Soft! Dry! She wiggled her toes inside them. Then Mama let Athena dry the apples with a towel. Rub, rub, rub. The apples went from wet to shiny and dry. Athena held one up to the window. It looked like a little red moon. "The apple is all dry," she said. "And me too!"

Beatrice loved school. At play time, she saw Tom and Mia in the corner. They fed a toy bunny with a tiny spoon. Beatrice wanted to play too. She stood and watched. The bunny got one spoon, then two spoons, then three spoons of pretend carrots.

Beatrice did not know how to start. She held her teddy bear tight. Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend we run a bear hospital!" she said.

Tom looked up. Mia looked up. "A bear hospital!" said Mia. "I will be the doctor." Tom grabbed a blanket for a bed. Beatrice bent down and laid her teddy in it. One bandage, two bandages, three bandages on the teddy's paw. "All better," said Doctor Mia.

Just like that, the game had begun. Beatrice smiled a happy smile. She had said the magic words, and friends came running. "Let's pretend we bake a cake next!" said Tom. Beatrice clapped her hands and stirred a pretend bowl round and round.

Milo ran to the block corner at school. Yesterday he had built a tall tower there. Today he wanted to build one again. But Ben was already playing with the blocks.

"You can play with the blocks later," said Miss Ana, a kind woman with a loose blue sweater.

Milo sat down at the little table. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Ana. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Milo watched Ben stack a red block, then a blue one. Ben dropped one block. It rolled under the shelf. Ben had to reach far to get it. While Ben reached, his tower wobbled. Down it fell. Blocks rolled everywhere on the soft rug.

Milo picked up a block and handed it to Ben. "Thank you," said Ben. "Do you want to help me build it now?"

"Now?" said Milo. He grinned. "Yes!"

They stacked the blocks side by side. Miss Ana came over and watched. "You two can paint together tomorrow," she said.

"Tomorrow is after later," said Milo.

"It sure is," said Miss Ana, and she put two brushes by the paint cups.

Lillian had a cold. Her nose was red. Her throat felt scratchy. She sat on the sofa with her blanket.

Grandma brought her a cup. It was a small blue cup. It had a star on it. "This is your special cup," Grandma said. "Try a little sip of water."

Lillian shook her head. "I am not thirsty," she said. Grandma put the cup in her hands anyway. Lillian took one small sip. Then she took another. The water was cool and fresh.

Grandma sat beside her. They watched a plane fly past the window. It left a long white line in the sky. Lillian sipped some more water while she watched.

Soon Lillian sat up a little taller. Her throat felt better. Her voice came back clear. "Grandma, can I have more water?" she asked. Grandma smiled and filled the little blue cup again. Lillian held it with both hands and took a big drink. Then she said, "That star cup is the best cup ever."

James was at the bank with Mom. It was cold outside. James had his red coat on his lap.

"Time to go," said Mom. James held up his coat. He put one arm in. He looked for the other sleeve. Where did it go? He turned and turned. The sleeve was hiding behind him.

A big kid named Ben was there too. Ben had a blue coat. "Watch this," said Ben. Ben laid his coat on the floor. The hood went down by his toes. Ben put his arms in the sleeves. Then Ben flipped the coat over his head. The coat was on!

Could James do that too? He laid his coat on the floor. The hood went down by his toes. He put his arms in the sleeves. He flipped it over his head. It worked! The coat was on, all by himself.

Now the zipper. James touched the zipper pull. He pushed it up, up, up. It went click, click, click. Mom smiled. "Good job, James."

On the wall was a picture of a snowman. "Look, Mom," said James. "He has a coat too." James patted his own warm coat and walked out the big door.

Mohamed went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought a big round loaf of bread. They bought a jar of golden honey. At home, Mohamed wanted to make breakfast for the family. "I will make honey toast," he said.

Dad got the butter from the fridge. Mohamed poked it with his finger. The butter was hard as a little hammer. "Ouch," said Mohamed. "It will not spread!" He tried to push it on the bread. The hard butter made a hole in the soft bread. "Oh no," said Mohamed. "The bread has a loose crumb now!"

Dad smiled. "Let's set the butter on the counter," he said. "We can wait." They set the butter down. They watched a fly buzz past the window. They washed the blueberries. They sang a toast song. Mohamed poked the butter again. Now it was soft! His finger went right in, squish.

Mohamed spread the soft butter all over the bread. He drizzled the honey on top. Mom took a big bite. "Mmm," she said. "Best toast ever!" Mohamed held up his plate. "More honey, please!"

Rosalie was going on a big trip. First she went to the airport. It was loud and busy. So many people! So many feet!

Then Rosalie saw the planes. Big planes in the window! "I want to run!" she said. She started to go. But the crowd was thick. Feet everywhere. Mama held out her hand. "Hold my hand in the crowd," she said. Rosalie took it. Her hand felt warm in Mama's hand. Together they walked and walked. In busy places, children stay close and hold hands. Rosalie held on tight.

At last they got to the beach. The sand was warm. The water went swish, swish. Rosalie found a tiny shell. It was pink. "Look, Mama! A tiny pink shell!" The waves came in. The waves went out. Rosalie held Mama's hand by the water. "Can we stay here all day?" she asked. Mama laughed and squeezed her hand.

Kai sat on Grandma's big soft rug. Grandma was humming a song. Kai wanted to sing it too. But he did not know the words yet.

Grandma clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Try it," she said. Kai clapped too. His claps were fast. Too fast! Grandma slowed down. Clap, clap, clap. Kai waited. Then he clapped with her. Now his claps were just right.

"Now sing," said Grandma. She sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Kai opened his mouth. He knew this tune! It was the same tune as his ABC song. He sang, "A, B, C, D." Grandma laughed. "Same song!" she said. Kai clapped and sang. He sang the ABC song all the way to Z. Then he sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Same tune, new words.

"You sing like a fish can swim," said Grandma. Kai clapped his hands. "Naughty song," he giggled. "It tricked me!" Grandma clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. "Sing it again," said Kai.

Jaxon woke up at Grandma's house. The sun made a warm line on his blanket. He wanted to go outside and play in the leaves. But first he had to get dressed.

Grandma laid out his clothes. Jaxon pulled on his pants. He pulled on his shirt. Then he pushed his feet into his shoes. He tried to walk. His bare toes felt cold and bumpy inside. He laughed and sat back down on the bed.

He pulled the shoes off. He wiggled his feet into his soft blue socks first. Then he pushed his shoes back on. Now his feet felt warm and cozy. He stood up and stomped. The shoes stayed on.

Grandma was waiting at the door. "Ready for breakfast?" she asked. Jaxon ate warm oatmeal that Grandpa made at the stove. After breakfast, he ran outside. The leaves crunched under his feet. A shy little cat peeked out from behind the bench. Jaxon knocked gently on the wood. "Hello, cat," he said. "Come play with me." The cat blinked and stepped out into the sun.

Jake went to the library with his mom. He saw a big wooden train table. He wanted to play with it so much. But a girl named Mia was already there. She held the long red train.

Jake reached for it. Mia pulled it back. "I had it first," she said. Jake felt like he might cry.

Then the librarian knelt down. She had a bee sticker on her sweater. "You can take turns," she said. "Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another." Mia nodded. "You first," she said to Jake. Jake pushed the red train all around the track. It went under the bridge and past the messy block tower. Then he stopped. "Your turn now, Mia," he said. Mia laughed and pushed the train fast. Jake clapped. When her turn was done, it was his go again. They played until the lights blinked. "Time to go," said Mom. Jake waved to Mia. "See you next time," he said, holding his bee sticker tight.

Mason lost his monkey. It was his favorite toy. The monkey had a long tail and a spotted tummy.

"Where did it go?" Mason asked. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. He looked in Grandma's big chair. No monkey.

"Maybe it went on the bus," said Grandma. "You took the bus yesterday." They walked to the bus stop. The bus driver smiled. He held up the monkey!

"This tag says Mason," the driver said. "So I knew it was yours." Grandma had written Mason's name on the tag.

"How does the tag know me?" Mason asked. He looked at the little letters. M for Mason. The letters spelled his name.

"Let's look for more tags," said Grandma. They went back inside. They wrote Mason's name on his toy truck. They wrote it on his red ball. They even wrote it on a block they used to build a tower.

"One name, two names, three names," said Mason. Every toy got a tag.

Then Mason hugged his monkey tight. "Now everyone knows you are mine," he said. "My name is on your tag!"

Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find the letter M. Her teddy bear had a tag with an M on it. But she did not know where M lived.

The library had a big rug with letters on it. Brooklyn sat down on the A. "A says ah," she said. Dad smiled. She hopped to B. "B says buh," she said. She hopped to C. Then she hopped to D.

But then she got stuck. She saw L, N, O and P. Where did M go? Brooklyn felt a little bad. She wanted M for her teddy's tag.

Then Dad began to hum a tune. Brooklyn knew that tune. It was the alphabet song. She sang along. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She kept singing. "H, I, J, K." Then she sang, "L, M, N, O, P."

The song put M after L! Brooklyn looked at the rug. She pointed to the spot right after L. "M goes here," she said. There it was, between L and N.

"M says mmm," said Dad. Brooklyn hugged her teddy. "M is for Moon," she said, pointing at a book about the moon. The moon could shine in the sky. Dad checked out the book for her.

Brooklyn waved to the letters. "Bye, A. Bye, B. Bye, M," she said.

Emile wants to read the book about the red truck. He finds it on the shelf. It is a thick book with a big flag on the cover. Emile opens it at the back. He points at the words. He starts at the right side of the page. He slides his finger to the left. The words do not match the pictures. The dog is on the wrong page.

"What is wrong?" he asks.

"You started at the back," says Miss Ana. She turns the book around. She opens the front cover. "Start here, on the left." Emile puts his finger on the first word. He slides it to the right. Now the words go with the pictures. The red truck beeps. Emile smiles and turns to the next page.

"Beep, beep," he says.

Ava sat at the dinner table. She had a big bite of pasta. The dog sat by her chair. "No begging," said Daddy. The dog begged anyway. Ava laughed.

"Can I stay up late?" Ava asked. "Pleeease?" Mommy looked out at the stormy sky. "You can try," she said. Ava tried. She stayed up long past her bath. She stayed up past her pajamas. She stayed up past her story.

The next morning, Ava was slow to get dressed. Her socks took a long time. She was too tired to play. She yawned at breakfast. Her milk sat untouched. "Does milk come from a cow?" she asked, yawning again.

That night, Ava took her bath early. She put on her pajamas. She went to bed on time.

The next morning, Ava jumped up. She dressed fast. She ran to her toys. "I can play!" she said. "I slept, and now I can play!"

Blake ran into Mia's house. Mia had a music box and a drum. "We can play a song!" said Mia. Mia's mom said, "I will count one, two, three, four. Then we all start singing together." Blake could not wait. She started singing right away. But Mia was still quiet. Blake had to stop. She had sung too soon! "Oops," said Blake. "I lose my spot when I go too fast." Mia giggled. Mia's mom smiled. "Let's try again," she said. "Wait for the count. It is easy. One, two, three, four!" This time Blake waited. One, two, three, four. Then both girls sang at the same time. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" They did not miss a word. Blake clapped her hands to the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Mia clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. Then Mia's dog barked on the last clap! The girls laughed and laughed. "Again!" said Blake. "One, two, three, four!"

Felix wanted a bedtime story. Grandma was busy, so Grandpa said, "I will read it."

Grandpa sat down. He opened the book. He started at the front. He turned the pages one by one. Then Grandma came in. "My turn," she said. She opened the book too.

Felix listened hard. Grandpa had said, "The moon was very sleepy." Now Grandma said the very same words. "The moon was very sleepy." Felix tapped the page. "Grandma, you said it just like Grandpa!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "The words are right there."

"The pencil words say it?" asked Felix.

"The printed words," Grandma said with a smile.

Felix looked closely. The little black marks sat on the page. They did not wiggle. They did not run away. Could paper really talk? Felix pointed at one word. "What does this one say?"

Grandpa leaned close. "It says moon."

Felix looked out the window. The noisy wind blew outside. The real moon was up in the sky.

"It is in the book and in the sky!" said Felix.

Grandma turned to the last page. She read the end. Then Felix closed the book himself, front cover down, just right.

"Again," said Felix.

Florence went to the library with her dad. She found a big book about a little mouse. The mouse had soft gray fur in the pictures. Florence loved those pictures. She wanted to know who drew them.

"Who made this mouse?" she asked her dad.

"Let's look," said Dad. He opened the front of the book. "We start here," he said. Florence pointed at the little black marks. Dad moved his finger under them. "These are words," he said. "They tell the story." The words said a name. "This is the illustrator," said Dad. "An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book."

Florence turned the pages one by one. The mouse moved to a barn. Then the mouse found some cheese. The pictures came after each other, front to back. At the end, the mouse slept in a nest.

Florence hugged the book. "This mouse is special," she said. "I want to take her home."

Dad helped her check out the book. Florence held it tight all the way to the door. "Good night, little mouse," she whispered. "I will read you again tomorrow."

Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. His paper had a big round pumpkin on it. But the paint jars had no orange. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. Hudson frowned at the jars.

Then he had an idea. He put a blob of red on his brush. He put a blob of yellow next to it. He mixed them with the brush. Round and round went the brush. The paint turned orange! Hudson gasped. "Mama, look! Orange!"

He painted his pumpkin all orange. He painted a green stem too. His bear sat on the chair beside him. Hudson held the bear up to see. "Nice pumpkin," said Mama with a smile. Hudson yawned a big yawn. Paint time had made him sleepy. He leaned his head on Mama's arm. "My pumpkin can sleep now," he said.

Isla went to the pharmacy with Dad. The shop smelled like cough drops. On a shelf Isla saw a little fox toy. It was soft and orange. Isla held the fox while Dad got his medicine. Her tummy made a growl. "Snack time soon," said Dad. Isla looked at her hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said. They looked clean and pale. Dad got soap and water from the sink by the counter. "Let's wash," he said. Isla rubbed the soap on her hands. It felt slippery and smelled like flowers. It was hard to wait, so they sang "Happy Birthday" two times. That made twenty seconds. Isla sang loud. The fox watched from the counter. Then the soap bubbles went down the drain. Isla held her hands up to the light. They shone. Then came a small surprise. Dad opened his bag and pulled out a banana. Isla took one bite. "Mmm," she said. "Wash again after the toilet too," said Dad. "Sing with me," said Isla. "Happy birthday to you."

Eli wanted his bedtime book. He looked at the shelf. There were so many books. Some were big. Some were small. He did not know which one was his.

Mom gave him a card from his drawer. It was his birthday card. It had marks on the front. "Those marks say Eli," said Mom. Eli traced the letters with his finger. E, L, I. Then he opened the card. He turned the pages one by one, front to back. The pictures went in order. The cat jumped first. Then the cat landed in a pot of flowers. Eli laughed.

He held the card next to a book on the shelf. One book had the same marks on a sticker. E, L, I. The letters sat in the same order. "That one is mine!" said Eli. He pulled it down slowly.

They sat on the bed. Eli opened the front cover first. He turned each page the same way as the card. On the last page was a photo of Eli as a tiny baby. "That is me!" said Eli. Mom smiled and kissed his head.

Eleanor was four today! There was a big cake on the table. Her friend Milo came in with a gift. It had a red wheel printed on the paper.

"Open mine!" said Milo. Eleanor tore the paper off. It was a pretend tool kit, with a strong little hammer inside. "Wow!" she said.

Then she saw more gifts. She ran to the next one. She ripped it open fast. It was a soft bunny from Grandma.

Mom tapped her chin. "Milo is still holding his empty bag," she said. Eleanor looked at Milo. Then she ran back to him.

"Thank you, Milo!" she said. "I love the hammer!" Milo smiled big. "You're welcome!" he said.

Eleanor hugged the tool kit to her chest. "Time for cake!" Dad called. Everyone ran to the table.

Leah held her doll tight. "Big cart!" she said. Mom picked the big cart, not the small basket. Leah loves the big cart.

They went fast on the moving floor. Then they walked slow by the milk. "Cold!" said Leah, touching the frozen door. "Careful," said Mom. "The frozen door is very cold." Leah saw hot bread, too. A baker with big gloves held the hot pan. Leah did not touch. She just smelled it. Yum.

At home, Leah ate a small cup of ice cream. Then she slept and slept. She woke up. It was dark! "Is it morning?" she whispered to her doll. Mom came in. "No, sweet girl. It is still night." Leah looked out. Dark sky, dark trees. "Day and night are opposites," said Mom. Leah yawned. She hugged her doll and closed her eyes. "Night, night, sun," she whispered.

Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But the paint cups sat in the far corner. The corner was dark and dim.

He picked a cup in the dark. "This one is green," he said. He painted. Then he moved his paper to the window. The sun came in. In the light, his frog was blue! Not green. Blue.

"I could not tell in the dark corner," said Miles.

"You could not tell," said his teacher, Miss Ana. "It is hard to tell what color things are in a very dark place."

Miles carried all the cups to the sunny window. Now he could see. Red. Blue. Yellow. Green. He picked green. He painted a new frog. It was green all over.

The class dog, Biscuit, barked once. Miles laughed. Biscuit put his nose right on the paper.

"Do not sniff my frog," said Miles. Biscuit wagged his tail.

Miles spun around in his chair, one time, two times. Then he stopped. "Whoa," he said. "That made me dizzy." He held the table till the room stood still.

He looked at his frog in the sun. Green. Green. Just right.

Xavier ran into the grocery store. His soft bunny was lost. "Bunny, where are you?" he called.

Xavier ran fast. He ran from the fruit to the bread. He ran to the milk. He ran to the lunch meat. "I don't see bunny!" he said.

Mom held his hand. "Let's slow down," she said. "Let's look at one place at a time. Then we won't miss any places."

They looked at the fruit. No bunny. They looked at the bread. No bunny. They looked at the milk. No bunny. They looked at the lunch meat. There was bunny! He sat by the cheese.

"Bunny!" said Xavier. He hugged his soft bunny tight. "You were hiding by the cheese. Silly bunny."

Bunny's ear flopped over, like a little wave hello.

Kinsley went to her friend Mia's house. Mia had a big toy box. But Kinsley felt shy. She did not know what to play.

Mia opened the dress-up box. "Look," said Mia. She put on a red hat. "Now I am a firefighter!" Mia held a pretend hose. She sprayed water at a pretend fire. Kinsley clapped.

Kinsley found a long white coat. She put it on. She put a small hat on top of her head. "I am a doctor!" she said. Her baby doll was sick. She wrapped the doll in a blanket. She gave it pretend medicine. The doll got all better.

Then Kinsley cleaned up the toys with Mia. They put each hat back in the box. "Come back soon," said Mia. Kinsley hugged her baby doll tight. "Next time, you can be the firefighter," said Mia. "Yes!" said Kinsley. "And you can be the doctor."

Julia stood in the kitchen on the gray mat. Baby Sam was napping. Julia wanted to play music for him.

She took a big pot and a small pot. She banged them fast. BANG, BANG, BANG! The noise was very loud.

Mama came in fast. "Shh," she said. "Sam is waking up." Mama held the pots. "Loud and quiet are opposites," she said. "Let's try quiet."

Julia tapped the small pot slow. Tap, tap. It was so quiet. Baby Sam stayed asleep. Julia tapped again. Quiet as a mouse.

Then Mama made tea. Julia stood back, far from the hot kettle. Mama gave her a cold cup of water instead. Julia drank it all up.

Baby Sam woke up with a small cry. Julia ran to him fast, with her little pot. She tapped it quiet and soft. Sam smiled at her.

Mama peeked in. "Your quiet song woke him happy," she said.

Julia tapped one more time. Tap.

Nova sat at the big art table. She wanted to paint a green cow. But the green paint pot was empty. "Oh no," said Nova.

The teacher knelt down beside her. "Let's mix some," she said. She poured yellow paint into a cup. Then she added blue paint. Nova stirred it with her brush. The paint turned green! Nova laughed and painted her cow on high, high grass.

Then it was clean-up time. "Sorting by color," said the teacher. Nova made a red pile, a blue pile, and a yellow pile of blocks. All the red ones together. All the blue ones together.

She counted her piles. One block looked funny in the yellow pile. It was hiding there! Nova picked it up. It was red. She put it with the red blocks.

"You found it," said her friend Sam. "Thank you." Nova smiled. Maybe she would dream about a green cow tonight.

Charles sat on the big rug at book club. Miss Amy held up letter cards. "This is A," she said. "A says ahh, like apple."

Charles clapped. "Ahh!" he said. "Like animal!"

The kids sang the alphabet song. Charles sang too. "A, B, C," he sang, "all the way to P." Then he stopped. "Done!" he said.

Miss Amy laughed. "Keep singing," she said. Charles sang on. "Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z. Z!" He looked around with wide eyes. "Where did Z come from?"

"Z was hiding in the song," said his friend Mila. She scratched her itchy sweater. "Z tickled my ears!"

"Does Z end the song?" asked Charles.

"Yes," said Miss Amy. "A starts it, and Z ends it."

Charles stood up. He found the letter cards in the basket. He laid them out on the dry, dusty rug. "A comes first," he said. "Z goes last." He put A at one end and Z at the other. He counted them all, one by one. Then he gave Z a big hug.

"Z waits so long," said Charles. "Poor Z. Now Z can sit by me."

Mila giggled. "Can A sit by me?" she asked.

"A is all yours," said Charles. "Ahh!"

Raphael sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He was excited! "Today I get a checkup," he said. His mom held his hand. An old truck went by the window. Raphael saw it with his eyes. Beep, beep! He heard it with his ears.

The doctor came in. She had a little stick and a lemon slice. "Open wide," she said. Raphael opened his mouth. First she looked with her light. Then she said, "Take a tiny lick of this." Raphael thought it would taste sweet like orange juice. He licked the lemon. Wow! His face scrunched up. His tongue told him it was sour!

The doctor laughed. "Good tongue!" she said. She let Raphael touch the lemon skin. It felt bumpy. Then Raphael smelled the lemon. It smelled sharp and fresh. "My tongue can taste that a lemon is sour," said Raphael. The doctor gave him a sticker. Raphael put it on his shirt. "Next year, lemon again?" he asked.

Kai stood in the garage next to Dad. Dad turned on a song. "Let's clap," said Dad. They clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Kai clapped too fast. Clapclapclap! The song ran away from him. "Chase the beat," said Dad with a grin. "It will wait for you." Kai slowed down. Clap, clap, clap. Now his hands landed right on the song.

Then Dad sang, "The itsy bitsy spider." He made his fingers climb up, up, up his arm. Kai tried too. But his fingers went down, down, down. Dad laughed. "Silly spider! Spiders climb up the spout." Kai giggled so hard his tummy wiggled. The spider went the wrong way!

Kai tried again. His fingers went up, up, up, just like Dad's. The garage smelled like warm oil and old paper. A cricket in the corner went quiet, then chirped along.

Kai sang the whole song by himself. Not one word missing. Dad scooped him up in a big hug.

Kai held very still, like a frozen popsicle. Then he whispered, "One more time?" His fingers climbed up, up, up.

Amelia woke up and saw white. Snow had fallen in the night. "A snow day!" said Mama. "No school today." Amelia put on her boots and her red mittens. Then she ran outside to the backyard.

The snow was deep and pretty. Amelia made a big snowball. She patted it and patted it. She made tracks like a little train, chugga chugga, all across the yard. Her mittens got wet from the snow. Her boots got wet too.

"I want to play more," Amelia said. She tried to put her mittens back on. They were cold and drippy. "Yuck," said Amelia.

"Your mittens are soaked," said Mama. "Hang them up to dry." Amelia hung her wet mittens on the line. She put her wet boots by the door. They dripped little spots on the mat.

Amelia watched from the window. She drank warm milk. Slowly the mittens stopped dripping. Slowly the boots stopped dripping too.

At last they were dry. "Now I can play again!" said Amelia. She pulled on her dry red mittens. She ran back out to her big snowball.

Mateo climbed into the car. He buckled his seat belt. Then he looked for Bunny. Bunny was not in his bag.

"Oh no," said Mateo. "Bunny is lost!"

"Let's look," said Mom. She turned on the light in the car. Mateo peeked under the seat. It was dark under there. He could not see anything at all.

"I can't see!" said Mateo. "It's too dark!"

Mom reached into her bag. She took out a flashlight. She clicked it on. "Here," she said. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots."

Mateo shined the flashlight under the seat. The light made the dark spot bright. And there was Bunny! Bunny was tucked next to a shoe and a clump of dog hair.

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He grabbed Bunny and hugged him tight. "The light showed me!"

Mom laughed. "You found him all alone under there."

They drove to the store. They would sell their old stroller there. Mateo held Bunny all the way. He shined the flashlight at his shoes too. Click, click. Dark, then light. Dark, then light.

"I see everything!" said Mateo. "Bunny, look at your soft ears!"

Mom smiled at the mirror. "Home soon," she said.

"Bunny, we found you," whispered Mateo. "The light found you."

Luke went to the mall with his mom. He was going to get his very first haircut. The salon had a big fish tank. The fish were blue and orange. They swam low in the water, then up, then low again.

Luke sat in the big chair. The hairdresser, Meg, put a low board across his lap. Then she picked up her scissors. But Luke heard a pop-pop sound. He turned to look at the fish tank. Snip went the scissors in the wrong place. "Oops," said Meg. "Your head moved."

Luke wondered, "If I sit still, will my hair look nice?" He tried it. He sat like a statue. He looked straight at the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little feathers on his arm. It tickled. Meg smiled. "Look now," she said. Luke saw a neat, short haircut in the mirror. "You sat very still," said Meg. "That helped me cut it neatly."

Mom brought Luke's jacket. On the way out, Luke stopped by the fish tank. One fish came up to the glass. It looked at him and did not move at all. Luke laughed. "You sit still too," he said. "Goodbye, fish."

Ava sat at the big table at writing club. Her paper was white. Her pencil was yellow. She wanted to write AVA all by herself.

She pushed the pencil on the paper. A. V. A. But her lines came out fat and fuzzy. "Oh no," said Ava. "My letters look like fuzzy bees!"

"Let me see," said Miss Kim. "Your pencil tip is dull. A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help." Miss Kim turned the pencil in the sharpener. Whir, whir, whir. Ava watched from her seat.

Miss Kim handed the pencil back. The tip was pointy now. Ava pushed it on the paper again. A. V. A. The lines were thin and clear. "Look!" said Ava. "My letters are not fuzzy bees anymore. They are just Ava!"

"Read it to me," said Miss Kim. Ava pointed at each letter. "A. V. A. That is me!" Then she drew one little bee next to her name, just for fun.

Harper held her mom's hand at the dentist's door. "First time today," said the lady at the desk. "One little girl, one big chair, one tiny tooth check."

Harper sat in the big chair. It went up and up. Then the dentist came in. His hands were blue! "Why are your hands blue?" Harper asked. The dentist wiggled his fingers. "These are my gloves," he said. "I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

He pulled one glove off. Under it, his hand was not blue at all. It looked just like Papa's hand. Then he put the glove back on. Snap! It was blue again. Harper counted as he snapped each glove. "One, two. One, two." He counted with her.

"Open wide like a little mouse," the dentist said. Harper opened her mouth. She was a small gray mouse, squeak, squeak. The dentist looked at her teeth with a tiny mirror. All clean and shiny.

"Can I try a glove?" Harper asked. The dentist gave her one. It was too big. It flopped like a sleepy sock. "I will wear mine next time," she said. The dentist laughed, and the big chair went slowly down.

Matteo ran to the park with his mama. He wanted to find something amazing. He saw a red bucket by the swings. He heard a dog bark, bark, bark. "I hear it with my ears!" he said.

Then Matteo took off his shoes. He stepped on the green grass. The soft grass tickled his bare toes. "My feet can feel it!" he laughed. "Mama, come feel!"

Mama sat down and took off her shoes too. "Ooh, it tickles me too," she said. Matteo smelled flowers nearby. He touched a smooth stone. He ate a sweet apple from his bag, being careful with each bite.

"Feet are for walking," said Matteo. "And feet can feel things too!" He wiggled his toes in the grass. The grass tickled, tickled, tickled.

Levi ran to the shape table at school. A big red clock sat there. "Look, the clock is a circle!" said his friend Mia. Levi grinned. He wanted to find a circle too.

He held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," said Mia. "It is too small. The clock is big." Levi put the button on the table. Then he put it next to the clock. He turned the button around and around. It stayed round, all the way, just like the clock.

"It is a circle!" said Levi. "A tiny circle!" Mia clapped. Then they found more. A square block. A triangle cracker. A rectangle book. "Big or small, they stay the same shape," said Levi. Miss Ana smiled. Levi put the button in his pocket. "My new circle," he said. "I will show my mom!"

Elizabeth went to the park with Dad. A picnic table sat under a big tree. Dad set up a little grill for hot dogs. Elizabeth wanted to help cook.

"Can I touch the grill?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it."

Elizabeth looked at the grill. It looked cool and gray. Was it hot? She did not touch it. She waited like Dad said.

Dad held his hand above the grill. Then he put a hot dog on. It went sizzle, sizzle. "It is hot," said Dad. "See the smoke?"

Elizabeth saw the smoke rise up. The grill did not look hot, but it was! The hot dog got brown and warm.

Elizabeth stayed close to Dad. She picked up her gentle blue blanket and hugged it. She sat on the safe side of the table. Soon the hot dogs were done.

Dad put one on her plate. It was warm and yummy. "You were a big helper," said Dad. "You waited so well."

Elizabeth smiled. "Can we cook again next time?" she asked.

Thomas put on his red coat. The zipper would not go up. He pulled and pulled. It stayed down by his tummy.

"Let's walk to the store," said Mom. "It is cold outside." Thomas held his coat shut with his hand. The cold wind came in anyway.

At the grocery store, Thomas tried the zipper again. His fingers pushed it. It went up a tiny bit. Then it stopped. "Almost," said Mom. "Try one more time."

Thomas lined up the two sides. He pushed the little slider up. It moved. It moved some more. Then it stopped at the very top. His coat was zipped all the way. Thomas smiled a big smile.

On the way home, Mom let him try again by the door. It took two tries. Then he zipped it up all alone. "I did it!" said Thomas. Mom clapped her hands. Thomas patted his neat red coat and walked with his hands swinging free.

Avery went to the store with her dad. She wanted the yellow cup on the high shelf. She had to wait for the shop lady to finish talking first.

Avery tugged her dad's sleeve. "Dad! Dad! Look!" she said. The shop lady was still talking about a phone on sale. Dad held up one finger. Avery puffed her cheeks and waited. The shop lady stopped talking. Then Dad said, "Yes, Avery?" Now it was her turn to talk.

"Can I have the yellow cup?" Avery asked. "Let's look at it together," said Dad. He reached the cup down from the shelf. "Is it sharp?" Avery asked. Dad felt the edge. "No, it is smooth," he said. "Good," said Avery.

At the till, a boy stood in front of them. He put his apples on the counter. Avery waited behind him. The boy paid and danced a little happy step out the door. Then it was Avery's turn. She put her cup on the counter. "Please and thank you," she said. The shop lady smiled and said, "You waited so nicely." Avery hugged the cup all the way home.

Jacob sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to know what was for dinner at home. His tummy gave a little growl. "Soon," said Mom. "We will eat after this."

Dr. Lee came in. She said, "Let's check your eyes." Jacob used his eyes to see a picture on the wall. Then he used his ears to hear a soft beep. "Good," said Dr. Lee. She gave him a small sticker to touch. It felt bumpy on his fingers.

At home, Grandma was cooking. Jacob played with his toy boat by the river rug. He sniffed the air with his nose. "I smell soup!" he said. He ran to the kitchen. There it was, bubbling on the stove. Grandma smiled and gave him a warm hug. "You knew before you saw it," she said. Jacob took one taste with his tongue. "Yum," he said.

Aubrey wanted to find the cookies at daycare. Miss Jo had put them somewhere. "Look for the word," said Miss Jo. Aubrey did not know how to look for a word.

She peeked into the kitchen nook. There was a big box on the shelf. The box had little marks on it. Miss Jo ran her finger under the marks. "This says cookies," she said. Aubrey opened the box. Cookies! The word had told her.

Then Aubrey saw more words. A sign on the door said OPEN. A label on the juice said JUICE. A card on the cubbies said NAMES. Words were all around her. They sat on signs, labels and boxes. They told her things.

Aubrey picked up a book. She opened it in the middle. "Start at the front," said her friend Ben. He turned to the first page. "We read this way." Aubrey held the book right. She turned the pages, one by one.

At story time, Aubrey had a question. She pointed at the cover. "What does that say?" Miss Jo smiled. "It says Aubrey's turn to pick." Aubrey giggled. She picked the cookie book. Ben peeked over her shoulder. "That word looks like the one on the box," he said. Aubrey pointed to it proudly. "That says cookies."

Ella held her bear at daycare. "The bear is sick," she said. "I will make him soup."

Sam came over with his dragon toy. "My dragon is sick too," he said.

"No," said Ella. "The dragon is scary."

Sam frowned. "My dragon is friendly."

They both stopped. Ella looked at the big dragon. Then she had an idea. "Can we say the dragon is friendly?" she asked.

"Yes!" said Sam. "Friendly dragon."

Ella patted the dragon's head. His wings felt soft, not scratchy like a brush. "Friendly dragon can help bear," she said.

The dragon gave the bear pretend soup. Ella hugged her bear close. "All better," she said. "Do you want soup too, dragon?"

"Yes, please," said Sam, in a big dragon voice.

They glued paper bowls for their soup. Teacher Mia smiled at them from her chair nearby.

"More soup!" roared the friendly dragon, and Ella laughed.

Nora woke up and looked out the window. "It is rainy today!" she said. Big drops tapped the glass. Tap, tap, tap. Nora wanted to jump in puddles. She put on her sneakers and ran outside. She stepped in a big puddle. Splash! Her socks got soggy. "Oh no," said Nora. "Wet socks, wet socks!"

Mama held up Nora's orange rain boots. "Try these," said Mama. Nora pushed her feet in. They went right on. She ran back outside. She stepped in the puddle again. Splash! She looked at her toes. "My feet are dry!" she laughed.

The wind blew and leaves spun around. "It is windy too!" said Nora. She stomped in every puddle. The wind tickled her hair. Back inside, she painted a picture. She painted a green turtle wearing orange rain boots. "Turtle stays dry," said Nora, and she stomped her boots one more time.

Isaiah sat on the big rug in the living room. Uncle Sam sat beside him. Friends came over to watch the soccer game. The TV showed players running on green grass.

Isaiah saw a net behind each player. He thought the ball had to fly over the net. "The ball goes over the top, right?" he asked.

Uncle Sam shook his head. "Watch," he said. A player kicked the ball. It went into the net, under the bar. The crowd jumped up. Everyone in the living room shouted, "Goal!" Isaiah's eyes went wide. Papa picked him up and spun him around. Isaiah laughed. "The ball goes in the net!" he said. He clapped his hands. On the TV, the player smiled a big, toothy smile. Isaiah hugged his teddy bear tight. "Kick it again," he said.

Max was at Grandma's house. A big truck went by. It made a loud rumble. Max did not like the loud sound.

Max put his hands over his ears. The rumble got quiet. He let go. The rumble came back loud. He put his hands back. It got quiet again. "Grandma, my hands make it quiet!" he said.

Grandma smiled. "Your ears hear sounds," she said. Max touched his ears. "Ears hear," he said. Then he touched his eyes. "Eyes see Grandma!" He smelled cookies baking in the oven. "Nose smells cookies!" He touched the warm cookie Grandma handed him. "Hands feel it!" Then he took a bite. "Mouth tastes it!"

"Five senses," said Grandma. "You are so brave with the loud truck." Max looked out the window. "Can we hear the ocean, Grandma?" he asked. "The ocean is far away," Grandma said. "But I can pour water in your bath. You can listen there." Max clapped his hands over his ears and off again, fast, like a game. Then he heard a bird sing, small and sweet. "I missed that bird before," he said. "My ears caught it now."

Ivy held the little box with two hands. Inside was her new puppy. He was small and brown and his tail went wag, wag, wag. Ivy named him Bean.

Dad stopped at the pet shop on the way home. "Bean needs a tag," Dad said. The tag was a small circle, shiny like a coin. Ivy picked a blue one. The lady put letters on it. Ivy pointed at the numbers. "What are those?"

"That is our phone number," Dad said. He helped Ivy squeeze the tag onto Bean's collar. The tag went jingle, jingle when Bean walked.

At home, Ivy took Bean out to the sidewalk. It began to snow, soft and slow. Bean saw a big leaf. He ran after it! He ran down the street, far, far away. Ivy could not see him. She felt a tear on her hand.

A neighbor came by, holding Bean in her arms. "This little one got lost," she said. "But look. His tag has a phone number. I called it, and Dad said to bring him here."

Bean licked Ivy's cheek. Ivy hugged him tight. "Your tag brought you home," she whispered. Bean wagged his tail, and the snow fell on them both.

Arya went to the library with her mom. She wanted a monkey song book. But all the monkey books were gone from the shelf. "Oh no," said Arya.

Then she saw a toy box. It had five little toy monkeys on top. A boy named Sam was there. Sam sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Then one monkey fell off. Sam put it in the box. Now there were four. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One fell off again. Arya counted with him. Three. Then two. Then one. Then the last monkey fell off. "No more monkeys!" said Sam.

"Let me try," said Arya. She put the monkeys back on top. She sang, "Five little monkeys!" She took one off each time. Five, four, three, two, one. Mom laughed. "You sing like salty popcorn pops," she said, "pop, pop, pop!"

Arya hugged the last monkey. "You fell down, little one."

Rosalie put on her red team shirt. Her team was playing soccer on the grass by the big pool. The sun made the light sparkle on the water. "Can we swim after?" she asked Mama. "After the game," said Mama.

The ball came to Rosalie. She looked at it. Where should it go? There was a net at the end of the field. She kicked the ball hard with her flat shoe. The ball rolled and rolled. It went right into the net!

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Rosalie clapped her hands. So that was the game! Kick the ball into the net, and you score. The other team kicked the ball toward the other net. It went in there too. Everyone cheered again.

Later, Rosalie jumped into the pool. The water was cool and splashy. "Did you like the game?" asked Mama. Rosalie kicked her feet in the water. "The ball goes in the net," she said, "and then everybody yells!"

Ali was in the backyard with Dad. They were waiting for Mom to come home. Mom was bringing the new baby.

Ali had a toy truck. He pushed it fast on the grass. "Babies like trucks," said Ali. Dad smiled.

Then Mom came out. She held a small bundle. "This is your baby sister," she said. Ali was so happy. He patted the baby on her head. He patted hard, like he patted his toy truck. The baby began to cry.

Mom said, "Pat very gently." Ali looked at his hand. He made his hand soft. He touched the baby's fingers, so so soft. The baby stopped crying. She held his finger.

Ali sat very still. Dad sat close by on the bench. The sun was warm. The baby looked up at Ali. "I will be gentle every day," said Ali. The baby squeezed his finger one last time.

Anthony sat in the car. Mom was driving to the salon. "Your hair is getting long," she said. "Today we will cut it."

Anthony held his hair. "Will the scissors hurt?" he asked.

"We will see," said Mom. "Maybe you can tell me."

At the salon, Anthony sat in a big chair. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Anthony closed his eyes. Then he opened them. Nothing hurt at all. It felt like nothing happening, just little sounds near his ears.

"Does it hurt?" asked Mom.

"No!" said Anthony. "Cutting hair does not hurt!"

Curls of hair fell down. One landed on his hand. He looked at it. It was so small and curly. How funny that it came from his own head.

Back in the car, Anthony found one more curl on his shirt. "Look, Mom," he said. "A souvenir."

Riley sat in the vet's waiting room. The sky outside looked cloudy. She held a small box with holes in the top. Inside was her new puppy, Ben.

Riley had a chocolate cookie in her pocket. She wanted to give it to Ben. She pulled it out slowly.

The vet saw the cookie and shook her head. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick," she said. "Dogs are never given chocolate." She opened a jar and handed Riley a small dog treat. "Try this instead."

Riley held out the treat. Ben sniffed it. Then he gobbled it up. His tail wagged fast.

Riley put the cookie back in her pocket. She picked up a toy snake from a basket and waved it. Ben jumped and barked. Then he sorted his toys into a pile with his nose.

At home, Riley fed Ben his dinner. She waited while he ate, bit by bit. Then Ben climbed into her lap and fell asleep.

Elena went to the park with her dad. She wanted a cold drink. Her juice box sat in the big cooler. The cooler lid was open. The lid made a shadow on the grass. "Open and closed are opposites," said Dad. He shut the lid. Then he opened it again.

Elena peeked inside. The ice was small and white. The cooler was big and cold. The sun outside was hot. "Close it please," said Dad. "The ice melts when it stays open." Elena pushed the lid down. Click. It was closed.

Then she heard a fast bird. It flew over the big slide. A slow snail sat by the tree. Elena sat down to draw the snail in her new notebook. She waited and waited. The snail moved one tiny step. Dad handed her a cold juice box from the closed cooler. Elena took a big, slow sip. "Nice and cold," she said.

Jasmine ran to the playground with her teddy bear. Her friend Mia was already there. Mia had a small toy pot and a wooden spoon.

"Let's play house," said Mia. Jasmine clapped her hands. She wanted to be the parent. She would stir the pot and mix the soup.

But Mia wanted to be the parent too. "I want to stir," said Mia. They both held the spoon. The pot tipped over. Pebbles rolled out like little beans.

Then Jasmine had an idea. "You be the parent first," she said. "I will be the baby." Jasmine sat in the sandbox. She hugged her teddy bear. "Ba ba," she said, very small. Mia laughed and stirred the soup.

"Now we switch," said Jasmine. She stood up and took the spoon. Mia sat down and drank from a tiny cup. "Ba ba," said Mia. The friendly sun shone on their pretend soup. Jasmine gave the teddy bear a taste too. "More, please," said Mia, holding out her cup.

Declan wanted to brush his teeth all by himself. He stood at the sink on his little step. The sink had two taps. He touched the left tap with one finger. It felt warm, warm, warm. Then he touched the right tap. That one was cold. "So one tap is hot and one tap is cold," he thought. "Which tap makes warm water for my toothbrush?"

He turned the cold tap a tiny bit. Water came out. It splashed into the bowl. Then it went down the hole. Where did the water go? Declan leaned close to look.

Then he saw something. It was a little box on the wall. It had two small holes. "What lives in there?" he wondered. Maybe his toothbrush could fit. Maybe his finger could fit too.

Declan did not put his finger in. He did not put anything in. He walked out of the bathroom. He found his grandma in the hall.

"Grandma, there is a little hole box on the wall," he said. "I did not touch it."

Grandma held his hand. They went back together. "That is called an outlet," she said. "No fingers, no sticks, no toys in there. Ever."

"Never put things in the outlet," said Declan.

"That's right," said Grandma. She turned the warm water on for him. Declan brushed his teeth. The water was warm, just right. Then he saw a shy little spider peek from behind the cup.

"Hello, spider," said Declan. He waved with his toothbrush. The spider ran away.

Emile was at daycare. It was snack time. He had a square napkin on the table. "Look, a square," said Emile. His napkin had four flat sides.

Emile had a wish. He wanted a little blanket for his toy bear. But the napkin was too big. So Emile folded the square napkin in half. He pressed the edge to the edge. He looked at it. The square was gone. Now it was a rectangle. "Teacher Nina, look!" he said. "My square is a rectangle now!" Teacher Nina smiled. "It is a nice long rectangle," she said.

Emile put the rectangle on his bear. It was just the right size. "It is not cold now," he said. Then his shoe tapped the floor, tap, tap. Emile folded his napkin again. He had an idea for tomorrow. He would fold it one more time and see.

Billie ran to the playground with Dad. The sun was hot on her head. The slide felt warm under her hand. Dad sat on a bench in the shade. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Billie waved. "I see you too!"

She went down the slide. She went up the ladder. Then she saw something far away. It was a red ball by the tall fence. She wanted that ball. She ran past the swings. She ran past the sandbox. The fence was far, far away.

Billie looked back at the bench. She could not see Dad. The tree was in the way. She could not see Dad at all. Billie stopped running. She stood very still. Then she ran back past the sandbox. She ran past the swings. There was the bench. There was Dad.

"I could not see you," Billie said. Dad held her hand. "Let's walk together," he said. They found the red ball by the fence. Dad picked it up. They took turns rolling it on the grass. Billie stayed close the whole time. "This is a good spot," she said. Dad smiled and rolled the ball back.

Matteo sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "One big truck!" he said. The truck went beep, beep. Two dogs ran by a fence. Three birds sat on a wire. "Count with me, Mama!" said Matteo.

Mama laughed. "One, two, three, four," she sang. "Five, six, seven," sang Matteo. They passed eight red apples at a fruit stand. Then they saw nine balloons by a door. "Ten!" shouted Matteo. He held up all his fingers.

At the red light, a girl in the next car waved. Mama rolled down the window. "How old is he?" the girl's daddy asked. Matteo held up four fingers, just like the girl did. "I am four!" said Matteo. The girl held up her fingers too. "I am four!" she said. The light turned green. The two cars honked goodbye.

Eloise sat high up in the big stadium. Dad sat next to her. Mama and Grandpa sat close too. The crowd was loud. The field below was green and bright. Eloise could smell popcorn. It was her favorite smell.

The game began. Little people ran on the field. "Dad, they all look the same," Eloise said. She could not tell who was on which team. Dad pointed down. "Look at the shirts. This team wears red shirts. That team wears blue shirts." Eloise looked hard. One, two, three red shirts ran one way. One, two, three blue shirts ran the other way. "I can tell them apart now," she said.

Eloise counted the red shirts. Then she counted the blue shirts. A red shirt kicked the ball. The blue team got it back. The crowd stood up and cheered. Grandpa clapped his big hands. Eloise clapped her small hands. She waved her red scarf. "Go red team," she called. Dad laughed. The popcorn smell drifted up again. "One more," Eloise said, pointing at the field.

Wyatt was at the grocery store with Dad. The freezer door was open. Cold air rushed out at him. Brrr! Wyatt jumped back.

"I want to try," Wyatt said. He put his arms in his coat. He pushed one side into the other side. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It went wrong at the bottom. He tried again. This time it zipped all the way!

Wyatt stood by the freezer. The cold air bounced off him now. His coat kept his body warm. He smiled a big smile.

"Look, Dad! I did it all by myself," Wyatt said.

"Big news," said Dad. "Now let's go find the bread."

Wyatt zipped his coat again, just to hear the sound. Ziiiip!

Miles ran to the picnic table. It was his birthday at the park. Mom had set out cups and a big cake. His friends were coming soon.

A girl named Nia came over. She had never met Miles before. "How old are you?" she asked.

Miles held up his hand. He lifted three fingers. Then he counted them in his head. One, two, three. That was not right. He was one more than three. He put up a fourth finger too.

"Four!" said Nia. "I am four too." She held up four fingers of her own. Their hands looked the same. Miles laughed. So did Nia.

"Can I have cake now?" Miles begged. Dad smiled. "First we light the candles," he said. Dad used a little match. He lit four candles, one for each year. Miles watched from far back, being safe. The candles glowed warm and small.

Everyone sang the song. Then Mom brought Miles a glass of cold juice. He took a big sip. It was sweet and icy. Nia sat right next to him on the bench.

Blow, blow, blow! Miles puffed out all four candles. His friends clapped loud. Nia gave him a high five with her whole little hand.

Maeve sat on the grass with Dad. The soccer game was on the big field. Lots of people ran after the ball. The crowd clapped and cheered.

Maeve wanted to see the ball go in the net. She stood up tall on her tiptoes. The players ran fast. Then a loud sound came. Toot! Toot! A man blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. They stood still on the field.

Maeve looked up at Dad. "Why did they stop?" she asked. "The referee blew his whistle," Dad said. "The whistle stops the game." Maeve watched the man with the whistle. He held up his hand. Then he blew the whistle again. The players began to run once more.

Maeve clapped her hands. Her tummy felt warm and happy. She skipped in a little circle on the grass. Later, the ball flew high and went in the net. Toot! Toot! The game stopped again. Maeve grinned and said, "The whistle did that."

Madelyn went to the library with Grandma. It was a sunny morning. Madelyn wanted a book about ducks.

The duck books were on a high shelf. Madelyn could not reach them. "I will help," said Grandma. "First, find them." Madelyn looked and looked. The duck book seemed to hide behind big books.

Grandma sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Madelyn sang too. Then she saw it. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" she sang. On the word "ten," her finger touched the duck book. It was the tenth book on the shelf.

Grandma took it down. "Can I have three books?" Madelyn asked. "Yes, three," said Grandma. Madelyn picked one duck book, one dog book, and one bear book. "Is that three?" she asked. Grandma nodded. "One, two, three," said Grandma. "Three means three books. Big ones and small ones too."

Madelyn counted her books all by herself. One, two, three. Then she counted the steps to the big chair. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. She was not alone. Grandma sat right beside her.

Madelyn hugged her three books. "Ten steps to the door," she said. Grandma laughed. "Let's count them together." They counted one, two, three, all the way to ten. "We made it," said Grandma. Madelyn held her hand tight.

Charlotte went to the store with Mama. She held Mama's hand. The store had crayons in big rows. Charlotte wanted crayons to draw pizza, and the sun, and the sky.

She picked a red crayon for the pizza. Then she picked a yellow crayon for the sun. Then she picked a gray crayon for the sky. "All done," she said.

Mama walked her to the window. "Look up," said Mama. Charlotte looked up. The day was sunny and clear. The sky was not gray. The sky was blue, all over, way up high. Charlotte put the gray crayon back. She took a blue one instead. Then she found a green crayon too, for the grass by her house.

At home, Charlotte tried to draw. She drew red pizza with yellow sun on top. She drew the blue sky over the green grass. Mama pointed at the sky in the picture. "Just like outside," said Mama. Charlotte smiled and held her picture up to the window.

Michael ran to the table. Grandma had put out warm bread. It smelled so good. He reached out his hand.

Then he stopped. He looked at his fingers. They had dirt on them. He had been helping plant flowers in the yard.

"First I wash," Michael said. He walked to the sink. Grandma smiled and followed him.

He pushed the soap pump. White soap came out. It felt smooth and slippery. He rubbed his hands together. Bubbles grew and grew.

"We wash our hands before we eat," Grandma said. She helped him count. "One, two, three." They counted all the way to twenty.

The water rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean now. He dried them on the soft towel.

Michael sat down and took a big bite of bread. Later, after the toilet, he ran to the sink again. He pumped the soap himself.

"Twenty seconds," he said, counting out loud.

Grandma clapped her hands.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a small bag of crackers. Her friend Ben sat next to her. Ben looked at the crackers. "Crackers, please?" said Ben. Sadie held out the bag. Ben took one cracker. He smiled big.

"Thank you," said Ben. Sadie did not know what to say back. She sat quiet. Then she heard her mama at the window. Mama gave the ticket man some money. "Thank you," said the ticket man. "You're welcome," said Mama. Sadie heard it. She tried it in her head. You're welcome. You're welcome.

"Thank you," said Ben again. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Ben laughed. Mama smiled in the mirror. Sadie gave Ben one more cracker. Then the car went over a bump. Sadie's cracker fell on the floor. "Oh no. Can you help, please?" she said. Mama reached back and got it. "You're welcome," said Mama. Sadie ate her cracker. It was cool how that worked.

It was snack time at school. Ruby had a job. She had to put out the cups. There were ten chairs at the table. Ruby held a stack of shiny cups.

She put one cup in front of one chair. "One cup, one chair," she said. She put a cup at the next chair too. "One cup, one chair." She went all the way around the table. Each chair got one cup.

At the last chair, her hand was empty. Ruby looked in the stack. No cups were left. She asked herself, "Do we have the same number of cups and chairs?" She counted the cups. Ten cups. She counted the chairs. Ten chairs. Each cup had one chair. Each chair had one cup. So yes, the same number.

Then Ben came with a string of crackers on a red thread. He had eight crackers. Ruby counted them. Ben asked, "Who has more, me or the table?" Ruby looked. The table had ten cups. Ben had eight crackers. "The table has more," she said. Ben lifted his string and laughed. Then everyone sat down, one cup in front of each chair, and the snack began.

Lea packed her little red bag. "We go to the beach today!" she sang. The car ride was long. Lea counted three cows, then she fell asleep.

At the beach, Lea found a shell. "Mama, look!" she said. Mama held up her phone. "Smile for a photo," said Mama. Click. Lea smiled. Click, click. Papa took a photo of the big waves. Lea took a photo of her toes in the sand. "My toes look funny!" she laughed.

Lea put her shell in the water. It did not float. It sat on the bottom. "Silly shell," said Lea. A wave came and tickled her knees. Click went Mama's phone again.

At home, the beach was gone. Lea felt sad. "I miss the sand," she said. Mama sat down next to her. "Let's look at our trip photos," she said. There was Lea and the shell. There were her funny toes. There was the big wave. Lea giggled and giggled. "Look, Papa, my toes!" she said. Papa laughed too. "That beach was different from our house," he said. Lea pointed at the last photo. "Again," she said. "Again and again."

Athena went to Miss Kim's music room. There was a big drum in the corner. Athena wanted to play it with her friend Tom.

Tom had sticks. Athena had sticks too. They began to tap. Tom tapped fast, fast, fast. Athena tapped slow. The sounds crashed like a stormy sea. It did not sound good.

"Why is it so messy?" Athena asked.

Miss Kim clapped her hands. Tap, tap, tap. She clapped slow and steady. Tom copied her. Athena copied her. Then they tapped the drum together. Tap, tap, tap. It sounded like one big drum!

"Now it sounds happy," said Athena.

They played a song. Miss Kim drew a picture of two drummers holding hands. She hung it on the wall.

Athena looked up at the picture. "Thank you, Miss Kim," she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "Play it again," she said.

Athena lifted her sticks. Tap, tap, tap.

Nolan ran to the community garden with his small watering can. He had planted lettuce seeds with Grandma last week. Now tiny green leaves peeked out of the dirt. "Hello, little plants!" he said.

The sun was hot that day. Nolan looked at his lettuce. The leaves were drooping. They hung down low, like sleepy heads. "Grandma, why are they sad?" he asked. Grandma filled his can at the pond. "Give them a drink," she said. Nolan poured the smooth, cool water over the leaves. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Nolan ran back to the garden. He gasped. The lettuce stood up tall! The leaves were perky and green. "Water made them wake up!" he said. He patted the dirt gently. "I will bring you water every day, little plants." Grandma smiled and gave him a big high five.

Theodore held his mama's hand at the farmers' market. "Strawberries!" he shouted. "Can we get some?" Mama laughed. "Yes. Today we bake a cake." Theodore jumped up and down. A cake! A whole cake! They knocked on the farmer's window to pay for the eggs. The farmer smiled and handed them over, one by one.

At home, Theodore helped at the big table. He cracked the eggs into the bowl. He poured in the flour. He stirred and stirred. A tiny taste of strawberry went in his mouth. The rest went in the bowl. Then Theodore looked in the bowl and stopped. The batter was runny. It was thin and wobbly like a puddle.

"Mama, it's broken!" he said. "Cake is big and round. This is just goo." His lip wobbled. "It will never be a cake." Mama carried the bowl to the oven. "In it goes," she said. Theodore stood far back, where it was safe. The oven door closed with a soft thump.

Theodore pressed his nose to the kitchen window. Outside, a cloud looked like a lion with a big fluffy mane. The kitchen began to smell sweet. "Sniff, sniff," said Theodore. "Mmm!" His tummy made a happy little growl. Then the timer went ding!

Mama opened the oven door. She used her big mitts. Out came a real cake! It was tall and golden. It was not runny at all. Mama set it down and cut one slice. The slice stood up on the plate, all by itself. Theodore clapped his hands. "It's a cake now!" he said. "Can we eat the lion-sized piece?"

Lucy woke up and saw snow. "No school today!" said Mom. Lucy put on her red boots and her funny hat with a leaf print on it.

Lucy went to the big sledding hill. She slid down, down, down. Whee! Then she made a snowball. It was round and white. She wanted to keep it. Mom helped her lock the door and they went inside, out of the cold.

Lucy set the snowball in a bowl on the table. "Now it will stay," she said. She ate lunch. She looked again. The snowball was small. She looked later. Where did it go? There was only water in the bowl. Lucy touched it with one finger. Mom smiled. "Want to make a new one outside?" Lucy ran for her boots. "Yes! A big one this time!"

Maverick sat at the little table. He had red paint, blue paint, and one big brush. He painted a cat. The cat had a long tail. "One tail, two ears, three whiskers," he said. He counted each part as he painted.

His friend Nia sat next to him. She painted a cat too. Her cat also had a long tail. The two cats looked almost the same. Then it was time for snack. The teacher said, "Put your papers on the big rack." Maverick put his cat on the rack. Nia put her cat on the rack too.

After snack, Maverick ran back. He saw two cats on the rack. "Which one is mine?" he asked. "I can't tell." Nia looked too. "I can't tell either," she said. The cats were the same size. The tails were the same brown. Both had one, two, three whiskers.

Then Miss Kim, the kind teacher, came over. She held up one paper. At the bottom were small letters. "This says Nia," she said. "Nia wrote her name on her art." Maverick looked at the other paper. No name. No letters. Just his cat. "That one is mine," he said. "It has no name on it." He took his cat and gave Nia hers. Nia smiled. "Thank you," she said.

Miss Kim gave Maverick a crayon. "You can write your name too," she said. Maverick held the crayon. He made an M. He made an A. He wrote every letter, one by one. Then he held up his cat. "Now it says Maverick," he said. "Now everyone knows it is mine."

Brielle ran into the sunny backyard. Dad held up a big red hoop. "Time to play!" he said. "Throw the beanbag in!"

Brielle held her yellow beanbag. She looked at Dad and waved. Then she threw the beanbag. It fell in the grass. Not in the hoop!

Mom rolled a big blue ball to Brielle. Brielle looked up at a bird. The ball bumped her tummy and rolled away. "Oh no!" said Brielle.

"Try again," said Dad. He blew a whistle. Pop! The sound made Brielle giggle.

Brielle picked up the beanbag. This time she looked at the hoop. Only the hoop. She threw the beanbag. In it went! "Yes!" she shouted.

Mom rolled the big ball again. Brielle looked at the ball. Only the ball. She held out both hands. Thump! The ball landed right in her arms.

"One beanbag, one ball, one hoop!" said Brielle. Dad clapped. Mom clapped. The wind blew the leaves around.

Brielle threw the beanbag again, looking at the hoop the whole time. In it went again!

Claare stood at the front door. She wanted to play outside. The sun was very bright. "It is sunny today," said Mom.

Claire ran to the yard. The sun shone on her face. She squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright to see the swing. "Ow," said Claire. She held her hand over her eyes.

Mom came out with a hat. It had a big brim. "Here is your sun hat," said Mom. Claire put it on. The brim made shade over her face. Now she could open her eyes wide. She could see the swing and the whole yard. "I can see now!" said Claire.

Then the wind blew. The wind took Claire's paper boat right off the step. Claire chased her boat to the fence. Dad picked it up for her. "It is windy too," said Claire. She held her boat tight.
