Dark clouds came. A few drops fell. "Rainy soon," said Dad. "Get your rain boots." Claire stomped inside in her boots, and the rain began to tap on the door.

Layla was at school. She saw a red truck on the rug. It had big black wheels. She wanted it fast.

But Tom grabbed the truck too. Layla pulled one end. Tom pulled the other end. The truck could not move.

"Let's ask Miss Jo," said Tom. Miss Jo came over. She held up the truck. "You can take turns," she said. "Tom first. Layla, you can have the next turn."

Layla sat on the rug. She waited. She watched Tom push the truck. It went far, far across the floor. Then Tom brought it back.

"Your turn now," said Tom. Layla took the truck. She pushed it fast. It rolled under the little table. Tom laughed and clapped.

"Here," said Layla. She held out the truck. "Your turn again."

Tom smiled big. "This is fun," he said. Then he pushed the truck past the blocks.

Ibrahim was at the park with his dad. He brought his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. He set it on the picnic table. Then he ran to the slide. When he came back, the car was gone.

"Where is my car?" said Ibrahim. He looked by the swing. No car. He looked in the grass. No car. He looked near the water fountain. No car. He tried one more look at the table. Still no car.

Dad sat down on the long bench. He patted the seat. "Small toys can roll or slide under furniture," said Dad. Ibrahim got down on his knees. He peeked under the bench. It was dark and cool there. He saw dust and a candy wrapper. Then he saw something blue. It was his car! It had rolled right under the bench.

Ibrahim reached in and pulled it out. The car felt cold from the shade. He held it up to the sun. "Found you!" he said. Then he put the car deep in his pocket, where it could not roll away, and ran back to the slide with Dad.

Leah sat on the living room rug. She wanted to draw a big red sun. Mom handed her the tablet.

"First, you press the round button," said Mom. Leah pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up. Then Leah tapped the little picture with the crayons. The drawing app opened.

Leah touched the blue spot first. Her finger made a blue line. "I want red," she said. "Where is red?" She looked at all the little circles. She found a red one and tapped it. Her next line came out red. "Red!" she laughed. She drew a big round sun with red rays. Then she drew green grass at the bottom.

"Now what do I do?" Leah asked.

"You hold the button again, and the screen goes to sleep," said Mom. Leah held the button. The screen went dark. She put the tablet on the shelf, right where it lives.

"Can I draw again after my nap in bed?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "The sun will wait for you."

Theo went to the community center with his mama. There was a music room with little chairs. On a table lay some recorders.

A girl named Mei had a yellow duck on her shirt. It was her favorite shirt. Mei picked up a recorder and blew. Squeak! The recorder made a loud squeaky sound. Mei frowned.

Theo picked up a recorder too. He put his fingers on the holes. He blew. A nice note came out. Theo lifted one finger off a hole. He blew again. A different note came out! He put his finger back down. The first note came back.

Theo tapped Mei's finger. "Your finger is not on the hole," he said. Mei looked down. She moved her finger. She covered the hole all the way. She blew. A nice note came out! No squeak.

Mei laughed. Theo laughed. They took turns. Theo covered one hole, then another. Each hole made a different note. The teacher played along on her big drum.

Theo blew a long note, and Mei blew one too.

Isabelle went to the cultural center with Mama and Grandpa. It was a rainy day, so the party was all inside. There was a big red and gold lion waiting by the door. Isabelle held Mama's hand.

Boom! Boom! Boom! The drums were so loud. Isabelle jumped and covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Grandpa knelt down beside her. "It is okay," he said. "Stay with me." Then Isabelle looked at the lion. The lion moved. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion shook his head.

"Is the lion dancing to the drums?" Isabelle asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Watch him go." The drums beat faster. The lion hopped and spun. Isabelle let go of her ears. She clapped her hands. Boom, clap, boom, clap! The lion blinked his big eyes at her. "He looked at me!" said Isabelle. Grandpa laughed and held her close. On the way home, Mama said Isabelle would get a warm bath before bed. Isabelle clapped one more time, soft and small.

David put muffin mix in a big bowl. His teacher, Miss Anne, helped him stir. David poured the sweet batter into cups. Miss Anne put the pan in the oven. She set a little timer on the table.

Then David's family came to visit. Mama and Papa played a game with David. It was a fox game with a picture of a red fox. David rolled the dice and moved his fox. He laughed a lot.

Then the timer rang. Beep, beep, beep. "The muffins!" said Miss Anne. She took the pan out with big mitts. David got to read the word "muffin" on the box. The muffins were warm and sweet. David gave one to Mama and one to Papa. "Yum," said Papa, and he took a big bite.

Florence sat in the car. They were going to the hospital. A new baby was coming today.

At the hospital, everyone looked at the baby. They held the baby. They talked to the baby. Nobody looked at Florence. She felt small, like a little mouse.

"I miss you, Mom," Florence said in the car. "Just you and me."

Mom held her hand. "That is okay," Mom said. "Big sisters can feel that way. I still love you."

Florence drew a picture at home. She drew the baby. She drew Mom. She drew herself, right beside them.

Mom put it on the fridge. "The baby is here," Florence said. "And I am here too."

Ali ran into the big kitchen. Snow was falling past the window. "Toast time!" he said.

Miss Jo gave Ali warm bread. A grown-up had cut it for him. Ali took his little knife. It was safe and soft. He spread the butter. The butter made the bread shiny. "Look, Mom! I did it!"

Next came the milk. Ali held the cup under the jug. He poured and poured. The milk went all the way to the top. Ali picked up the cup. He took one step. The milk sloshed. Milk spilled onto the floor.

Miss Jo mopped it up. "Try again," she said. Ali poured the milk again. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He picked it up. He walked slowly. Not one drop fell out!

"I did it! No spill!" Ali blew on his milk like it was hot cocoa. "You are so cute," said Mom. Ali drank it all up.

Eva wants to find the cat book at the library. She grabs a big red book from the shelf. She sits down and opens it.

But the pictures look funny. The cat is upside down! His tail hangs by his ears. His whiskers point at the floor.

"Hello, silly cat," says Eva. "You are upside down!"

The librarian smiles. "Books go this way," she says, turning the book around.

Now the cat stands on his feet. Eva looks at the squiggly marks under the cat. "That says cat," says the librarian. Eva points at each mark. The words tell the cat where to sit.

Eva turns one page, then the next page. The cat walks through the snow on the last page. "The end," says Eva, and she pats the book.

Leah saw a big cardboard box at school. She wanted to play with it. "A house!" said Leah. She put her doll inside and gave the doll a pretend bottle.

Then Ben came. "A car!" said Ben. He wanted the box too. "It is my house," said Leah. "It is my car," said Ben. Their teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "You can take turns," she said. "First the house. Then the car."

Leah fed her doll. She tucked her in with a small cloth. Then she said, "Your turn, Ben." Ben sat in the box. "Beep beep!" he said. He drove the car fast. Leah held his pretend bucket of gas and filled the tank.

After that, Ben tipped the box onto its side. "Now it is a boat!" he said. Leah climbed in too. They rowed across the pretend sea. The doll sat between them and looked out. "Faster!" said Leah. The boat rocked hard, so they rowed slow. Then Miss Kim called, "Snack time!" They hurried out of the boat and left it floating on the blue rug.

Everly was at Grandma's house. Her new baby brother was there too. He was small and soft. He made tiny sounds.

Everly had a cracker in her hand. She wanted to give it to the baby. She held it out to his mouth. "Here, baby," she said. Grandma came over fast. "Wait, Everly," she said. "The baby cannot eat a cracker yet. A baby drinks milk, not big kid food."

Everly looked at her cracker. Then she looked at the baby. Grandma picked up a little bottle. It was warm from the hot water pot, and now it was cool enough. Grandma held it for the baby. The baby drank and drank. His eyes closed. His little hand held Grandma's finger.

Everly ate her cracker all by herself. Then she patted the baby's blanket. "Next year you can have one," she whispered. At the table, Grandma smiled and put a cookie on Everly's plate. Everly shared her cookie with Grandma, one half each.

Nova's tooth felt wiggly at daycare. She was scared to open her mouth wide. "I don't want it to fall out," she said.

Her teacher Sam sat down next to her. "I felt that way too," Sam said. "My tooth wiggled when I was small. I was nervous. Even grown-ups feel that way. Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Nova looked up. "You were afraid?" she asked. Sam nodded. Nova felt a little braver.

A boy named Max ran by with a big smile. He was so happy. Then he dropped his truck and looked angry. "My truck!" he shouted. Nova picked it up and gave it back. Max smiled again.

"Now I am excited," said Nova. She opened her mouth wide in the mirror. The tooth stayed put, just a little wiggly.

Sam laughed. "It will come out when it is ready," Sam said. Nova wiggled it with her finger and smiled back.

Mason wanted to hold the lion puppet. His sister Lily had it. She waved it up and down. The lion gave a big shake of its mane.

Mason reached out. He grabbed the lion's tail. Lily pulled it back. "No," she said. "You didn't ask."

Mason felt like crying. Mama came close. "Say, 'May I have a turn?'" said Mama. Mason took a big breath. "May I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Lily smiled. "Yes! Here you go." She put the lion in his hands. The lion gave Mason a kiss on his nose. "Thank you," said Mason. Then the lion jumped too high and bumped Lily's head. "Sorry," said Mason. He patted her arm.

Mason shook the lion gently. Lily clapped. "What a polite lion," said Mama. Mason hugged the puppet tight. "May I keep him a little more?" he asked. "Yes," said Lily. And the lion danced on Mason's knee.

Weston ran to the toy corner at daycare. There was a big basket on the floor. His friend Mia tipped it over. Lots of picture cards fell out everywhere.

"Let's put them in piles," said Mia. Weston picked up a card. It had a cow on it. Mia held up a card with a dog. "Dogs and cows are animals," she said. "They go in one pile."

Weston found a card with a banana. It did not go with the cow. He found a card with an apple. Bananas and apples were foods. He made a new pile for foods. Then he found a ball card and a triangle block card. Those were toys. Toys got a pile too.

Soon all the cards were in three neat piles. Teacher Jo smiled. "What nice piles," she said. "Look, animals, foods, and toys." Weston clapped his hands. Then he and Mia picked one card from each pile. A cat, a carrot, and a drum. "The cat eats the carrot," Weston said. Mia laughed. "Then the cat plays the drum."

Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad held her hand. They walked to the playground.

A boy was hiding behind his mom. He peeked out at Violet. He did not say a word. Violet wanted a friend to play with. She waved and said, "Hello!" The boy peeked out more. "Hello," he said back. His mom smiled. "Let's go on the swings," said the boy.

Violet ran to the swings. She sat down. But the swing would not go. Her coat felt itchy and stuck. "Dad, can you help, please?" she asked. Dad gave the swing a little push. Up went Violet, high like a bird. The boy swung next to her. "Thank you," said Violet to Dad. Dad laughed and pushed them both again and again.

Sienna sat by the train window. She was going on a big family trip. Her friend Bear sat on her lap. "One suitcase, two snacks, three hugs," Mama counted. Papa held a big paper map.

The train stopped at a little station. The family got off. They walked to the car. Papa drove and drove. Then the road looked wrong. "Oh dear," said Papa. "I think we took a wrong turn."

Mama opened the map. Sienna peeked at it. The map had roads, small and thin like noodles. It had towns, little dots. "Look," said Sienna. She put her finger on a dot. "That is our town." Her finger slid along a road. "This road goes to the sea."

Papa smiled. "Let us follow the road on the map." He turned the car around. They drove past a cow. They drove past one windmill, two windmill... no, three windmills!

The air smelled fresh and salty. "The sea!" said Sienna. She rolled down the window a little bit. Her ice cream began to melt in the sun. She licked it fast. "The map found the way," she said. Papa laughed. "It did, little helper." Sienna gave Bear a sticky, sweet hug.

Aaron was at Grandma's house. He wanted a story, but Grandma was fixing lunch. "Find a book," she said. "Then we will read it together."

Aaron hurried to the book shelf. He picked his favorite book. It had a bear on the front. He saw little marks all over the pages. "Grandma, what are these marks?" he asked.

"Those are words," said Grandma. "Words tell the story." She opened the book. "We start at the front," she said. "Then we go page by page." Grandma read the words out loud. The bear found a honey pot! Aaron clapped. The words made that happen.

Then Aaron asked, "Who made up the bear story?" Grandma pointed to the cover. "See this name?" she said. "That is the author. The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Aaron said the name out loud. "The author wrote my bear!"

Every night after that, Aaron looked for the author's name. He found it on his truck book. He found it on his dog book. "The author wrote the words," he said, and smiled at the name.

Willow sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "But I don't know what happens there," said Willow. "We can find out together," said Dad.

At the dentist's office, Willow saw a big chair. She did not want to sit in it. The dentist smiled. "Just sit and try," she said. Willow sat down. Then she pressed nothing at all, and the chair began to move. It slowly tipped back! Willow was lying down now, just like in bed. "It moved!" she said. "It tips back so I lie down!" "Yes," said the dentist. "Now I can look in your mouth." Willow opened her mouth wide. She felt brave and smart.

On the ride home, Willow smiled. "Dad, the chair fell back like a ride at the park!" "It did," said Dad. Willow said, "I want to lift my hand and wave goodbye to the chair." She lifted her hand and waved all the way out the door. "Bye, big chair!"

Joshua sat at the picnic table at summer camp. He wore his big yellow hat. The sun was high in the sky. He was painting a picture of grass. But Joshua had a problem. He had blue paint and yellow paint. He did not have green paint. Grass is green, and his paper grass looked all wrong in blue.

"I need green," Joshua said. His friend Mia sat down next to him. She sang a little song while she painted. Joshua dipped his brush in the blue paint. Then he dipped it in the yellow paint. He stirred them together on his plate. The paint turned green! Joshua opened his mouth wide. He looked at his brush. It was green, really green.

"Look, Mia!" he said. He painted tall green grass all over his paper. Then he painted a green hill, too. The birds sang up in the trees. Joshua held up his painting so Mia could see it. "Blue and yellow make green," said Joshua, and he painted one more blade of grass.

Gabriella went to Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Rosie. They were playing house. Mia was the mom. Gabriella was the doctor.

Then Mia tripped on the rug. Rosie fell too. She slid under the chair. Mia began to cry.

Mia's dad came in. He picked up Rosie. He looked at her arms and legs. "Rosie cannot really feel hurt," he said. "She is just a toy. But you can give her a pretend hug."

Mia stopped crying. She hugged Rosie tight. Gabriella watched. Then she had an idea. She patted Rosie's head very soft. "All better!" she said. Mia smiled a big smile.

Then they made Rosie swim across the blue blanket. They spotted a spotted sock and made it a fish. Rosie chased the fish. "Swim fast, Rosie!" said Mia.

At dinner time, Gabriella told her mom everything. "Rosie fell down," she said. "But we fixed her with pretend hugs."

Asher went to the store with Mama. He wanted a book about trucks. He found one with a big red truck on the front. He hugged it. It was soft and smooth.

Asher opened the book. But wait. The pages looked all mixed up. He turned one page. Then another page. Then another. "Silly book," said Asher. "Your truck is hiding!"

Mama smiled. "Turn the book around," she said. Asher flipped it over. Now the truck was on the front. He opened the front cover. Page one, page two, page three. The story made sense now. The truck went beep, beep!

"Read it to me all day," said Asher. "Front to back, front to back." Mama laughed. "Front to back it is." They sat down on a little red seat. Asher turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back cover. Then he turned the book over and started again.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor wanted to do something big with her. "Can we make your bread?" she asked. "The bread you always bring?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. My mother taught me. Her mother taught her. Our family has made it for a long, long time."

So they began. Eleanor poured flour. It made a tiny white cloud. "Look!" she said. "My hands made the cloud!" Grandma laughed. Eleanor poked the dough. It was soft and squishy in the middle. "Why does it get big?" she wondered. Grandma said, "Wait and see."

They waited. The dough grew puffy. Eleanor skipped around the kitchen while it grew. Then Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. Eleanor watched from her chair.

Out came warm bread. "I helped make this," Eleanor said. She took a big bite. "It tastes just like your bread, Grandma!"

Cooper ran to the art table. He wore his favorite blue shirt. He wanted to paint a big yellow sun.

The class was noisy with happy painters. Everyone put on an apron. Cooper did not. He was too excited to wait.

He dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He made a circle. Then a drop fell. It landed on his blue shirt. He looked down. A big yellow spot sat on his sleeve.

Cooper's eyes got wide. The teacher came over with a soft smile. She helped him put on an apron. It was red with white dots. It covered his shirt all the way down.

He painted more suns. He painted rays and stars. No more paint got on his clothes. Not one drop.

Then he found a surprise under the paint cups. A tiny glass jar of sparkles! He shook it gently. The sparkles looked like stars on his sun.

"Look at my sun!" said Cooper. The teacher held it up to the window.

Raphael sat by the big window at the community centre. Miss Dana put out two baskets. One basket held three big balls. The other basket held three tiny beads.

"The balls are more!" said Raphael. "They are so big." He counted the balls. "One, two, three." Then he counted the beads. "One, two, three." He sat very still. "The same? But the beads are so small!"

Miss Dana smiled. "Count them again," she said. He did. Balls: one, two, three. Beads: one, two, three. Big balls and tiny beads both made three.

Then Raphael saw his friend Sam with a broken crayon. Sam looked sad. Raphael tipped the beads into Sam's hand. "Here, you can hold three," he said. "Three beads, three balls. Same!"

Sam laughed and held them up to the window so the sun made them shine.

Nolan was at Grandma's house. Today was a big day. "You get your first haircut!" said Grandma. Nolan clapped his hands. His hair had little curls. Soon they would be short and clean.

Grandma drove Nolan to the salon. A man named Sam smiled. "Hop up!" said Sam. The chair was very big. Nolan tried to sit. But Sam stood and looked and shook his head. "You are too short for the big chair," said Sam. "I cannot reach your hair from up here."

Nolan wanted his haircut. He wanted it now! Sam went away. He came back with something. It was a booster seat. It was like the one at the playground, but clean and red. Sam put it on the big chair. "Climb on," said Sam.

Nolan sat on the booster seat. Up, up he went! Now his head was high. Now Sam could reach his hair. Snip, snip went the scissors. Curly bits fell down. They landed on the floor like little clouds.

"All done!" said Sam. Nolan looked in the mirror. His curls were short. His hair was clean. "I sat on the booster seat!" said Nolan. Grandma hugged him tight.

Eliana sat on the big rug. The room smelled like warm popcorn. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Grandpa was in his soft chair. Mama and Papa sat on the couch.

"Who is winning?" Eliana asked. "Who has more points?"

"Can you remember the score?" asked Grandpa.

Eliana tried. She forgot the numbers. She pulled her teddy close.

Then Grandpa pointed up high. "See the scoreboard," he said. Eliana looked at the big bright board on the screen. It showed two teams. It showed numbers for each team. The red team had more points. The blue team had less.

"The red team is winning!" Eliana said.

The blue team ran fast. They kicked the ball. The crowd on TV got loud. Eliana looked back at the scoreboard. The blue numbers went up. Now the two teams had the same points.

"It changed!" said Eliana. "The scoreboard changed!"

She watched the board the whole time now. The door was closed so it was quiet and cozy.

Later the red team got one more point. Grandpa clapped his hands. Eliana clapped her teddy's paws.

"We won," said Grandpa.

Eliana pointed at the scoreboard and smiled. "The red team has the most points!"

Kai sat at the art table. It was a hot summer day. He wanted to make a traffic light for the class game.

First he found the red paint. He painted the top circle red. Then he painted the middle circle yellow. The bottom circle was green. His friend Mia painted a blue car for the game.

"Now we can play crossing the street," said Mia. She held the blue car up high. Kai held up the traffic light. He turned the red circle to the top.

"Red means stop," said Mia. The blue car stopped right away. Vroom. It sat so still.

Kai turned the green circle to the top. "Green means go," said Mia. The blue car went, "Zoom, zoom!" It went fast past the crayon box.

"What about yellow?" asked Kai. He turned the yellow circle to the top. Mia drove the car a little bit. Then she stopped it. "Yellow is in the middle," she said. "Not stop and not go."

Kai laughed. He wondered if a bad driver would mix up the colors. He held up red again. "Stop, stop!" he called. Mia stopped the car with a little screech.

At pickup time, Kai held his teacher's hand at the real crossing. The real light turned red. All the cars stopped. "Red means stop," said Kai. Then it turned green. The cars zipped by, one after another. Kai squeezed his teacher's hand and whispered, "Green means go."

Emile was at Grandma's house. Dinner was hot on the table. There was warm soup and bread.

Emile wanted to eat right away. He grabbed his spoon. Grandma held up her hand. "Wait, Emile. First we say grace."

"What is grace?" asked Emile.

"It is a short prayer of thanks," said Grandma. "Many Christian families say it before meals. Would you like to say it?"

Emile nodded. He put down his spoon. He folded his little hands. "Thank you, God, for soup. Thank you for bread. Thank you for Grandma."

"Emile said it!" he cheered.

Grandma laughed and poured him some milk. "Very good. Now we can eat."

Emile took a big sip of soup. "Grace first, soup next!"

Grandma patted his hat. "That's right, my boy."

Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture of a house. She had paper, crayons, and a box of stickers. But her house looked wrong. The roof would not sit on the walls.

Her friend Leo was there too. He had a toy block. "This is a cube," Leo said. "It has six flat faces." Gabriella picked up the block. She turned it over and over. She put a sticker on each flat face. One, two, three, four, five, six. Every face was a square, just like her stickers.

Gabriella looked at the block. Then she drew a square for her house. She drew a triangle for the roof. The triangle sat on the square just right. She drew a rectangle for the door. Then she drew a circle for the window. A paper rabbit crawled out of Leo's pocket and sat by her picture. "The rabbit wants to come in," Leo said. Gabriella drew a little square door just for him.

Then she washed her hands until they were clean. She hung her picture up high. "Look, a house!" she said. Leo clapped, and the rabbit ear wiggled.

Sienna ran outside to play. She patted the big red dog. "Soft fur!" she said. The dog wagged his tail. Then Mom called, "Lunch time!"

Sienna ran to the table. She reached for her sandwich. Mom shook her head. "You petted the dog. Hands first!" Sienna looked at her hands. They looked the same as before. But she ran to the sink anyway.

Mom turned on the water. Sienna pumped the soap. "Now we count to twenty," said Mom. "One, two, three..." Sienna rubbed her soapy hands. "Four, five, six..." Bubbles grew big and white. "Seven, eight, nine, ten..." They looked like clouds! "Eleven, twelve, thirteen..." Sienna lifted her hands up high. The bubbles wiggled. "Fourteen, fifteen!" A bubble floated off her thumb.

"A bubble is flying!" Sienna laughed. It popped in the air, far above her head. "Sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" Mom gave her a towel. Sienna dried her clean hands all by herself.

She ran back to the table and took a big bite. "Yum!" said Sienna. Then she held up her hands. "Dog fur all gone!" Mom clapped. "Wash them again after the toilet too," she said. "Twenty seconds, every time." Sienna grinned. "I can count to twenty!" At nap time, she whispered the numbers to her teddy on the bed. "One, two, three, four..."

Asher sat in the big barber chair. It went up, up, up! The barber put a cape on him. "First haircut!" said Mom. Asher smiled a big smile.

The barber picked up the scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some bits landed on Asher's neck. Asher wiggled. He wiggled some more. His neck felt itchy! "I don't like this," said Asher.

The barber got a soft brush. She brushed the little bits away. Whoosh, whoosh. The itch went away! Asher sat very still. "All done," said the barber. Asher jumped down and ran to Mom. "The brush made the itch go away!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. "What a big boy," she said. "I am so happy!" said Asher. At home, Dad would miss his little baby hair. But Asher did not miss it one bit. He touched his new short hair and grinned.

Beatrice loved the big red blocks at school. She wanted to build a robot. A tall, nice robot with block arms.

At free play time, Beatrice ran to the block corner. Her friend Tom was already there. Tom grabbed all the blocks. He hugged them close. "They are all mine," said Tom. Beatrice had zero blocks. Her robot could not start.

Then Mia came over. Mia had zero blocks too. Tom sat alone with every block. Nobody could build with him. Tom looked around. He saw two sad friends and one full arm.

Tom put the blocks in the middle. "You take some. You take some. I keep some," he said. Beatrice got a big pile. Mia got a big pile. Tom got a big pile too. Everyone got a chance to build.

Beatrice stacked two blocks, then two more. Mia made legs for the robot. Tom gave it block arms. The robot grew tall. It was the nicest robot ever. Miss Kay came to look. "What a fine robot!" she said. Beatrice waved her hand at the robot. "We all built it," she said. "Everyone helped."

Everett ran to the feely bag at daycare. "My turn!" he said. Teacher Mia held out the bag. Everett pushed his hand in. He felt something round. He felt something smooth. "A ball!" he said. "It is a red ball!"

"Are you sure it is red?" asked Teacher Mia. Everett pulled out the ball. It was blue! His friend Ana laughed. "You have to look," she said. "Your fingers cannot see colors." Ana took her turn next. She felt a soft square. "A cloth!" she said. "But I do not know the color yet." She peeked. The cloth was yellow!

Then Everett felt something bumpy in the bag. It was small and cold. He pulled it out. It was a green truck, so cute, with snow painted on top. "A green truck with snow on it!" he cheered. Ana clapped her hands. Teacher Mia smiled. "One more turn," she said. Everett reached into the bag with a big grin.

Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big basket of apples. She wanted the bright red apple on top.

Avery reached out and grabbed for it. Another little boy was reaching too. The basket wobbled. Mama held it steady. "One at a time," said the store man. The boy went first. He took one apple and said, "Thank you."

Then it was Avery's turn. She took the bright red apple. She held it with both hands. Mama said, "We say please when we ask for something." Avery looked at the store man. "Please," she said. He smiled and gave her a little sticker.

At the checkout, they waited in the line. Avery stood by the cart. A man let them go ahead. "You can go first," he said. "Thank you," said Mama. Avery waved her sticker. At home, she sat on her pillow and held her apple. "Please," she said to Mama, "can I have a bite?" "Yes, you can," said Mama, and she cut the apple into slices.

Mia wanted her horse at bedtime. She looked under her bed. The horse was missing. Mia felt sad. She stomped her foot. "I am angry!" she said. Her tummy felt tight.

Mama came in. "Where is my horse?" Mia asked. "Let us look together," said Mama. They looked in the toy box. They looked by the window. Snow was falling outside, soft and slow. There was the horse, on the shelf! Mia felt excited. She hugged him tight.

Then she felt worried. "Will he be cold?" she asked. "No," said Mama. "He is warm and safe." Mia felt better. Mama sat close. "Try slow, deep breaths with me," she said. Mia breathed in slow. She breathed out slow. Her tummy felt soft. Her eyes felt sleepy. Mia yawned and held her horse all night.

Grandma was coming to stay. Grandma would come for a whole week. Harrison stood by the door. He held his teddy bear tight.

"I want to hide," Harrison said.

Mom knelt down next to him. "You can give Grandma a big hug," she said. "Or you can wave. Or you can just say hello."

The car pulled up. Grandma got out. She had a big bag and a happy face. Harrison held his teddy tighter. His foot stayed on the bottom step. He was not ready for a hug yet.

So Harrison lifted his hand. He waved.

Grandma waved back. "Hello, Harrison!" she called. Her voice was warm like soup.

Harrison's tummy felt better. He came down one step. Then one more. He tapped his foot on the mat. "Hello, Grandma," he said, very small.

Grandma sat on the step beside him. She smelled like flowers. "Would you like to see what is in my bag?" she asked.

Harrison nodded. Grandma pulled out a soft blanket. It was blue and big.

Harrison put teddy on the blanket. Then Harrison leaned over. He gave Grandma a hug after all.

Grandma hugged him back. "Hello to you too," she whispered.

Benjamin ran to the playground. He wanted to swing up high. The swing was his favorite thing. But then he saw his friend Milo on the bench. Milo sat all alone. His mouth was turned down. His eyes looked wet. Benjamin could tell how Milo felt just by looking at his face. Milo looked sad.

Benjamin walked over. "Why are you sad?" he asked. "My dog ran to the farm and I can't find him," said Milo. Just then a big dog came running. It barked very loud. Milo's face changed. His eyes got wide. He looked scared. "That bark was scary," said Milo. "But look," said Benjamin. "It is your dog! He came back from the farm!"

Milo smiled a big smile now. He jumped up and down. "I am so excited!" he said. Benjamin laughed. Then a big boy pushed past them and grabbed the swing. Benjamin's face got hot and red. He made two fists. He felt angry. But the big boy's face looked sorry. "Sorry," the boy said. "You can go first." Benjamin's fists opened. He felt happy again. He got on the swing. "Push me, Milo!" he called. Milo pushed, and up Benjamin went, high into the blue sky.

Sarah sat at a big desk in the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. A game was on. Her family and friends watched too.

The red team ran fast. The blue team ran fast too. Sarah clapped her hands and shouted, "Go red team!" But everyone at the table went quiet. Then Daddy said, "We like the blue team, sweetie." Sarah giggled. "Oops. I am sorry, blue team!"

Then the blue team kicked the ball in the net. Everyone jumped up. They cheered and clapped for the blue team. Sarah clapped too. She clapped so hard her hands felt warm.

"Now I know," Sarah said. "You clap when your team scores!" She smiled and waved her little flag. The waiter brought lemonade for everyone. Sarah took a big sip. "Go blue team!" she shouted, one more time.

Henry walked with Mom into the hospital. He held Dad's hand. They went to a big room with a bed. In the bed was a tiny baby. "That is your baby sister," said Mom.

The baby made a loud cry. "Waa! Waa!" Henry covered his ears. "Why is she crying?" he asked. Dad said, "A new baby cannot talk yet." Henry waited. The baby cried again. Dad gave her some milk. Then she stopped crying. Henry saw that. The cry asked for milk, and Dad gave it.

The baby cried one more time. Henry got a soft blanket. He put it near her, very slow. She stopped crying and made a small sound. "She talks with cries," said Henry. He gave his sister a kiss on her head. "I will listen to you," he said. The baby held his young finger tight.

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet book. She pointed at the letter S. "That one is tricky," she said.

Mom sat down next to her. "S says sss," said Mom. "Like a little snake."

Brielle looked around the nook. She wanted to find an S word all by herself. She saw her red sock on the floor. She held it up. "Sss sock!" she said. "Sock starts with S!" Mom clapped.

Then sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the book. "Sss sun!" said Brielle. Mom laughed. "You found two," she said.

Brielle hunted for more. She looked under the cushion. She looked in the basket. Then she wiggled her toes in her toy box of sand from the beach. "Sss sand!" she shouted. She was not mad about the mess. She was happy.

Mom helped her clean up the sand. "Sss sweep," said Mom, with a wink.

"I found S everywhere," said Brielle. She hugged her book.

Kayden woke up in the dark. "Is it morning now?" he asked. He heard a plane go by, high in the sky. It was still night. Night was not morning yet.

He felt shy in the dark hallway. He went to find Dad. Dad said, "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast. It is not morning yet. It is morning later, when the sun comes up." Kayden climbed into the big bed. Dad tucked the blanket around him.

"Now we sleep," said Dad. "Tomorrow is morning. Yesterday was morning too, and you ate eggs." Kayden thought about eggs. Yesterday he had eggs. Today he would have pancakes. He wanted pancakes so much.

The sun came up. It was morning now! Kayden ran to the kitchen. Mom was at the table. "Good morning, Kayden," she said. She had made pancakes. Kayden ate three. He did not cry about the dark night anymore. Morning was here at last, just like Dad said.

He licked the syrup off his fork. "Today is a good day," he said.

Elizabeth lived on a farm with her grandma. One morning grandma said, "Let's play the senses game." Elizabeth wanted to win, but she did not know all the answers yet.

Grandma held up a red apple. "What do you call this sense?" she asked. "Seeing!" said Elizabeth. "And you see with your eyes." Grandma rang a big black bell. "Hearing," said Elizabeth. "I hear with my ears." She petted a soft lamb. "Touching! I touch with my hands." Then grandma gave her warm bread. "Tasting. I taste with my mouth," said Elizabeth, and she took a big bite.

"One sense left," said grandma. She pointed to the rose garden. Elizabeth ran to the pink roses. She sniffed one, then another. The little white one smelled best of all. "Smelling!" she shouted. "We smell with our nose!" Grandma laughed and clapped. Elizabeth picked the white rose and put it on grandma's hat. "Now you smell sweet too," she said.

Sadie was at summer camp. It was time for snack. The teacher said, "Wash your hands first." Sadie ran to the small sink. She wanted to wash all by herself.

Sadie turned the tap. The water came out. She put one finger near it. It felt very hot. She pulled her finger back. "Teacher Sam!" she called. "Please check my water."

Teacher Sam came over. He put his hand under the water. "It is too hot," he said. He turned the tap the other way. He put his hand under again. "Now it is warm," he said. "Warm is just right."

Sadie put her hands in the water. It felt good. She took the soap. She rubbed and rubbed. The class sang the hand song. It was a long song. "This song takes twenty seconds," said Teacher Sam. Sadie kept rubbing until the song was done. Bubbles covered her hands.

She rinsed the bubbles off. Then she got her snack. The crackers tasted good. After snack, it was nap time. Sadie lay down on her mat. "I can wash my hands now," she whispered. "All by myself." Then she closed her eyes to sleep.

Ryan was at summer camp. Lunchtime was coming. The camp man, Ben, called everyone to the sink. "Soap first," said Ben. "Rub for twenty seconds. Then rinse."

Ryan rubbed the soap on his hands. One, two, three. He counted to twenty. His hands felt slippery and bubbly. He ran them under the water. The water washed the soap off. Now his hands were not slippery at all. They felt clean.

Ben held out the sandwiches. But Milo's hands were still soapy. "Feel my hands," said Milo. They were slippery. Ryan pointed to the sink. "Rinse again," said Ryan. "The water washes the soap off." Milo rinsed and rinsed. His hands were clean too.

Milo smiled. "Thank you, Ryan. That was polite." The boys sat down together. Ryan took a big bite of his sandwich.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil and white paper. He wanted to write his name.

Mama sat next to him. "Show me the L," she said. Lucas gripped the pencil tight. "One, two, three, letters," he said. "L, U, C!"

He began at the right side of the page. He drew a big L. Then a U. Then the C went squish, right off the edge. Lucas frowned. "No room, Mama!"

Mama turned the paper around. "Try here," she said, pointing to the left side. Lucas looked. The whole long page stretched out in front of his letters.

He started at the left edge now. One L, smooth and beautiful. One U, round like a cup. One C, curvy like the moon. All the letters went across the page, one after another, left to right.

"LUCAS!" he shouted. The letters fit! They did not fall off the paper at all.

Mama clapped her hands. Lucas picked up the paper. He held it up high and grinned.

"I can write it again!" he said, and grabbed a fresh page.

Bennett ran to the park. He wanted to be a rocket today. Rockets go up, up, up.

First he found a big red slide. Next to it was a small blue slide. His dad gave him a cold juice box from the cooler. "Brr, cold," said Bennett. His dad held a hot cup of coffee. "Hot," said Dad. "I hold it, not you."

Bennett saw the tall ladder. "Rockets climb up," he said. He put one foot on the ladder. Up he went, one step at a time, slow like a snail. At the top he shouted, "Up and down are opposites!"

Then a fast puppy ran by. It looked up at Bennett and wagged its tail. Bennett sat down. Whoosh! He slid straight down, fast like a rocket.

The puppy licked his shoe. It climbed the little steps of the small slide. Down it came, tail first.

"Again!" said Bennett.

Addison played at Grandma's house. She built a big tower of blocks. She sent one block sliding across the rug. Then she sent another one. Soon blocks were all over the floor.

Grandma called, "Time for a snack!" Addison jumped up. She ran to the kitchen. Grandma gave her a tasty apple slice. Addison ate it all up. Then she looked back at the door. The blocks were still on the floor. Grandma had not played with them. Addison had.

Addison went back to the playroom. She picked up a block. She put it in the basket. Then another block, and another. Her bottom sat down on the rug as she reached the last ones. The floor was clear. Grandma peeked in and smiled. "All clean," said Grandma. Addison clapped her hands and patted the empty basket.

Josephine went to Rosa's house. Rosa had a tablet. Rosa's mom said, "You can draw on it." Josephine looked at the black screen. She did not know what to do. "How do I make it wake up?" she asked. Rosa pushed the little round button with one finger. The screen lit up. Josephine tried it too. Tap. The screen woke up. She smiled big.

Rosa showed her the drawing app. It was a little pink square with a crayon on it. Josephine tapped it. Colors filled the screen. She picked the thin green pen. She drew a long, wiggly snake. Then she drew a red sun. "My snake is winning the race," she said. Rosa laughed and drew a fast rabbit.

Then the screen went black. Josephine's snake was gone. Her tummy felt tight. "Oh no," she said. "Did I break it?" Rosa's mom came over. "No, it just ran out of power," she said. "It needs charging." She plugged the charger into the wall. The screen showed a small battery. Josephine waited. Soon the picture came back. Her snake was still there.

Rosa's mom said, "All done for now. Let's put it away." Josephine pressed the button. The screen went dark. She laid the tablet on the soft rug, face up. Rosa's mom set it by the charger. "You learned a lot today," Rosa said. Josephine nodded. "Tap to wake. Tap to draw. And it sleeps when the power is all gone." Rosa's mom plugged in the charger and said, "Snack time, girls."

Weston ran to the big tree in his backyard. He wanted to find blue things for his blue box. He found a blue jay feather. He put it in the box. He found a blue bottle cap. He put that in too.

Then he found a small toy car. It was very dark blue. Weston frowned. "Is this blue?" he asked. His sister Mia ran over. "No! That is too dark!" she said.

Weston held the feather by the car. Both looked blue to him. He put them side by side in the grass. The feather was light blue. The car was dark blue. "They are both blue," he said. Mia leaned down and looked. "Oh! Light blue and dark blue!" she said. She clapped her hands. Weston put the car in the box. Then he found something new. A green leaf sat on a red wagon. "Mia! Come see!" he called. "Which green is this one?"

Sophie sat at the dinner table. She looked at her spoon. "Mom," she said, "is today the library day?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now. And right now we are eating dinner. So we go after dinner."

Sophie tapped her cup. "Yesterday we went to the park," she said. "Yesterday is not now."

"That's right," said Mom. "Yesterday is done. Today is here."

Sophie ate one pea. Then she ate another. The clock ticked slowly. She reached for the bread, but it was far away. Dad passed it to her.

"Can we go now?" she asked.

"Not yet. First we eat. Later we go."

Sophie waited. She looked out the window. The last light was soft and pink. She saw the flower on the table, a yellow one in a little jar.

At last Mom stood up. "Now we go," Mom said.

Sophie jumped down from her chair. She held Mom's hand at the door.

"Today is my day," said Sophie.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big yellow pencil. "Now you can write your name," she said. Jackson was so happy. He jumped up and ran to show Dad. The pencil waved up in his hand, point out. Mom caught his arm gently. "Point down," she said. Jackson looked. He turned the pencil so the point faced down. He held it tight like that all the way to the door.

Then Jackson sat back down. He gripped the pencil low, near the tip. He made a shaky J. He made a wobbly a. Some letters missed the paper and went on the table. Mom wiped a wet cloth over it. "Try again," she said. Jackson tried again and again. Then he saw it. "JACKSON," all in a row. He held the paper up high. "I did it, Mom! Look!"

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Sienna jumped up and down. "One, two, three hugs!" she counted.

They made pancakes. Dad held the hot pan. Sienna watched and stirred the bowl. They read stories. They drew a big truck with crayons. Sienna wore her itchy new sweater to show Grandma. It was the best week ever.

Then Grandma had to go home. Sienna stood at the door. Her eyes were wet. "I will miss you," she said.

"You can call me on the phone," said Grandma. "Or we can see each other on a video call. Or you can send me a letter!"

"A letter?" said Sienna.

She ran to the table. She drew the truck. She drew Grandma. Mom helped her mail it.

Three days later, the phone rang. It was Grandma! "Your letter came!" she said. "I love my truck picture. Want a video call tomorrow?"

"Yes!" said Sienna. "One, two, three, four, five o'clock?"

"Five o'clock," laughed Grandma. "See you then!"

Arlo ran to the park today. Yesterday the big slide was wet. Today the sun made it dry. "Now I can slide!" said Arlo.

A girl named Mia was at the swing. "I went to this park tomorrow," she said. Then she stopped. She thought hard. "No, not tomorrow. I went yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." Arlo nodded. "Yesterday the slide was wet," he said. "Today it is dry."

Mia had a small red ball. She threw it high. The ball went up, and then it came down. It rolled under a bench. Arlo went to grab it. The ball was stuck. He tried once. He tried twice. Then Mia helped. Together they pulled it out. "Now we can play," said Mia.

"Can you come back tomorrow?" asked Arlo. "Yes," said Mia. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Arlo smiled. Tomorrow they would play again. At home, Arlo drew the park at his little desk. He drew Mia's red ball, and a snowy hill he would slide down some day. Then Mama called, "Dinner later, Arlo!" Arlo got one more crayon and drew the slide. "See you tomorrow, slide," he said.

Matteo went to the temple with Grandma. The bell rang once. The wood smelled like rain. People bowed and folded their hands. Matteo bowed too, just a little.

After the visit, Grandma took him to a small room. Rice and soup were on the table. Grandma put her hands together. "We say itadakimasu before we eat," she said. "In Japan, everyone says it. It gives thanks for the food." Matteo tried. "Ita... daki?" The word felt bumpy in his mouth, like his shoes bumping the table leg. "One more try," said Grandma. He tried again. "Itadaki... masu?" "Almost," said Grandma. She smiled and waited.

Matteo looked at the rice. He looked at his hands. He folded them like Grandma. He took a big breath. "Itadakimasu!" he said. Grandma clapped softly. "Just right," she said. "Now we can eat." The rice was warm. The soup was salty. Matteo ate it all up.

Later, Matteo drew a picture with a red crayon. He drew the temple. He drew Grandma. He drew a big bowl of rice. On the top he wrote some wiggly letters. "That says itadakimasu," he told Grandma. Grandma hung it on the wall. "What a lucky wall," she said. Matteo laughed. Then he folded his hands and said it one more time, all by himself.

Maverick dug a small hole in the dirt. He dropped in one seed. Then he patted the soil down flat. "Now grow, little seed," he said. Every day he came back. He looked and looked. No green. No leaf. Nothing at all.

"Maybe my seed is lost," said Maverick. Miss Ada, the garden helper, gave him a little stick of wood to mark his spot. "Water it, then wait," she said. Maverick gave the seed a drink. The sun made the dirt warm, but not too hot. He waited. One day, two days, three days, four days. Still nothing.

On day five, Maverick bent down low. Something green was poking up. It was very small. It looked like a tiny curl. "Miss Ada! Come quick!" he called. Miss Ada knelt beside him. "That is a sprout," she said. "A tiny new plant poking up is called a sprout." Maverick grinned. He slipped his finger next to it, soft and slow. "Hello, sprout," he whispered.

Eliana went to the store with Mama. She wanted to pick the apples. "Stay close to my cart," said Mama. Eliana held the side of the cart. One hand, two hands, hold on tight.

They walked past the bakery. It smelled warm and sweet. "The oven is very hot," said Mama. "The baker uses big gloves. We watch from here." Eliana saw the baker pull out bread. The bread was hot. The milk by the door was cold. Eliana touched the cold milk jug. Brrr.

Then Eliana saw something on the floor. It was small. It was a lighter. She counted to herself, one, two, three steps back. She did not touch it.

"Mama, I see a lighter," she said.

The kind store man came over. He picked it up. "Good job telling me," he said. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." He put it in his pocket, far away.

Later a doctor came in to shop. She had a clean white coat. She smiled at Eliana.

At home, Mama washed the apples. "You were my big helper," she said.

Eliana bit her apple. Crunch.

Emilia stood at the park gate. "Is it time to swing now?" she asked.

"Now it is," said Mom. "Today we can swing. Yesterday it rained, so we stayed home."

Emilia ran to the swings. She pumped her legs. The swing went up, up, up. "The swing is big now!" she said.

After swinging, Emilia wanted a turn on the slide. But a boy was there. "Can I go later?" she asked Mom.

"Yes, later, when he is done," said Mom.

Emilia waited. She watched the boy slide down. Then it was her turn. "Now it is my turn!" she said. Down she went, fast.

Then Emilia looked around. "Where did the sun go?" she asked. The sky was getting dark at the edge.

"It is almost time to go home," said Mom. Mom held up her phone. A clock was on it. "Look. The clock shows what time it is."

Emilia looked at the clock. "Will we come back?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow we will come back. It will be a beautiful summer day again."

Emilia smiled. She held Mom's hand. "Swing tomorrow?" she asked.

"Swing tomorrow," said Mom. They walked home together.

Grayson walked on the nature trail with his mom. He found a small purple feather on the ground. He picked it up. "This is a puzzle," he said. "Some things feel different."

His mom smiled. "Your hands can tell," she said. Grayson touched the feather. It felt soft. He put it in the soft pile.

Then he found a pinecone. He touched it. The pinecone felt bumpy and rough. He put it in the rough pile. His mom held out a small blanket from the bag. Grayson rubbed it with his fingers. "Soft," he said. It went in the soft pile too.

"Now close your eyes," said Mom. Grayson closed his eyes. She put something in his hands. His skin felt little bumps. "Rough!" he said. He opened his eyes. It was the pinecone.

Grayson laughed and held the soft feather to his cheek.

Hannah sat on the train with Mama. The window made a whoosh sound. Trees went by, fast. Hannah held her little pig toy. "We are going to the sea," said Mama. "The sea has big water."

The train stopped. Then the train went again. Hannah looked and looked. At last they got off. The sand was warm under Hannah's feet. Far away, the water went splash, splash. Hannah wanted to run to it now.

She started to run. "Wait," said Mama. "At the beach, a child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching. Let me put down the bag first." Hannah stopped. She waited. She held her pig and watched the waves. They went up and down, up and down.

Mama put down the bag. Mama took Hannah's hand. They walked to the water together. The water was cool on Hannah's toes. It splashed her pig too. "Same wet toes, same wet pig!" said Hannah. Mama laughed and held her hand tight.

Lydia stood in the reading corner. She was holding something new. It was her very first library card.

"I want a dinosaur book!" she shouted. A boy next to her looked up. He pointed at the big rug. Two kids were reading there. One had a book about bears. The other had a book about the moon.

The librarian bent down. "We use quiet voices here," she said softly. "So others can read." Lydia looked at the kids on the rug. Then she whispered, "A dinosaur book, please." The librarian smiled and whispered back, "Top shelf, little friend."

Lydia found a big green dinosaur book. She carried it with two hands. At the desk, she gave her card. Beep! The librarian scanned the book. "All yours for now," she whispered.

Lydia clapped her hands, very quietly. "A tiny clap," she said with a giggle. "For a big dinosaur." The boy next to her laughed. "Tiny clap for a T. rex," he whispered. Lydia hugged her book and tiptoed to the door. "Bye, library," she sang in a small, small voice.

It was animal day at school. Weston brought his toy fish to show. His friend Ben brought a toy dog. Mia brought a toy cow.

"Your fish is not an animal," said Ben. "It has no legs. My dog has legs. Mia's cow has legs."

Weston felt sad. He wanted his fish to count. Miss Rosa said, "Let's look at the animal wall." The wall was full of pictures. Weston saw a dog there. He saw a cow there. Then he saw a fish there, too!

"Dogs, cows and fish are all animals," said Miss Rosa. Weston smiled big. "My fish is an animal!" he said.

Then it was snack time. Miss Rosa gave out foods. There were apples and crackers. Weston took a bite of his apple. Then he held his fish up high.

"Fish can swim," he said. "Dogs and cows cannot swim like that."

Ben listened. "My dog can swim a little," he said. "But not like a fish."

The class sat on the floor. They lined up all the animals in a row. Dog, cow, fish, dog, cow, fish. Weston counted them one by one.

Then came the surprise. Miss Rosa opened a box. A real bunny was inside! "This is an animal, too," she said. Weston laughed and clapped. "Animals, animals, everywhere!"

Sofia went to the library with her dad. She saw a circle rug on the floor. She saw square books on the shelf. A song was playing, and some kids began to clap.

At the craft table, Sofia wanted to make a paper sailboat. She needed two triangle sails. She looked in the paper box. She found only one square paper. "Where can I get triangles?" she asked. Miss Amy, the librarian, came over. "Bring the square here," she said. Miss Amy took the scissors. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open in Sofia's hands. Two triangles!

Sofia held one triangle up. Then she held the other up. Her loose tooth wiggled when she smiled. She taped both triangles to her boat. "Look, Dad! My boat has two sails!" Dad clapped for her. Sofia put her boat on the circle rug and gave it a little push.

Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She folded her napkin into a little square. "Dad, is the story time now?" she asked.

Dad stirred the pot. "The story is not now. The story is after dinner."

Eleanor looked at her plate. The carrots were still there. She ate one. Then she ate another. "Is it now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Now you are eating carrots. Later we will read."

Eleanor ate slow. She watched Dad take the pot off the stove. He poured the soup carefully. Eleanor waited. She folded her napkin again.

"Now?" she asked.

"Now," said Dad.

Eleanor was brave about the hot bowl. She let it cool while Dad sat down. Yesterday they had soup too. Tomorrow they would have pasta. Today was soup day, and story day.

After the last spoonful, Dad wiped her chin. "Is it after dinner now?" Eleanor asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "It is now story time."

Eleanor ran to get her book. Dad patted the chair beside him. Eleanor climbed up and opened the cover.

"Now," she whispered, and Dad began to read.

Madeline went to the park with Daddy. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower. "I only have red paint," said Daddy. Madeline made a sad face.

First she played on the swing. Daddy pushed her high, high, high. "One, two, three," she counted. Then she saw a green frog by the pond. She saw a blue bird up in a tree. She saw a yellow duck waddle by. "Green frog, blue bird, yellow duck," she said.

Then a girl named Bella sat at the paint table. Bella had white paint. Madeline had red paint. "Let's mix," said Bella. Madeline stirred white into her red paint. She stirred and stirred. "Pink!" she yelled. Red and white made pink. It was pink, pink, pink!

Madeline painted a pink flower on the card. She helped Bella fold the card into a square. "For Grandma," said Madeline. "You did it," said Daddy. He gave her a big hug.

Madeline ran to the car. She held the pink flower card up high. "Pink flower for Grandma!"

Rowan played on a basketball team. He wore a red shirt with the number five. His sister came to watch every game. She sat on the long bench by the court.

Bounce, bounce, bounce went the ball. Rowan ran. He passed. He shot. The ball hit the rim. Then Rowan ran fast with it. A whistle blew. Loud and sharp.

"Who is that man?" Rowan asked. "Why did he blow the whistle?"

"He is the referee," said Coach. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Rowan had run too far with the ball. That was not the rule. So the other team got the ball now. Rowan puffed out his cheeks. Then he nodded.

Next practice, Rowan counted his steps. One, two, then he stopped. Bounce, bounce, bounce. He passed to his friend Ben. Ben shot. The ball went in. The referee gave a thumbs up.

After the game, Rowan waved to his sister. "The referee watched me," he said. "I followed the rules." He yawned all the way to the car, and he fell fast asleep before they got home.

Kinsley held her toy pig tight. "Pig needs a haircut too," she said.

Mom laughed. "You are the one getting a haircut today. We must not be late."

At the mall, the hairdresser smiled. She put a big cape around Kinsley's shoulders. The cape was red and shiny.

"I am a superhero!" said Kinsley. "Zoom, zoom!"

The hairdresser began to cut. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off the cape. Plop, plop, plop.

Kinsley watched one hair. It fell on her arm. She blew it away. "Bye bye, hair!" she said.

Then more hairs fell. One, two, three. They all slid off the cape. None went on her dress.

"Pig is safe too," said Kinsley. She tucked pig under the cape. Pig peeked out.

"Superhero pig," said the hairdresser.

Snip, snip, snip. Then the cape came off. Kinsley's dress was clean. No hairs on it at all.

"Look, Mom! Nothing on me!"

Mom spun her around. Kinsley hugged pig and zoomed out the door.

Penelope wants to make pancakes for her family. She asks her dad to help. Dad says, "We need the recipe." The recipe is a card that hangs on the wall.

Penelope stirs the flour and the milk. She cracks two eggs into the bowl. Dad cooks the pancakes in the hot pan. But the pancakes come out flat. They look like little flat clouds. Penelope says, "Oh no, they are so flat!"

Dad reads the recipe card again. "Look," he says. "We skipped a step. The recipe says to add the baking powder." Penelope adds it and stirs. Dad cooks the new pancakes. They come out big and puffy. The family eats them all. Penelope's little brother, a boy with smelly socks, laughs and asks for more. Penelope says, "The recipe told us what to do, one step at a time."

Hunter ran into the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a table with a cake. Grandma held the cake carefully. Four little candles stood on top. Daddy lit the candles with a match. Hunter watched from his chair.

A girl named Mia came over. She had a feather in her hair. "You can touch it," she said. Hunter touched the feather. It was soft. Then Mia asked, "How old are you?"

Hunter held up three fingers. "I am three," he said. Mia shook her head. "No. Today is your birthday," she said. "On your birthday, you turn one year older."

Hunter looked at his fingers. He put one more finger up. One, two, three, four. "I am four now!" he said. Grandma smiled. She held the cake near him. "Be careful," she said. "The candles are little flames." Hunter blew and blew. The flames went out. Everyone clapped.

Then everyone sang. Hunter sat up tall. Four candles, four years old. "I will be five next time," he said. Daddy laughed and gave him a big hug.

Alexander dug a small hole in the backyard. His dad helped him plant three little seeds. "Now what?" Alexander asked. "Seeds need water," said Dad. Alexander filled his watering can. He poured the water over the dirt. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He looked at the dirt. There was only dirt. No sprout. No green. He touched the soil with one finger. "Still wet," he said. He watered the seeds again. A bird watched him from the swing. Alexander swung slowly and waited.

The next day, only dirt again. Alexander watered the seeds one more time. Then he saw something new. A tiny green sprout was peeking out. "It came up!" Alexander shouted. He stuck out his tongue at the bird. "See? Water helped it grow!" The sprout stood there, small and green, in the morning sun.

Iris wanted to sort her toys. She put the robot in one pile. She put the white bear next to it. Then she found a carrot on the rug. It had rolled off the table. She put the carrot with the toys.

At lunch, Mom set out plates. "Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Mom. Iris looked at her toys. The carrot did not belong there! She ran back and wiped the rug where the carrot had been. Then she carried the carrot to the food bowl.

The carrot went crunch when she bit it. It tasted sweet. Mom put apple slices beside her. The bread was soft and warm. Iris fed the robot a pretend apple. The robot said nothing. Iris laughed and patted his white round head. "You can't eat," she said. "You're a toy."

Alexis ran to the big drum at the park. He hit it with his hands. Boom! Boom! Boom! His whole body felt excited. "I am a giant!" he shouted. His voice was big like thunder.

A girl named Mia came close. Then the drum went boom again. Mia covered her ears with both hands. She ran behind the bench. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked scared.

Alexis stopped drumming. He felt sad that Mia was sad. He thought hard. Then he patted the drum very softly. Tap. Tap. Mia peeked out. Her hands came down. She smiled a happy smile. "I like it quiet," she said. "I like it loud," said Alexis. They looked at each other. Same drum. Different feelings.

"I know!" said Alexis. "We can count the taps." He tapped softly. Mia counted. "One, two, three." They sat close together on the cozy grass. Then Mia took a paper plate from her bag. She held it up like a tiny drum. Tap, tap, went the quiet plate. Alexis tapped his big drum. Soft, then loud, then soft. They made a drum song all their own, one giant and one small, playing side by side in the sun.

Norah sat at the paint table. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. "Where is the orange?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Beth, smiled. "Let's look at the cups."

The cups held red, blue, yellow, and green paint. Norah sniffed one cup. "This red one smells stinky," she said, and she giggled. Miss Beth laughed too. "That is okay. Paint can smell like that." Sam, who sat close by, pushed his brush toward her. "Put red in the yellow," he said. "Watch what happens."

Norah dipped her brush in red. She stirred it into the yellow cup. Swirl, swirl, swirl. The paint turned orange! "It changed!" she cried. She painted her pumpkin orange. It looked round and bright. Miss Beth hung it up to dry. "I want to pay you a sticker," Miss Beth said, and she stuck a shiny gold star on Norah's hand. Norah held it up high. "My pumpkin is orange," she said.

Theodore ran into art class. "Today we hunt for shapes!" said Miss Amy. She held up a red card. It had four sides and four square corners. "This is a rectangle," she said. "Can you find one?" Theodore looked and looked. He saw a round clock. "No, that's a circle," he said. He saw a block with equal sides. "No, that's a square." Then he saw the big door. He ran to it and put his finger on a corner. "One, two, three, four!" He counted four corners. "The door is a rectangle!"

"I found one! I found one!" Theodore shouted. Miss Amy clapped. The other kids came to see. Theo pointed up. "The door has four sides too. Just like my red card." Everyone counted the corners together.

Then Theodore got to work. He drew a tiny door on his paper. He painted a rectangle door with blue paint from the bucket. "My rectangle can open!" he said. He cut it out and taped it on. Miss Amy spelled his name at the top. Theodore held up his picture and smiled. "Look at my door!"

William sat on the clean grass in the backyard. He wanted to name his five senses. He touched a smooth seed with his fingers. "Fingers are for touching," he said. He sniffed a red flower with his nose. "Nose is for smelling," he said.

Then a bee went buzz, buzz. William turned his head. "Which body part hears that?" he asked himself. He covered his ears with his hands. The buzz got very small. He took his hands away. The buzz came back. "Ears! We hear with our ears," he said.

William sat very still. His ears heard a bird sing. His ears heard leaves go swish. His ears heard water drip from the hose. He smiled and cupped his hands behind his ears. A dog barked next door. William laughed and said, "Hello, dog!"

Myles sat at the big art table. He had a paper and a pencil. He wanted to draw a furry dog. The teacher, Miss Ana, hung a picture of a dog on the wall.

Myles began to draw. He pressed down very, very hard. He wanted the dog to be dark. He pressed even harder. Then something went snap! The pencil point broke off. It began to fall to the floor. Myles watched the little point land by his shoe.

"Oh no," said Myles. "My pencil broke." Miss Ana came over. She gave him a new pencil. "What will you try now?" she asked. Myles looked at the new pencil. He held it softly.

This time he pressed gently. The line was light and soft. He made one small mark, then another. The furry dog began to appear. Myles drew two ears and a happy tail. He smiled and looked at his paper.

"Look at my dog!" he said.

Jake was eating breakfast with his fork. His tummy felt funny. Today he had to get a shot.

"Will the shot hurt?" Jake asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then it is done."

Mom gave him a cute teddy bear to bring. "His name is Boo," Jake said. He put Boo in his bag. They got in the car.

At the doctor's office, Jake sat on the big chair. Boo sat on his lap. Jake's hands squeezed Boo tight. His legs wanted to wiggle. The nurse came in with the tray.

Grandpa held Jake's hand. "Smell the flower," Grandpa said. He held up one finger like a flower. "Breathe in slow. One, two, three."

Jake sniffed the flower finger. One, two, three. Then he blew out slow, like blowing out a candle. His shoulders came down. His hands let Boo go soft.

"Again," said Grandpa.

One, two, three in. Slow breath out. Jake did it two more times. His tummy felt less jumpy.

"Can Boo do it too?" Jake asked.

"Yes," said Grandpa. "Help him."

Jake lifted Boo to his nose. One, two, three in. Slow breath out.

"Ready?" said the nurse.

Jake kept breathing. In slow, out slow. He felt a tiny pinch, and then it was done.

"All done," said the nurse. She gave Boo a bandage too.

At home, Mom made lunch. Jake used his fork to feed himself bite by bite. He fed Boo a pretend bite. One, two, three, yum.

"Boo did it," Jake said. "And I did it too."

Yesterday Athena went to the store with Mom. Today they went again. Athena wanted the pink yogurt with the strawberry on it. Yesterday the shelf was empty. Today she hoped it was there.

Athena ran to the dairy case. She looked and looked. The pink yogurt was not there. A man in a green shirt was stacking milk. "Excuse me," said Athena. "Do you have the pink yogurt?"

"The truck comes today," said the man. "More yogurt soon."

"Soon?" asked Athena.

"Soon means in a little while," said the man. "Not a long wait."

Athena tapped her toes. She counted to ten. Then the doors opened wide. A big truck backed up slow. Men rolled in boxes on a noisy cart. Athena watched from her spot by the cart.

"Now we can stock the shelf," said the man. He opened a box. He put out pink yogurt, row after row.

"There it is!" said Athena. She took two. Mom smiled and put them in the cart.

"Later we will eat one," said Mom. "Tomorrow we can have the other one. Can you show me where the bus stop is?"

Athena pointed out the window. "The bus will come soon," she said.

The bus rolled up. Athena held Mom's hand. In her bag, the pink yogurt sat cold and safe. The doors opened with a hiss. "All aboard," called the driver.

Lennon went to the library with Dad. She saw the big red tablets on the small table. She wanted to draw a cloud on one.

Dad pushed the round button. The screen lit up. "Now tap the little pictures," Dad said. "They are called icons." Lennon tapped a cat icon. A cat game came up. That was not drawing.

She looked again. She saw a little paintbrush icon. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. There were colors everywhere. Lennon drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a noisy blue bird next to it.

A boy came to the table. He wanted a turn. Lennon was done anyway. She pressed the button and the screen went dark. Dad put the tablet back on the shelf. The boy waved at her. "Thank you," he said.

Rowan sat at the dinner table. He ate his pasta with a spoon. The pasta was warm and squishy in his mouth. He patted his full tummy.

Then Rowan needed the toilet. He ran down the hall. He used the toilet. He pulled up his pants. He ran back to the table.

"Did you flush?" asked Mom.

Rowan stopped. Oops. He had forgotten. He ran back. He pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. Then he washed his hands with soap. The bubbles smelled like flowers. He dried his hands on the towel.

Rowan ran back again. "I flushed and washed my hands!" he said.

"Good job," said Mom. "Now finish your pasta. Then it will be bath time, and after that, your cozy sock and sleepy time."

Rowan looked at his clean hands. They smelled like flowers too. He smiled and ate one more bite.

Ayla went to the park with her grandma. Ayla brought Bear and Bunny. She wanted to have tea with them. But she had no tea.

Ayla sat on the grass. She found two little cups by the sandbox. Someone had left them there. The cups were empty. No water. No tea. Nothing.

"Grandma, no tea!" said Ayla. Grandma smiled. "You can pour pretend tea," she said. Ayla tipped the empty cup over Bear. Nothing came out. But Ayla made a poury sound. "Glug, glug!"

Bear got a pretend drink. Bunny got a pretend drink too. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" said Ayla. Bunny tipped over. "Oops, Bunny!" said Ayla. "Don't break your cup." She set Bunny up straight again.

Then Grandma pretended to sip. "Mmm," she said. "Yummy pretend tea." Ayla giggled. She poured more pretend tea. "One more cup, Grandma?" she asked. Grandma held out her hands and said, "Yes, please."

Felix wanted to taste the honey cake. Grandma was baking it in the oven. "Not yet," said Grandma. "This cake is for tonight."

"But why?" asked Felix. "Cake is cake!"

Grandma laughed. "This cake is for the holiday. We make it just for this day."

Felix watched Grandma take the pan out. She used big mitts. The cake looked brown and warm. Felix sniffed the air. "It smells yummy now," he said.

"We wait for Papa and Nia," said Grandma. "Then we eat it together."

Felix waited. He looked at the cake. He looked at the clock. The clock was very slow.

At last Papa came home. Nia came too. Felix helped Grandma lift the cake onto a big plate. Nia put out plates and forks.

"Now?" asked Felix.

"Now," said Grandma.

Everyone sat at the table. Felix took a big bite. "Happy holiday!" he said, with crumbs on his chin.

Papa patted his sleepy head. "One more little piece," said Papa, "and then bed."

"Two pieces," said Felix.

Grandma laughed. "Okay, one big one."

Iris went to the salon with Grandma. Her hair was long and it went into her eyes. "Time for your first haircut," said Grandma. Iris felt her tummy jump. She wanted to see, but she also wanted to hide.

A hairdresser named Jo came over. Jo held a comb and a small card with hair pictures on it. Iris picked the card. "This one," she said. Jo smiled.

Then Jo combed Iris's hair. Comb, comb, comb. Then one little snip. Iris kicked her feet under the cape. "Why do you comb so much?" she asked. "Watch and see," said Jo. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. The comb made the hair lie flat and neat. Then the cut was tidy too. Iris counted, "Three combs, one snip!" Jo laughed.

At the end, Iris looked in the mirror. No hair in her eyes. She was happy. "Grandma, the comb helps the hair stay neat!" said Iris. Grandma took a photo, and Jo gave her the little card to keep.

Levi stood at the running track. The sun made the red track feel warm under his shoes. Coach Ana had a big bag of beanbags and a hoop on the ground.

"Watch me," she said. She threw a beanbag. It landed in the hoop. Levi clapped. Then Levi threw one. It went in too. He grabbed another beanbag. Then another. Then another.

"Levi," said a kid named Mia. "I want a turn too." Coach Ana held up her hand. "Taking turns means one throws, and then the next kid throws." Levi looked at the beanbags in his arms. He counted them in his head. Then he passed them down the line, one by one. Mia threw hers. It missed. She tried again and it landed in the hoop with a soft plop.

Levi picked up the big ball next. He held out both hands. "Ready?" asked Mia. She rolled it to him. He caught it and hugged it tight. It smelled like rubber and grass.

"My turn again?" Levi asked. Coach Ana smiled and pointed at the kid at the end of the line. Levi marched the ball over to him. "Here you go," Levi said.

Charles sat on the big couch. It was Sunday morning. Everyone came to watch the big game. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too.

A man ran onto the field. He wore a black and white striped shirt. "Who is that?" Charles asked. "He is not playing ball." Uncle Ben laughed. "That is the referee," he said. "The referee watches the game. He makes sure the players follow the rules."

The referee blew his whistle. One player had pushed another player. The whistle made everyone stop. Then the game started again.

"The whistle is loud," Charles said. "It is not scary," Grandma said. "It keeps the game fair."

Later, Charles swept his toy cars off the floor with his hands. "I am the referee," he said. He held up his toy whistle. "Beep! Everybody follow the rules!"

Dad laughed and pulled Charles onto his lap.

The lights went out. The big TV went dark too. Leo stood very still in the dark living room. "Mama!" he called.

Mama came with a candle. The flame tickled the air with its little light. "A power cut," said Mama. "The lights are off. We will use candles."

Leo looked at the window. He pressed his nose to the cold glass. All the houses on the street were dark! Next door was dark. The yellow house was dark. Every house on the street was dark at once. "Mama, look! All dark!"

Mama came to look. "Yes," she said. "All the houses went dark together." Leo clapped his hands. The dark street felt like a big night team, everyone the same.

Mama lit one more candle. Then another. The room got brighter and brighter. Leo got his blanket. He and Mama sat by the candles. "Now we tell a story," said Mama. "Story time can start early tonight." Leo snuggled close. The candle flames wiggled on the wall. Outside, the street stayed dark, all of it, all at once.

Then the lights popped back on. Leo blinked. "Again!" he shouted, pointing at the candles. Mama laughed and blew them out, one by one.

Gabriel was at Grandpa's house. Outside, snow was falling. It covered the grass. It covered the big green tree. Now the tree was white. "Snow is white," said Grandpa.

Gabriel wanted to draw the snow. Grandpa gave him white paper. Gabriel drew with his red crayon. He drew with his yellow crayon. He drew with his green crayon. Then he looked for a white crayon. He had no white one. The white paper had no snow on it at all. Gabriel frowned. "My snow will not show up," he said.

Grandpa looked in the drawer. He pulled out blue paper. "Try this," he said. Gabriel drew on the blue paper. He drew white snow with a cotton ball. The snow showed up! It was white on the blue. Gabriel laughed.

He drew a white hill. He drew a white snowman with a red hat. Grandma came in with warm soup. "Is it salty?" asked Gabriel. He took a little sip. Then he held up his drawing. "Look! Snow!" Grandma gave him a wave. Gabriel waved back.

Luca sat in the car with Dad. They were going to get the new baby. "I want to hold her," said Luca. "First we wash our hands," said Dad. "Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby."

At home, the baby was in a soft blanket. Luca ran in fast. "Hold baby now!" he said. Mom stopped him. "Hands first," she said. Luca looked at his hands. They had dirt on them.

Luca went to the sink. Dad turned on the water. Luca washed one hand, then the other. He counted, "One, two, three bubbles!" Then his hands were clean.

Mom put the baby in Luca's arms. The baby made a tiny sound. Luca gasped. She grabbed his finger! "She likes me," said Luca. Dad said, "Yes. Big brother, clean hands, warm baby." Luca smiled and held on.

Asher stood at the school gate. He held his new backpack in his hands. It was very heavy. He could not lift it onto his back.

A girl named Maya stood by him. She wore rain boots. The gate was wet and slippery from the morning rain. "My backpack goes on my back," Maya said. She turned around to show him. It sat on her back like a little nest.

Asher tried again. He pulled and pulled. The backpack slid off. It fell with a thump. Asher sat down on the step and opened it. Inside were his toy truck, three rocks, and a small plastic cow from the farm set.

Asher took out the rocks. He took out the truck. He kept the cow. Now the backpack was light. He slipped his arms through the straps. It sat on his back, just like Maya's.

Asher waved to his mom by the fence. "Look! It's on my back!" he called. The cow peeked out of the top pocket, as if she wanted to wave too.

Charlie was building a tall tower. Her blocks went up and up. Her brother Sam made a tower too. Sam's tower was very tall.

Charlie wanted to see it close. She stepped back. She bumped right into Sam's tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sam's face went funny. His lip wobbled. "My tower," he said.

Mummy knelt down by Charlie. "Say sorry," she said softly. "Sorry shows Sam you know you hurt him."

"Sorry, Sam," said Charlie.

Then Charlie picked up a block. She put it at the bottom. Sam put one on top. They took turns. One for Sam, one for Charlie.

Soon a new tower stood tall. It was even taller than before.

"Better tower?" asked Charlie.

"Yes," said Sam. "Best tower."

Zoey sat at the little red table. Miss Pam held up a big card. "This is Z," she said. "Z says zzz, like a bee."
